intro.heading: Two facts that shape every Al Jaddaf tutoring conversation
paragraphs: Al Jaddaf sits on the creek between Dubai Healthcare City and the Ras Al Khor side, and two features of the neighbourhood do most of the work in any scheduling discussion. The first is that Swiss International Scientific School Dubai is inside the community, so a meaningful share of secondary children here have a school run measured in minutes rather than in interchanges. The second is the Green Line terminus at Creek, which makes Al Jaddaf one of the few creek-side communities where an older teenager can get home without a car at all.

Those two facts together produce a weekday with more usable slots than most Dubai neighbourhoods have. A student walking or taking a short ride home from a school inside the development can be settled by around quarter past four. A Year 12 student coming back on the Green Line from a school nearer Deira arrives on a predictable schedule rather than a traffic-dependent one. Both are genuine advantages, and both are only convertible into an actual appointment if nobody has to drive across the city to teach it.

The third shaping fact is employment. Dubai Healthcare City is immediately adjacent, and a disproportionate number of Al Jaddaf households include someone working clinical shifts. A rotating pattern breaks the assumption most tutoring plans rest on, which is that a parent is reliably home at the same time every week. Families here need a slot that works whether or not an adult is present, plus a record of what happened in the lesson for the parent who was not there.

The academic mix in this community is distinctive too. Swiss International Scientific School Dubai runs a bilingual IB continuum, which means students here are more likely than elsewhere in Dubai to be working in a second language of instruction and to be weighing a bilingual Diploma. That changes the tutoring brief: language route decisions, Language A and Language B choices, and written work produced in a language the student is still consolidating.

Lessons for Al Jaddaf families are one-to-one and delivered live over video. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. For this community the point is specific rather than general: a bilingual Diploma student needing Chemistry taught in clear English, or Arabic as a first language taught to the KHDA expectation, needs a narrow match. Narrowing it further by driving distance is how families end up with a generalist.

What follows is written for this community rather than for Dubai in general: the household patterns a clinical rota produces and the slot that holds for each, the language routes available in a bilingual setting and whether the bilingual award is worth its workload, what KHDA requires alongside the international programme, the AED market bands with their sources, the boundary a tutor must not cross on a second-language draft, and what to do when the specialist you need has no slot in the hour you wanted.

dubai/al-jaddaf.programmesIntro: Al Jaddaf families sit across the IB continuum and the British route, with the bilingual element distinguishing this cluster from the rest of the creek. Each programme asks something different of a student working in a second language.

programmes.name: IB Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Transdisciplinary inquiry organised around units rather than subjects, with the exhibition in the final year. Assessment is formative and continuous, which makes a parent's read on progress harder than a percentage system allows. Literacy and numeracy foundations are being laid in two languages in a bilingual setting.
programmes.countryNote: PYP requests from Al Jaddaf are almost entirely about language balance rather than academic difficulty. A child consolidating reading in two languages at once can look behind in both for a term and be ahead in both by the end of the following year. Short frequent sessions in the weaker language are what help; general tutoring is rarely the answer at this stage.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, marked out of eight, with command terms determining the shape of a correct answer. Year 11 may sit MYP eAssessment on screen. In a bilingual setting students also meet subject content in their second language of instruction, which raises the writing demand.
programmes.countryNote: The characteristic Al Jaddaf problem in MYP is a student whose understanding is ahead of their written expression in the language of assessment. The criterion scores reflect the writing rather than the thinking, and the fix is targeted work on subject-specific language and command-term phrasing rather than more content teaching.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internal Assessments carry a substantial share of each subject grade. Students taking two languages at Language A level across two different language groups may qualify for the bilingual Diploma award.
programmes.countryNote: For Al Jaddaf students the Diploma conversation frequently starts with the language route rather than the science or mathematics choice. Taking two Language A subjects is a real commitment in written workload, and the honest advice sometimes is that a strong single Language A plus a Higher Level science serves a university application better than a bilingual award pursued at a cost.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses examined at the end of Year 11, with Cambridge syllabuses such as 0580 Mathematics and 0625 Physics or Pearson equivalents including 4MA1 and 4PH1. Cambridge tiers several subjects Core or Extended, and first-language and second-language English are separate qualifications with different papers.
programmes.countryNote: Al Jaddaf families whose children attend British-curriculum schools nearby most often ask about the English route: whether a bilingual student should sit English as a first language or as a second language. That decision affects university recognition and should be made on evidence from written work rather than on how confidently the student speaks.

dubai/al-jaddaf.subjectsIntro: This list reflects what Al Jaddaf households actually book, which includes more language work than a typical Dubai area. Each note says what the component demands of a student who is working in a second language.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: Taught in Standard Arabic under KHDA requirements, graded separately from the international curriculum. Grammar and composition carry the marks, and the usual difficulty is retention between weekly school lessons rather than comprehension.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Required for non-Arab students in Dubai private schools. Script fluency and vocabulary recall respond to frequency, which is why two short sessions a week outperform a single long block at this level.

subjects.name: IB Language B, including Arabic and French
subjects.description: Assessed across reading, writing, listening and an individual oral. Students lose marks on register and text type rather than vocabulary: a formal letter written as an essay loses credit the student did not know was at stake.

subjects.name: IB Language A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The unseen non-literary paper and the individual oral are the components most often underprepared. For a bilingual student the demand is analytical vocabulary rather than fluency, and that is directly teachable.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and energetics take most of the time. For a student working in a second language, the explanation questions and the Internal Assessment evaluation section are where precision costs marks.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics and fields reward method. Marks go on units, significant figures and explanation questions where a correct idea is written too loosely, which is a language problem as much as a physics one.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: High content volume and heavy terminology. Mapping the student's existing vocabulary onto the syllabus terms early saves weeks of apparent confusion, particularly for a student taught the subject previously in another language.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The least language-dependent subject on this list and often where bilingual students are strongest. The Exploration is the exception, since criterion B rewards mathematical communication in written form.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with a heavy calculator component. The written interpretation of results is where marks are lost, and that is a writing task rather than a mathematics one.

subjects.name: IGCSE English as a first or second language
subjects.description: Two separate qualifications with different papers and different university recognition. The decision between them should rest on marked written work, and getting it wrong in Year 10 is expensive to reverse.

sections.heading: Scheduling around a clinical shift pattern
paragraphs: Almost every tutoring plan assumes a parent is home at roughly the same hour each weekday. In Al Jaddaf, with Dubai Healthcare City next door, that assumption fails often enough to be worth designing around rather than apologising for. A rotating rota means an arrangement has to work on a week when nobody is home at five, and the family has to be able to see afterwards what happened in the lesson.

Two design choices make that workable. The first is a slot that does not depend on supervision: for students from Year 9 upwards this is usually straightforward, and Al Jaddaf's short school run means the early afternoon window is available rather than theoretical. The second is a written record. Worked solutions and a short summary saved after each session mean a parent coming off a night shift can see what was covered without having been present or having to ask a tired teenager.

The table sets out the household patterns we see in this community and the slot that holds for each. Two rows deserve note. Where both adults work clinical shifts, a fixed weekday slot with a standing fallback day is more robust than a flexible arrangement, because flexibility in practice means the session gets postponed and then skipped. And where a younger child genuinely needs an adult present, the honest answer is to put the session on the days that can be covered and accept fewer of them.

What does not work is booking a slot around the shift and moving it every week. The sessions that survive a year are the ones with a fixed place in the week, even if that place is a Friday morning or a Sunday evening. A tutor also builds a better picture of a student from a regular contact than from an irregular one, and that picture is a substantial part of what you are paying for.

sections.heading: The bilingual Diploma, and whether it is worth the workload
paragraphs: This is the question Al Jaddaf families ask more than any other, and it rarely gets an honest answer elsewhere because the honest answer is sometimes no. The bilingual Diploma is awarded where a candidate completes two languages at Language A level from different language groups, or completes certain subjects in a second language. It is a genuine distinction and it is also a substantial amount of additional written work in a programme that already has six subjects and three core components.

The decision should rest on evidence rather than aspiration. A student whose written analytical work in the second language is already strong at the end of MYP is in a good position to take it on. A student who speaks the language fluently at home but writes it at a conversational level is being asked to develop academic literacy in a second language at the same time as sitting three Higher Levels, and something usually gives. Which thing gives is often the Higher Level science, which is the component a university offer actually depends on.

A tutor's useful contribution here is diagnostic and specific. Reading two pieces of the student's own written work, one in each language, against the Language A criteria tells a family more than a term of discussion. If the gap is register and analytical vocabulary, that is closeable in a term of targeted work. If the gap is sentence-level accuracy across extended writing, the honest assessment is that pursuing the bilingual award will cost more than it returns.

sections.heading: What KHDA requires alongside the international programme
paragraphs: Families in this cluster meet the mandatory UAE subjects in a particular way, because a bilingual school is already running more languages than most. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, under KHDA requirements schools were to implement from the start of the 2025-26 academic year, and the grades are reported separately from the Diploma or IGCSE result.

KHDA sets out how these subjects are organised in some detail, and the detail matters for anyone buying support. Schools must run separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, with the school's licensed-curriculum language used for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in moral, social and cultural studies.

Instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit. Schools may vary the lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and KHDA advises that any mandatory subject lesson should run at least twenty-five minutes. That figure is a useful benchmark for a parent planning a tutoring session, since a support session shorter than the school's own minimum is unlikely to achieve much.

Two constraints apply to the content itself. Teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education in Dubai schools must hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, which a parent can reasonably ask about. And for the mandatory UAE subjects, use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited. Support in these subjects therefore works from the school's own material rather than a parallel syllabus, and any provider offering a different curriculum here is offering something that does not fit the rules.

sections.heading: What tutoring costs in this market, and where language work sits
paragraphs: Three of the six best-ranking Dubai tutoring pages publish no price, and the two that do quote in US dollars, which is not the currency an Al Jaddaf family transacts in. The bands below are AED market rates taken from providers' own published pages and a 2026 Dubai tutoring cost survey, with the source named on each row. They are market figures and not an IB Gram price list, and nothing here is a quote.

Language work sits in a slightly different place in the market from subject work, and it is worth understanding why. Arabic and Language B support at the volume that actually helps means two short contacts a week rather than one hour, so the useful comparison is the weekly total rather than the hourly rate. Two forty-minute sessions a week is roughly five and a half hours a month, which at the qualified band produces a different monthly figure from four single hours even though the hourly rate is the same.

The other distinction is specialism. A tutor teaching Arabic as a first language to the KHDA expectation, in Standard Arabic, is a narrower specialism than a general subject tutor, and so is a Language B examiner-style oral rehearsal. Scarcity shows up in availability rather than in the published rate, which is why the coverage question at the end of this page matters as much as the price question.

Three questions separate a real quote from a headline figure anywhere in this market. Is the number all-in, or does it precede assessment fees, materials and a minimum booking period. Is value added tax included in what is shown. And what happens if the first pairing is wrong, which for language and bilingual work is a realistic risk because the match is more specific than for a mainstream subject.

sections.heading: In-home tutoring in Al Jaddaf compared with one-to-one online
paragraphs: In-home tutoring is a legitimate service and plenty of Dubai families use it well. Market rates run roughly AED 180-500 an hour with travel priced into the figure, according to a 2026 cost survey and tutors' own published pages, and for a younger child who needs an adult physically present it has a real advantage. The honest question for an Al Jaddaf household is what it costs in match quality when the brief involves a specific language route.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE. Home visits are a service we run only in India. What we arrange for Al Jaddaf families is one-to-one tuition delivered live over video, selected from the whole roster by subject, level and language. For Arabic as a first language taught in Standard Arabic, or a Language B oral rehearsal at Higher Level, that pool is narrow before any geographic filter is applied.

Two features of this community sharpen the comparison in opposite directions. The short school run and the metro terminus mean Al Jaddaf students can realistically take an early afternoon slot, which is both less contested and only bookable if no travel is involved. On the other hand, a household with both adults on clinical rotas may genuinely value an adult arriving at a fixed time, and we do not pretend otherwise.

The table compares the two formats on the terms that matter for this brief rather than on general convenience. The final row is the honest limitation, stated as plainly as the rest: a young child who will not stay on task alone is harder to teach on a screen, and the right answer for that child is shorter sessions with a parent nearby, or a home visit from a provider who offers them.

sections.heading: Where a tutor stops on a bilingual student's written work
paragraphs: This boundary needs stating with more care for a bilingual student than for anyone else, because the temptation is greater and the line is less obvious. A student writing an Internal Assessment or an Extended Essay in their second language will produce prose with grammatical errors and awkward phrasing. A tutor who corrects every sentence has produced a document the student did not write, and the fact that the ideas were the student's own does not fix that.

The legitimate version is teaching rather than correcting. A tutor can explain the assessment criteria and their mark allocations, show what academic register looks like in that language, teach the sentence patterns that subject writing uses, point to a paragraph and say that the argument is not visible here, and ask the student to rewrite it themselves. That approach develops the capability the examination will test again in a room where nobody can help. Line-by-line correction does not.

What a tutor must not do is supply text, rewrite a passage into its final form, or take over in any way that makes the submission not the student's own. IB Gram does not supply assessed work, does not edit a draft into a finished submission, and declines requests framed that way. Submitting work that is not the student's own is malpractice under IB rules, and the investigation and the consequence fall on the student rather than on anyone else.

There is also a practical point specific to language assessment. Where the written component is partly assessing language itself, as in Language A and Language B, correction is not merely a rules problem; it directly inflates the mark for a skill the student has not acquired. The predicted grade then sits above the real one, the university offer is made on the wrong basis, and the gap appears in May. Teaching the register is slower and it is the only version that holds.

sections.heading: The exam calendar for a bilingual cohort, counted backwards
paragraphs: Exam administration catches language candidates in a particular way, because oral components sit earlier in the year than written papers and are often the first assessed thing a student does. For a Language A or Language B student the internal oral window can fall months before the examination series, and a family planning around the written papers can miss it entirely. The school's internal deadline list is the document to ask for, in September, for the whole year.

On the written side the board calendars are published and usable. Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level in a June series and a November series, with a March series as well. For the March 2027 series, final entries are due 27 November 2026, the exam period runs 3 February to 4 March 2027, forecast grades are due 27 February 2027 and results reach centres on Direct on 13 May 2027. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that the correct zone timetable must be used, because it cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who missed a paper after using the wrong version.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November, with the November 2026 final timetable running from late October to 19 November 2026. For reference on the results interval, June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so the live PDF on the Pearson site is the version to work from.

For the IB this page publishes no session or results date. The IB's own site blocks automated checking, and an unverified date on a page a family might plan around is worse than none. Confirm the May session window and the results date with your school's IB coordinator or on ibo.org. The deadlines that actually govern an Al Jaddaf autumn are the school's internal ones for the oral components, the Internal Assessments and the Extended Essay, all of which fall earlier than anything the board publishes.

sections.heading: Coverage and fallback for language and Higher Level subjects
paragraphs: No provider covers every subject and language at every hour, and the ones that imply otherwise substitute a generalist and leave you to notice. For an Al Jaddaf brief the scarce combinations are predictable: Arabic as a first language taught to the KHDA expectation, Language B at Higher Level with oral preparation, and the familiar Higher Level trio of Chemistry, Physics and Maths Analysis and Approaches in the hour between five and seven o'clock.

This community has a structural advantage worth using. The school inside the development and the metro terminus mean an Al Jaddaf student can realistically take an early afternoon slot that families elsewhere physically cannot reach. The quarter-past-four window is markedly less contested than the five-to-seven block, and a household prepared to use it has access to specialists that a later booking does not.

Where a slot still cannot be filled, three honest options exist and we name them. A different time, usually earlier or at the weekend. A dated wait for a slot to open, with the date given rather than implied. Or a tutor based outside the UAE teaching the same named syllabus at a time that suits both sides, disclosed in advance with any rate difference stated plainly. Several competitors in this market conceal non-UAE delivery behind a local-looking contact number; we state the tutor's location before the first session.

What we will not do is place a student with someone who does not know the component. For a language brief that matters more than usual, since a tutor who speaks the language fluently but has never taught the Language B assessment criteria will teach conversation, which is not what the examination rewards. Fluency and assessment knowledge are different qualifications, and only one of them is what you are buying.

process.title: Tell us the shift pattern as well as the school
process.description: Whether an adult is reliably home at the same hour each week changes what arrangement will hold. For households on a clinical rota, a fixed slot with a standing fallback day and a written record after each lesson is more robust than a flexible one.

process.title: Settle the language route before the subject plan
process.description: For a bilingual student the Language A and Language B decisions shape the whole programme. A diagnostic on two pieces of the student's own written work, one in each language, tells you more than a term of discussion about the bilingual award.

process.title: Confirm the board, the stream and the syllabus code
process.description: English as a first language and English as a second language are different qualifications with different papers and different recognition. Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are different courses. The statement of entry settles both.

process.title: Choose frequency over length where recall is the problem
process.description: Arabic, Language B vocabulary and subject terminology respond to two short contacts a week rather than one long session. We will recommend the pattern the subject needs rather than the one that bills most conveniently.

process.title: Diagnostic first session on the student's own work
process.description: The tutor works through a recent marked paper, written task or draft and reports where the marks are going. For a bilingual student that report distinguishes a content gap from a written-expression gap, which are different jobs.

process.title: Plan the oral and coursework windows in September
process.description: Internal oral windows for Language A and B often fall months before the written series, and coursework deadlines are set by the school rather than the board. Getting the internal deadline list in September is the single most useful administrative step.

whyPoints.title: The arrangement is designed for a rota, not a routine
whyPoints.description: A fixed slot that runs whether or not a parent is home, plus a written record after every session, is what survives a clinical shift pattern. Flexibility sounds helpful and in practice means the lesson is postponed and then dropped.

whyPoints.title: Language route advice comes with evidence attached
whyPoints.description: The bilingual Diploma is a real commitment in written workload. We read two pieces of the student's own writing against the criteria before encouraging it, and we will say when the honest answer is a strong single Language A instead.

whyPoints.title: Fluency and assessment knowledge are not the same purchase
whyPoints.description: A tutor who speaks a language fluently but has never taught its assessment criteria will teach conversation. We match on the component, which for Language B means text type, register and the oral, not general practice.

whyPoints.title: The honesty line on written work is explicit
whyPoints.description: A bilingual student's draft will contain errors. We teach register and sentence patterns and the student rewrites their own paragraphs. We do not correct line by line, supply text or edit a draft into a submission.

whyPoints.title: Rates and sources are both published
whyPoints.description: Every AED band here names the provider or survey behind it, with the weekly pattern that language work actually needs priced as a weekly pattern rather than disguised as an hourly comparison.

whyPoints.title: No regulator or board approval is claimed
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no accreditation from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. Those bodies are named here to explain a requirement or source a date, nothing more.

faqs.question: Is the bilingual IB Diploma worth the extra workload?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the honest answer depends on written evidence rather than spoken fluency. The award recognises two languages studied at Language A level from different groups, which is a substantial amount of additional written work alongside six subjects and the Diploma core. A student whose analytical writing in the second language is already strong at the end of MYP is well placed. A student who speaks it fluently at home but writes at a conversational level is being asked to build academic literacy while sitting three Higher Levels, and what usually suffers is the Higher Level science a university offer depends on.

faqs.question: Should my bilingual child sit English as a first language or second language at IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Decide it on marked written work, not on how confidently they speak. They are separate qualifications with different papers and different recognition by universities and by some employers, and the choice is effectively locked at the entry deadline in Year 10 or 11. A tutor can read two pieces of recent written work against both syllabuses and give you an evidence-based view in a single session. Getting this wrong is expensive to reverse, and the school's head of English will usually be direct about it if you ask for their reasoning rather than their recommendation.

faqs.question: Can a lesson run when nobody is home because of a hospital shift?
faqs.answer: For most students from Year 9 upwards, yes, and in Al Jaddaf that is a common arrangement given how many households work clinical rotas next door at Dubai Healthcare City. The two things that make it work are a fixed slot rather than one that moves with the rota, and a written record: worked solutions and a short summary saved after each session so a parent coming off a night shift can see what was covered. For younger children, put the sessions on the days that can be covered and accept fewer of them rather than booking a weekly hour and cancelling half.

faqs.question: Why do you recommend two short sessions a week for Arabic rather than one hour?
faqs.answer: Because the difficulty is retention between contacts, not a shortage of explanation. Script fluency and vocabulary recall decay on a predictable curve, and two thirty to forty minute contacts interrupt that curve twice rather than once. KHDA's own instructional-time guidance is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit and advises that a mandatory subject lesson should run at least twenty-five minutes, which is a useful benchmark: a support session shorter than the school's own minimum achieves little. For composition and grammar at first-language level, a longer session has more value, so the pattern changes with the level.

faqs.question: What does the Green Line terminus at Creek change for an older student?
faqs.answer: Predictability, which is worth more than speed. A Year 12 student travelling home on the metro arrives on a timetable rather than at the mercy of the Ras Al Khor interchange, which means a five o'clock slot can be booked with confidence rather than hope. For families where neither adult is home at that hour, that reliability is the difference between a slot that holds for a year and one that gets moved every third week. The usual thing that breaks it is a school activity shifting the return by half an hour, so build that into the chosen time.

faqs.question: My son's understanding is ahead of his written English. Which does tutoring fix?
faqs.answer: Both, but they are different jobs and worth separating explicitly. A diagnostic on a marked paper will show whether the lost marks are content he does not know or explanation he cannot yet phrase precisely enough to score. The second case is extremely common in a bilingual setting, and the work is subject-specific language: the sentence patterns an examiner credits, what a command term requires, and the register that analytical writing uses. That is teachable in a term. More content teaching will not touch it, which is why so many families feel their tutoring is not working.

faqs.question: Where exactly does a tutor stop when helping with writing in a second language?
faqs.answer: At correction. A tutor can explain the criteria and their marks, show what academic register looks like in that language, teach the sentence patterns subject writing uses, and point at a paragraph and say the argument is not visible. The student then rewrites it themselves. A tutor must not supply text, rewrite a passage into final form or correct line by line, because that produces a document the student did not write and inflates a mark for a skill they have not acquired. IB Gram does not supply assessed work and declines requests framed that way.

faqs.question: Which school is actually inside Al Jaddaf?
faqs.answer: Swiss International Scientific School Dubai sits within the community, running a bilingual IB continuum through to the Diploma. That single fact explains most of what is distinctive about tutoring here: a very short school run, an early afternoon slot that is genuinely usable, and far more language-route questions than other creek-side areas generate. Families wanting a British or American route generally look east to Dubai Festival City or north-west to Oud Metha. Confirm current programmes and language streams with the school and against the KHDA school listing, since both change by year group.

faqs.question: When do Language A and Language B oral components actually happen?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most families expect, and often months before the written papers. The internal oral windows are set by the school rather than by the board, which means they do not appear on any published board calendar a parent might find. The practical step is to ask the IB coordinator in September for the internal deadline list covering the whole year, including oral windows, Internal Assessment drafts and Extended Essay checkpoints. A family planning around the May papers can otherwise discover the oral has already happened, which is not a recoverable situation.

faqs.question: Does my non-Arab child have to study Arabic in a Dubai private school?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, under KHDA requirements schools were to implement from the start of the 2025-26 academic year, and the grades are reported separately. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, since the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. For non-Arab students, Islamic Education and moral, social and cultural studies are taught in the school's licensed-curriculum language.

faqs.question: Can a tutor use their own Arabic materials instead of the school's?
faqs.answer: Not for the mandatory UAE subjects. KHDA states that for these subjects the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry of Education, is prohibited. Support therefore has to work from the school's own material and the prescribed content rather than a parallel syllabus, which is a genuine constraint and worth knowing before buying. It also means a provider advertising its own Arabic curriculum for these subjects is offering something that does not fit the rules. Teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education in Dubai schools must also hold appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects.

faqs.question: Do tutors come to apartments in Al Jaddaf or Jaddaf Waterfront?
faqs.answer: Not through IB Gram. We do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Independent in-home tutors operate across Dubai at market rates of roughly AED 180-500 an hour with travel priced in, per a 2026 Dubai cost survey and tutors' own published pages. The trade-off is sharper here than in most areas: a twice-weekly short-session pattern, which is what language work needs, means two visits a week rather than one, and the travel premium multiplies across them.

faqs.question: Is a tutor who speaks the language fluently good enough for Language B?
faqs.answer: Not on its own. Fluency and assessment knowledge are separate qualifications, and only one of them is what the examination rewards. Language B is assessed across reading, writing, listening and an individual oral, and marks are lost on text type and register rather than on vocabulary: a formal letter written as an essay loses credit regardless of how natural the language sounds. A tutor who has taught the criteria knows what a conceptual question in the oral requires. A fluent speaker without that knowledge will teach conversation, which is pleasant and does not move a grade.

faqs.question: What should I budget monthly for twice-weekly language support?
faqs.answer: Two sessions of thirty to forty minutes a week is roughly five and a half hours a month, so the monthly figure follows from the hourly band rather than from a package headline. Published market rates for a qualified online subject tutor in Dubai run roughly AED 150-300 an hour, with Unitors listing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. A 2026 Dubai cost survey puts weekly one-hour tutoring at roughly AED 600-1,200 monthly in the mid tier. Those are market figures, not IB Gram prices. Ask whether the quote is all-in and whether value added tax is included.

faqs.question: What if no Standard Arabic or Higher Level Language B tutor is free at our time?
faqs.answer: We say so and give you three real options rather than substituting someone who does not know the component. The first is the early afternoon slot, which Al Jaddaf's short school run and metro access make genuinely available and which is far less contested than five to seven o'clock. The second is a dated wait, with a date given rather than implied. The third is a tutor outside the UAE teaching the same named syllabus at a time that suits both sides, with the location and any rate difference stated before the first session rather than discovered later.

dubai/al-jaddaf.closingHeading: Tell us the rota and the language route
dubai/al-jaddaf.closingBody: Two pieces of information get an Al Jaddaf arrangement right at the first attempt: whether an adult is reliably home at the same hour each week, and which language route your child is on or considering. The first decides the slot and whether a written record after every lesson matters. The second decides the tutor, because Standard Arabic, Language B at Higher Level and a bilingual Diploma brief are narrow specialisms rather than general subject work. Lessons are one-to-one and delivered live over video, which is what makes the early afternoon window this community uniquely has into an appointment you can actually book.

dubai/al-khail-gate.tutorsIntro: Tutors matched to Al Khail Gate households are chosen for two things beyond subject knowledge: they can hold an evening slot after a long bus run, and they teach one named board and tier rather than a subject in general, so no hour is spent on content the student will never be examined on.

intro.heading: Two fixed constraints: the bus and the monthly figure
paragraphs: Al Khail Gate sits in Al Quoz 4, a set of mid-rise residential blocks arranged in phases along the Al Khail Road side of the district, with its own retail plaza, mosque, clinic and nursery, and the Al Quoz industrial area and Times Square Center close by. It was built as affordable family housing rather than as a lifestyle community, and it works: households here are stable, often long-settled, frequently with three children rather than one, and overwhelmingly commuting rather than walking to school.

The first constraint that shapes everything is the bus. There is no large school inside the community, so children are collected early and returned late. A route that serves Al Quoz blocks and then continues to Al Barsha, Al Barsha South or Motor City is a long route in both directions, and for a secondary student it frequently means leaving before seven in the morning and arriving home between half past four and half past five. Younger children on primary routes are often home earlier, which matters because it means the household's two age groups are available at different times.

The second constraint is the monthly figure. In most of the communities this website covers, the limiting factor on tutoring is the diary. Here it is usually the budget, and it is a genuine budget rather than a preference: a number per month that has already been allocated and cannot be exceeded without something else being cut. Published Dubai market rates run from AED 45 an hour at the generalist end to AED 650 at the top, which means the same subject can cost four times as much depending on who teaches it, and nobody in this market will explain which difference is worth paying for.

The third feature is the household shape. An Al Khail Gate apartment with three school-age children has one dining table, often one laptop that is good enough for a video lesson, and parents whose working hours do not reliably end at six. That combination makes the usual advice, book a tutor for each child who needs one, both unaffordable and physically impossible. The planning problem is a household problem rather than a student problem, and it is solvable, but only if it is treated as one from the start.

So this page answers the questions those three constraints produce. When can a session actually happen here. How do you schedule three children and one device. What does each monthly budget buy, in AED, with sources. Is a group of four better value than one hour one-to-one, honestly. What does the Core or Foundation tier decision cost if it is wrong. How do you check that whoever is teaching your child is legally permitted to do it. And what IB Gram actually delivers, which is one-to-one tuition online over live video rather than a visit to your building.

dubai/al-khail-gate.programmesIntro: Al Khail Gate children sit a wider spread of systems than most Dubai communities, because the schools reachable from Al Quoz cover British, Indian and IB routes at very different fee levels. These four cover the great majority.

programmes.name: IGCSE at Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel
programmes.description: The qualification most Al Khail Gate students actually sit. Cambridge splits most subjects into Core and Extended, with Core capped at grade C and Extended running A* to E. Pearson Edexcel tiers mathematics as Foundation and Higher, with Higher reaching grade 9 and Foundation capped at 5. The tier is chosen by the school, often in Year 9, and it sets the grade ceiling two years before the papers are sat.
programmes.countryNote: This is the decision with the largest financial consequence for a household here, and almost nobody discusses it in those terms. A student placed on Core who could have managed Extended loses access to grades above C, which affects sixth-form entry and the Ministry of Education equivalency count. Ask for the tier in writing and ask what evidence it was based on.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four published criteria marked out of eight, converted to a grade from 1 to 7. Unlike an examined course, the grade depends on habits such as investigating and communicating as much as on content knowledge, so a student who knows the material can sit in the middle bands for years. There is no tier and no ceiling, which removes the Core or Extended problem entirely.
programmes.countryNote: Several IB continuum schools are reachable from Al Quoz. For a household weighing fees, the honest point is that the Middle Years Programme asks for more independent work at home than an examined course does at the same age, which costs parental time rather than money and is worth knowing before choosing it.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, usually three Higher and three Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internal assessment carries 20% in the sciences and both mathematics courses. A Standard Level subject is built around 150 guided hours and a Higher Level subject around 240, so each Higher Level choice adds substantial content rather than simply more difficulty.
programmes.countryNote: For a household with a fixed tutoring budget, the Diploma's structure matters: six subjects plus a core means tutoring every weak subject is not affordable, so choosing which one or two to support is the real decision. The highest return is usually a Higher Level subject where the internal assessment is at risk, because 20% of a grade is a large thing to lose.

programmes.name: A Level, as the post-16 route
programmes.description: Three or four linear subjects with no core, assessed almost entirely through terminal written papers. For a budget-conscious household this has a practical advantage over the Diploma: fewer components, no Extended Essay, no Theory of Knowledge, and support can be concentrated on one subject rather than spread across six. The disadvantage is that everything rests on the final papers.
programmes.countryNote: Several schools reachable from Al Quoz offer A Level after IGCSE. The question worth asking at sixteen is which route the student's intended next step actually requires, and whether the sixth form inside their current school is available to them, because a transfer at sixteen adds both cost and disruption.

dubai/al-khail-gate.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Al Khail Gate households ask about most, with a note on where the marks are won in each. The emphasis is on what a single weekly hour can realistically change.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580)
subjects.description: The most requested subject in this community. Core and Extended are different papers with different ceilings, and the Extended route includes a non-calculator paper. One weekly hour spent on worked past paper questions with honest marking moves this subject faster than any other, because the marks are lost in method and presentation rather than in understanding.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Pearson Edexcel 4MA1)
subjects.description: Two papers with a calculator permitted in both, tiered Foundation and Higher. Foundation caps at grade 5 and Higher reaches 9 with a 3 allowed, so the tier decision is a grade-ceiling decision. Students who rely on written methods for arithmetic lose time rather than marks, and that is fixable in a handful of sessions.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 and Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.description: Cambridge 0625 assesses practical skills through either a practical test or a written alternative paper, and which one the school enters for changes what matters. Electricity and circuits are the topic that most often decides a grade here, and they respond well to short, repeated, diagram-based practice rather than to long explanation.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 and Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: Mole calculations, concentration and yield are where Extended candidates separate from Core, and they are drillable. At Diploma level the scientific investigation carries 20% at both levels, which makes it the single most valuable thing to support when a budget allows only one component.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 and Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: Content-heavy and decided by command terms. A student who answers every question as describe caps well below their understanding, and correcting that is a matter of hours rather than months. For a household buying a single weekly hour, command-term work across the sciences gives the broadest return.

subjects.name: Coordinated and Combined Sciences
subjects.description: Two or one IGCSE grades covering all three sciences, common in schools that need to fit a broad curriculum into a timetable. The content is genuinely broad and shallow, so the main risk is a student treating it as three separate subjects and running out of revision time. A single structured plan across the paper is usually enough.

subjects.name: English as a second language
subjects.description: A different specification from First Language English, with different papers and a different purpose. Schools sometimes enter a bilingual student in the route that suits the timetable rather than the student. Reading comprehension technique and timed writing structure are where the marks sit, and both improve with frequent short practice.

subjects.name: English as a first language
subjects.description: Directed writing and the analysis of unseen passages decide the grade. Some sixth forms set First Language English as the entry requirement for literature courses, so the route matters beyond the grade itself. The highest-value hour here is a timed attempt marked honestly against the published scheme rather than a discussion of technique.

subjects.name: Mathematics and Science at MYP level
subjects.description: Criterion-based rather than examined, so the work is about demonstrating the strands the criteria name rather than about covering content. A student who is strong on knowledge and weak on investigating or communicating will sit at a 4 or 5 indefinitely, and that pattern is fixable once it is explained.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Studies
subjects.description: Usually chosen at fourteen and often the subject where a student can gain the most quickly, because the marks are procedural: accurate diagrams, labelled axes, and a justified recommendation where one is asked for. Answers that list advantages and disadvantages instead of recommending lose marks in every paper.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Every student in a Dubai private school takes Arabic regardless of curriculum, as a KHDA mandatory subject. The mandatory stream and the examined IGCSE qualification are different things, and progress in one does not automatically appear in the other. Support has to work from the school's own material rather than a parallel course.

dubai/al-khail-gate.regionsIntro: Al Khail Gate's neighbours matter as school destinations and as bus routes. These notes are about travel and timing rather than about amenities.

regions.name: Al Quoz 1, 2 and 3
regions.note: The surrounding district, part industrial and part residential, with several schools and a large number of the city's tuition centres. Short journeys in distance, and routinely slow at the Umm Suqeim Street and Sheikh Zayed Road junctions at both ends of the school day.

regions.name: Al Barsha and Al Barsha South
regions.note: Across Al Khail Road, with a concentration of large all-through campuses at a range of fee levels. Most secondary bus routes from this community head in this direction, which is what sets the typical arrival home after half past four.

regions.name: Motor City and Dubai Sports City
regions.note: South along Al Khail Road, with several campuses and residential communities. A straightforward run outside peak and a long one during it, so households with children at schools here see the latest arrival times in the community.

regions.name: Al Safa and Umm Suqeim
regions.note: Towards the coast along Umm Suqeim Street, with a number of British-curriculum schools. The journey is short when the junctions are clear and unreliable when they are not, which makes a measured arrival time more useful than a map estimate.

regions.name: Oud Metha and Bur Dubai
regions.note: Towards the creek, where several long-established schools serving Indian and British curricula sit. These are longer bus routes with earlier pickups, and the pickup time is the constraint that limits how late an evening session can run.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate and Al Quoz 4 border
regions.note: Immediately adjacent across Al Khail Road, with newer campuses and clinics. Several Al Khail Gate households use services here, and children at these schools have the shortest bus run available from the community.

regions.name: Jumeirah Village Circle and Al Furjan
regions.note: Further along Al Khail Road, with their own school provision and a similar mixed-tenure household profile. Families here face the same budget-versus-format question and reach the same conclusions about group teaching.

schoolClusters.city: Al Quoz and the Al Khail corridor
schoolClusters.note: The nearest campuses, reachable on short bus routes, covering British and Indian curriculum provision at a range of fee levels. These produce the earliest arrivals home in the community and therefore the widest choice of session times.

schoolClusters.city: Al Barsha, Al Barsha South and Motor City
schoolClusters.note: The inland and southern ring across Al Khail Road, with several large all-through campuses including British and IB routes. These are the longest bus runs from this community and the reason most secondary sessions here start after five.

dubai/al-khail-gate.modesIntro: Three formats are built around a fixed budget rather than around an ideal. All run online over live video, and the honest ranking between them depends on how much of the problem is content and how much is confidence.

modes.title: One subject, one hour, one term
modes.description: The format most households here should start with: a single weak subject, one weekly hour, for one term, then a decision. It is the cheapest arrangement that can produce a measurable result, and it avoids the common mistake of spreading a fixed budget so thinly across four subjects that none of them moves.
bullets: One subject chosen on where the marks are actually being lost
Same tutor weekly, named before anything is paid

A clear decision at the end of the term rather than a rolling renewal

modes.title: Household timetable for two or three children
modes.description: Back-to-back slots on the same evening so one table and one device serve the whole household, with the exam-year child given the stronger hour. Different tutors where the boards differ, one shared calendar, and one review conversation covering every child rather than separate calls that say the same thing.

modes.description: A fixed, countable number of sessions immediately before an examination series, built entirely on timed questions, mark-scheme marking and an error log the student maintains. For a household that cannot fund a whole year, this is where a limited number of hours buys the most marks.

sections.heading: The Al Khail Gate school run is a bus run, and it starts early
paragraphs: Scheduling here begins with a timetable the family does not control. There is no large school inside the community, so children are collected from the blocks and driven out, usually to Al Barsha, Al Barsha South, Motor City, Al Safa or towards the creek. A secondary route serving several Al Quoz stops before continuing inland is a long route, and it is long in both directions. The practical result is a school day that starts before seven for many students here and ends with an arrival home between half past four and half past five.

That has two consequences parents rarely connect. The early pickup caps how late a session can run the previous evening without costing sleep, which is why a nine o'clock slot that looks available is a bad idea for a child who has to be at the stop at ten to seven. And the later arrival narrows the usable window at the other end, so the realistic weekday hour here is a single one rather than a choice of three. Where a household has children on both a primary and a secondary route, those children become available at different times, which is useful rather than inconvenient: it is what makes back-to-back slots possible on one device.

The table below gives the pattern by school cluster. These are planning figures from the households we work with rather than published timetables, so measure your own: write down for two weeks the time the child is actually at a desk, fed, rather than the time the bus arrived. The average of that fortnight is the number to build around, and it is usually later than a parent would guess. Then set the session fifteen minutes after it and keep that hour every week, because a slot attended thirty-six times beats a better slot attended twenty-four.

sections.heading: Three children, one table, one laptop
paragraphs: The standard advice about tutoring assumes one student in a house with spare rooms. A great many Al Khail Gate households have three school-age children, one dining table that works, and one laptop that is good enough for a video lesson. That is not a problem to be apologised for; it is a scheduling constraint with a known solution, and ignoring it is why arrangements collapse in week three rather than why they fail outright.

The solution is sequencing and prioritising rather than simultaneity. Children arrive home at different times because they are on different routes, so the natural pattern is the primary child in the earlier slot and the secondary child later, on the same device, with the table handed over cleanly. Where two children are both in examined years, the one sitting a series this year takes the better hour by default. And where the budget supports only one child being tutored at all, that decision should be made on where the marks are most recoverable rather than on who complains loudest, which is a harder conversation and the right one.

There are three cheap pieces of equipment that make a shared setup work properly, and together they cost less than one hour of tutoring. Over-ear headphones with a boom microphone, so a student can be heard without raising their voice over a shared living space. A wired connection or the 5 GHz band rather than whatever the laptop joins by default. And an old phone propped as a document camera, so the tutor sees the written working rather than the student's face, which changes mathematics and science lessons more than any other single thing. The table below gives the household patterns we see here and the plan that works for each.

sections.heading: Supervision when both parents are still at work at four
paragraphs: A quieter issue in this community is that the hours between a child arriving home and a parent arriving home are often unsupervised, and the habits formed in those hours do more to decide a grade than any weekly session does. A student who spends four until six on a phone and then starts work at eight is not helped much by one paid hour on a Tuesday. A student who has a fixed, short, unglamorous routine in that window can do without tutoring in several subjects entirely.

What works in practice is small and specific. A written list of what is to be done each weekday, left on the table rather than communicated by message, because a list a child can tick is harder to ignore than an instruction they can forget. Thirty to forty minutes rather than two hours, since nobody supervises the second hour and nobody does it. The same task type each day, so no decision is required: ten marked questions, one page of vocabulary, one past paper section. And an evening check that takes two minutes rather than a conversation that takes twenty.

An online tutoring slot can be built to support this rather than to replace it. The session sets the week's short daily task and then checks it at the start of the next session, which means the paid hour buys five days of unsupervised work rather than one hour of supervised work. For a household with a fixed monthly figure, that is the single largest multiplier available, and it costs nothing extra. It also solves the supervision problem without requiring a parent to be home, because the accountability is to the tutor at a fixed point rather than to whoever happens to be in the room.

sections.heading: What each monthly budget actually buys in this market
paragraphs: This is the section most pages in this market refuse to write. Three of the six ranking pages reviewed for this project publish no price at all, and two quote in US dollars. The table below works the other way round: it starts from a monthly figure in AED and says what that figure realistically buys, with the source of each band named. The figures are market rates surveyed in October 2026 from published platform and agency rate pages and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table. They are not an IB Gram price list and nothing here is a quote.

The pattern in the table is worth stating plainly because it is counter-intuitive. More hours of weaker teaching is usually worse value than fewer hours of the right teaching, up to a point, and then the curve flattens hard. One weekly hour with a tutor who teaches your child's exact board and tier, marking against the published scheme, outperforms three weekly hours of general homework supervision for an examined subject. But a specialist at the top of the market is not three times better than one in the middle; past a certain point you are paying for scarcity and for a name.

Two further things save money in this community specifically. First, choose the subject by where the marks are recoverable rather than by which grade looks worst, because a student two grades below their potential in mathematics is a better investment than one who was never going to pass a language. Second, ask the three questions that reveal the real cost of any arrangement: is the figure per hour or per session and how long is a session; does it include VAT and will that appear on the invoice; what happens to money already paid if you stop after one lesson. Get all three in writing before paying anything.

sections.heading: A group of four, or one hour one-to-one?
paragraphs: For a household working to a fixed figure this is the real question, and the honest answer is that it depends on what is actually wrong. If a student has missed content and knows it, a group class covering that content is good value, because the teaching is the same whether four people hear it or one. If a student understands the content and keeps losing marks, a group is poor value, because the thing that needs fixing is specific to them and will not be addressed in a room of four with one worked example on a board.

There is a second distinction that matters more than group size: whether the group is matched by board and tier. Four students sitting Cambridge 0580 Extended can be taught together efficiently. Four students where one sits Core, one sits Extended, one sits Pearson Edexcel Foundation and one sits the International Mathematics syllabus cannot, whatever the advertised subject. Tuition centres in Al Quoz vary enormously on this point, and it is a fair question to ask before enrolling: which board, which tier, and are all the students in this group entered for the same one.

The table below compares the formats on the dimensions that decide value for a budget household. Note the last row. Free or low-cost support run by the school itself is frequently the best-value option available and is routinely under-used, because it is not marketed. Ask the head of year what after-school or intervention support exists before paying for anything, because in many schools there is a Year 11 clinic, a maths drop-in or a subject surgery that costs nothing and is staffed by the teacher who will mark the coursework.

sections.heading: Core or Extended, Foundation or Higher: the ceiling decision
paragraphs: The most consequential decision in an Al Khail Gate student's school career is often made quietly in Year 9 by a department, and most parents here never hear it discussed. Cambridge Core and Extended are different papers with different grade ranges: Core is capped at grade C, Extended runs A* to E. Pearson Edexcel mathematics is tiered Foundation and Higher: Foundation caps at grade 5, Higher reaches 9 with a 3 allowed. A student placed on the lower tier cannot access the higher grades no matter how well they perform.

Schools place students on evidence, and the evidence is usually right. But placements are made in a cohort rather than about an individual, they are sometimes made on a single set of Year 9 results, and they are occasionally made on timetable convenience. A student who was placed on Core in Year 9 after a bad term, and who has since improved substantially, may be sitting a paper that cannot give them the grade they now deserve. The correct response is not an argument; it is a request for the evidence and a conversation about whether a move is possible within the board's entry deadlines.

Those deadlines are the hard constraint, and they are earlier than families expect. Cambridge's published key dates for the March 2027 series put final entries on 27 November 2026 for an examination period beginning 3 February 2027, which means board, tier and option codes are locked more than two months before the first paper. A tier change requested in January for a February series is usually impossible. Ask the question in the autumn term, not in the spring, and ask it with evidence: a set of Extended past paper questions attempted under timed conditions and marked honestly is the most persuasive thing a parent can bring to that meeting.

sections.heading: Is whoever teaches your child legally permitted to do it?
paragraphs: Informal tutoring is common across Dubai and particularly common where budgets are tight, which makes this worth setting out plainly rather than hinting at. Private tutoring in the UAE operates under a permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years. Because there is no fee, there is no cost reason for a tutor not to hold one, which makes its absence a straightforward signal rather than a financial hardship.

Eligibility is broader than most parents assume. It includes teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. The application route is MoHRE's own service, Issuance of a New Work Permit for Private Tutor Licensing, applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system, with a stated completion time of two working days and no fee listed. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws; no fine schedule has been published, so any specific amount circulating online should be treated with caution.

There is one further condition worth knowing, and it protects your child rather than the tutor. The permit carries a code of conduct which press reporting indicates bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school, and in Abu Dhabi, ADEK has set professional-ethics rules prohibiting private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school. Those positions are press-reported rather than quoted here from current policy documents, so verify with the school. A separate point: a tutoring business with premises and staff is a different legal animal from an individual tutor and requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit, so a centre and a person are not governed by the same rule.

sections.heading: Why the search says home tutor, and what we actually deliver
paragraphs: Home tuition is the arrangement most families here know, and the preference for it is practical rather than nostalgic. A person who comes to the building supervises attention in a way a screen cannot, needs no device, and solves the problem of three children and one laptop by bringing their own presence instead. For a parent who is still at work at four o'clock, somebody physically in the room is a form of supervision as well as of teaching. Those are real arguments.

The market answer is also practical. Published in-home rates in Dubai run roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour, with the tutor's travel inside the figure, against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online and AED 200 to 450 for a specialist. For a fixed monthly budget, the travel component is the first thing worth removing, because it buys nothing. The pool of people willing to drive into Al Quoz on a weekday evening also skews towards generalists, which matters most for an examined subject where the board and tier have to match exactly.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Home visits are a service we provide only in India, and nobody will be sent to an Al Khail Gate address. Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video, with screen sharing for marked work and a document camera for written working. For the supervision problem specifically, the answer is not presence but structure: the session sets a short daily task and checks the previous one, so the paid hour creates accountability on five days rather than one. That costs nothing extra and does not depend on anyone being home.

sections.heading: Starting from Al Khail Gate, with costs and limits stated plainly
paragraphs: Begin with three facts and one number. The school, the board and syllabus code, the tier or level, and the monthly figure you are actually working to. Saying the budget out loud at the start is not awkward; it is the fastest way to a sensible arrangement, because it determines the format before the tutor. If the honest answer is that the figure supports a short pre-series block rather than a year of weekly sessions, we would rather plan that properly than sell a year that gets cancelled in month three.

Before paying anyone, including us, ask the head of year what free support the school already runs. Year 11 clinics, subject surgeries and maths drop-ins exist in many schools reachable from Al Quoz, cost nothing, and are staffed by the teacher who will mark the work. They are under-used because they are not advertised. Any tutoring plan that has not first established what is available at no cost is spending money unnecessarily, and we will say so rather than let it pass.

The limits: coverage is uneven in narrow Higher Level subjects, in less common languages and in uncommon Pearson Edexcel options, and the honest answer is a different hour with the right specialist, an adjacent level or board where the overlap is genuine, or a plain statement that we cannot cover it. On assessed work, an internal assessment or Extended Essay must be the student's own work, authenticated by the school; a tutor teaches the criteria, reads the student's draft and comments on it, and authors nothing. We do not supply board syllabus documents, past papers or mark schemes, because those belong to the boards. Data collected through this site is handled under UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021.

process.title: Say the monthly figure first
process.description: The budget determines the format before it determines the tutor, so stating it at the start saves everybody time. A figure that supports one weekly hour in one subject for a term is a workable plan. A figure spread across four subjects is not, and we would rather say that in the first message than discover it when the arrangement is abandoned.

process.title: Ask the school what it already provides free
process.description: Year 11 clinics, subject surgeries and drop-in sessions exist in many schools in this corridor, cost nothing and are run by the teacher who marks the work. They are under-used because nobody advertises them. Establish what is available at no cost before paying for anything, including this.

process.title: Send the board, the code and the tier
process.description: Cambridge Core and Extended, and Pearson Edexcel Foundation and Higher, are different papers with different grade ceilings. The code and tier on the school's entry confirmation remove the guesswork and make sure no paid hour is spent teaching content the student will not be examined on.

process.title: Measure the bus, then set one hour and keep it
process.description: Record for two weeks the time your child is actually at a desk, fed, rather than the time the bus arrived. Set the session fifteen minutes later and hold that hour every week. A slot attended thirty-six times over a year is worth considerably more than a better slot attended twenty-four.

process.title: Review at the end of the term and decide
process.description: One term is enough to see whether the arrangement is working, measured against the school's own report rather than against our session notes. At that point there is a decision rather than a drift: continue, change subject, change tutor, or stop because the job is done. Rolling arrangements nobody reviews are how a fixed budget quietly disappears.

whyPoints.title: The budget is treated as the design constraint
whyPoints.description: This page publishes what each monthly AED figure buys, with sources, because a household working to a fixed number deserves that before a sales conversation. Where the honest answer is a short pre-series block rather than a year of weekly lessons, that is what gets planned.
