For a household where nobody is home at four, that structure does more than physical presence would and costs nothing extra.

whyPoints.title: Board and tier matched exactly
whyPoints.description: Cambridge Core, Cambridge Extended, Pearson Edexcel Foundation and Pearson Edexcel Higher are different examinations. A tutor teaching the wrong one is a wasted hour, which for a fixed budget is the most expensive mistake available. We ask for the code and tier before any teaching begins.

whyPoints.title: Free options named before paid ones
whyPoints.description: School clinics and subject surgeries are frequently the best value available in this corridor and are routinely overlooked. We will tell you to ask about them first. A provider that does not mention the free option is not giving you the full picture of your choices.

whyPoints.title: The permit rules set out so you can check
whyPoints.description: The MoHRE private tuition permit is free and valid for two years, so its absence is a signal rather than a hardship. This page sets out who can hold one and how it is applied for, including the condition about a tutor's own school's students, so a parent can verify rather than take a claim on trust.

faqs.question: When can a tutoring session start in an Al Khail Gate household?
faqs.answer: For a secondary student, usually between a quarter to five and half past five, depending on the school cluster. There is no large school inside the community, so children are collected early and returned late on routes that serve several Al Quoz stops before continuing to Al Barsha, Motor City or towards the creek. Primary children are often home by half past two or three, which is what makes back-to-back slots possible on one device. Measure your own figure for two weeks: the time the child is at a desk and fed, not the time the bus arrived.

faqs.question: How do we manage tutoring for three children in one apartment?
faqs.answer: Sequentially rather than simultaneously, which the bus timetable already helps with because children arrive home at different times. The pattern that works is the primary child in the earlier slot and the secondary child later, on the same device, with the table handed over cleanly. Where two children are in examined years, the one sitting a series this year takes the better hour by default. Where the budget supports only one, choose on where marks are most recoverable rather than on who asks loudest.

faqs.question: What can we get for AED 500 a month?
faqs.answer: Roughly four sessions with a generalist tutor, or two with a qualified subject tutor, based on published Dubai market bands surveyed in October 2026. At that level the highest-return use is not general homework help: it is exam technique in one examined subject, with work marked against the published mark scheme. Published monthly estimates for a single weekly hour run roughly AED 240 to 600 at the budget end. Before spending it, ask the school what free clinics or subject surgeries exist, because in many schools that support costs nothing.

faqs.question: Is a group class at a centre better value than one hour one-to-one?
faqs.answer: It depends on what is wrong. If your child has missed content and knows which content, a group class is good value, because the teaching is identical whether four people hear it or one, and centre group rates run from roughly AED 45 to 120 an hour per student. If your child understands the content and keeps losing marks, a group is poor value, because the fix is specific to them. Ask one question before enrolling: are all the students in this group entered for the same board and the same tier?

faqs.question: My child was put on Core. Can that be changed?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and only within the board's entry deadlines, which sit months before the papers. Cambridge Core is capped at grade C while Extended runs A* to E, so the placement sets a ceiling. Schools place on evidence and are usually right, but placements are made across a cohort, sometimes on one set of Year 9 results. Ask for the evidence, then bring your own: a set of Extended past paper questions attempted under timed conditions and marked honestly. Raise it in the autumn term, because a January request for a February series is generally too late.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Pearson Edexcel Foundation and Higher?
faqs.answer: Grade range and paper content. Foundation caps at grade 5 and Higher reaches grade 9 with a 3 allowed, and the two tiers sit different papers, though a calculator is permitted in both. A student capable of a 4 or better belongs on Higher; a student for whom a 4 or 5 would be a strong result is often better served by Foundation, where the questions are accessible and the marks are there to be collected. Getting it wrong in either direction costs grades, which is why the decision deserves evidence rather than assumption.

faqs.question: Does a tutor in Dubai need a licence, and does it cost them money?
faqs.answer: A permit is required and it is free. Private tutoring in the UAE operates under a work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years. Eligibility covers registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18, and applications go through MoHRE's service, Issuance of a New Work Permit for Private Tutor Licensing, with a stated two working day completion time. Because there is no fee, the absence of a permit has no cost excuse behind it.

faqs.question: A teacher at my child's school has offered paid lessons. Should we accept?
faqs.answer: Treat that as a question for the school before it is a question about money. The MoHRE permit carries a code of conduct which press reporting indicates bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school, and in Abu Dhabi ADEK has set professional-ethics rules prohibiting private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school. Those positions are press-reported rather than quoted here from current policy documents, so verify directly with the school. A tutor with no connection to the school avoids the conflict entirely.

faqs.question: Nobody is home between four and six. Does that make tutoring pointless?
faqs.answer: No, but it changes what the paid hour should be used for. Those unsupervised hours shape a grade more than one weekly session does, so the session's most valuable output is a short daily task that gets checked the following week. Thirty to forty minutes a day, the same task type each time so no decision is needed, left as a written list rather than sent as a message. The accountability runs to a fixed checkpoint rather than to whoever is in the room, which is why it works without a parent being present.

faqs.question: Which subject should we spend the money on first?
faqs.answer: The one where marks are most recoverable, not the one with the worst grade. A student sitting two grades below their potential in mathematics is a better investment than one who was never going to pass a language they started late. Across the sciences, command-term work gives the broadest return for a single weekly hour, because a student who answers every question as describe caps well below their understanding in three subjects at once. For a Diploma student, an internal assessment worth 20% of a grade usually outranks everything else.

faqs.question: Can a tutor come to our building in Al Khail Gate?
faqs.answer: Not through us. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India, and nobody will be sent to an Al Khail Gate address. Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. Published in-home rates in Dubai run roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel inside the fee, against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online. For a fixed monthly budget, removing the travel component is the first saving available, and it costs nothing in teaching quality.

faqs.question: What equipment do we need for online lessons?
faqs.answer: Three things, bought once, together costing less than a single hour of tutoring. Over-ear headphones with a boom microphone so a student can be heard without raising their voice over a shared living space. A wired connection or the 5 GHz band rather than whatever the laptop joins by default, because a dropped connection costs more than a slow processor. And an old phone propped as a document camera, so the tutor sees the written working rather than the student's face, which changes mathematics and science lessons more than any other single item.

faqs.question: Does the price include VAT, and what if we stop after one lesson?
faqs.answer: Ask both questions of any provider and get the answers in writing before paying, including from us. Ask whether the figure quoted is per hour or per session and how long a session is, because an hour and a ninety-minute session are frequently quoted at the same number. Ask whether VAT is included and whether it will appear on the invoice. And ask what happens to a prepaid balance if you stop after one lesson. A provider who will not put those three answers in writing is telling you something useful.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting tutoring if the exams are only weeks away?
faqs.answer: Often yes, if the content is broadly in place and marks are being lost in execution, because timed papers marked against the published mark scheme move grades faster than anything else at that stage. A short, countable block of sessions built entirely on past papers and an error log the student keeps is the right shape, and it should have a stated end date rather than rolling on. If most of a specification was never taught, the honest answer is triage: pick the subjects where the return is highest and accept that not everything can be rescued.

If the honest answer is a short block before the series rather than a year of lessons, that is what we will propose.

intro.heading: The gap between the lesson and the paper
paragraphs: Al Khawaneej is villa Dubai at the edge of the city, past Mirdif and towards the desert boundary, with farms, the Last Exit and a sense of being outside the dense emirate rather than in it. It is also a community without a private secondary school inside it. Children travel, usually to Mirdif, Al Warqa or Al Qusais, and the day accordingly ends with a bus route or a drive rather than a walk.

That geography has a specific academic consequence, and it is not the one families expect. The issue is not the loss of time, though that is real. It is that a student out here spends a smaller proportion of their working week in the presence of a teacher and a larger proportion of it alone at a desk. Whatever a school covers in a lesson, the conversion from covered to understood happens later, somewhere with no teacher in the room.

A school lesson of forty minutes, across a year, is enough to deliver a syllabus. It is not enough to make a student fluent in it. Teachers know this and plan around it: the lesson introduces, models, checks, and sets practice, and the practice is where the learning finishes. The students who do well are not the ones who listened hardest. They are the ones whose independent hour was spent doing something that actually worked.

Most independent hours are not spent doing something that works. They are spent reading notes, highlighting, copying out definitions and watching videos, all of which feel productive and almost none of which produce recall under pressure. This is a well-known pattern among teachers and almost never discussed with parents, which is why so many families describe a child who "works hard and still gets a six".

There is a second reason the independent hours matter more out here. A student who leaves on a bus a few minutes after the bell cannot attend a lunchtime clinic, cannot stay for a departmental catch-up and cannot ask the question that occurred to them in the last ten minutes of a lesson. Whatever free support the school runs, a travelling student reaches less of it, and the questions pile up until somebody is available. Teaching a student to unstick themselves is therefore worth more here than a perfectly explained topic.

So this page is about the independent half of the week. What a syllabus actually demands against the weeks available. Why the common revision methods fail. How to mark your own script against the official scheme, which is the single most useful habit available to a sixteen-year-old. What the market charges for help that closes a gap rather than restating a lesson. And what a tutor may and may not do with work that has to be the student's own.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every Al Khawaneej lesson is one-to-one over live video, which matters more here than in most districts, because nobody has to add a thirty-minute drive in each direction to a week that already loses an hour a day to the road.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Terminal papers at sixteen on one of two boards, Cambridge in June and November series with Core and Extended tiering on many codes, Pearson Edexcel in May/June and November on a 9-1 scale. Eight or nine subjects run in parallel, so the independent work is divided across more fronts than at any other stage of school.
programmes.countryNote: An Al Khawaneej Year 11 student is managing nine subjects' independent work with less time at a desk than a student living next to their school. Prioritising matters more here, which is why we start by asking which two subjects are closest to a boundary rather than attempting all nine.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. The Diploma is explicitly designed around independent work: the internally assessed components, the essay and the reflective elements all assume sustained effort outside lessons, against school deadlines set well before any board date.
programmes.countryNote: For students travelling in from the eastern edge, the Diploma's independent load is the binding constraint rather than the content. The practical intervention is usually structural: deciding what gets done on which day, and making the student own that schedule rather than reacting to deadlines.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four lettered criteria with task-specific descriptors rather than percentages. Because assessment is continuous, independent work is assessed work, and a student who does not understand what a criterion rewards loses marks steadily rather than in one visible event.
programmes.countryNote: The most useful thing a Middle Years student out here can learn is to read a task sheet against the criteria before starting. It takes fifteen minutes and it is the difference between a task that addresses what is being marked and one that addresses the topic.

dubai/al-khawaneej.subjectsIntro: Demand here concentrates on the subjects where independent practice is the whole mechanism of improvement, and where a student who cannot start a question alone loses the most.

subjects.name: Mathematics 0580 and 4MA1
subjects.levels: Cambridge IGCSE Extended and Pearson Edexcel
subjects.description: The clearest case of fluency built by practice rather than explanation. A student who understands every worked example and cannot begin an unseen question has a starting problem, not a knowledge problem, and that is fixed by attempting questions badly before attempting them well.

subjects.name: Chemistry 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and quantitative work. This is the subject where students most often stall at the first line of a calculation, and the fix is a decision procedure for starting rather than another explanation of the concept.

subjects.name: Physics 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Circuits, waves and the practical paper. Independent practice works well here because the question types repeat across series, so a student who has worked through enough of them recognises the structure before reading the detail.

subjects.name: Biology 0610 and 4BI1
subjects.description: The subject most improvable by a student working alone, because the dominant loss is mark-scheme vocabulary and that responds to retrieval practice from a marked script. A good candidate for self-managed work while a tutor covers something harder.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Higher Level assumes algebraic automaticity that only accumulates through volume. Students arriving without Additional Mathematics usually need a short foundational block before the course's own problems become attemptable alone.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and calculator fluency, with marks lost on interpretation. Interpretation can be practised independently from a mark scheme, because the scheme states what the examiner wanted in words the student can learn to anticipate.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy is the most self-drillable skill in any humanities subject: axes, curves, labels, shifts, repeated until correct without reference. Higher Level adds quantitative questions and a policy paper that rewards precise named examples.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Two external papers and oral assessment. The independent work that pays is planning: writing essay plans against past questions rather than full essays, because a plan takes fifteen minutes and tests the same skill the examiner is marking.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case studies where students describe a tool instead of applying it. Independent practice means taking a real organisation and forcing the tool onto it, which can be done without a tutor once the habit is established.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Compulsory in every Dubai private school, taught in separate classes for Arab and non-Arab learners because the expectations and the language of instruction differ. Vocabulary retention depends on short daily work rather than a weekly session.

regions.name: Mirdif
regions.note: The nearest cluster with secondary options inside it, including IB continuum and British-curriculum schools. Students attending here have the shortest journey of anyone in this group.

regions.name: Al Mizhar
regions.note: Between Al Khawaneej and Mirdif, villa housing with the same school options and the same long bus routes. Timings here are close to identical to Al Khawaneej's.

regions.name: Al Warqa

regions.name: Al Khawaneej 2 and Al Aweer
regions.note: The furthest edge, where journeys are longest and the first workable weekday session is rarely before 5:00pm. Weekend mornings matter more here than anywhere in this group.

regions.name: Nad Al Hamar
regions.note: West towards Ras Al Khor with shorter runs into the Festival City schools. One of the easier catchments for an earlier weekday slot.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis

regions.name: Al Rashidiya

regions.name: Dubai International Academic City
regions.note: South-east, with university campuses and a few schools. Older students travelling here arrive late enough that timed paper work belongs on a weekend.

schoolClusters.city: What Al Khawaneej has, and what it does not
schoolClusters.note: The community contains early-years and primary provision and a Dubai Schools campus, but secondary students travel. That is the single fact around which an Al Khawaneej family's week is organised, and it is why the independent half of the week carries more weight here than in districts where the school is a few minutes away. Students we support attend schools in this group.

schoolClusters.city: The Al Warqa and Al Qusais secondary options
schoolClusters.note: The second direction, with the largest cohorts in the eastern half of Dubai and the longest bus routes serving them. Journeys from Al Khawaneej into this cluster can approach an hour, which is why so much of the advice on this page concerns what happens at a desk rather than in a classroom.

sections.heading: No secondary school inside the community, and what that decides
paragraphs: Al Khawaneej families make one structural choice that families in Mirdif or Oud Metha do not have to make: which direction to travel for school. Everything else follows from it. The bus route, the arrival time, the activity options, which other families your children know, and how much of the week is spent at a desk rather than in a classroom.

The effect on tutoring is not that there is less time, although there is. It is that the balance shifts. A student living beside their school can be in a teacher's presence for a lunchtime clinic, an after-school catch-up, a quick question at the end of a lesson. A student on a bus leaving at 2:45pm cannot attend the clinic, cannot stay for the catch-up, and asks the question next week or not at all.

This is worth knowing because it changes what a family should buy. For a student with easy access to their teachers, paid tutoring frequently duplicates free support. For an Al Khawaneej student, the free support exists but is physically out of reach, and the paid hour is genuinely filling a gap rather than restating something available at lunchtime. That is one of the few cases where the economics clearly favour tutoring.

The second thing it changes is what the session should contain. If a student cannot ask their teacher a question for a week, the most valuable thing a tutor can do is make them capable of unsticking themselves: a procedure for starting a question, a habit of checking against a mark scheme, a way of recording what they did not understand so it survives until somebody can address it. Those transfer across subjects and across years, and they matter more out here than a perfectly explained topic.
bullets: The school direction decides the whole shape of the week
Lunchtime clinics are physically out of reach on a bus route
The paid hour fills a real gap rather than duplicating one
Teach unsticking, not just the topic

sections.heading: The arithmetic of a syllabus against the weeks available
paragraphs: Parents are often surprised at how thin the teaching time for an examined subject actually is when it is written out. A subject taught in four or five lessons a week, across the teaching weeks that remain once holidays, mock weeks, inspection days and examination leave are removed, has a finite and not especially generous allocation. The syllabus has to fit inside that, and something always gets compressed.

What gets compressed is predictable. Content is delivered because it has to be; a teacher cannot leave a topic untaught. Practice volume is what gives, along with the slower, less efficient activities that build fluency: attempting questions badly, getting stuck, trying again. Those are exactly the activities that a class of thirty cannot afford and an individual student can.

The table sets this out by subject type rather than by specific code, because the exact lesson allocation differs between schools and your child's timetable is the authoritative version. Ask the school how many lessons a week the subject gets and how many teaching weeks remain before the final paper. The two numbers together explain most of what a parent needs to know about where the pressure will appear.

The practical conclusion is that independent practice is not a supplement to the course. It is a structural component of it, assumed by the design, and in a household where the student spends an hour a day travelling it is the component most at risk. A tutoring plan that adds more explanation to a student who already has enough explanation is solving the wrong half of the problem.

sections.heading: Why re-reading notes does nothing, and what replaces it
paragraphs: The commonest independent study method among students at this level is also close to the least effective. Reading notes, highlighting, copying out definitions and watching explanation videos all share one property: the information is in front of the student while they work. That makes the work feel easy and fluent, and fluency while looking at the answer is not evidence of anything.

What produces recall under examination conditions is retrieval: attempting to produce the information or the method without looking, discovering what is missing, and then correcting it. It is uncomfortable, it feels less productive, and it is the thing that works. A student who closes the book and writes down everything they can remember about a topic, then checks, has learned more in fifteen minutes than in an hour of re-reading.

The second component is spacing. Returning to a topic after a gap, when some of it has decayed, is harder and more productive than revisiting it immediately. This is why a tutoring session on consecutive days is worth less than two sessions separated by three days, and why a final-week revision cram produces a short-lived performance rather than a durable one.

The third is practice under the real constraint. A student who can do a question with unlimited time, their notes open and no pressure has not demonstrated what the examination measures. Working from a past paper, closed book, against the clock, is the only practice that tests the actual skill. Everything else is preparation for that. A tutor who does not eventually put the student into those conditions is leaving the last and most important step undone.
bullets: Fluency while looking at the answer is not evidence of learning
Retrieval beats re-reading, and feels worse while doing it

sections.heading: Marking your own script against the scheme, properly
paragraphs: If a student out here learns one thing from a tutor, it should be how to mark their own work against the official mark scheme. It is the skill that converts every future past paper into feedback without needing anybody present, which matters most for a student who cannot reach a teacher between Monday and the following Monday.

Almost nobody does it properly without being taught. Students read the mark scheme, see that their answer is roughly similar, and award themselves the mark. That is not marking; it is confirmation. Real marking is adversarial: the student has to look for the reason an examiner would refuse the mark, which is usually a missing term, an unstated unit, an unshown step or a point the scheme requires and the answer only implies.

The procedure is mechanical and takes a few sessions to establish. Sit the question closed book and timed. Put the answer aside. Open the scheme and list what it requires, point by point, before looking at your own work. Then mark against that list and write the mark you have earned rather than the mark you deserved. Then write one sentence saying what the loss had in common across the paper, because the pattern is more useful than any individual question.

The last step is the one that produces grade movement. A student who notices that eleven of their fifteen lost marks across a paper came from not stating units, or from answering around the command verb, has found something they can fix in an afternoon. A student with a list of fifteen unrelated errors has found work with no end to it. The pattern is where the leverage is, and seeing it is a learned skill rather than an obvious one.

sections.heading: What the market charges for help that closes a gap
paragraphs: Most tutoring pages in this market publish no price, and two of the ones that do quote US dollars rather than dirhams. The figures below are market rates attributed to the providers that published them, presented as the market rather than as an IB Gram price list. They are organised here by what the money is actually buying, because that is the question a family out here should be asking.

Budget online tutoring from university students or generalists is advertised from roughly AED 45 to AED 65 an hour, with one platform quoting from about AED 33. That band is well suited to supervision of independent practice: keeping a student working, checking answers, maintaining accountability. Those are real services and they are what many students actually need.

Qualified subject tutors working online sit between about AED 150 and AED 300, with one agency publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. That band buys board-specific technique: command verbs, mark-scheme reading, method precision. Specialist IB, IGCSE and A Level tutors are quoted at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with one agency at AED 270 and one premium provider at AED 650, and that band exists for Higher Level depth and criterion-level coursework feedback.

In-home visits run roughly AED 180 to AED 350 on one published index and AED 200 to AED 500 among independent tutors, with travel inside the rate. For Al Khawaneej specifically, expect the upper end: the drive out here in the late afternoon is long. Monthly packages in circulation include about AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits.

sections.heading: An in-home tutor in Al Khawaneej against one-to-one online
paragraphs: The in-home option exists in this market and the comparison should be honest. An adult at the table sees written working without asking, can take a pen to a page, and provides a presence some younger students respond to better than a screen. For families where that matters most, other providers will arrange it and it may be the right call.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. Out at the eastern edge there is a particular reason this holds up. The journey here is long enough that the pool of tutors willing to make it weekly is small, local and not selected for subject expertise. For a family whose problem is technique on a specific board's papers, choosing from that pool means choosing on geography when the whole point is to choose on marking experience.

There is also a direct trade-off in hours. A tutor driving out here loses most of an hour in each direction, which is priced into the rate whether or not it appears as a line item. The same money spent online buys either more sessions or a better-matched specialist. For a student whose problem is that they need more practice with feedback, more sessions is often the better purchase.

What we lose, stated plainly: unprompted sight of the page, which we replace with a phone or tablet camera angled over the working and a tutor who insists on seeing the method rather than hearing the answer. And the social presence of an adult, which genuinely matters more for younger children than for a Year 11 student working on past papers.

sections.heading: Past papers and board material: what you may legitimately use
paragraphs: A student relying on independent practice needs practice material, and this is where families get into trouble without intending to. The internet is full of sites offering past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents and grade-boundary tables, some legitimate and many not. Using material from an unauthorised source is a copyright problem, and for unreleased material it can become a malpractice exposure for the student.

The legitimate routes are straightforward. The boards themselves publish specimen and past materials through their own channels and through the school's examinations officer. Schools hold licences and access that individual families do not, which is why the right first request is to the subject teacher or the examinations officer rather than to a search engine. Where a school has issued a paper, using it is unambiguous.

What we will not do is send out board material. Syllabuses, past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables and subject guides belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB. We reference them, name the official source, and work with what the school has legitimately issued. A tutoring provider advertising a downloadable library of board documents has told you how it treats rules, which is worth noticing before a deadline rather than after one.

One further caution specific to timetables. Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for the zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong zone timetable. A family revising from a timetable found online rather than from the school's own copy is carrying a real and avoidable risk.

sections.heading: Feedback on work that has to be the student's own
paragraphs: Everything on this page points towards the student doing more, not less, which makes the academic-honesty boundary particularly relevant here rather than a formality at the end. One provider found in this search sells completed Internal Assessments outright. Under board malpractice rules the consequence falls on the candidate who declared the work as their own, and no refund exists for a withdrawn qualification.

The legitimate boundary is specific. A tutor may teach the content the assessment rests on, explain each criterion and what its marks reward, say whether a research question is viable before weeks are spent on it, warn that a method will not generate usable data, read a draft and name the criterion that is under-served, and ask the questions that make a student see their own gap. A tutor may not supply text, rewrite sections, generate data, choose the question, or edit a draft into a finished state.

For a student who has learned to mark their own work, there is a useful equivalence here. Marking your own script and judging your own draft against a criterion are the same skill applied to different material. A tutor who teaches that is making the student less dependent, which is the opposite of what the essay mills sell and better value over two years.

The test a student can apply alone, at eleven at night with a deadline the next morning: if the help would still work with you absent from the room, it is substitution rather than teaching. Everything legitimate requires the student to be the one thinking.

sections.heading: A first month that produces evidence
paragraphs: The first month should end with something a parent can look at, not an impression. We structure it that way deliberately, because an arrangement judged on feelings continues indefinitely and an arrangement judged on evidence either improves or stops.

Week one is a diagnostic. Send a recent marked script, the board and syllabus code, and the bus arrival time. The tutor works through the script with your child and writes a short note naming the actual gap, which is frequently not the one the school report named, and stating the order to address it.

Weeks two and three teach the two highest-leverage habits for an independent learner: a procedure for starting an unseen question, and marking against the scheme. Both are generic, both transfer to every subject, and both produce visible artefacts, a marked script with the student's own annotations on it, that a parent can read without understanding the subject.

Week four is a timed paper on a weekend morning, marked by the student and then reviewed. At the end of it there is a number, a pattern statement naming the dominant loss, and a specific plan for the next six weeks. If that package does not exist at the end of the first month, the arrangement has not started properly and we would rather say so than let it continue on goodwill.

The reason for insisting on artefacts rather than reports is that a parent who does not teach the subject cannot evaluate a verbal summary. A marked script with the student's own annotations on it can be read by anybody: either the annotations identify real refusals of marks, or they do not. A timed paper with a date on it can be compared with the next one. A sentence naming the dominant loss can be checked against the following month's script to see whether that loss has gone. None of that requires subject knowledge, which is exactly why we produce it.
bullets: Week one: diagnostic from a marked script, written note
Weeks two and three: starting procedure and self-marking

process.title: Teach self-marking against the scheme

whyPoints.description: A student travelling in from the eastern edge spends more of their working week alone at a desk and less of it near a teacher. That is where the grade is decided, and it is what the sessions are designed to improve.

whyPoints.title: Self-marking is taught explicitly
whyPoints.description: Reading a mark scheme and awarding yourself the mark is confirmation, not marking. We teach the adversarial version, where the student looks for why the examiner would refuse the mark, until their marking agrees with ours.

whyPoints.title: Retrieval and spacing over re-reading
whyPoints.description: Highlighting and re-reading feel productive and do not produce recall under pressure. We set closed-book retrieval, space the return to a topic, and put the student into timed conditions, which is the only practice that tests the real skill.

whyPoints.title: Board material handled properly
whyPoints.description: Past papers, schemes, syllabuses and boundary tables belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB. We reference and explain them and work from what your school issued, including always using the school's own zone timetable.

whyPoints.title: Rates matched to the actual problem
whyPoints.description: Every dirham figure here belongs to the provider that published it, and we set the bands against the problem each one solves. If your problem is that the work is not being done, the cheapest band is the honest recommendation.

whyPoints.description: A diagnostic note, a self-marked script, a timed paper with a real mark, and a named pattern of loss. An arrangement judged on artefacts either improves or stops, which is better for a family than one judged on goodwill.

faqs.question: My child works hard and the grade will not move. What is going wrong in Al Khawaneej households?
faqs.answer: Usually the method rather than the effort. Reading notes, highlighting, copying definitions and watching explanation videos all keep the information in front of the student while they work, which makes it feel fluent and produces little recall under pressure. What works is retrieval: closing the book, producing the method or the content from memory, finding what is missing and correcting it. It feels less productive and does considerably more. A student travelling in from the eastern edge has fewer supervised hours, so method matters more here.

faqs.question: How does a student learn to mark their own past paper properly?
faqs.answer: By being taught the adversarial version, which takes three or four sessions. Sit the paper closed book and timed, then put the script away before opening the scheme. Write out what the scheme requires point by point first, so you cannot read it to fit your own answer. Then mark looking for why an examiner would refuse each mark: a missing unit, an unstated term, an unshown step. Record the mark earned, not deserved, and write one sentence on what the losses had in common.

faqs.question: Does living in Al Khawaneej actually affect my child's results?
faqs.answer: Indirectly, and it is worth understanding. There is no private secondary school inside the community, so students travel and the bus leaves soon after the bell. That puts lunchtime clinics, after-school catch-up and the quick question at the end of a lesson physically out of reach. The result is a larger share of the working week spent alone at a desk. It also means paid tutoring here is genuinely filling a gap rather than duplicating free support that is a short walk away.

faqs.question: Why is my child able to follow the lesson but unable to start a question at home?
faqs.answer: Because following and starting are different skills, and only one of them is practised in a lesson. Watching a worked example is comprehension; facing a blank unseen question requires a decision procedure, choosing what kind of problem this is and what the first line should be. That procedure can be taught directly and generically, and it is usually the highest-value thing a tutor does in the first month. More explanation of the concept will not fix it, because the concept was never the problem.

faqs.question: How much teaching time does an IGCSE subject actually get?
faqs.answer: Less than parents expect once the calendar is written out. A subject taught in three to five lessons a week, across the teaching weeks remaining after holidays, mock weeks and examination leave, has a finite allocation that the whole syllabus must fit inside. Content gets delivered because it must be; practice volume and the slower fluency-building activities are what give way. Ask the school how many lessons a week the subject gets and how many teaching weeks remain. Those two numbers explain most of the pressure.

faqs.question: Where should we get past papers and mark schemes from?
faqs.answer: From the school. The examinations officer and the subject teacher have access and licences that individual families do not, and material issued by the school is unambiguous. Boards also publish specimen and sample assessment material through their own sites, which is the right place to look for public versions. We reference and explain these documents and work from the copy your school issued; we do not send out board material, because past papers, schemes, syllabuses and boundary tables are the boards' copyright.

faqs.question: Why does the Cambridge exam timetable zone matter?
faqs.answer: Because using the wrong version can cost a paper. Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for the zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong zone timetable. A family revising from a timetable found through a search engine rather than from the school's own issued copy is carrying an avoidable risk, and the fix takes one email to the examinations officer.

faqs.question: Is spaced revision really better than revising a topic until it is finished?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it feels worse, which is why most students do the opposite. Returning to a topic after a gap, when part of it has decayed, forces reconstruction rather than recognition, and reconstruction is what builds durable recall. Revisiting immediately feels smooth and produces a short-lived performance. In practice this means two tutoring sessions separated by three days outperform two on consecutive days, and a final-week cram produces something that holds for days rather than weeks.

faqs.question: What does the budget end of the tutoring market actually do well?
faqs.answer: Supervision of independent practice, which is exactly what a large share of students need. Published figures put budget online tutoring from university students or generalists at roughly AED 45 to AED 65 an hour, with one platform quoting from about AED 33. That band keeps a student working, checks answers and maintains accountability. What it does not reliably provide is board-specific technique or criterion-level coursework feedback, which is what the AED 150 to AED 300 band and above exists for.

faqs.question: Do tutors travel out to Al Khawaneej for home lessons?
faqs.answer: Some providers arrange it; we do not. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE, and home visits are a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. Out here the journey is long enough that the pool of tutors willing to make it weekly is small and local rather than selected for subject depth, and the drive is priced into the rate whether or not it appears as a line. The same money online buys more sessions or a better match.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with an Internal Assessment if the work must be my child's own?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a specific boundary. A tutor may teach the underlying content, explain each criterion and what its marks reward, say whether a research question is viable before weeks are spent on it, warn that a method will not produce usable data, read a draft and name the criterion that is weak, and ask the questions that make a student find their own gap. A tutor may not supply text, rewrite sections, generate data, pick the question or edit a draft into a finished state.

faqs.question: How do we judge whether the first month of tutoring has worked?
faqs.answer: By what exists at the end of it rather than by how the sessions felt. Week one should produce a written diagnostic note from a marked script. Weeks two and three should produce artefacts you can see: a script with your child's own marking annotations on it, and evidence that they can start an unseen question. Week four should produce a full timed paper with a real mark and one sentence naming the dominant pattern of loss. If that package does not exist, the arrangement has not started properly.

faqs.question: Should we tutor the weakest subject or the one closest to a grade boundary?
faqs.answer: The one closest to a boundary, almost always. A grade two marks short can often be moved in a term with technique work alone, because the knowledge is already there and the loss is procedural. A subject three grades adrift needs a structural rebuild across two terms and will not respond to the same intervention. Ask the school which is which, send the marked script, and sequence subjects across terms rather than running several in parallel on an evening that already loses an hour to the road.

faqs.question: What is the single most useful habit a student out here can build?
faqs.answer: Marking their own work against the official scheme, honestly. It converts every past paper the school issues into feedback without needing anyone present, which matters most for a student who cannot reach a teacher between one Monday and the next. It also transfers directly to coursework, where judging your own draft against a criterion is the same skill applied to different material. A student who can do both is less dependent on tutoring, which is the point.

dubai/al-khawaneej.closingHeading: The independent hour is where the grade is decided
dubai/al-khawaneej.closingBody: Al Khawaneej students spend more of the week alone at a desk than students who live beside their school, and that is the half of the week worth working on. Teach a procedure for starting an unseen question, teach honest marking against the official scheme, set closed-book retrieval rather than re-reading, space the return to a topic, and put a full timed paper on a weekend morning where there is no journey behind it. Then send a recent marked script, the syllabus code and the bus arrival time, and the first month will end with a mark, a named pattern of loss and a plan rather than an impression. Every lesson is one-to-one over live video.

intro.heading: The real Deira timetable, not the one on the prospectus
paragraphs: Al Mamzar sits on the coast at the northern edge of Deira, next to Al Nahda and close to the Sharjah boundary, with the beach park on one side and some of Dubai's longest-established private schools within a few minutes. The families here are different from those in the newer western communities: more of them are long-settled, a higher proportion are Arabic-speaking households, and more of their children have been at the same school since kindergarten.

That produces a specific academic shape. The international curriculum, whether IB or IGCSE, is not the whole of the week. Every private school in Dubai teaches Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies regardless of the curriculum it is licensed for, and KHDA's mandatory subject guidelines required implementation by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. For an Arab student the Arabic and Islamic Education load is substantial and taught in Standard Arabic.

Tutoring pages for Dubai almost never mention any of this. Search for IB or IGCSE support and you will find six subjects, three Higher Levels and an exam calendar, as though the student had nothing else on the timetable. Parents in Deira know better, because they see the homework. A Diploma student here is not managing six subjects plus a core; they are managing six subjects plus a core plus three further assessed subjects with their own tasks and their own reporting.

The practical consequence is a scheduling problem dressed up as an ability problem. A capable student with a full week does the work that is due tomorrow and defers the work that compounds, which means the Arabic vocabulary load slips, or the cumulative science revision slips, and by the mock it is visible. The intervention that helps is not another subject tutor added on top; it is an honest look at where the hours are going and which of them are producing nothing.

This page covers what the mandatory subjects actually require, the real difference between Arabic as a first language and as an additional language, the KHDA rules that govern how both are taught and what material may be used, where the two loads collide across the school year, and why Arabic and Islamic education do not count towards the equivalency total despite being compulsory. Lessons are delivered online, one to one, over live video, and IB Gram does not make home visits in Dubai, which is a service offered only in India. Every KHDA rule quoted below is taken from the authority's own published mandatory-subject guidelines, and every AED figure is a market rate attributed to the provider that published it in October 2026 rather than a price of ours.

dubai/al-mamzar.programmesIntro: Each programme interacts differently with the mandatory subject load, and that interaction is the thing a Deira family actually needs described. The notes below set out each one against the full week rather than against its own subject list.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, marked out of 8 and converted to a 1-7 grade. The MYP already includes language acquisition and individuals and societies, so for a Dubai student the mandatory subjects either map onto those groups or sit beside them. Which of the two it is varies by school and changes the weekly load considerably.
programmes.countryNote: Ask your Deira school directly how Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are timetabled against the MYP groups, and how each is reported. Two schools a few minutes apart in Al Mamzar and Al Qusais can handle this differently, and the difference shows up as hours in the week rather than as a line on a report.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Arabic can sit inside the Diploma as Language A or Language B, which resolves part of the load, but Islamic Education and Social Studies remain separate requirements with their own lessons and assessments on top of a programme that is already full.
programmes.countryNote: For an Arabic-speaking Diploma student in Deira, taking Arabic A rather than Arabic B is often the single most effective structural decision available, because it folds a compulsory subject into the Diploma's own six. Whether the school offers it, and at what level, is the question to ask in Diploma Year 1.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Eight or nine subjects sat as terminal papers, with coursework in several. Arabic is available as an IGCSE subject in both first-language and foreign-language forms, which lets some of the mandatory requirement be examined rather than simply taught. Islamic Education and Social Studies still sit outside the examined set.
programmes.countryNote: The composition of the option block matters twice over for a Deira family. It decides which subjects are examined, and it decides which five count towards the Ministry's equivalency requirement, since Arabic and Islamic education are excluded from that count. Both decisions are taken in Year 9.

dubai/al-mamzar.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Al Mamzar and wider Deira families ask about most, including the ones almost no tutoring platform lists. Each note names the specific demand rather than describing the syllabus.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: A full Diploma language and literature course taught in Standard Arabic, with unseen textual analysis and an individual oral. Strong colloquial speakers routinely under-score because the course assesses literary analysis in Standard Arabic, which is a different competence from fluency at home.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: The acquisition route, assessed on productive and receptive skills against defined themes. The common problem is placement: a student with household Arabic placed in Arabic B can find the course easy and limited, while one placed in Arabic A can find the literary analysis beyond them.

subjects.name: IGCSE Arabic
subjects.levels: Cambridge first language and foreign language routes
subjects.description: Two distinct qualifications with different demands. The first-language paper assumes Standard Arabic reading and writing at length; the foreign-language route assesses communication. Being entered for the wrong one is one of the most consequential and least discussed errors in Dubai schools.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with the graphic display calculator assumed throughout. Marks leak where an answer arrives with no stated assumption or a correlation with no comment on its limits. Check destination prerequisites before treating it as the lighter mathematics route.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The highest-volume Diploma science, and the one that suffers most in a full week because it rewards cumulative retrieval rather than last-minute reading. The scientific investigation is marked on research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation, so design work has to come before any data is collected.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study application under time pressure rather than recall, with a Higher Level extension adding extended response. Students lose marks by defining a term instead of applying it to the stimulus organisation, which is a technique fault and quick to correct.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy decides a substantial share of the marks and improves fast. The commentary portfolio is the slower piece: each commentary has to be anchored to a genuine published article inside a word limit, and a poor article choice caps the analysis before writing begins.

subjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics
subjects.description: The tier decision caps the grade in Cambridge subjects, and Extended candidates lose marks on method and on questions spanning two topics. In a full week this is the subject where deferred practice shows up first, because it is cumulative in a way the others are not.

subjects.name: IGCSE Physics
subjects.description: Electricity produces most of the enquiries from Deira families, and it is concentrated in a small number of recurring question types. That makes it an efficient target: a handful of sessions against mark schemes moves it more than a term of general revision.

subjects.name: IGCSE English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Distinct from first-language English and frequently the right entry for a student in an Arabic-speaking household. Marks sit in the reading comprehension technique and the structure of the writing tasks rather than in vocabulary breadth, which is why targeted practice outperforms general reading.

dubai/al-mamzar.regionsTitle: Al Mamzar and the Deira districts around it
dubai/al-mamzar.regionsIntro: This part of Dubai has a dense cluster of long-established schools and a different household profile from the newer western communities. These are the areas Al Mamzar families actually move through.

regions.name: Al Nahda
regions.note: Immediately inland and running towards the Sharjah boundary, with heavy cross-border traffic in both peaks. A family here plans the evening around the border movement rather than around school distance.

regions.name: Hor Al Anz
regions.note: South-west along the coast road, densely populated and feeding several of the same schools. Households here and in Al Mamzar ask for the same subjects, often in the same term, which is why slots in this cluster fill together.

regions.name: Al Qusais
regions.note: Inland, holding a large number of established private schools across British and Indian curricula. Many Al Mamzar children are enrolled here, which makes the inland run rather than the coast road the daily journey.

regions.name: Deira
regions.note: The wider district to the south, with the oldest private schools in the emirate inside it. Long-settled families and multi-generational enrolment are common, and so is a school choice made twenty years ago.

regions.name: Al Garhoud
regions.note: Across towards the creek and the airport, with British and IB schools that take a steady share of Al Mamzar students. The airport traffic is an extra variable in the afternoon that western Dubai does not have.

regions.name: Abu Hail and Al Muteena
regions.note: Directly inland from the coast strip, dense and well served by the metro Green Line. Students here often travel independently, which widens the range of workable session times.

regions.name: Al Twar
regions.note: Further inland, where several large school campuses sit. The journey is longer and more predictable than the coastal routes, which paradoxically makes a fixed slot easier to hold.

regions.name: Sharjah border communities
regions.note: A significant number of Deira school families live across the boundary and commute in. For them the afternoon return is the single largest constraint on when a session can start.

schoolClusters.city: Al Mamzar, Al Nahda and Al Qusais
schoolClusters.note: The closest cluster, mixing American, British, IB and Indian curricula within a short drive. These are long-established schools with large year groups, which is why individual feedback on written work is the scarcest resource in the week.

sections.heading: The timetable nobody counted: three mandatory subjects alongside the curriculum
paragraphs: Start with what the rules actually say, because most families have never been shown them. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA's requirements had to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. These are not enrichment lessons. They are assessed subjects with timetabled hours.

The organisational rules are specific and they explain why the experience differs so much between two children in the same class. KHDA requires separate classes by group: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. An Arab student and a non-Arab student in the same year group are therefore on genuinely different courses.

The language of instruction rules follow from that. KHDA requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students, and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies. For an Arab student in Al Mamzar, a meaningful part of the school week is taught and assessed in Standard Arabic.

Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and KHDA advises that any mandatory subject lesson should be at least 25 minutes. The table below sets out the structure. The point of it is not compliance detail; it is that a Diploma or IGCSE student here carries a genuinely larger week than the same student in a school outside the UAE, and any plan that ignores that is planning for somebody else's child.

sections.heading: What class covers in Arabic, and what the student has to do alone
paragraphs: Arabic is taught in a class, to a group, at the pace of the group, in a limited number of 40-minute units a week. What that can deliver is content: vocabulary introduced, grammatical structures explained, texts read together, tasks set and marked. What it cannot deliver for every student is individual correction of extended writing in Standard Arabic, which is the thing the assessment actually measures and the thing that improves slowly.

The gap shows up most starkly in Arabic-speaking households, which is counter-intuitive until it is explained. A child who speaks Arabic at home arrives with fluency in a dialect and confidence in conversation, and is then assessed on Standard Arabic reading, extended writing and literary analysis. Those are different competences. Parents hear the fluency and assume the subject is secure; the marked work says otherwise, and nobody has a clear explanation for the mismatch.

For non-Arab students in the additional-language stream, the gap is different and more familiar. Vocabulary and script are built by repetition, which almost nobody does voluntarily in a week already full of IGCSE or Diploma work. Twenty minutes a day of genuine retrieval practice outperforms an hour of passive reading, and it is the one subject where that small, daily, boring input is the whole of the answer.

The useful intervention in both streams is the same in shape: individual correction of the student's own extended writing, against the criteria the school is actually using. That is one-to-one work by definition, and it is what a class of twenty-eight structurally cannot provide. It is also why generic Arabic tutoring often disappoints, because it teaches a parallel course rather than fixing the written work the school will mark.

sections.heading: Arabic as a first language against Arabic as an additional language
paragraphs: This distinction decides more than families realise, and placement errors persist for years because nobody revisits them. The two streams have different content, different assessment and, under KHDA's rules, different classes. A student in the wrong one is either bored and unchallenged or permanently behind, and in both cases the grade on the report is not a useful signal about their Arabic.

The commonest error runs in one direction. A student from an Arabic-speaking household is placed in the first-language stream on the basis of the household language, and then struggles with Standard Arabic literary analysis and extended writing that the dialect does not prepare them for. Their spoken fluency masks the problem in class and the written assessment exposes it. The correct response is targeted work on Standard Arabic writing, not a move to the additional-language stream, which is usually neither available nor appropriate.

The reverse error is less common and more quietly damaging. A student with real Arabic competence placed in the additional-language stream coasts, builds nothing, and arrives at sixteen without the written Arabic they would need for Arabic A at Diploma level or a first-language IGCSE entry. For a Deira family that has deliberately chosen to keep Arabic strong, that is a significant loss and it is invisible on a report full of high grades.

The table below sets the two side by side. The practical action is to look at a piece of your child's marked extended writing in Arabic and ask the teacher which stream the task was set for and what the assessment criteria were. That conversation takes ten minutes and settles a question that otherwise runs for several years.

sections.heading: Islamic Education, Social Studies and the content rule that limits what any tutor may use
paragraphs: These two subjects sit outside the international curriculum entirely and are often treated by families as lower stakes, which is a mistake for a straightforward reason: they occupy real hours in the week and they are assessed. A student deferring them to Sunday night is deferring a subject with a mark attached, and the time that work takes has to come from somewhere, which in practice means from cumulative revision in mathematics or a science.

There is a constraint on support in these subjects that families should know about, because it explains why a credible tutor will refuse certain requests. KHDA states that for the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry of Education, is strictly prohibited. A tutor cannot therefore bring a parallel syllabus, an imported workbook or a substitute scheme of work into Islamic Education or Social Studies. Legitimate support works from what the school is using.

The staffing rule is the second thing worth knowing. Schools are required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate approval from KHDA to teach these subjects. That applies to school staff rather than to private tutors, and it is a useful question to ask of the school if your child's Arabic teaching has changed three times in two years, which happens more often than it should in large Deira year groups.

The practical position for a family is therefore narrower and clearer than in the international subjects. Support in Islamic Education and Social Studies means explanation of the school's own material, help with how answers should be structured, and organisation of the revision, rather than a substitute course. Where a family genuinely wants content beyond the school's, the route is a conversation with the school, not a tutor.

sections.heading: Where the two loads collide across the school year
paragraphs: A week that is full but balanced is manageable. The problem is that the two loads do not spread evenly, and their peaks overlap. Diploma internal assessment deadlines, IGCSE coursework and mock examinations cluster in particular windows, and so do the assessment points in the mandatory subjects. When a Deira student has an Arabic assessment and a science internal assessment draft in the same fortnight, something is going to be sacrificed, and it will be whichever one has no deadline attached.

That is nearly always cumulative revision. Revision of material from two months ago is the only commitment in the week with no due date, so it is the one that gives, and it is also the one that decides a terminal paper in June. The sequence is predictable: a busy February, a quiet collapse in the oldest topics, and a mock result in a subject the student was previously comfortable in. Parents read that as the subject becoming harder, which it has not.

The table below maps the year so the collisions are visible in advance. It is worth building a household version with your own school's dates, because the mandatory subject assessment points are set at school level and are not published anywhere a parent can find them. Asking for them in September takes one email and prevents most of this.

The honest conclusion from the mapping is sometimes that there are too many commitments, not too few hours. A Diploma student carrying six subjects, the core, three mandatory subjects and two extracurricular commitments does not have a tutoring problem. Adding a weekly session to that week displaces something, and if nobody chooses what gets displaced, the student chooses, and they will choose the thing with no deadline.

sections.heading: The marks that go missing in the main subjects when the week is full
paragraphs: A full week does not damage all subjects equally, and knowing which ones it damages first is how a family spends efficiently. The subjects that suffer are the cumulative ones: mathematics, where a deferred topic blocks later ones, and the sciences, where cross-topic questions require material from several months earlier to be simultaneously available. Those subjects punish deferral with a lag, so the damage is invisible when it is being done.

The subjects that survive a full week better are the ones assessed on technique applied to unseen material. English language analysis, business case application and economics diagram work can be held at a reasonable standard with less frequent input, provided the technique is secure. That is a real distinction and it should drive the order in which a busy student allocates time, rather than the order in which homework happens to be set.

The losses themselves are mostly the same three. Command terms, where a thorough description scores in the lowest band because the paper asked for an evaluation. Timing, where a six-mark question takes eighteen minutes and twelve minutes of marks are lost elsewhere in the paper. And mark-scheme form, where a correct answer is written in a way that does not collect the available marks. None of those require content coverage to fix, which is why they are the right first target for a student with no spare hours.

The diagnosis has to come from the student's own marked work, not from a general list. Two students in the same Deira classroom with the same grade usually lose their marks in different places, and the first useful session is spent reading a marked mock and categorising every lost mark as knowledge, technique or timing. A tutor who does not ask for that paper before starting is guessing, and in a week this full, a guess costs hours that are not available.

sections.heading: What support costs here, and what cannot be bought at any price
paragraphs: The market rates are the same across Dubai, so the table below prices by need rather than repeating the bands. For reference: a budget online tutor, generally a university student, runs AED 45-150 an hour, with EdFlik listing from AED 45-65 and Tutopiya from AED 33-52; a qualified subject tutor online is AED 150-300, with Unitors listing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200; a specialist is AED 200-450 or more, with TutorChase publishing AED 270; and premium named tutors reach AED 500-650, with BartyED publishing AED 650. Those are market figures gathered in October 2026 and attributed to those providers, not IB Gram prices.

The column that matters on this page is the last one, because in the mandatory subjects there are things no amount of money can legitimately buy. Substitute content in Islamic Education or Social Studies is prohibited without prior Ministry of Education permission, so a tutor offering a parallel programme in those subjects is offering something the rules do not allow. A move between the Arabic streams is a school decision, not a purchasable one. And no provider can supply coursework that has to be the student's own work.

There is also a value point specific to a full week. The cheapest effective intervention for a busy, capable Deira student is often not a subject tutor at all; it is a single session auditing where the hours go, followed by a rebuilt weekly schedule. Families arrive expecting to buy three sessions a week and leave with one plus a schedule, and the results are usually better because the displaced activity was producing nothing.

One honest observation about Arabic specifically. It is the subject with the thinnest supply of genuinely qualified one-to-one tutors relative to demand across the whole emirate, particularly for first-language Standard Arabic writing at Diploma level. That means booking early in the school year matters more here than in mathematics, where the pool is deep. If the slot is not available, you should be told rather than handed a conversational tutor for a literary analysis course.

sections.heading: Who may teach these subjects, and what approval actually means
paragraphs: Two different rules operate here and they get confused constantly. The first applies to schools: KHDA requires schools to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate approval from KHDA to teach these subjects. That is a condition on a school's staffing, and it is a reasonable thing for a parent to ask about if the Arabic teaching in a large year group has been unstable.

The second applies to individuals offering private lessons anywhere in the UAE. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is administered by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. It is granted free of charge for two years, and MoHRE's own service page, Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, lists no fee, gives a two-working-day completion time and is applied for through the smart app, website and e-services system.

The eligible categories are broad: teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so any page quoting an amount is not working from a source, and that is worth remembering.

The condition most relevant to a Deira family is the one about your child's own school. The permit carries a code of conduct that bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school, and ADEK's professional-ethics rules prohibit Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school. In a district where the same families have used the same schools for years, hiring your child's own teacher privately can feel like the obvious move. It is the arrangement these rules exist to prevent.

sections.heading: Why Arabic does not count towards the equivalency five
paragraphs: This is the point where the two halves of a Deira student's week produce a genuinely odd result, and almost no page explains it. Arabic and Islamic Education are compulsory under KHDA's rules for every private school in Dubai. They are also explicitly excluded from the five subjects the Ministry of Education's British-track equivalency route counts. A student can therefore spend years on two compulsory subjects that do not contribute to the certificate recognition they will eventually need.

The published requirement is specific. A student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. Alongside that, one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level with the same grade, is required. One ranking competitor page states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects; the sourced requirement is five, and the composition matters more than the count.

The practical consequence lands in the Year 9 option meeting. A student taking Arabic and Islamic Education plus four other IGCSE subjects has four counting subjects, not six, and discovers it two years later when the entry list has long closed. In a Deira school where Arabic is a serious, examined subject taken at first-language level, this is a real and common trap, and the fix is to count the counting subjects deliberately rather than assuming the total is the total.

None of this is a reason to treat Arabic as wasted effort, and it should not be read that way. For an Arabic-speaking family it is the subject with the longest-term value, and at Diploma level taking Arabic A folds a compulsory requirement into the six subjects that are scored. The point is narrower: the equivalency arithmetic has to be done separately, and it has to be done before the option block is signed. Equivalency itself is completed through the official channel, and no tutoring provider performs, accelerates or guarantees it.
