process.title: Tell us the whole week, not the subject
process.description: We ask what the full timetable contains, including Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies, plus coursework and activities. In a Deira school the week is larger than the curriculum suggests, and a plan that ignores the mandatory subjects is a plan for a student in a different country.

process.title: Send marked work in the subject that worries you
process.description: For an international curriculum subject that means a marked mock or unit test. For Arabic it means a piece of extended writing with the teacher's marking on it, because that is the only thing that distinguishes household fluency from assessed Standard Arabic competence.

process.title: Ask the school two questions we will give you
process.description: Which Arabic stream your child is in and what criteria their written tasks are assessed against, and what the mandatory subject assessment dates are for the year. Both answers come by email, neither is published, and together they prevent most of the collisions described on this page.

process.title: Trial the tutor in the real slot
process.description: The session runs at the time you intend to keep, on a normal weekday after the actual journey home. From Al Mamzar and the Al Nahda side, that usually means allowing for the border and airport traffic rather than for the map distance.

process.title: Review, and be willing to buy fewer hours
process.description: Progress is judged on the next marked assessment against the named targets. If the audit showed that the week was overcommitted rather than undersupported, the honest recommendation is one session and a schedule rather than three sessions and a fuller week.

whyPoints.title: We plan for the real Dubai week
whyPoints.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are compulsory, assessed and timetabled, and almost no tutoring page accounts for them. A Diploma student in Deira carries six subjects, a core and three further assessed subjects, and that is the week a plan has to fit.

whyPoints.title: The two Arabic streams are treated as different courses
whyPoints.description: Household fluency is not first-language readiness, and a placement error in either direction is invisible on a report and persists for years. Support in the first-language stream means individual correction of Standard Arabic writing, not conversation practice.

whyPoints.title: We work from the school's own material where the rules require it
whyPoints.description: KHDA prohibits different or additional content in the mandatory UAE subjects without prior Ministry of Education permission. A tutor offering a parallel Islamic Education or Social Studies programme is offering something the rules do not allow, and we will say so.

whyPoints.title: The equivalency arithmetic is done separately
whyPoints.description: Arabic and Islamic education are compulsory and excluded from the five subjects the British-track equivalency route counts. Four counting subjects plus two compulsory ones is not five, and that is discovered after the entry list closes unless somebody counts in Year 9.

whyPoints.title: We will recommend fewer hours when the week is overfull
whyPoints.description: A capable student carrying six subjects, a core, three mandatory subjects and two activities does not have a tutoring shortage. Adding a session displaces something, and if nobody chooses what, the student defers the one thing with no deadline: cumulative revision.

whyPoints.title: We say when Arabic supply is short
whyPoints.description: Genuinely qualified one-to-one tutors for first-language Standard Arabic writing at Diploma level are the scarcest category in this market. If the slot is not available you are told, rather than handed a conversational tutor for a literary analysis course.

faqs.question: Why does my child's Deira school teach Arabic and Islamic Education alongside the IB?
faqs.answer: Because every private school in Dubai must, regardless of the international curriculum it is licensed for. KHDA's mandatory subject guidelines required implementation by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. These are assessed subjects with timetabled hours, calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, with KHDA advising at least 25 minutes for any mandatory subject lesson. The practical consequence is that your child's week is larger than the curriculum's own subject list suggests.

faqs.question: My child speaks Arabic at home but scores poorly in Arabic. How?
faqs.answer: Because household fluency and assessed Standard Arabic are different competences. A child who speaks a dialect confidently is then assessed on Standard Arabic reading, extended writing and, at Diploma level, literary analysis. The spoken fluency masks the gap in class and the marked written work exposes it. The fix is individual correction of the student's own extended writing against the criteria the school is using, which a class of twenty-eight cannot provide and which generic conversational tutoring does not address.

faqs.question: Can my child move between the first-language and additional-language Arabic streams?
faqs.answer: That is a school decision rather than something a tutor can arrange, and KHDA requires the two streams to be taught in separate classes, with combined classes for Arab and non-Arab groups strictly prohibited. Start by asking the teacher which stream your child is in and what criteria their written tasks are assessed against. If a student from an Arabic-speaking household is struggling in the first-language stream, the usual answer is targeted Standard Arabic writing work rather than a move downwards.

faqs.question: Can a tutor use a different Arabic or Islamic Education syllabus than the school's?
faqs.answer: No, and a credible tutor will decline. KHDA states that for the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. Legitimate support therefore explains and reinforces the school's own material, helps with how answers should be structured, and organises the revision. A provider offering an imported workbook or a parallel scheme of work in these subjects is offering something the rules do not allow.

faqs.question: If Arabic is compulsory at my Al Mamzar school, does it count in the equivalency five?
faqs.answer: No, and this catches Deira families regularly. The British-track route requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. A student taking Arabic and Islamic Education plus four other subjects therefore has four counting subjects, not six. One ranking competitor page states six are required; the sourced figure is five. Count the counting subjects before the Year 9 option block is signed.

faqs.question: Which schools around Al Mamzar do your students attend?
faqs.answer: The nearest cluster spans Al Mamzar, Al Nahda and Al Qusais, including Al Ittihad Private School Al Mamzar, Deira Private School, The Westminster School, Dubai Scholars Private School and Al Diyafah High School. The second cluster, towards Al Garhoud and Oud Metha, includes Deira International School, Al Mawakeb School Al Garhoud, St Mary's Catholic High School, Dubai Gem Private School and The Indian High School. These are long-established schools with large year groups, which is why individual feedback on written work is the scarcest thing in the week. Named as context only.

faqs.question: Should an Arabic-speaking Diploma student take Arabic A or Arabic B?
faqs.answer: Where the school offers it and the student can handle Standard Arabic literary analysis, Arabic A is often the single most effective structural decision available, because it folds a compulsory requirement into the six subjects that are actually scored. Arabic B is the acquisition route and can leave a genuinely competent student coasting. The test is a piece of extended writing in Standard Arabic, marked honestly, rather than a judgement based on how the student speaks at home. Ask in Diploma Year 1, while a change is still possible.

faqs.question: Which subjects suffer first when a Deira student's week is too full?
faqs.answer: The cumulative ones. Mathematics punishes a deferred topic because later work depends on it, and the sciences punish it because cross-topic questions need material from several months earlier to be simultaneously available. Both damage with a lag, so the loss is invisible while it happens and shows up in a mock. Subjects assessed on technique applied to unseen material, such as English analysis and business case application, survive less frequent input better, provided the technique is already secure.

faqs.question: When do the curriculum and mandatory assessment loads collide?
faqs.answer: Most sharply from November to March. Coursework and internal assessment deadlines cluster, mocks fall in January, the mandatory subjects have their own mid-year assessment points, and Ramadan often lands in February or March with shortened school days. When two deadlines coincide, the commitment with no due date is sacrificed, and that is always cumulative revision. Ask the school in September for the mandatory subject assessment dates, because they are set at school level and are not published anywhere a parent can find them.

faqs.question: Is it better to add a tutoring session or to cut something from the week?
faqs.answer: Frequently the second, which is not what a tutoring provider is expected to say. A student carrying six subjects, the Diploma core, three mandatory subjects and two extracurricular commitments does not have a shortage of input. Adding a weekly session displaces something, and if nobody decides what, the student defers the activity with no deadline. A single session auditing where the hours actually go, followed by a rebuilt schedule, often produces better results than three new sessions.

faqs.question: Can I hire my child's own Arabic teacher privately?
faqs.answer: It is the arrangement the rules exist to prevent. The MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school, and ADEK's professional-ethics rules prohibit Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school. In a district where families have used the same schools for years this can feel like the natural choice. Choose a tutor from outside your child's school instead.

faqs.question: What approval does a school's Arabic teacher need?
faqs.answer: KHDA requires schools to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate approval from KHDA to teach these subjects. That rule applies to a school's staffing rather than to private tutors, and it is a fair question to raise with the school if the Arabic teaching in a large year group has changed repeatedly. Separately, individuals offering private lessons in the UAE need the MoHRE private tuition work permit, which is a different instrument with different conditions.

faqs.question: Do private Arabic tutors in Dubai need a permit?
faqs.answer: Yes, like any individual offering private lessons in the UAE. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is administered by MoHRE, and is granted free of charge for two years, with a two-working-day completion time stated on MoHRE's service page and applications made through the smart app, website and e-services. Eligible categories include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. No fine schedule is published for non-compliance.

faqs.question: Is it harder to find a good Arabic tutor than a maths tutor?
faqs.answer: Yes, measurably so. Genuinely qualified one-to-one tutors for first-language Standard Arabic writing, particularly at Diploma level, are the scarcest category in this market relative to demand, while the mathematics pool is deep. The practical consequence is that booking early in the school year matters more for Arabic than for anything else, and that a conversational tutor is not a substitute for someone who can mark extended Standard Arabic writing against the criteria. If no suitable tutor is free, you should be told.

faqs.question: How should a student in Al Mamzar schedule twenty minutes of Arabic a day?
faqs.answer: Attached to something that already happens, and with retrieval rather than reading. Twenty minutes of producing vocabulary and structures from memory, in writing, outperforms an hour of passive reading, and daily beats weekly in this subject more than in any other. Fix it to an existing routine, after dinner or immediately after the journey home, so it survives a busy week. For the additional-language stream, that small, boring, daily input is close to the whole answer, and almost nobody does it unprompted.

dubai/al-mamzar.closingHeading: Count the real week, then decide what to buy
dubai/al-mamzar.closingBody: A student at a Deira school is not carrying an IB or IGCSE timetable; they are carrying that plus Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies, all assessed and all taking hours. The useful first step is to write the whole week down, get the mandatory subject assessment dates from the school, and find out which Arabic stream your child is in and what their written work is marked against. Send us that, plus a marked paper in whichever subject worries you, and you will get a plan sized for the real week. Lessons run online, one to one, over live video.

dubai/al-manara.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover the two halves of an Al Manara student's week: the Diploma and IGCSE subjects the school is licensed for, and the Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies streams that run alongside them under KHDA requirements.

intro.heading: Two timetables, one week
paragraphs: Al Manara is a villa community inland of Umm Suqeim, bounded by Sheikh Zayed Road on one side and the Al Khail corridor on the other, and its households send children out in both directions: towards the Jumeirah and Umm Suqeim schools on the coast, and inland towards Al Barsha and Al Sufouh. Most of those schools are licensed to teach a British or International Baccalaureate curriculum. All of them also have to teach something else.

Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific national curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but they must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. In Dubai, KHDA turns that federal baseline into a detailed requirement: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA's own guidelines state the requirements must be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April.

That is the half of the week that no tutoring page in this market writes about. Search for tutoring in Dubai and you will find Mathematics, the sciences and English in abundance, with Arabic appearing as a subject chip and nothing more. Yet it is a subject every child in a Dubai private school carries, it is examined and reported on, and for many families it is the grade that causes the most anxiety precisely because the parents cannot help with it at home.

So this page covers both halves. It sets out exactly what KHDA requires, including the rules on which language each subject must be taught in and the prohibition on combining Arab and non-Arab students in the same class. It explains how much of the school week the mandatory subjects consume, using KHDA's own forty-minute lesson unit. Then it covers the IB and IGCSE subjects Al Manara families combine them with, and the commute that decides when anything can be slotted in.

Delivery is straightforward. IB Gram arranges one-to-one tuition online, over live video, with a shared whiteboard and the student's own work on screen. Nobody is sent to an address in the UAE; home visiting is confined to the India service. For Arabic in particular this is a genuine advantage, because a first-language Arabic specialist who can teach to the Dubai requirement is not necessarily someone living a fifteen-minute drive from Al Manara Road.

One boundary is worth stating at the start. For the mandatory UAE subjects, KHDA's guidelines state that the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry of Education, is strictly prohibited. That is a real constraint on how any tutor may describe their material, and this page describes it accurately rather than ignoring it.

dubai/al-manara.programmesIntro: Three programmes dominate in the schools Al Manara children attend, and all three run with the mandatory UAE subjects sitting alongside. These notes describe how the two timetables interact at each stage.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, transdisciplinary and without external examination. The mandatory subjects are at their most time-consuming proportionally at this stage, because the PYP day is shorter and the weekly Arabic and Islamic Education allocation takes a larger slice of it. Early Arabic exposure is also where the gap between first-language and additional-language streams opens up.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Manara the commonest primary request is Arabic as an additional language for a child who started Dubai schooling after the early years and is behind the stream they have been placed in. That is a specific, fixable gap, and it is far easier to close at primary than at Year 9.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight, converted to a 1-7 grade through subject boundaries. Language acquisition is already a programme requirement, and in Dubai the mandatory Arabic provision sits alongside it rather than replacing it, which is the point at which the week starts to feel genuinely full for a Year 9 or Year 10 student.
programmes.countryNote: MYP students in Al Manara frequently carry Arabic twice over, once as the KHDA-mandated subject and once inside the MYP language acquisition requirement, depending on how the school has structured it. Ask the school which arrangement applies before buying tutoring, because the two have different assessment criteria.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS, with an Internal Assessment in every subject. By this stage the mandatory UAE provision has usually reduced in weekly hours, but it does not disappear, and a Diploma student juggling six subjects plus the core plus Arabic has the densest week in the school.
programmes.countryNote: The practical consequence for Al Manara Diploma families is that the mandatory subjects are the first thing to be quietly dropped from a revision plan and the first thing to appear as a problem in a report. Keeping a modest, regular slot on them is cheaper than an emergency block in the final term.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects examined at the end of Year 11, with syllabus codes that matter: Cambridge Mathematics is 0580, Pearson International GCSE Mathematics is 4MA1, and the papers differ. Some Dubai schools enter Arabic as an IGCSE subject in addition to the KHDA-mandated provision; others keep them entirely separate.
programmes.countryNote: Confirm with the school whether your child's Arabic is being examined as an IGCSE or delivered purely as the KHDA-mandated subject, because the two need different tutoring. An IGCSE entry has a specification and past papers; the mandatory provision follows the Ministry's curriculum.

dubai/al-manara.subjectsIntro: An Al Manara student's subject list has two parts. The first is the curriculum the school is licensed for. The second is the set of subjects KHDA requires regardless. Both are listed below, because both appear on the report.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.levels: Mandatory for Arab students in Dubai private schools
subjects.description: Taught with Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction under KHDA's requirements, and taught in classes separate from non-Arab students. Grammar, comprehension and formal written register carry the marks, and the gap between spoken dialect at home and Standard Arabic on the page is where most students lose them.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.levels: Mandatory for non-Arab students in Dubai private schools
subjects.description: A different syllabus and a different expectation from the first-language stream, with KHDA requiring the two to be taught separately rather than combined. Progress is built on vocabulary, script fluency and sentence patterns, and a student placed in the wrong stream struggles for reasons that have nothing to do with ability.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.levels: Mandatory, delivered in separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students
subjects.description: KHDA requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students, and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arab students. The content is prescribed, and schools must ensure teachers hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach it.

subjects.name: UAE Social Studies
subjects.description: KHDA requires Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students. The subject covers UAE history, geography, civics and national identity, and because its content is prescribed by the Ministry, it is examined on specific material rather than on general knowledge.

subjects.name: Moral, Social and Cultural Studies
subjects.levels: Mandatory, licensed-curriculum language for non-Arab students
subjects.description: Delivered in the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arab students under KHDA's requirements. Assessment is usually coursework and discussion-based rather than examination-heavy, which makes it the subject most often neglected and most often flagged in a report.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebra, calculus and proof, with Paper 1 sat without a calculator. Method marks are written into the markscheme, so a correct answer with no working scores a fraction of the available total. This is the subject where an Al Manara Diploma student's week is most often rebalanced.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with the calculator permitted throughout. Marks go missing in interpretation rather than calculation: describing statistical output instead of naming the variables, the test and the significance level the question specified.

subjects.name: Chemistry and Physics
subjects.levels: HL and SL · Cambridge 0620 and 0625, Pearson 4CH1 and 4PH1 at IGCSE
subjects.description: The two subjects Al Manara families most often buy alongside Arabic, and the two with the heaviest content load at Higher Level. In both, extended-response marks are lost to command-term confusion rather than to gaps in knowledge.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: HL and SL · Cambridge 0610 at IGCSE
subjects.description: Content-dense and sensitive to missed weeks, with the HL extension sitting largely in genetics, plant biology and physiology. Retrieval practice between sessions does more for the grade than additional coverage inside them.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.levels: HL and SL · Cambridge 0500 and 0510 at IGCSE
subjects.description: Paper 1 unseen analysis, Paper 2 comparative essay, plus the Individual Oral and the HL Essay. For students whose home language is Arabic, the Individual Oral is often the component that moves furthest with structured, timed rehearsal.

dubai/al-manara.regionsIntro: Al Manara sits between two very different commute corridors, and the communities around it divide along that line. These notes are about which direction the school run goes and what that does to the afternoon.

regions.name: Al Manara
regions.note: Villa plots between Sheikh Zayed Road and the Al Khail corridor. Households here split between coast-facing and inland-facing school runs, which means two neighbours can have afternoon windows forty minutes apart.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim
regions.note: Directly seaward, with several schools inside a short run. Coast-facing Al Manara families usually route through here, and the beach road at pick-up is the slow section rather than the inland leg.

regions.name: Umm Al Sheif
regions.note: Between Al Manara and the coast, villa stock with school provision inside the community. Families here often have the earliest workable slot in this cluster, around 4pm on a normal weekday.

regions.name: Al Safa 2
regions.note: North across Al Manara Road. Shares bus routes with Al Manara in both directions, so comparing arrival times with an Al Safa 2 neighbour is a quick way to sanity-check a proposed slot.

regions.name: Al Barsha 1 and 2
regions.note: Inland across Sheikh Zayed Road, a major school destination for Al Manara students. The return leg crosses the motorway at peak, which is the single slowest part of any inland run from here.

regions.name: Al Sufouh
regions.note: Along the coast towards the university area, with established school provision. The run back along Al Sufouh Road is reliable outside pick-up and unpredictable within it.

regions.name: Al Quoz 3
regions.note: Immediately inland of Al Manara's eastern edge. Worth knowing because tutors quoting in-home rates for Al Manara often start from this side and price the Sheikh Zayed Road crossing into the hour.

regions.name: Jumeirah 3
regions.note: Seaward along the coast, overlapping with Al Manara on several bus routes. Secondary students on these routes arrive later than their primary siblings, which splits a household into two different windows.

schoolClusters.city: Coast-facing from Al Manara
schoolClusters.note: The schools Al Manara families reach by heading seaward. Every one of them, whatever curriculum it is licensed to teach, must also deliver Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies under KHDA's requirements, and each must ensure its Arabic and Islamic Education teachers hold appropriate KHDA approval.

sections.heading: The half of the week nobody writes about
paragraphs: Search for tutoring in Dubai and the results describe one timetable: Mathematics, the sciences, English, the Diploma core. Arabic appears, if at all, as a chip in a list of subjects. Islamic Education and UAE Social Studies appear nowhere. Across the pages competing for these searches, there is essentially no content on the subjects every child in a Dubai private school is required to take.

That is a strange gap, because these subjects are not optional and they are not marginal. The federal position is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. Dubai's regulator then specifies how. KHDA's mandatory subjects guidelines state that Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with implementation from the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools on an April start.

For an Al Manara parent the practical point is that these grades appear on the same report as the Mathematics grade, and for many households they are the ones the parents cannot help with at home. A British or Indian expatriate parent can usually sit down with a Year 9 algebra problem. Standard Arabic grammar is a different proposition, and the usual result is that the subject is left entirely to the school until a report says it has gone wrong.

The rest of this page treats that half of the week as seriously as the examined subjects, because KHDA does, and because for a significant number of Al Manara families it is the actual reason they are searching.

sections.heading: What KHDA actually requires alongside your child's curriculum
paragraphs: The requirements are specific rather than general, and the specifics are what a parent needs. KHDA sets not only which subjects must be taught but which language each must be taught in, and how classes must be organised. Those rules are published in KHDA's mandatory subjects guidelines and they are checkable.

On language, KHDA requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and for Arabic as a first language; Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students; and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arab students in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies. That means two children in the same year group can be taught the same nominal subject in different languages, legitimately.

On class organisation the rule is unambiguous. For Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and KHDA states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited due to the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. If your child has been placed in a stream, that placement determines the syllabus they are being taught, and tutoring has to match it.

There is also a credential requirement worth knowing. KHDA states that schools are required to ensure all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate KHDA approval to teach these subjects. That applies to the school's own staff. It is not a licence any tutoring provider holds, and no provider should imply that it is.

sections.heading: How much of the school week the mandatory subjects take
paragraphs: Parents often assume the mandatory subjects are a token allocation. They are not, and KHDA sets out exactly how the time is calculated. The guidelines state that mandatory-subject instructional time is calculated based on a forty-minute lesson unit, that schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and that it is advised that the length for any mandatory subject lesson is at least twenty-five minutes.

Those three clauses between them explain a lot of the variation parents see between schools. Two schools can meet the same weekly requirement with very different timetables: one running fewer, longer lessons and another running more, shorter ones. Both are compliant. The practical effect on a child is not identical, because a language subject taught in three short slots behaves differently from the same total delivered in one long one.

The advised twenty-five minute floor matters too. It exists because a language lesson shorter than that achieves very little, and it is the clause to point at if a school has compressed Arabic into fragments. A parent asking how the school calculates its mandatory-subject time, and how many lesson units each subject receives, is asking a question the school can answer from its own timetable documentation.

The reason to understand this before buying tutoring is simple. If the school is already delivering a substantial weekly allocation and the grade is still weak, the problem is not quantity of exposure, and more hours of the same thing will not fix it. If the allocation is thin, a modest regular slot outside school may close the gap quickly. Those are different purchases.

sections.heading: Arabic as a first language against Arabic as an additional language
paragraphs: These are two subjects with one name, and confusing them is the commonest reason Arabic tutoring fails to help. The first-language stream assumes a student who speaks Arabic at home and teaches them to read, write and analyse Standard Arabic to a formal academic standard. The additional-language stream assumes no household Arabic and builds from script, vocabulary and sentence construction upwards.

The difficulty for first-language students is rarely comprehension. It is register. Spoken Gulf or Levantine dialect at home differs substantially from Standard Arabic on the page, in vocabulary, in grammar and in sentence structure, and a student entirely fluent in conversation can still produce written work that loses marks on every line. That is a teachable, specific problem and it responds to structured grammar work and marked writing rather than to more reading.

The difficulty for additional-language students is different and more straightforward: insufficient exposure. Script fluency and vocabulary accumulate through frequent short practice, which is why two thirty-minute sessions a week outperform one ninety-minute session for a student who is behind. It is also why a student who joined Dubai schooling late is behind for a reason that has nothing to do with ability and everything to do with starting years after their classmates.

KHDA requires the two groups to be taught separately, so your child is already in one stream or the other. The first question to a prospective Arabic tutor is which stream they are teaching to, and the first thing to send them is a piece of the student's own marked work. A tutor teaching first-language grammar to an additional-language student, or the reverse, is wasting the hour politely.

sections.heading: Islamic Education, Social Studies and the content restriction
paragraphs: Islamic Education and UAE Social Studies are prescribed subjects, and that word carries weight. KHDA's guidelines state that for the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry of Education, is strictly prohibited. That is a real constraint and it shapes what legitimate tutoring in these subjects looks like.

What it means in practice is that a tutor in these subjects works from the material the school is using, not from a parallel course of their own devising. There is no scope for a tutoring provider to offer its own Islamic Education syllabus or its own version of UAE Social Studies, and any provider advertising one should be asked where the Ministry permission came from. The useful work is explanation, structure, examination technique and help with the prescribed content itself.

For Social Studies specifically, the content is UAE history, geography, civics and national identity, examined on specific prescribed material rather than on general awareness. Students lose marks by answering from general knowledge where the question expected the taught content, which is a technique problem a tutor can address directly by working through the student's own notes and past assessments.

Moral, Social and Cultural Studies is usually the most neglected of the group, because its assessment tends to be coursework and discussion rather than examination, and it therefore produces no obvious crisis until a report comment arrives. A modest amount of attention to it, early, is far cheaper than the alternative. For all of these subjects, the right opening move is to ask the school which Ministry material the class is following.

sections.heading: Why Arabic and Islamic Education sit outside your equivalency five
paragraphs: Here is where the two timetables diverge in a way that surprises parents. The UAE Ministry of Education's equivalency requirements for the British track specify that students must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade no lower than E or grade 3, plus either one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. And the Ministry's clarification states that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects.

So a student can be carrying Arabic and Islamic Education as mandatory school subjects, be graded and reported on both, and still find that neither counts towards the five the Ministry wants to see for equivalency. That is not a contradiction. The school requirement and the equivalency requirement are different instruments with different purposes, and both apply.

The planning consequence is concrete. A Year 11 student entering exactly five IGCSE subjects plus Arabic and Islamic Education is entering five that count, with no margin. If one of the five goes wrong, the margin is zero. That is a reason to plan the subject block in Year 9 with the equivalency count in mind, rather than discovering the arithmetic in the summer of Year 11.

It is also worth noting that one page currently ranking in this market states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects. The Ministry's own clarified rule is five, excluding Arabic and Islamic education. Verify the current requirement on the Ministry of Education's own site before acting on any figure, including this one. IB Gram does not perform equivalency or attestation and this page is describing the process, not operating it.

sections.heading: Two commute directions, two different afternoons
paragraphs: Al Manara's geography creates an unusual scheduling problem. The community sits between Sheikh Zayed Road and the Al Khail corridor, and its school runs go in both directions. A coast-facing run to Umm Suqeim or Jumeirah 3 is short in distance and slow only on the beach road. An inland run to Al Barsha or Al Sufouh means crossing the motorway at pick-up, which is the single least predictable leg available from here.

The practical result is that two Al Manara households on the same street can have afternoon windows forty minutes apart. A family whose child attends a school in Umm Al Sheif may be home before four. A family on an Al Barsha route may not be home until a quarter to five. Both will be offered the same generic four o'clock slot by a provider who has not asked, and one of them will spend a term rearranging it.

The table below works through the pattern by direction. It gives the typical finish, the realistic arrival window in Al Manara, the earliest start that works and the slot most likely to survive a full term. For the mandatory subjects in particular, the short-session format helps here: a thirty-minute Arabic slot fits into a window that a full hour does not.

The other factor in this cluster is activity scheduling. Al Manara is well served by sports and music provision inland, and those commitments tend to arrive mid-term rather than in September. Fixing the tutoring slot first and arranging activities around it is the only approach that survives, because the tutoring hour is otherwise always the item with the most flexible counterpart.

sections.heading: Combining the mandatory subjects with a full IB or IGCSE load
paragraphs: The honest problem for an Al Manara family is capacity. A Diploma student carries six subjects, Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS, and the mandatory UAE provision on top. An IGCSE student carries eight to ten subjects plus the same mandatory provision. There is no version of that week with unlimited room in it, and a tutoring plan that ignores the arithmetic will fail on contact with November.

The approach that works is triage with a stated priority, revisited each term. In Year 10 the priority is usually the IGCSE subjects that will be continued post-16, with a small maintenance slot on Arabic to stop it drifting. In Year 12 it inverts for many families: the examined Diploma subjects dominate, but the mandatory subjects are the ones most likely to produce an unpleasant surprise precisely because nobody is watching them.

The table below sets out a realistic footprint by stage. The right-hand column is the one most families get wrong, because the instinct is to add hours to the subject causing visible pain and ignore the one quietly accumulating a problem. A half-hour maintenance slot on Arabic costs a fraction of an emergency block in the final term and is considerably more likely to work.

One structural point helps. Short sessions suit the mandatory subjects and long sessions suit the examined ones, which means the two compete for different parts of the afternoon rather than the same part. A thirty-minute Arabic slot at four and an hour of Chemistry at five is a more achievable week than two hours of anything.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do, across both halves of the week
paragraphs: Two separate boundaries apply in an Al Manara household, and they are worth stating together because they are often confused. The first concerns assessed coursework in the IB and IGCSE subjects. The second concerns the prescribed content of the mandatory UAE subjects.

On coursework, the rule is authorship. A tutor may teach the content an Internal Assessment rests on, explain each criterion in the IB's own wording, read the student's own draft and put the criteria to them as questions, and teach referencing, data handling and timeline discipline. A tutor may not produce any part of the submission, including a rewritten conclusion or an edit heavy enough that the words cease to be the student's. There are providers in this market advertising completed Internal Assessments; the malpractice consequence of buying one falls on the student, not the seller.

On the mandatory subjects, the rule is content. KHDA's guidelines state that the use of any different or additional content for these subjects, without prior permission from the Ministry of Education, is strictly prohibited. A legitimate tutor therefore works from the material the school is teaching. Nobody should be selling an alternative Islamic Education or UAE Social Studies syllabus, and a provider offering one is describing something it has no permission to deliver.

Neither boundary limits the useful work much. Explaining prescribed content clearly, drilling examination technique, fixing register in written Arabic, teaching a student to structure an answer that addresses the command term: all of that is substantial and all of it is within the rules. What both boundaries rule out is the shortcut, which is the thing a parent under pressure is most likely to be offered.

faqs.question: Does my child have to study Arabic in a British curriculum school in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of which international curriculum the school is licensed to teach, and KHDA's guidelines set implementation from the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. The federal position behind that is that private schools need not follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. So a British or IB school still delivers all three.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language?
faqs.answer: They are two different subjects with different syllabuses, and KHDA requires them to be taught in separate classes. The first-language stream assumes Arabic at home and teaches reading, writing and analysis of Standard Arabic to a formal academic standard, with Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction. The additional-language stream builds from script, vocabulary and sentence construction for students with no household Arabic. A student placed in the wrong stream struggles for reasons unrelated to ability, so confirm the placement before arranging any tutoring.

faqs.question: Can Arab and non-Arab students be taught Arabic in the same class?
faqs.answer: No. KHDA's guidelines are explicit: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. If you are told your child's class combines both groups in one of those subjects, that is worth raising with the school directly. The rule exists because the two groups are following genuinely different material at genuinely different levels.

faqs.question: How much Arabic teaching time should my child be getting each week?
faqs.answer: KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit and allows schools to vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, while advising that any mandatory subject lesson should be at least twenty-five minutes. That means two compliant schools can look very different in a timetable. The useful questions to ask your school are how many lesson units each mandatory subject receives and how it has chosen to distribute them, since fragmented sessions below the advised floor achieve very little in a language subject.

faqs.question: Do Arabic and Islamic Education count towards UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: No. The Ministry of Education's clarification of equivalency requirements for the British track states that students must pass five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, plus one Advanced Level subject at E or two Advanced Subsidiary Level subjects at the same grade, and that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. A student entering exactly five countable subjects therefore has no margin if one goes wrong. Verify the current rule on the Ministry's own site, because IB Gram does not perform equivalency.

faqs.question: Can a tutor teach a different Islamic Education syllabus from the school's?
faqs.answer: No, and a provider offering one should be questioned. KHDA's guidelines state that for the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. Legitimate tutoring in these subjects therefore works from the material the school is teaching: explaining prescribed content, building examination technique, and structuring answers that address the command term. That is substantial work. What it is not is an alternative course of somebody else's devising.

faqs.question: My child speaks Arabic at home but gets poor Arabic grades. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost always register rather than comprehension. Spoken Gulf or Levantine dialect differs substantially from Standard Arabic in vocabulary, grammar and sentence structure, so a student entirely fluent in conversation can lose marks on every line of written work. It is a specific and teachable problem that responds to structured grammar work and marked writing rather than to more reading or more conversation. Send a prospective tutor a marked piece of your child's own written Arabic; the pattern is usually visible immediately.

faqs.question: Is Moral, Social and Cultural Studies actually assessed?
faqs.answer: It is delivered and reported on, and KHDA requires it in the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arab students. Its assessment tends to be coursework and discussion-based rather than examination-heavy, which is precisely why it is the most neglected of the mandatory subjects: it produces no visible crisis until a report comment arrives. A small amount of attention early, usually just making sure the coursework is submitted properly and on time, costs very little compared with addressing it after the fact.

faqs.question: What time can lessons start for an Al Manara family on an Al Barsha school run?
faqs.answer: Later than most families hope. An inland run crossing Sheikh Zayed Road at pick-up typically puts arrival between 4pm and 4.45pm, which makes 5.05pm the earliest realistic start and 5.15pm the time that holds across a term. Coast-facing Al Manara runs towards Umm Al Sheif or Umm Suqeim are considerably better, often allowing 3.50pm or 4pm. Since two households on the same street can differ by forty-five minutes, the slot should be set from your own measured arrival rather than a general assumption.

faqs.question: Should Arabic sessions be long or short?
faqs.answer: Short and frequent, in both streams. Language and script fluency accumulate through repetition rather than through extended sitting, so two thirty-minute sessions a week outperform one ninety-minute session for a student who is behind. That also helps practically in Al Manara, because a thirty-minute slot fits an afternoon window that a full hour does not, and it lets a shorter mandatory-subject session sit at four o'clock with a longer science hour behind it at five.

faqs.question: My child joined a Dubai school late and is behind in Arabic. Is that fixable?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and the reason for the gap matters. A student who began Dubai schooling after the early years is behind because they started later than their classmates, not because of ability, and the additional-language stream content accumulates in a predictable order. Script fluency, core vocabulary and sentence patterns can be built systematically with frequent short practice. The earlier it is addressed the smaller the job: a gap opened in Year 3 is a far cheaper repair than the same gap discovered in Year 9.

faqs.question: Does the IB Diploma leave room for the mandatory subjects?
faqs.answer: It has to, and the week is genuinely tight. A Diploma student carries six subjects, Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS, with the mandatory UAE provision alongside, usually at reduced weekly hours by that stage. The practical risk is not the timetable but the revision plan: mandatory subjects are the first thing dropped when pressure rises and the first thing to appear as a surprise in a report. A protected half hour a week through Year 12 is much cheaper than a crisis block in Year 13.

faqs.question: Which schools do Al Manara families usually use?
faqs.answer: Al Manara households split between coast-facing and inland runs. Seaward there are Raffles World Academy and Raffles International School in Umm Suqeim, Kings' School Dubai, Horizon International School in Umm Al Sheif, Jumeirah Baccalaureate School in Al Safa and Al Ittihad Private School Jumeira. Inland across Sheikh Zayed Road sit GEMS Wellington International School in Al Sufouh, Dubai American Academy and Kings' School Al Barsha, Al Mawakeb School and Dubai National School. These are named as context only; check each school's current KHDA band on the KHDA site.

faqs.question: Are the mandatory subject teachers at my school approved to teach them?
faqs.answer: They should be, and it is a reasonable question to ask. KHDA states that schools are required to ensure all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. That is a requirement on the school, checkable with the school, and it is a useful question if your child's Arabic class has had several changes of teacher in one year. It is worth adding that this approval applies to school staff and is not something a tutoring provider holds or can claim.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover both Arabic and a science subject?
faqs.answer: Occasionally, but it is not the arrangement to aim for. Teaching Standard Arabic grammar to the first-language stream and teaching Higher Level Chemistry are different specialisms, and a tutor strong in one is rarely strong in the other. The format also differs: Arabic wants short frequent sessions and Chemistry wants longer ones. Two tutors at the right level, in slots of the right length, costs more administration and wastes considerably fewer hours. Ask each what they have actually taught to assessment.

Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are required in every Dubai private school whatever the licensed curriculum, they are graded, and they are the subjects most expatriate parents cannot support at home. Ask the school which stream your child is in and how many lesson units each subject gets, send a marked piece of their own Arabic writing, and protect a short regular slot rather than waiting for a crisis. intro.heading: The part of the course nobody supervises
paragraphs: A Year 11 teacher in Bur Dubai has a specification, a term calendar and twenty-four other students in the room. By June every topic on that specification will have been taught. That is a different claim from saying every student learned it, and the distance between the two is where private tuition earns its money. Parents in Al Mankhool tend to notice that distance in one of three places: a mock paper that comes back well below what the classwork suggested, an internal assessment nobody has started six weeks before the school's own deadline, or a topic the class finished during the fortnight your child was away.

The IB Diploma turns this into a structural problem rather than an occasional one. Six subjects, three at Higher Level, each carrying an internal assessment the student designs and drafts outside lesson time. Above that sit a 4,000-word Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay of 1,600 words and the TOK exhibition. None of it is homework in the ordinary sense, because there is no exercise to finish by Thursday. It is a project-management task handed to a sixteen-year-old, and the students who come unstuck are rarely the ones who find the content hard. They are the ones who were never shown how to cut a long piece of work into weekly pieces.

IGCSE has its own version of the same gap. Cambridge and Pearson both reward a volume of past-paper practice that no school timetable has room for, and command-term discipline that only shows up under timed conditions. A student can know every definition in Physics 0625 and still lose eight marks on Paper 4 because 'explain' was answered as 'describe'. That failure is diagnosable within one marked paper, which is why a first session with a specialist usually starts with a script rather than a topic list.

Al Mankhool shapes the practical side of this. It is a dense mid-rise district between Kuwait Street, Al Mankhool Road and the BurJuman interchange, and most families here live in apartments rather than villas. There is no spare study room, the school run goes out towards Oud Metha, Al Garhoud or across the creek, and a tutor driving in would be parking in a paid zone. The IB continuum schools these families use sit outside the neighbourhood, which means a 7am departure and a return after 15:30 on most days.

IB Gram works to that reality. Tuition for UAE families is delivered online, one-to-one, over live video, and IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the Emirates; the in-home service exists only in India. For a Bur Dubai parent the trade is a good one. Instead of whoever teaches the right subject within a twenty-minute drive of Al Mankhool, your child works with a tutor chosen for the exact paper they sit, in a slot that survives a traffic day on Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Road.

What follows is the honest version. What a school covers and what it leaves to the student, what the assessments actually require, what tuition costs in this market and who charges it, where the academic-honesty line falls, and what happens when no specialist is free in the week you ask.

dubai/al-mankhool.programmesIntro: Bur Dubai families split across three routes at sixteen: IGCSE then A Level, IGCSE then IB Diploma, or an IB continuum from MYP straight into DP. The notes below say what each demands of a student working at home in an Al Mankhool apartment, rather than repeating what the programme is.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across six groups, three at Higher Level and three at Standard, plus the three core elements. Every subject carries an internal assessment worth roughly a fifth of the grade, and the final score runs to 45 points including up to three bonus points from the Extended Essay and TOK matrix. Higher Level means more content, an extra paper in most subjects and a heavier IA expectation, not simply harder questions on the same material.
programmes.countryNote: An Al Mankhool DP student is usually travelling to a school in Al Garhoud, Al Jaddaf or further out, which removes most of the afternoon. The practical consequence is that IA and Extended Essay work lands late in the evening and at weekends, with no supervisor in the room. That is the single most common reason a Bur Dubai family calls in the first term of DP1 rather than the exam year.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, marked out of eight and reported as a 1-7 grade per subject. The programme rewards process: investigating, communicating, reflecting. It does not drill algorithms, so a student can hold strong MYP grades and still arrive in DP1 or Year 10 without the procedural fluency that timed papers assume.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP-to-DP step is the one Bur Dubai parents underestimate. A student who scored 6s on criterion-based tasks meets a Mathematics Analysis and Approaches paper with no criteria, no redrafting and a clock. Work in MYP 4 and 5 is best spent on fluency and notation rather than on more projects, because the criteria will not be there in Year 12.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two years, typically eight or nine subjects, terminal written papers with an alternative-to-practical or practical component in the sciences. Cambridge tiers many subjects into Core and Extended, which caps the grade available; Pearson International GCSE runs a single tier in most subjects with an allowance for modular entry in some. The board decides the paper structure, so the board matters more than the subject name.
programmes.countryNote: Several schools serving Al Mankhool and Oud Metha run Cambridge, others run Pearson, and a few enter different subjects with different boards in the same year group. Check the exam entry slip rather than the prospectus. A tutor prepared on 0580 Extended who meets a student entered for Pearson 4MA1 is teaching the right mathematics against the wrong paper.

programmes.name: International A Level
programmes.description: Three or four subjects in depth, examined in a June or November series, usually with no coursework in the sciences beyond a practical endorsement or a written practical paper. It suits a student who already knows which faculty they want, because the narrowing happens at sixteen rather than at eighteen.
programmes.countryNote: Families in Bur Dubai often compare A Level against DP on workload alone. The sharper comparison is the UAE Ministry of Education equivalency route: the British track asks for five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3, plus one A Level at E or two AS Levels at the same grade, with Arabic and Islamic Education excluded from the count of five.

dubai/al-mankhool.subjectsIntro: Requests from Al Mankhool and the surrounding Bur Dubai blocks cluster around the subjects where the gap between class coverage and independent work is widest: the two mathematics routes, the three sciences and the essay subjects whose internal assessments nobody sees until they are late.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof, calculus and algebraic fluency carry the paper. Marks go on unjustified steps, on sloppy notation in differentiation and on the Paper 3 extended investigation at HL, where students stop one inference short of the result. The 20-mark exploration is graded on five criteria, and personal engagement is the one most often left thin.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and technology use. The content reads friendlier than Analysis and Approaches and the grade boundaries do not reflect that. Students lose marks by reporting a regression without testing whether the model fits, and by using the graphical calculator without recording what was entered.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics and fields reward quick diagram work; thermodynamics and circuits punish vague wording. The scientific investigation is marked out of 24 on four criteria, and the design stage is where most of the difference between a 5 and a 7 is made, long before the data is collected.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms account for most lost marks at HL. Students who can name a mechanism often cannot draw the curly arrows in an order an examiner accepts. Data-based questions need unit-by-unit care, and significant figures quietly cost a mark per paper.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Volume is the problem rather than difficulty. Command terms decide the marks: 'outline' wants a list, 'explain' wants a mechanism with cause and effect. The investigation needs a variable that can be controlled in a school lab, which is where a tutor saves weeks by ruling out an unworkable question early.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams are the grammar of the subject. Three commentaries of 800 words each, built on news articles, carry the internal assessment, and the common failure is choosing an article that cannot carry a diagram or a key-concept link. HL adds policy calculation and a quantitative paper.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Tools are easy to name and hard to apply. Examiners reward evaluation anchored in the stimulus, not a recited SWOT. The research project at HL needs a real organisation willing to answer questions, which is a logistics problem a tutor should flag in the first week.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The Paper 1 guided analysis is the fastest grade to move, because students usually write about content rather than technique. The individual oral needs a global issue narrow enough to argue in ten minutes, and a weak choice limits the mark before a word is spoken.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Paper 1 rewards precise pseudocode and a clear grasp of system fundamentals. The solution development for the internal assessment needs a client with a genuine problem and documented consultation, and students who skip the planning record lose marks they cannot recover later.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Studies must be used as evidence rather than retold. Essay marks hinge on a critical thinking line that actually engages with method, sampling or ethics. The experimental study report runs to 2,200 words and needs a replication simple enough to run with classmates.

dubai/al-mankhool.igcseSubjectsIntro: Year 10 and Year 11 requests from Bur Dubai cluster on a shorter list, and the board matters as much as the subject. The codes below are the ones most often printed on exam entry slips at schools serving Al Mankhool.

igcseSubjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
igcseSubjects.description: Cambridge Extended reaches grade 9 while Core caps at grade C or 5, so the tier decision taken in Year 10 sets a ceiling. Pearson runs Foundation and Higher papers with a different question style. Algebraic manipulation and multi-step problems carry the marks in both.

igcseSubjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Pearson 4PH1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
igcseSubjects.description: Electricity and waves produce the most lost marks. Paper 6 or the practical paper tests method, variable control and graph plotting, and students who have only read practicals rather than run them lose marks on the detail an examiner expects.

igcseSubjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Pearson 4CH1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
igcseSubjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and qualitative analysis are where the grade is decided. Many students can balance an equation and still not convert a volume to moles under time pressure. Observation questions need the colour and the state, not one of the two.

igcseSubjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Pearson 4BI1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
igcseSubjects.description: Transport in plants, enzymes and genetics recur every series. Extended-response marks depend on using the stem's own terms, and students lose marks by answering with examples when the question asked for a process.

igcseSubjects.name: English as a Second Language and First Language English
igcseSubjects.description: The directed-writing task rewards audience and register more than vocabulary. Summary questions are mark-dense and quick to improve: most students write a paraphrase instead of selecting discrete points, and lose half the available marks in ten minutes.

igcseSubjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
igcseSubjects.description: Case-study papers need numbers used in the answer, not quoted beside it. A six-mark evaluation wants a judgement with a reason drawn from the case. These are among the quickest IGCSE subjects to move with four or five marked-script sessions.

dubai/al-mankhool.regionsTitle: Bur Dubai, Deira and the blocks either side of the creek
dubai/al-mankhool.regionsIntro: Al Mankhool does not work as an island. Families here use schools, clinics and tuition in a ring of older districts, and the notes below are the operational detail that decides when a lesson can actually start.

regions.name: Al Mankhool
regions.note: Mid-rise apartments between Kuwait Street and Al Mankhool Road, with BurJuman at the eastern edge where the Red and Green metro lines meet. Study space is a desk in a shared room for most students, which is why a scheduled online slot works better than open-ended homework time.

regions.name: Bur Dubai and Al Fahidi
regions.note: The oldest residential grid in the city, heavily served by abra and metro rather than car for secondary students. Session timing here is set by the school bus, not the parent's commute, and most students are home by 15:45.

regions.name: Karama
regions.note: Dense low-rise blocks immediately south, with a large long-settled Indian and Filipino community and schools drawing from both. Requests from Karama skew towards IGCSE mathematics and the sciences in Year 10 and 11.

regions.name: Oud Metha
regions.note: The school district for this whole corridor, holding several of the larger private schools plus the Dubai Police Academy roundabout that governs afternoon traffic. A 16:00 start is unrealistic on a weekday; 16:45 holds.

regions.name: Al Garhoud
regions.note: Across the creek near the airport, with British and IB schools and a shorter run from Al Mankhool than the map suggests outside peak hours. Families here often need a slot that survives an evening flight-shift parent being absent.

regions.name: Al Mamzar and Hor Al Anz
regions.note: Northern end of Deira towards the Sharjah boundary, with a mix of apartment families and schools running Indian and British curricula. Lesson slots after 18:00 are common because the inbound commute lands late.

regions.name: Al Muteena and Al Qusais
regions.note: Established Deira districts along the Red Line towards Sharjah, with a strong CBSE and British presence. Students switching from an Indian board into IGCSE in Year 9 or 10 are the typical request from these blocks.

regions.name: Al Jaddaf and Dubai Healthcare City
regions.note: The nearest IB continuum option for many Bur Dubai families, reached over Al Garhoud or Floating Bridge. The crossing adds twenty to thirty-five minutes each way in term time, which pushes DP coursework sessions into the late evening.

schoolClusters.city: Oud Metha and Al Mankhool
schoolClusters.note: The immediate catchment. These schools run Indian and British curricula, with IGCSE at 16 in the British stream, and they are reachable from Al Mankhool inside twenty minutes outside peak hours. Students we support attend schools in this cluster.

schoolClusters.city: Al Garhoud and Dubai Festival City

schools: Deira International School, Dubai Festival City

dubai/al-mankhool.modesIntro: Three shapes of support cover almost every request from this part of Dubai. All of them run online, one-to-one, over live video, with the tutor and the student sharing a screen and a working document.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one, term-long
modes.description: A fixed slot in the same subject each week, working a term ahead of the school's scheme of work rather than behind it. This is the shape that fixes a structural gap: a student who understands each lesson but cannot assemble a full paper. Most Al Mankhool families start with one subject at one session a week and add a second only if the first is holding.
bullets: Same tutor, same slot, reviewed at the end of each half-term

modes.title: Assessment-cycle block
modes.description: A short, dense block tied to a mock window or a final series. Six to ten sessions, built around marked scripts and timed papers rather than new content. The first session diagnoses from a real script; the last runs a full paper under exam conditions with the clock visible. This is what families ask for in January and again in March.
bullets: Diagnostic from a marked mock before any teaching happens

modes.title: Coursework clinic for IA, EE and TOK
modes.description: Structured sessions for the self-managed work: choosing a question that can be answered, building a timeline backwards from the school's internal deadline, and reading drafts against the published criteria. The student writes every sentence. The tutor gives feedback in writing on what the criteria reward and what is missing, which is the boundary IB rules set.

sections.heading: What an Al Mankhool parent is really asking for
paragraphs: The search is for a tutor in Al Mankhool. The need is almost always narrower: one subject, one level, one specific failure that showed up in a report or a mock. Answering the literal question first, lessons for Al Mankhool students run online, one-to-one, over live video, usually in a 17:00 or 18:30 slot, and the tutor is chosen for the paper your child sits rather than for proximity to Kuwait Street.

That substitution is worth examining rather than glossing over. A neighbourhood search assumes the useful variable is distance. For a Year 11 mathematics student it might be, because almost any competent mathematics teacher can help. For a Chemistry HL student three weeks from a scientific investigation deadline it is not. The useful variable is whether the tutor has marked that component, knows what the four criteria reward and can tell in ten minutes whether the proposed research question will survive contact with a school lab.

Bur Dubai is dense enough that a local pool exists. It is not deep enough to guarantee a specialist in Economics HL internal assessments or Computer Science solution development within a short drive of Al Mankhool. Online delivery widens the pool from one neighbourhood to the whole network, which is the entire argument for it. The counter-argument parents raise is attention, and it is a fair one: a teenager on a laptop can drift. The answer is structural rather than rhetorical, and it sits in how the session is run, which the next sections set out.

What this page will not do is pretend the neighbourhood is irrelevant. Where your child goes to school, how long the run takes and what time the house goes quiet all decide whether a tutoring plan survives past week three. Those are local facts, and they are in here.

sections.heading: What the school covers, and what your child is left holding
paragraphs: Every private school serving Al Mankhool teaches the full specification. The question is which parts of the course the timetable can supervise and which parts it can only set. The table below splits an IGCSE or DP course into those two columns, because almost every tuition request that reaches us is somewhere in the right-hand one.

Content delivery sits firmly with the school and generally works. A competent department will get through the syllabus, set homework against it and run two assessment points a term. What a timetable cannot do is sit beside one student while they attempt a full past paper under timed conditions, mark it against the published scheme and then talk through each lost mark. There are not enough teacher hours in a week for that across a cohort of ninety.

The self-managed components are where the gap widens into something a parent can see. An internal assessment has no weekly checkpoint. The Extended Essay has a supervisor who may be managing fifteen others. Past-paper practice is recommended rather than scheduled. A student with strong executive function handles all three; a student without one quietly does none of them until the deadline arrives, and the first visible sign is a predicted grade that drops in the spring of DP1.

Reading the table honestly tends to change what a family buys. Parents often arrive asking for help with the whole subject and leave with a six-session block on examination technique and an internal assessment timeline, which is usually what the evidence actually supported.

sections.heading: The self-managed assessments, with their actual limits
paragraphs: Parents are often surprised by how much of an IB or IGCSE grade is decided by work produced at home, and by how specific the constraints are. The limits in the table below are the ones students have to design to, and they change what a realistic timeline looks like. A 4,000-word Extended Essay cannot be written in a half-term; a set of three 800-word Economics commentaries can, if the articles are chosen early.

The internal assessment weighting is the figure worth internalising. In most IB Diploma subjects it accounts for roughly twenty per cent of the final subject grade, and in some it is higher. That is a full grade band available on work completed without an examiner in the room, against criteria published in the subject guide. A student who reads the criteria before planning rather than after drafting is working with information the school has already given them and most do not open.

Mark allocations by criterion matter just as much. The mathematics exploration is marked out of twenty across five criteria, with the largest single allocation on use of mathematics and the smallest on personal engagement and reflection. A student who writes beautifully about why they chose the topic and then uses mathematics at the level of the course rather than above it has optimised the wrong criterion. Reading the descriptors backwards from the top band is the single highest-value hour of coursework support available.

Confirm every limit and weighting against the current subject guide your child's school is teaching, because the IB revises guides on a rolling cycle and two cohorts in the same building can sit different versions. A tutor's job here is feedback on the student's own draft against those descriptors, and nothing further.

sections.heading: Where IGCSE marks actually go missing between Year 10 and the final paper
paragraphs: IGCSE failure modes are repetitive enough to be diagnosed from one marked paper. The most common is command-term drift: a question asks the student to explain and gets a description, or asks for a calculation and gets a method with no evaluated answer. Examiners mark to a scheme, and a scheme rewards the instruction given. This costs a strong student between four and ten marks per paper, which is often the difference between a 6 and a 7.

The second is unit and significant-figure discipline in the sciences and mathematics. A correct calculation recorded to the wrong precision, or with a unit dropped, loses the accuracy mark while keeping the method mark. Across three science papers that adds up to a grade boundary. It is pure habit and responds quickly to drilling, which makes it the first thing a good tutor fixes.

Third is time allocation. Students who have never run a full paper against a clock spend disproportionate effort on the first long-answer question and arrive at the last two with nine minutes. The marks lost there are not knowledge marks, and no amount of extra content teaching recovers them. One full timed paper, marked and talked through, usually changes a student's pacing permanently.

Fourth, and most consequential, is the Core and Extended tier decision in Cambridge subjects. Core caps the grade at C or 5. A student placed in Core in Year 10 because of a weak start, and never reviewed, carries that ceiling into the final series regardless of how much they improve. Any family in Al Mankhool whose child was tiered early should ask the department directly whether the entry can still be changed, and the deadline for that sits months before the exam.
bullets: Command-term errors are the largest single recoverable loss on most scripts

sections.heading: What tutoring costs in Bur Dubai, with the rates attributed
paragraphs: Most pages in this market refuse to publish a number. Three of the six strongest competing pages carry no price at all, and the two that do quote US dollars, which is not the currency a Dubai family transacts in. The table below gives the market bands in dirhams, with the provider who publishes each figure named beside it, so a parent can check the source rather than take our word for it.

These are market rates, not an IB Gram price list. What they are useful for is calibration. If a tutor in Bur Dubai quotes AED 500 an hour for IGCSE mathematics, that sits at the premium examiner end of the market and the family should ask what justifies it. If a quote comes in at AED 50 an hour for Chemistry HL, that is the university-student band, and it may be fine for content revision and unsuitable for internal assessment design.

Format changes the figure more than subject does. In-home visits carry travel inside the rate, which is why the published in-home bands sit well above the online ones for the same level of tutor. In a district like Al Mankhool, where parking is paid and the approach roads are slow between 16:00 and 19:00, that travel component is being paid for a journey that produces no teaching.

Monthly packages are also published in this market: around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and roughly AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Bestimate's 2026 estimates for a single weekly hour run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support.
