sections.heading: Online lessons against a home tutor for an Al Mankhool apartment
paragraphs: Home tutoring is a real service in Dubai and parents are right to ask about it. A tutor in the room reads body language, takes a book off the table and holds a distractible thirteen-year-old's attention more easily than a screen does. Anyone who claims otherwise is selling rather than explaining. The question for an Al Mankhool family is what that advantage costs and what it displaces.

The cost is visible in the market bands above: published in-home rates run materially higher than online rates for comparable tutors, and part of the gap is travel. In this district the journey is not trivial. Approach roads around BurJuman and Kuwait Street are slow through the late afternoon, parking is metered, and a tutor crossing from Barsha or Mirdif is pricing in forty minutes each way. That money buys transport.

What it displaces is choice. The pool of tutors willing to drive to Al Mankhool for a 17:00 session is a subset of the pool who teach that subject, and for a narrow requirement, Computer Science solution development, say, or Economics HL commentaries, the subset can be empty. Online delivery removes the geographic filter entirely. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE, so this is the trade we are describing rather than a neutral comparison, and it is better stated plainly than implied.

The attention problem is answered by how the session runs, not by where it happens. A shared document both parties write in, a visible timer on timed sections, screen sharing on the actual paper and a written note to the parent afterwards all do the work that presence in the room was doing. Families who try one trial session usually settle the question themselves within a week.

sections.heading: The academic-honesty line, written out
paragraphs: This part of the market has a problem, and a parent in Al Mankhool should know about it before engaging anyone. Operators in this SERP sell finished internal assessments at four-figure dirham prices. Buying one is academic malpractice under IB rules, and the consequence falls on the student: a withdrawn grade, potentially a withdrawn diploma, and a record that follows a university application. No tutor should be anywhere near that boundary, and a tutor who offers to cross it is a liability dressed as a shortcut.

The permitted side of the line is wide and genuinely useful. A tutor can teach the content a project needs. They can discuss whether a research question is answerable with the equipment available. They can explain what each criterion descriptor rewards, read a draft the student wrote and say in writing which descriptor is not yet met. They can help build a timeline backwards from the school's internal deadline and hold the student to it. All of that is teaching, and all of it is recorded.

The prohibited side is narrow and absolute. A tutor does not supply text. They do not restructure a draft so the student copies it back. They do not generate data, analyse it on the student's behalf, or edit prose to a finished state. They do not hand over material from another student's project. Each of those transfers authorship, and authorship is the thing being assessed.

The practical safeguard is documentation. Ask any tutor how they record coursework feedback, and ask to see it. Written feedback against criterion descriptors, kept and shareable with the school, protects the student in the only situation that matters: a question from the coordinator about where the work came from. A verbal-only arrangement leaves nothing to show.
bullets: Permitted: teaching content, scoping a question, explaining criteria, feedback in writing
Prohibited: supplying text, generating data, editing a draft to a finished state
Ask how coursework feedback is recorded before the first session
Keep every draft and every piece of feedback until the grade is confirmed

sections.heading: KHDA, the mandatory UAE subjects and the permit question
paragraphs: Private schools in Dubai are overseen by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which u.ae describes as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. KHDA publishes inspection outcomes on a six-band scale from Outstanding down to Very Weak. For a parent in Al Mankhool choosing between two schools, the useful reading is not the headline band but the subject-level judgements inside the report, because a school rated Good overall can be Acceptable in secondary mathematics, and that is the band your Year 11 student lives in.

Dubai's private-school market is large. The Dubai Media Office reported 387,441 students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, offering seventeen curricula, with the UK curriculum at 37 per cent of enrolment, Indian at 26, US at 14 and the International Baccalaureate at 7. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private-school fees in the emirate would not rise for 2026-27 under Dubai's second economic incentives package. For a family budgeting tuition alongside fees, that is a real and checkable anchor.

Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum. KHDA's guidelines require separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and state that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, and schools are required to ensure teachers of these subjects hold appropriate KHDA approval. Material for these subjects is tightly controlled: using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited.

On tutors themselves, the position is simple and parents should check it. Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone offering private tutoring without that permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule has been published, so any page quoting an amount is guessing. Ask a prospective tutor whether they hold the permit; it costs nothing to obtain and takes two working days through MoHRE's own service.

sections.heading: Starting, and what happens when no specialist is free
paragraphs: The sequence is short. A parent describes the subject, the level, the board and what prompted the call, ideally with a marked script or a school report attached. A specialist in that exact component is identified. A trial session runs at a time that fits the Al Mankhool school run. After it, the tutor says what they think the problem is and how many sessions it plausibly takes, and the family decides.

The honest part is the availability limit, which no competing page in this market discloses. Some combinations are thin. A Computer Science HL internal assessment, Economics HL commentaries in a specific week, Further Mathematics, Arabic as a first language at DP level: for these, a match can take several days rather than the same evening, and occasionally the right person is not free at the hour a family wants. When that happens we say so and offer the nearest real alternative, which may be a different slot, a different tutor profile or a short wait. What we do not do is put a general science tutor in front of a Chemistry HL investigation and hope.

Timing matters more than families expect. A student starting in October of DP1 is working with the whole internal assessment cycle ahead of them. A student starting in March of DP2 is doing damage limitation on examination technique, which is worth doing and is a smaller job than it needed to be. For IGCSE, the useful start points are the beginning of Year 10, the week after the Year 10 end-of-year exams, and the week the Year 11 mock results land.

Six weeks before a paper is not too late, and it does change what the sessions can achieve. At that distance the work is marked scripts, command terms, pacing and the three highest-yield topics, rather than a reteach of the syllabus. Families who come in at that point and accept the narrower scope generally get more out of it than families who insist on covering everything.
bullets: Send a marked script or report with the first enquiry; it halves the diagnosis
Trial session at a Gulf-time slot that fits the Bur Dubai school run
Availability on narrow components is disclosed, not papered over
Six weeks out, the work is technique and triage, and it still moves a grade

process.title: Tell us the component, not just the subject
process.description: Subject, level, board and the specific thing that went wrong: a mock paper, an internal assessment with no start, a topic missed during an absence. A syllabus code from the exam entry slip is the most useful single detail a parent can send, because it fixes which paper the tutor prepares for.

process.title: We match on the paper, then on the clock
process.description: A specialist in that subject and level is identified first, and availability is fitted around the Oud Metha and Al Garhoud school runs second. Most Al Mankhool students settle on a 17:00 or 18:30 Gulf-time slot, because anything earlier collides with the inbound afternoon traffic.

process.title: Trial session, working from real evidence
process.description: The first session runs on a marked script or a piece of the student's own coursework wherever one exists, rather than a general assessment. The tutor is looking for repeated error patterns, not a grade, and the student leaves with one concrete thing to change.

process.title: A plan with a session count attached
process.description: After the trial the tutor sets out what they think the problem is, what they would do about it and roughly how many sessions it takes. A plan without a number is not a plan. If the honest answer is four sessions rather than a term, that is what gets said.

process.title: Review at each half-term
process.description: Progress is checked against the school's own assessment points rather than our impression of it. If the plan is not working, the tutor changes or the scope narrows. Families pause during school exam weeks instead of doubling up, which protects the slot for the term after.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the component, not the year group
whyPoints.description: A tutor is assigned to Chemistry HL internal assessments or Cambridge 0580 Extended, not to 'secondary science' or 'Year 11 maths'. That is the difference between someone who can explain a topic and someone who knows what the mark scheme rewards on the paper your child sits in May.

whyPoints.title: Rates on this page are sourced
whyPoints.description: Every dirham figure here is attributed to the provider or research that published it, with the band stated. Three of the strongest competing pages in this market publish no price at all. A parent should be able to check a number rather than trust a claim about it.

whyPoints.title: The honesty line is written down
whyPoints.description: Coursework support is teaching, scoping and written feedback on the student's own draft. Operators in this market sell finished internal assessments; that risk lands on the student, not the seller. Our boundary is published so a family can hold us to it.

whyPoints.title: Availability is disclosed before you pay
whyPoints.description: Where a component is thinly covered, we say so and give a realistic match time rather than filling the slot with whoever is free. No competing page in this market discloses a coverage limit, which tells you something about how often the limit is hidden.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling that survives a Bur Dubai afternoon
whyPoints.description: Slots are set after the inbound run from Oud Metha, Al Garhoud or Al Jaddaf, not at a time that looks tidy on a timetable. Sessions move for a school exam week or an iftar timing shift rather than being lost, which is what keeps a plan alive past week three.

whyPoints.title: Written record after every session
whyPoints.description: A short note of what was covered, what the student got wrong and what to practise goes to the parent. For coursework, feedback against criterion descriptors is recorded and can be shown to the school if a coordinator ever asks where the help came from.

faqs.question: What do IB and IGCSE tutors charge for an Al Mankhool family?
faqs.answer: Market rates in Dubai run roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour for a qualified subject tutor working online, and AED 200 to 450 or more for an IB, IGCSE or A Level specialist. Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200; TutorChase publishes AED 270; Bestimate's 2026 tutoring-cost table puts the specialist band at AED 200 to 450 and above. In-home visits are quoted higher, roughly AED 180 to 500, because travel sits inside the fee. Those are market figures from the providers named, not an IB Gram price list. Our own figure depends on subject, level and weekly frequency, and comes with a trial session first.

faqs.question: My son's school taught the whole syllabus, so why is he still dropping marks?
faqs.answer: Because teaching a specification and rehearsing an examination are different tasks, and a timetable can only do the first properly. Marks on a strong student's script are usually lost to command-term drift, precision and unit errors, and pacing, rather than to missing knowledge. A question that says explain and receives a description gets the description marks only. Those losses are invisible in homework, which is untimed and marked kindly, and they only appear under a clock. One full paper run to time, marked against the published scheme and talked through line by line, usually identifies three repeated habits that account for most of the gap.

faqs.question: How many hours a week outside school does an IB Diploma really need?
faqs.answer: More than most families plan for, and the shape matters more than the total. Six subjects each setting homework, three internal assessments in progress, a 4,000-word Extended Essay and a 1,600-word Theory of Knowledge essay add up to a workload that cannot be absorbed in the hour before bed. The students who cope treat coursework as a weekly commitment of one or two protected hours per component from the start of DP1, rather than a block to be cleared later. The ones who struggle have no weekly deliverable on any of it, which is exactly the thing a scheduled session supplies.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with my daughter's Internal Assessment without crossing the honesty line?
faqs.answer: Yes, within clear limits. A tutor can teach the content the project needs, discuss whether the research question is answerable with the equipment available, explain what each criterion descriptor rewards, read a draft your daughter wrote and say in writing which descriptor is not yet met, and build a timeline backwards from the school's internal deadline. A tutor cannot supply text, restructure a draft for her to copy back, generate or analyse her data, or edit prose to a finished state. The authorship has to stay hers, because authorship is what the criteria assess. Ask any tutor to record coursework feedback in writing so the school can see it.

faqs.question: Which IB schools do Al Mankhool families usually drive to?
faqs.answer: The IB Diploma options nearest Bur Dubai sit across the creek rather than in the neighbourhood itself. Families from Al Mankhool commonly use schools in Dubai Festival City and Al Garhoud, and for an IB continuum from the primary years, Al Jaddaf and the Sobha Hartland area. Those runs are manageable off-peak and slow between 07:00 and 08:30. The practical effect on tutoring is that the student's afternoon is largely consumed by the return journey, so coursework sessions land at 17:00 or later. Named schools here are neighbourhood context; IB Gram has no affiliation with any of them.

faqs.question: Is there an IB World School inside Al Mankhool itself?
faqs.answer: Al Mankhool and the surrounding Bur Dubai blocks are mainly served by Indian-curriculum and British-curriculum schools, with IGCSE at sixteen in the British stream. The IB Diploma and IB continuum provision that these families use is a short drive away rather than on the doorstep, which is a genuine feature of this part of the city rather than a gap in our coverage. Check the KHDA school listing for current programmes at any specific school, because programmes are added and withdrawn between academic years and a prospectus is not always current on this point.

faqs.question: My child missed two weeks of Year 11 chemistry. Can that still be caught up?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and it is one of the cleaner tutoring jobs. A fortnight of a Cambridge 0620 or Pearson 4CH1 course is a defined block of content, and a specialist can establish exactly which specification points were covered from the scheme of work, teach them in two or three focused sessions and then test them with past-paper questions on those points only. The risk is not the content itself but the assumption later in the course that it is secure. Electrolysis and moles in particular reappear constantly, so a gap there compounds quietly until a mock exposes it.

faqs.question: Do lessons start after the BurJuman and Oud Metha traffic clears?
faqs.answer: That is how slots are set for this district. The inbound afternoon run along Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Road and around the Oud Metha roundabouts makes a 16:00 start unrealistic on most weekdays, so Al Mankhool students generally settle on 17:00 or 18:30 Gulf time. Because lessons are delivered online over live video, the session begins when the student sits down rather than when a tutor finds parking, which is the practical reason these slots hold through a bad traffic week. Weekend mornings are available and work well for coursework, where a longer block is more useful than an hour.

faqs.question: Does a private tutor working in Al Mankhool need a permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by a work permit introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so treat any page quoting an amount with caution. Ask a tutor directly whether they hold it.

faqs.question: What are the word limits on the IB work my child has to hand in?
faqs.answer: The Extended Essay runs to 4,000 words and the Theory of Knowledge essay to 1,600 words on a prescribed title. A science investigation is limited to around 3,000 words and marked out of 24 across four criteria. The mathematics exploration is a page-length rather than a word-count expectation, commonly around twelve to twenty pages, and is marked out of 20 across five criteria. Economics asks for three commentaries of 800 words each. An MYP personal project report sits between 1,500 and 3,500 words. Confirm each against the current subject guide your school teaches, because the IB revises guides on a rolling cycle.

faqs.question: How does the Extended Essay get supervised if the school supervisor is stretched?
faqs.answer: The school supervisor remains the person who signs the work off and who the IB holds responsible, and that cannot be delegated. What a stretched supervisor often cannot provide is weekly structure, and that is where external support is legitimate and useful. A tutor can help test whether a research question is answerable in 4,000 words, build a backwards timeline from the school's internal deadline, point to what the assessment criteria reward, and give written feedback on a draft the student wrote. The supervisor meetings still happen and still matter. Keep every piece of external feedback in writing so the school can see its scope.

faqs.question: What happens if no tutor covers my child's component in the week I ask?
faqs.answer: We tell you, and we give a realistic match time rather than filling the slot. Some combinations are genuinely thin: Computer Science solution development, Further Mathematics, Arabic as a first language at Diploma level, or a specific internal assessment window where several schools share a deadline. In those cases a match can take several days, and occasionally the right person is not free at the hour you want. The alternatives we offer are a different slot, a different tutor profile, or a short wait. Putting a general science tutor in front of a Chemistry HL investigation would waste your money and the student's time.

faqs.question: Are Arabic and Islamic Education compulsory at an Al Mankhool private school?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum. KHDA's guidelines require separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and state that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit. For the UAE Ministry of Education equivalency count on the British track, Arabic and Islamic Education are not included among the five required IGCSE or GCSE subjects.

faqs.question: How do we find out whether Cambridge or Pearson sets my child's IGCSE papers?
faqs.answer: Look at the exam entry slip or the statement of entry rather than the school prospectus, because several schools serving Bur Dubai enter different subjects with different boards in the same year group. The code is the giveaway: 0580 and 0625 are Cambridge, 4MA1 and 4PH1 are Pearson. It matters because the papers differ in structure, tiering and question style. Cambridge tiers many subjects into Core and Extended with a grade ceiling on Core; Pearson runs single-tier entry in most subjects. A tutor prepared for the wrong board is teaching correct content against the wrong assessment.

faqs.question: Does my child need five IGCSE subjects for a UAE university place?
faqs.answer: For UAE Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, the published requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two accredited Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic Education are not included among the five. One competing page in this market states six subjects, which does not match the published rule. Verify the current requirement on moe.gov.ae or with the attestation authority before acting on it, and note that equivalency is a ministry process, not something a tutor performs.

dubai/al-mankhool.closingHeading: Start with the script, not the subject
dubai/al-mankhool.closingBody: If there is a marked mock paper, a school report or an internal assessment draft in the house, send it with your first message. It tells a specialist more in five minutes than a conversation about the subject does in half an hour, and it usually narrows the job from a term of general tuition to a handful of targeted sessions. Tell us the subject, the level, the board and the slot that works after the Bur Dubai school run, and we will say honestly whether we have the right person free and what we think the work involves. Lessons are one-to-one and online, and the trial session comes before any commitment.

dubai/al-mizhar.tutorsIntro: These tutors cover both IGCSE boards, the IB Middle Years and Diploma programmes and the American-curriculum stages taught around the eastern suburbs. Tell us the bus arrival time rather than the school finish time, because in Al Mizhar those two numbers can be forty minutes apart.

intro.heading: The bus route is the first thing a tutoring plan has to respect
paragraphs: Al Mizhar is low-density villa housing on Dubai's eastern edge, bounded by Al Khawaneej Road and reaching towards the desert boundary. It is quiet, spacious and well suited to family life, and it has one characteristic that shapes every weekday: almost nobody attends school inside the district. The schools families use sit in Mirdif, Al Warqa, Al Qusais and the newer communities further out, and most children reach them by bus.

A school bus is not a car journey with more passengers. It collects along a route, which means the first child boards twenty or thirty minutes before the last, and in the afternoon the order reverses. A student living at the far end of a route can leave school at 2:45pm and walk through the door at 3:40pm, having spent nearly an hour sitting still without being able to work. Parents reasonably describe this as a short commute, because the distance is short. The clock disagrees.

The consequence for tutoring is specific. A session booked at 4:00pm meets a student who has been home for twenty minutes, has not eaten properly and has not changed out of uniform. The first ten minutes of a paid hour go on settling, and the student's useful attention is already partly spent. Push the same session to 4:45pm and it meets a different child. Nothing about the tutor changed; the plan changed.

The second feature of this district is that the evening has more in it than a tutoring page usually assumes. Homework from a full timetable. The mandatory UAE subjects, which Dubai private schools must run alongside the licensed international curriculum and which generate their own written work. Often an activity, because villa communities out here build their social life around sport and clubs. In many households a religious or community commitment on specific evenings. Adding an hour to that week without removing anything is how a tutoring arrangement dies in week nine.

Third, this is a district of long-settled families rather than short-term arrivals. Children frequently stay at the same school from primary through to sixteen, parents know the school well, and expectations are set by siblings who went before. That is an advantage: the decision to bring in a tutor here is usually made deliberately, in response to something specific, rather than in a panic. It also means a family will notice quickly if an arrangement is not producing anything.

So this page starts with the clock and the evening, then moves to building a plan that survives a full term, what the market charges in dirhams, the comparison with a tutor who has to drive out here, and what a tutor may and may not do with internally assessed work. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every Al Mizhar lesson is one-to-one over live video, which is also why a session can start at 4:45pm without anyone adding a second journey to the afternoon.

A bus route can add forty minutes to a short journey

dubai/al-mizhar.programmesIntro: Three systems account for most Al Mizhar enquiries. For each, the detail that matters here is how the workload lands on an evening that is already short.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Terminal papers at sixteen, with Cambridge examining in June and November series and tiering many subjects into Core and Extended, and Pearson Edexcel examining in May/June and November on a 9-1 scale. Year 11 generates sustained written homework across eight or nine subjects at once, which is what makes the evening arithmetic bite.
programmes.countryNote: An Al Mizhar Year 11 student with a long bus route is trying to fit nine subjects' homework into the hours between four and nine, alongside the mandatory UAE subjects. The useful tutoring decision here is often to cover one subject properly and let the rest be managed, rather than to add two hours and lose sleep.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four lettered criteria with task-specific descriptors rather than percentages. Assessment is continuous, so the pressure arrives as a steady stream of tasks rather than a single examination, and the final year carries the Personal Project, which is self-managed.
programmes.countryNote: Mirdif and the eastern suburbs contain IB continuum schools, so many Al Mizhar students are in this programme from an early age. The Personal Project in the last year is the usual trigger for an enquiry, because it is the first assessment the student has to structure without being told how.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internally assessed components carry real weight and run on school-set deadlines that arrive well before anything the board publishes. The second half of DP1 is where content, coursework and mocks collide.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students out here face the longest afternoons in the district, because the nearest continuum schools still involve a journey and sixth-form timetables often finish later. Sessions are usually placed from 4:45pm, with longer technique work moved to a weekend morning.

programmes.name: American-curriculum stages and AP preparation
programmes.description: Continuous assessment through coursework, quizzes and a grade point average, with Advanced Placement examinations for students targeting selective universities. The grade point average means a weak term has a longer shadow than it does in a terminal system, so early intervention is worth more.
programmes.countryNote: The eastern suburbs include American-curriculum schools, and families here often ask about equivalency as well as grades. The published Ministry of Education requirements for the American track are test-based, and they are set out later on this page with the standards as published.

dubai/al-mizhar.subjectsIntro: Demand here follows the school mix: mathematics and the sciences at the top, Arabic and Islamic Education as a steady second stream, and coursework support in the Middle Years and Diploma years.

subjects.name: Mathematics 0580 and 4MA1
subjects.levels: Cambridge IGCSE Extended and Pearson Edexcel
subjects.description: The highest volume subject in the district. Because fluency decays without practice, two shorter sessions across a week outperform one long block for a student who is already tired by five o'clock after a bus route.

subjects.name: Physics 0625
subjects.description: Electricity and circuits take most of the losses, and the practical paper rewards a method precise enough for a stranger to follow. Both are drillable in short bursts, which suits a short evening better than a long explanation.

subjects.name: Chemistry 0620
subjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and quantitative questions separate the upper grades. This is the subject students most often cannot start alone, so it is the poorest candidate for being left to independent homework in a crowded week.

subjects.name: Biology 0610
subjects.description: Mark-scheme vocabulary is where the marks go. A confident paraphrase scores nothing where a specific term is required, and correcting that is quick, visible and achievable in short sessions.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The proof-and-calculus Diploma route. Higher Level assumes automaticity built over months, and a student who reaches it without Additional Mathematics usually needs a short foundational block before the course content is workable.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and calculator fluency. Marks leak on interpretation questions that ask what a value means in context, which is a different skill from calculating it and has to be taught explicitly.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: Dubai private schools must run Arabic for every student, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab learners because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. The first-language route carries a heavier written load than families expect.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.description: Required alongside the international curriculum, taught in Standard Arabic for Arab students and in the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arab students. Additional or different content needs prior ministry permission, so tutoring works strictly from the school's material.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Two external papers and oral assessment, with the individual oral linking a global issue to two texts, one in translation. Preparation and structure carry more marks than style, and the planning can be done in short sessions.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Tools applied to a real organisation rather than described in the abstract. The research project needs a narrow question and genuine source material, and students in business-owning households frequently have better access than they realise.

dubai/al-mizhar.regionsIntro: These are the communities sharing Al Mizhar's roads, bus routes and school options. The timing advice shifts with the length of the route rather than the distance.

regions.name: Mirdif
regions.note: The nearest school cluster, with IB continuum and British-curriculum options inside the community. Children who attend school here have the shortest afternoon in the district and can sometimes hold a 4:15pm start.

regions.name: Al Khawaneej
regions.note: Villa communities further east with no private secondary school inside them. Routes are longer again, and a 4:45pm start is the realistic earliest for a student on a full bus run.

regions.name: Al Warqa
regions.note: South-west towards Al Aweer, with large schools and correspondingly long bus routes. Families here often share Al Mizhar's timetable almost exactly.

regions.name: Al Rashidiya
regions.note: West towards the airport. Shorter runs into Al Garhoud and Dubai Festival City, but the routes cross airport traffic, which congests earlier than purely residential roads.

regions.name: Nad Al Hamar
regions.note: South towards Ras Al Khor, with quieter roads and a shorter run into the Festival City schools. One of the easier catchments in this group for an earlier session.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis
regions.note: South-east along Sheikh Mohammed Bin Zayed Road, apartment living with schools serving the community. Working parents often prefer a later slot to overlap with arriving home.

regions.name: Dubai International Academic City
regions.note: Further south-east, with university campuses and a few schools. Older students travelling this way arrive late enough that weekday technique work is better moved to the weekend.

regions.name: International City
regions.note: Dense apartment housing to the south with mixed curricula. Bus routes are long and often shared between several schools, which pushes arrivals past four.

schoolClusters.note: The nearest cluster, mixing IB continuum, British and American curriculum schools with catchments drawn from the eastern villa communities. Because the schools sit in Mirdif rather than in Al Mizhar itself, almost every secondary student here takes a bus or a car. Students we support attend schools across this cluster.

It is deliberately short because an hour of real attention at that point in the day is more than most students have left, and a shorter session that lands fully beats a longer one that drifts.

sections.heading: What a long bus route actually takes out of the day
paragraphs: A school bus serving a villa community collects along a route with several stops, which means the child who boards first in the morning is the child who disembarks last in the afternoon, or the reverse, depending on how the route is run. For a family at the far end that produces a journey of forty to fifty minutes in each direction over a distance a car covers in fifteen.

The time is not neutral. A student on a bus cannot write, cannot spread out a past paper, and in practice cannot revise beyond looking at a phone. Parents sometimes propose using it for flashcards, which works for a fortnight and then stops. Treat the journey as lost time for planning purposes and the plan becomes realistic; treat it as potential study time and the plan assumes an hour that never materialises.

There is a second effect that matters more than the first. A child who has been sitting still, often in warm conditions, for most of an hour arrives flat rather than energetic. The restorative sequence, a drink, food, a change of clothes, twenty minutes of nothing, is not indulgence; it is what makes the next two hours usable. Families who skip it to start tutoring earlier reliably report that the sessions were fine at first and then the child became resistant.

The practical rule we use in this district: session start equals bus arrival plus forty-five minutes, or bus arrival plus thirty if the student is older and eats quickly. For most Al Mizhar households that puts the first honest weekday slot at 4:45pm, and for the longest Al Warqa and Al Qusais routes at 5:00pm or later.

sections.heading: The evening arithmetic: what time does a Year 11 student sleep?
paragraphs: This is the calculation almost no tutoring page performs, and it is the one that decides whether an added hour helps or harms. Take a Year 11 student in this district on a long bus route. Home at 3:45pm. Food, change, decompress until 4:30pm. Homework across eight or nine subjects, realistically ninety minutes to two hours in Year 11, including written work for the mandatory UAE subjects. That is 6:30pm at best.

Then the household. An evening meal, family time, a shower, possibly an activity on two or three evenings and a community or religious commitment on another. Teenagers also need some genuinely unstructured time, and removing it entirely is not a neutral decision. By the time that is accounted for, a reasonable lights-out at ten leaves perhaps one spare hour on a good evening and none on a busy one.

An hour of tutoring has to come from somewhere in that sequence, and the options are limited: from homework, from the activity, from family time, or from sleep. Three of those four are defensible depending on the family's priorities. The fourth is not, and it is the one that quietly gets chosen, because sleep is the only item nobody has to negotiate for.

The honest recommendation that follows is to add less than families expect. One subject, forty-five minutes, twice a week at most, placed where it replaces the least productive hour rather than stacking on top. Where two or three subjects genuinely need attention, sequence them across terms rather than running them in parallel. A rested student working on one subject outperforms a tired student working on three, and that is not a slogan; it is the only version of this plan that is still running in March.

sections.heading: The UAE week, and why Monday is the wrong day to start
paragraphs: Most Dubai private schools now run a Monday to Friday week with a Saturday and Sunday weekend, and that shape has consequences for where a tutoring session should sit. Monday afternoon is the worst available slot. The student has just come off a weekend, the week's homework has not yet been set, and there is nothing concrete to work on, so the session fills with general revision that nobody remembers by Wednesday.

Tuesday and Wednesday are the strongest weekday slots. By then the week's work exists, the student knows what they do not understand, and there is still time to act on the session before the end of the week. Thursday is serviceable but competes with end-of-week fatigue. Friday afternoon, in most households, is the least productive hour of the week by a wide margin.

The second scheduling point is the gap. Two sessions on consecutive days give the student no time to attempt anything alone, which means the second session reviews the first rather than the student's own work. Two sessions separated by two or three days produce independent practice in between, which is where the learning actually consolidates. Tuesday and Thursday is a better pair than Tuesday and Wednesday, every time.

Finally, the weekend. A Saturday or Sunday morning is the highest-quality hour available to a student in this district, because there is no journey, no fatigue and no evening pressing on it. For anything requiring sustained concentration, a full timed paper, essay planning, a coursework review, that is where it belongs. Families protective of the weekend often change their minds after comparing one weekend session with one Thursday session.

sections.heading: Building a plan that still exists in week nine
paragraphs: Tutoring arrangements rarely end with a decision. They thin out. Week one is excellent. Week four is good. Week six has a clash and gets moved. Week seven is cancelled for an activity. Week eight is rescheduled and then forgotten. By week ten nobody has formally stopped and nothing is happening. Recognising the pattern early is worth more than any individual lesson.

The first defence is to schedule for the busy week rather than the quiet one. If the student has football on Wednesdays for two terms, a Wednesday slot is not a slot. If an activity runs in one term only, plan the change now rather than discovering it. A plan written against the real calendar survives; a plan written against an average week does not.

The second is to name the warning signs in advance, so that a reschedule is treated as information rather than an inconvenience. One moved session is noise. Two moved sessions in three weeks means the slot is wrong and should be changed, not endured. A session where no independent work has been attempted means the format is wrong, usually too much content and not enough practice. A student who arrives unable to say what they want from the hour has disengaged, and more hours will not fix that.

The third is the review. At six weeks we compare the school's next assessment to the position recorded before the first session, and the tutor explains the result either way. Four outcomes are honest: continue, change the format, change the subject, or stop. In a district of long-settled families who talk to each other, an arrangement that cannot explain itself is correctly abandoned, and we would rather reach that conclusion at six weeks than at six months.

sections.heading: What tutoring costs around Al Mizhar and Mirdif, in dirhams
paragraphs: Most tutoring pages serving this market publish no price, and two of the ones that do quote US dollars rather than dirhams. The figures below are market rates attributed to the provider that published them. They describe the market and are not an IB Gram price list.

Budget online tutoring from university students or generalists is advertised from roughly AED 45 to AED 65 an hour, with one platform quoting from about AED 33. Qualified subject tutors working online sit between roughly AED 150 and AED 300, with one agency publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one visits run roughly AED 180 to AED 350 on one published index and AED 200 to AED 500 among independent tutors, because travel sits inside the rate. Specialist IB, IGCSE and A Level tutors are quoted at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, one agency at AED 270, and one premium provider at AED 650.

In the eastern suburbs the in-home premium is larger than the published ranges suggest, for a reason specific to the geography. A tutor driving out to Al Mizhar at five in the afternoon is making a long journey in the wrong direction, and the ones who will do it regularly are either local, which narrows the pool, or charging for the drive, which raises the rate. Families here are more likely than most to be quoted at the upper end of the in-home band.

Monthly figures circulating in this market include about AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits. One published index estimates weekly one-hour tutoring at roughly AED 240 to AED 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 or more for specialist examination-year support. Set against school fees, which KHDA confirmed will not rise in Dubai for 2026-27, one subject is a modest addition and three is not.

sections.heading: A tutor driving out to Al Mizhar against one-to-one online
paragraphs: The in-home option is a genuine part of this market and it deserves an honest comparison rather than a dismissal. An adult at the table sees written working without asking, can annotate a page, and gives a younger child a presence that no screen reproduces. For some children that outweighs everything else, and other providers will arrange it.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. In the eastern suburbs the arithmetic is unusually one-sided. A tutor reaching Al Mizhar for five in the afternoon is driving out against the flow at the worst hour, and the pool of people willing to do that weekly is small and local. A family needing a Higher Level chemistry specialist or a Pearson Edexcel mathematics specialist is asking for a narrow skill; adding a geographic constraint to a narrow skill usually produces whoever is available rather than whoever is right.

There is also the practical point about the arrival. An in-home session scheduled for 5:00pm starts when the tutor gets there, and in this part of Dubai that is an estimate. For a household already working with a short evening, a tutor arriving fifteen minutes late does not shorten the lesson; it pushes homework, the meal and bedtime back by fifteen minutes each.

What we give up is real and worth naming. Unprompted sight of the page, replaced by a phone or tablet camera angled over the working. The social presence of an adult, which matters more for younger students. And independence from a connection, which is a genuine advantage on the days when the connection is poor.

sections.heading: Coursework: the Personal Project and the Internal Assessment
paragraphs: The Middle Years Personal Project is the first assessment most students in this district have to structure by themselves, and it arrives in the same year as mock examinations. The Diploma Internal Assessments follow the same pattern at a higher level: self-managed work, published criteria, school-set deadlines ahead of anything the board publishes. Both are the point at which families most often look for help and most often encounter the worst offers in this market.

One provider found in this search sells completed Internal Assessments outright. That is an academic-integrity breach which triggers a malpractice investigation, and under board rules the consequence falls on the candidate who declared the work as their own. No part of that risk sits with the seller.

The legitimate boundary is specific. A tutor may teach the underlying content, explain each criterion and what its marks reward, say whether a research question or project goal is viable before weeks are spent on it, warn that a method will not generate usable evidence, read a draft and name the criterion that is under-served, and ask the questions that make a student see their own gap. A tutor may not supply text, rewrite sections, generate data, choose the question, or edit a draft into a finished state. The student declares the work and must be able to discuss it.

We also do not redistribute syllabuses, past papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables. Those belong to the IB, Cambridge and Pearson. We reference them, name the official source, and work with what the school has legitimately issued. A provider offering a downloadable library of board material has told you something useful about how it operates.

sections.heading: Starting, and the coverage limits we will tell you about
paragraphs: Three things before a first session: a recent marked script or school report, the board and syllabus code with the tier where one applies, and the bus arrival time rather than the school finishing time. The third is the one families leave out and the one that determines whether the slot works.

The first session is a diagnostic. The tutor works through the script with your child and writes a short note afterwards naming the actual gap, which is often not what the report named. Sometimes that note says a fortnight of structured independent practice would do more than a tutor would, and we would rather write it than sell a term to a family who will notice.

On availability, plainly. The weekday window from 4:30pm to 6:00pm is the one every family in the eastern suburbs wants, and for scarce Higher Level subjects it fills. When the hour you want is gone there are three honest options: a different hour with the specialist you want, your hour with a tutor whose subject fit is good rather than ideal, or a weekend morning. For a student on a long bus route the weekend morning is frequently the better choice on its own merits.

And where we cannot help: a narrow Higher Level subject with a coursework deadline inside six weeks, or an unusual language pairing, can take over a week to match with the right person. We say that at the enquiry rather than accepting the booking. No competitor page in this market publishes a coverage limit, which is exactly why families keep discovering one after paying for it.

faqs.question: What time should a tutoring session start for a child on a long school bus route in Al Mizhar?
faqs.answer: Bus arrival plus thirty to forty-five minutes. A route serving the eastern villa communities can keep a child on the road for forty to fifty minutes over a distance a car covers in fifteen, and they arrive flat rather than energetic. A drink, food, a change of clothes and twenty minutes of nothing are what make the next two hours usable. For most Al Mizhar households that puts the first honest weekday slot at 4:45pm, and later again on the longest Al Warqa and Al Qusais routes.

faqs.question: Can my child revise on the school bus?
faqs.answer: In practice, no, and planning on the assumption that they can is how a schedule ends up an hour short. A student on a bus cannot write, cannot spread out a past paper and cannot concentrate reliably in a moving vehicle with other children. Flashcards work for a fortnight and then stop. Treat the journey as lost time when you build the week; the plan becomes realistic rather than optimistic, and nobody ends up blaming the child for an hour that never existed.

faqs.question: How many hours of tutoring can a Year 11 student in the eastern suburbs actually absorb?
faqs.answer: Less than most families assume. Count the evening: home at 3:45pm, settled by 4:30pm, ninety minutes to two hours of homework across eight or nine subjects plus written work for the mandatory UAE subjects, a meal, an activity on some evenings, and a reasonable bedtime. That leaves roughly one spare hour on a good evening and none on a busy one. One subject, forty-five minutes, twice a week at most, placed where it replaces the least productive hour, is the honest answer.

faqs.question: Which weekday is the best one for a tutoring session?
faqs.answer: Tuesday or Wednesday. Monday afternoon is the worst available slot, because the week's work has not been set and the session fills with general revision nobody remembers. By Tuesday the student knows what they do not understand and there is still time to act on the session before the week ends. Thursday competes with fatigue and Friday afternoon is usually the least productive hour of the week. If you need two sessions, separate them by two or three days rather than putting them on consecutive days.

faqs.question: Is it worth using a weekend morning for tutoring instead of a school night?
faqs.answer: For anything requiring sustained concentration, yes, and it is the highest-quality hour available in this district. There is no journey behind it, no fatigue from a full school day and no evening pressing on the end of it. A full timed paper, essay planning or a coursework review belongs there. Families protective of the weekend often change their view after comparing one weekend session with one Thursday session, because the difference in what gets done is visible rather than theoretical.

faqs.question: Do you send tutors to villas in Al Mizhar or Al Khawaneej?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. Out here the arithmetic is unusually clear: a tutor driving east for a five o'clock session is travelling against the flow at the worst hour, the pool willing to do it weekly is small and local, and the arrival time becomes an estimate that pushes homework, the meal and bedtime back by however long the road takes.

faqs.question: Why are in-home tutoring rates higher in the eastern suburbs?
faqs.answer: Because the drive is long and the willing pool is small. Published market figures for in-home visits run roughly AED 180 to AED 350 on one cost index and AED 200 to AED 500 among independent tutors, with travel sitting inside the rate. Families in Al Mizhar, Al Khawaneej and Al Warqa are more likely to be quoted at the upper end of that band than families in central Dubai, because a tutor making an afternoon journey out here is giving up more of their working day to reach you.

faqs.question: How do we stop a tutoring arrangement from quietly fading out by week nine?
faqs.answer: Name the warning signs before they happen. One moved session is noise. Two moved sessions in three weeks means the slot is wrong and should be changed rather than endured. A session that begins by doing last week's set task means the format is wrong, usually too much content and not enough practice. Three weeks with no written note from the tutor means nobody is tracking it. Schedule against the busy week rather than an average one, and record a starting position so the six-week review has something to measure.

faqs.question: What is the Personal Project and can a tutor help with it?
faqs.answer: It is the self-managed project at the end of the Middle Years Programme, assessed against published criteria, and for most students it is the first piece of work they have to structure without being told how. It lands in the same year as mock examinations, which is why it generates so many enquiries. A tutor can explain the criteria, say whether a project goal is viable, warn where the evidence will not support it, and review a draft to name the weak criterion. A tutor cannot write any part of it.

faqs.question: Which subjects should an Al Mizhar family tutor first if they can only afford one?
faqs.answer: The subject where the grade sits closest to a boundary, not the subject the child finds hardest or dislikes most. A grade that is two marks below a boundary can often be moved in a term with technique work alone, while a subject that is three grades adrift usually needs a structural rebuild across two terms. Ask the school which it is, send the marked script, and sequence the subjects across terms rather than running two or three in parallel on an evening that has no room.

faqs.question: Does Arabic or Islamic Education tutoring have to follow the school's material?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is a real constraint rather than a preference. KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies in all Dubai private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students because the expectations and the language of instruction differ. For these subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited, so tutoring works from what the school teaches rather than from an outside scheme.

faqs.question: Our school is American curriculum. What will my child need for UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: The published requirements are test-based. English proficiency can be shown with a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT. Mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Mathematics test, and the guidance states that should be in place before applying. No EmSAT requirement appears in the guidance we have read, and no IB points figure is published that we can source. Confirm the current position with the Ministry of Education directly.

faqs.question: How long does it take to match a tutor for a specialist Higher Level subject out here?
faqs.answer: Longer than for mainstream subjects, and we say so at the enquiry. For IGCSE and Standard Level subjects a first session is usually arranged within a few days once we have the marked script, the code and your preferred slot. A narrow Higher Level subject with a coursework deadline inside six weeks, or an unusual language pairing, can take over a week to fill with the right person. No page in this market publishes a coverage limit, which is why families keep discovering one after they have paid.

faqs.question: What should we send before booking a first session in Al Mizhar?
faqs.answer: Three things. One recent marked script or report, so a specialist can see where the marks actually went rather than hearing it described. The board and syllabus code, with the tier for Cambridge subjects. And the bus arrival time on a normal weekday, which is the detail families leave out and the one that determines whether the slot holds. With those, the first session is a diagnostic that ends in a written recommendation rather than an hour spent establishing basics.

dubai/al-mizhar.closingHeading: Count the evening, then book the hour
dubai/al-mizhar.closingBody: Al Mizhar families rarely have a teaching problem. They have a clock problem that looks like a teaching problem. A bus route adds forty minutes nobody budgeted for, nine subjects' homework and the mandatory UAE subject work fill the next two hours, and the spare hour that tutoring is supposed to occupy turns out to be the one the student was sleeping in. Work out where the hour is coming from first. Then set the session at bus arrival plus a proper break, put it on a Tuesday or a Thursday, move the long timed papers to a weekend morning, and record a starting point so six weeks later the question has an answer. Every lesson is one-to-one over live video.

dubai/al-muteena.tutorsIntro: Enquiries from Al Muteena often start with a problem the school cannot solve: an option block that excluded the subject a student now needs, a repeat decision, or an entry sat outside the school. The tutors below are matched to a syllabus code rather than to a timetable, which is what a candidate without a class actually requires.

intro.heading: The student with no class, and the syllabus with no teacher
paragraphs: Al Muteena sits inland from the Deira coast strip, dense, long-established and well served by the metro, with Abu Hail and Hor Al Anz either side of it and the oldest private schools in the emirate within a short ride. It is a district of apartments and long tenancies, and the families here are more likely than most in Dubai to have been using the same schools for a decade or more.

Among the enquiries that come from this part of the city, a particular group recurs. A Year 11 student needs an additional IGCSE subject the school's option block never offered. A student has missed a grade and the family has to decide between a November resit and a repeat year. A candidate is out of step with their year group after a move, an illness or a family year abroad. In each case there is a syllabus and no class, which is self-study in its purest and least supported form.

This is the hardest situation in secondary education and the least written about. A student inside a class has a teacher setting the pace, a cohort to calibrate against, mock examinations on a fixed date and somebody noticing when a deadline approaches. A candidate studying alone has none of those. The syllabus is public, the papers are available, and the entire burden of sequencing, pacing, timing and self-assessment sits on a sixteen-year-old.

The second thing these cases have in common is administrative. An entry outside the normal school route involves decisions a family has never had to make: which series, which centre, which components, what a practical or coursework element requires when there is no laboratory and no teacher to supervise it. Those decisions have deadlines that close months before the paper, and nobody sends a reminder.

This page is built for those cases. It covers what to do when a school cannot offer a subject, what a private candidate actually has to arrange and in what order, how practical and coursework components work without a class, how to structure self-study with no teacher setting the pace, the calendar counted backwards from a private entry, and how to decide between a resit and a repeat. Lessons are delivered online, one to one, over live video, and IB Gram does not make home visits in Dubai, which is a service offered only in India. One structural note before any of it: this page separates what a tutor can do from what only a board or an examination centre can do, because a candidate outside a school has nobody else drawing that line for them. Every date quoted comes from Cambridge or Pearson directly, and every AED figure is a market rate attributed to the provider that published it in October 2026.

dubai/al-muteena.programmesIntro: The three structures below behave very differently for a student outside a normal class, and the differences are practical rather than philosophical. Private entry is routine in one of them and close to impossible in another.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: The most accessible route for a candidate outside a class, because many subjects are assessed entirely by written paper and the syllabuses are public. Cambridge runs June and November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Component availability varies, and some options carry alternatives designed for candidates without laboratory access.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the practical question is which centre will accept the entry and which components it offers. Independent examination centres in the emirate do accept private candidates in some subjects, and the board's own centre list is the place to start rather than a tutoring site. Ask about components, fees and deadlines in the same enquiry.

programmes.name: A Level and AS Level
programmes.description: Also commonly sat outside a school, particularly for an additional subject or a retake. The content depth makes self-study harder than at IGCSE, and the practical endorsement in sciences is the component that most often blocks a private entry. For Ministry of Education equivalency, one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, is what the published guidance states.
programmes.countryNote: A retake decision at this level is usually driven by a university offer rather than by the grade itself, so the first question is what the institution will accept and by when. Ask them in writing before committing to a series, because a resit that arrives after a deadline is an expensive way to confirm a place already lost.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Not a programme a candidate can realistically take outside a school. It requires a registered IB World School to deliver it, with internal assessment marked by teachers and moderated externally, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. A student out of step with a Diploma cohort has a school conversation ahead of them, not a private entry.
programmes.countryNote: For a Diploma student in difficulty, the realistic options are school-internal: adjusting levels early in Diploma Year 1, or in some cases moving to the Diploma Courses route for individual certificates rather than the full Diploma. Both are school decisions. Ask the IB coordinator what is administratively possible and by what date.

dubai/al-muteena.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects most often studied without a class in this part of Dubai, usually because an option block excluded them or a grade needs retaking. Each note names what makes it workable or difficult alone.

subjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics
subjects.description: The most commonly retaken subject and one of the more manageable alone, because it is assessed entirely by written paper and the question types repeat predictably across series. The risk is pacing: a candidate without deadlines covers the comfortable topics and leaves the cumulative ones until there is no time to secure them.

subjects.name: IGCSE Additional Mathematics
subjects.description: Taken by students who need more mathematics than their option block allowed, often ahead of A Level Mathematics. Demanding but self-containable, since it is paper-assessed. It is a reasonable private entry for a strong candidate and a poor one for a student still insecure in Extended material.

subjects.name: IGCSE Economics
subjects.description: Workable alone because the assessment is written and the syllabus is clearly bounded. Marks are lost on command terms and on diagram accuracy, both of which need correction by somebody reading the candidate's own answers rather than self-marking against an answer key.

subjects.name: IGCSE Business Studies
subjects.description: Case application rather than recall, which is harder to self-assess than it looks: a candidate marking their own work tends to credit accurate content that the scheme would not reward because it never engaged with the stimulus organisation.

subjects.name: IGCSE Sociology
subjects.description: Frequently added by students whose school does not offer it. Self-study suits the content, but the extended evaluative answers require someone to mark them against the criteria, since the gap between a competent description and a credited evaluation is invisible from inside.

subjects.name: IGCSE Computer Science
subjects.description: Theory is self-containable; the problem-solving paper rewards pseudocode conventions that a self-taught programmer will not naturally follow. A candidate who codes well can still lose heavily on the written conventions, which is quick to fix with correction.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Within the Diploma rather than a private route, but included because students repeating a Diploma year often change mathematics route at the same time. Modelling and statistics with the calculator assumed; check destination prerequisites before switching for difficulty reasons.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy decides a large share of the marks. For a student repeating Diploma Year 1, this is one of the subjects where a second pass genuinely helps, because the commentary portfolio benefits from having been attempted once already.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Evaluation of studies rather than recall of them is what the scheme rewards, which is the single most common reason an able student stalls in the middle band. The internal assessment requires a replication to a specified structure and is marked within the school.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Placement matters more than tutoring: a student in English B who should be in English A, or the reverse, is mismarked rather than badly taught. Settle the placement from a marked timed piece before buying any support.

dubai/al-muteena.regionsTitle: Al Muteena and the Deira districts around it
dubai/al-muteena.regionsIntro: This is a dense, well-connected part of old Dubai, and the journeys here are short but congested. These are the districts an Al Muteena family actually uses.

regions.name: Abu Hail
regions.note: Immediately north on the Green Line, equally dense and sharing school choices. Students here and in Al Muteena often travel independently by metro, which makes an early-evening session slot genuinely workable.

regions.name: Hor Al Anz
regions.note: East towards the coast road, densely populated and feeding the same cluster of schools. The two districts ask for the same subjects in the same terms, so specialist slots in this cluster fill together.

regions.name: Al Muraqqabat
regions.note: South, mixed residential and commercial, with heavy daytime traffic that lingers into the afternoon. A fixed session time after half past four avoids most of it.

regions.name: Naif and Deira
regions.note: The historic core to the south-west, containing some of the oldest private schools in the emirate. Multi-generational enrolment is common, and so is a school choice that was made for an older sibling a decade ago.

regions.name: Al Qusais
regions.note: Inland, with a large concentration of established private schools across Indian, British and IB curricula. Many Al Muteena students are enrolled here, and it is also where option blocks most often fail to include a wanted subject.

regions.name: Al Garhoud
regions.note: Towards the creek and the airport, with British and IB campuses taking a share of students from this district. Airport traffic is an extra afternoon variable that the western suburbs do not have.

regions.name: Oud Metha
regions.note: Across the creek, with several of the emirate's largest schools. The journey is longer and more predictable, which makes a weekly slot easier to hold than the shorter but less reliable inner-Deira runs.

regions.name: Al Nahda
regions.note: North-east towards the Sharjah boundary. Families living that side plan around the border movement, which is the single biggest constraint on when a weekday session can start.

schoolClusters.city: Al Muteena, Abu Hail and Al Qusais
schoolClusters.note: The nearest cluster, dominated by long-established schools with large year groups across Indian and British curricula. Option blocks here are efficient rather than broad, which is precisely why a student sometimes needs a subject the school does not run.

schoolClusters.city: Deira, Al Garhoud and Oud Metha
schoolClusters.note: The wider ring, holding the emirate's oldest schools alongside British and IB campuses. Families here commonly ask what happens if a subject, a level or a whole year has to be repeated, because the schools are large and the cohorts are fixed.

dubai/al-muteena.modesIntro: Three formats match the cases that come from this district. All run over live video, which is the only practical way to put a specialist on a syllabus nobody nearby is teaching.

modes.title: Class of one on a full syllabus
modes.description: For a candidate studying a subject with no class attached. The tutor becomes the pace-setter: a sequenced plan across the available months, weekly content targets, scheduled internal checkpoints that function as mocks, and timed papers from early rather than late. The structure is the product here as much as the teaching.
bullets: A written sequence across the months remaining, with weekly targets
Checkpoint assessments on fixed dates, marked against the scheme
Timed full papers from the midpoint, not the final fortnight
Explicit coverage of the topics a candidate would naturally avoid

modes.title: Resit block on a named gap
modes.description: For a student who has missed a grade and is entering a further series. The work starts from the marked script where one is available, or from a timed paper sat cold where it is not, and targets the specific question types that failed rather than the whole syllabus again.
bullets: Diagnosis from the actual script or a cold timed paper
Targets the failed question types, not a full re-teach
Honest early judgement on whether the series is realistic
Review point before the entry deadline, while the decision is reversible

modes.title: Decision session before committing
modes.description: A short piece of work for a family choosing between a resit, a repeat year, a changed subject or a changed level. The tutor reads the evidence, tests the student on real past-paper material, and gives a written view on what is achievable in the time available. It sometimes concludes that the right answer is not to enter.
bullets: Tests the student on genuine past-paper questions, cold
Separates a two-mark gap from a two-grade gap
Names what the time remaining can and cannot deliver
Written conclusion you can take into the school conversation

sections.heading: When a Deira school cannot offer the subject your child needs
paragraphs: This happens for sound reasons and it still leaves a family stuck. A large school runs option blocks that work for the majority, which means some combinations are impossible: a student cannot take both of two subjects timetabled against each other, and a minority subject with eight interested students may not run at all. The school is making a reasonable staffing decision and your child still needs the subject.

The first move is always to ask the school rather than to assume. Some schools will arrange a supervised independent study route for a motivated student, some will enter a candidate for a subject taught outside school hours, and some will decline. The answer varies by school and by year, and it is worth asking in writing in Year 9 rather than discovering the position in Year 10 when the timetable is fixed.

If the school declines, the second route is an entry outside it. Many IGCSE subjects are assessed entirely by written paper, which makes a private entry genuinely feasible, and the syllabus is published so the content is not a mystery. What has to be arranged is the centre, the series, the components and the fee, and those decisions have deadlines that close well before the paper. The table below sets out the options against the common situations.

There is one honest caution. A subject added outside school is a subject with no teacher, no cohort and no mock timetable, and a student already struggling with the eight subjects they have should not be adding a ninth. The right candidates are students with capacity who need a specific subject for a specific reason, most often a university prerequisite or a mathematics requirement that the option block did not accommodate.

sections.heading: What a private candidate actually has to arrange, and in what order
paragraphs: The administration is the part that catches families, not the studying. A candidate entering outside a school has to find a centre that will accept them in that subject, confirm which components that centre offers, confirm the series, pay the fee by the centre's own deadline rather than the board's, and then obtain the correct timetable for that centre's administrative zone. Each step depends on the one before it, and skipping any of them is discovered late.

Start with the board, not with a tutoring provider. Cambridge and Pearson both publish information on entries and on centres, and the board's own guidance is the authority on what is possible for a private candidate in a given subject. A tutoring company cannot enter a candidate, cannot guarantee a centre will accept one, and should not be the source of the answer on whether a component is available.

The deadline discipline is stricter than families expect. Cambridge set final entries for the March 2027 series at 27 November 2026, with the exam period running 3 February to 4 March 2027. A centre will set its own internal deadline earlier than the board's, often by several weeks, so the practical cut-off is earlier again. The table below puts the sequence in order with an honest note on what goes wrong at each step.

One detail that is easy to miss and expensive to get wrong. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. A private candidate has no school checking this for them. Ask the centre which zone it is in, in writing, and build the revision plan on that version.
