sections.heading: Practical and coursework components without a class
paragraphs: This is where a private entry most often breaks down, and it should be checked before any money is spent on tutoring. Some subjects contain components that must be assessed inside a school: coursework marked by a teacher, a practical examination requiring laboratory supervision, or a speaking assessment conducted by a centre. If a component of that kind is compulsory and the candidate has no school to host it, the entry is not viable in that form.

In several science subjects the boards offer alternative components intended for candidates without laboratory access, and in some subjects the practical skills are assessed by written paper instead. Whether that applies to your child's subject and series is a question for the board and the centre, and the answer should be obtained in writing. It is not a question a tutoring provider can answer reliably, and a provider who answers it confidently without a source is guessing.

A tutor can do useful work around a practical component even where it exists, and it is worth being clear about what that work is. Experimental design, data handling, uncertainty treatment, graph work and the written interpretation of results are all taught well over video using genuine data sets, and in most papers those are where the practical marks actually sit. Handling the apparatus is the part that requires a laboratory, and no amount of tutoring substitutes for it.

For coursework that must be school-assessed, the position is simpler and stricter. A tutor cannot supervise, authenticate or submit it, and no tutor should offer to supply it. If a subject requires a teacher-assessed component and the candidate has no teacher, the honest answer is that this subject needs a school route rather than a private one, and a family is better served by hearing that early than by discovering it after an entry fee has been paid.

sections.heading: Self-study with nobody setting the pace
paragraphs: A student in a class is carried by structure they never notice. The teacher decides what is covered this week. The cohort shows them whether they are keeping up. Mock examinations arrive on a date nobody chose. Homework deadlines create small, frequent obligations. Remove all of that and a sixteen-year-old is left to sequence a two-year syllabus, pace it across months, decide when to stop reading and start practising, and judge their own standard without a reference point.

Almost everybody fails at the same two things. The first is sequencing: a self-studying candidate covers the parts of the syllabus they find approachable and defers the hard cumulative material, so the structure that should have been built first is missing when the harder work depends on it. The second is self-assessment, because marking your own work against an answer key tells you whether the answer matched and nothing at all about whether the marks would have been awarded.

The structure that works is unremarkable and has to be imposed from outside. A written sequence across the available months, with the hard foundations first. Weekly content targets that are small enough to be met. Checkpoint assessments on fixed dates, marked by somebody else against the published scheme. Timed full papers starting from the midpoint rather than the final fortnight, because pacing is a skill that needs months of practice rather than a week of panic.

The third element, and the one most often absent, is a reference point. A candidate studying alone has no idea whether their work is at a grade 5 or a grade 8 standard, and their own estimate is usually wrong in both directions. Somebody marking their timed papers against the real scheme supplies that calibration, and the calibration is frequently more valuable than the teaching, because it tells the family whether the entry is realistic while there is still time to change the decision.

sections.heading: The calendar counted backwards from a private entry
paragraphs: For a candidate inside a school, deadlines arrive through the school and someone else is watching them. For a private candidate, every date has to be found and tracked by the family. Counting backwards from the paper rather than forwards from today is the only way to see whether the plan fits, and the table below does that using dates published by Cambridge and Pearson themselves.

The Cambridge March 2027 series is the cleanest illustration. Final entries were due on 27 November 2026, the exam period runs from 3 February to 4 March 2027, forecast grades are due on 27 February 2027, results reach centres on Cambridge Direct on 13 May 2027, and certificates follow in late June. Cambridge also runs June and November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. A centre's own registration deadline sits earlier than the board's, so the real cut-off is earlier again.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations are available in May or June and in November each year. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, including International GCSE November 2027, and revises them, so the live official PDF is the only version to plan against. Pearson's June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026.

No IB session or results date appears on this page. The IB's own site could not be confirmed directly for this project, so publishing one here would mean repeating something unverified, and for a Diploma student the binding dates are the school's internal ones anyway. If a date matters to your decision, get it from the IB coordinator or the board in writing rather than from any tutoring page, including this one.

sections.heading: Repeating a year against resitting a subject
paragraphs: This decision arrives suddenly and gets made under pressure, usually in the days after a results release. It deserves better treatment than that, because the four available options differ enormously in cost, in time and in what they actually fix. The table below sets them against each other. The honest starting point is a question most families skip: how big is the gap, in marks, and in how many subjects?

A candidate two marks below a boundary in one subject has a targeted problem. Eight weeks of work on the specific question types that failed, entered into the next available series, is a proportionate response and it frequently succeeds. A candidate several grades below in three subjects has a different problem entirely, and attempting it in a single short window produces a second disappointing result plus the cost of the entries.

The repeat year is the option families resist most and it is sometimes right. It fixes content comprehensively, it restores a cohort and a teacher, and it removes the self-study burden that makes private entries hard. Against that it costs a year, it costs a year of fees, and it has a social cost that should not be dismissed because an adult finds it unimportant. The decision belongs to the family and the school; what a tutor can add is an honest measurement of the gap.

One further option is frequently overlooked. Sometimes the right answer is to change the subject or the level rather than to repeat the attempt. A student who has failed twice at Higher Level Chemistry for a degree that does not require it has a subject-choice problem dressed up as a performance problem, and another resit solves nothing. Checking what the destination actually requires is free and it should be the first step, not the last.

sections.heading: What this costs, and what a tutor cannot do for a candidate
paragraphs: Market rates in Dubai are the same for this work as for any other, so the table below prices by case and adds the limits. For reference: a budget online tutor, generally a university student, runs AED 45-150 an hour, with EdFlik listing from AED 45-65 and Tutopiya from AED 33-52; a qualified subject tutor online is AED 150-300, with Unitors listing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200; a specialist is AED 200-450 or more, with TutorChase publishing AED 270; premium named tutors reach AED 500-650, with BartyED publishing AED 650. Market figures gathered October 2026, attributed to those providers, and not IB Gram prices.

Examination entry fees are a separate cost and this page does not quote them, deliberately. They are set by the board and the centre, they vary by subject and series, and a private candidate often pays a centre administration charge on top of the board fee. Ask the centre for a written quote covering both before committing, and ask whether late entry carries a surcharge, because for a private candidate it usually does.

The limits matter more here than in ordinary subject tutoring, because a candidate without a school has nobody else to tell them. A tutor cannot enter a candidate for an examination. A tutor cannot guarantee that a centre will accept a private entry in a given subject. A tutor cannot supervise or authenticate a school-assessed coursework component, and should not offer to supply one. And a tutor cannot sit in a laboratory on the candidate's behalf.

What a tutor can do is the part that decides the outcome. Supply the structure a class would have provided, set the sequence, mark timed papers against the real scheme, and give an honest calibration of where the candidate currently stands. For a self-studying candidate that calibration is the single most valuable deliverable, because it answers the question the family cannot answer alone: is this entry realistic in the time remaining?

sections.heading: Equivalency for a candidate who sat subjects outside school
paragraphs: A student who has assembled qualifications across more than one route eventually has to put them in front of the Ministry of Education for equivalency, and the arithmetic is worth doing early rather than at the point of application. The published British-track requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level with the same grade.

Two details matter particularly for a candidate with a mixed record. The first is that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects for the GCSE or IGCSE count, so a student who took both at school and three other counting subjects has three, not five. The second is that one competitor page ranking for these queries states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects, where the sourced requirement is five. Working from the wrong figure changes which additional entry is needed.

For the American track, English proficiency is met by a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. No IB points threshold appears anywhere on this page, because the sources consulted state none and nothing could be read on the Ministry's own site. Treat any unsourced IB equivalency figure as unreliable.

Two cautions to carry. Equivalency is a regulatory process the family completes through the official channel, and no tutoring provider performs it, accelerates it or guarantees it. And tutoring is not a requirement for equivalency, for university admission or for school progression; any page implying otherwise is manufacturing urgency about a process it does not control. Where tutoring helps is in making sure the counting subjects are passed at the grade the rule requires.

sections.heading: Academic honesty when nobody is supervising
paragraphs: A candidate studying alone is the most exposed student in this market, and it is worth naming why. There is no teacher reviewing drafts, no cohort to compare against, and no school declaring authenticity until the point of submission. Research for this project found a provider in this market selling finished Internal Assessments at AED 3,750, and services offering completed coursework and assignments circulate widely in Dubai. A candidate without supervision is the easiest person in the system to sell to.

The rules do not soften because a student is working alone. Submitting work that is not the student's own is malpractice under IB rules and the investigation falls on the candidate, with consequences that can reach a whole Diploma rather than one subject grade. For a board coursework component, authenticity is declared, and a false declaration is a matter between the candidate and the board. The provider who supplied the document is not part of that conversation.

The legitimate boundary is the same for a private candidate as for anybody else, and it is specific enough to check. A tutor may explain what each published criterion rewards and the marks it carries. A tutor may question a research design until it can generate usable data in the time available. A tutor may teach how an evaluation or an argument should be structured, and may read a draft the candidate has produced and say in writing where it falls short. The candidate writes every word.

There is a further point worth making to a family in this situation. A private candidate has fewer people vouching for them, which means their own work has to be defensible on its face. A candidate who has genuinely done the work can discuss the method, the choices and the limitations. One who has not cannot, and for a student already outside the normal route, that is a much worse position to be in than a disappointing grade.

process.title: Tell us what the school has already said
process.description: Most of these cases start with a school answer: the subject cannot run, the option blocks clash, the year cannot be repeated, the level cannot be changed. Knowing exactly what has been ruled out, and by whom, saves a fortnight of exploring routes that are already closed.

process.title: Measure the gap with a cold timed paper
process.description: Before any decision about entering, repeating or resitting, the student sits a genuine past paper under timing and somebody marks it against the real scheme. Two marks below a boundary and two grades below are different problems, and only a marked paper distinguishes them.

process.title: Confirm the administration before the teaching
process.description: For a private entry, the viability questions come first: can the subject be sat without school-assessed coursework, will a centre accept the entry, which components does it run, and what are the centre's own deadlines. Those answers come from the board and the centre, not from us.

process.title: Build the sequence backwards from the paper
process.description: A written plan across the months remaining, hard cumulative foundations first, weekly targets small enough to be met, checkpoint assessments on fixed dates, and timed papers from the midpoint. For a candidate with no class, that structure is the service as much as the teaching is.

process.title: Recalibrate at each checkpoint
process.description: Every checkpoint is marked against the published scheme and compared against the target grade, so the family always knows whether the entry is still realistic. If a checkpoint says it is not, that should be said while the decision is still reversible rather than after the fee is paid.

whyPoints.title: We supply the structure a class would have given
whyPoints.description: A self-studying candidate fails at sequencing and at self-assessment, not at effort. A written sequence, weekly targets, fixed checkpoints and timed papers from the midpoint are the structure that is missing, and imposing it from outside is the whole job.

whyPoints.title: Calibration against a real mark scheme
whyPoints.description: A candidate alone has no reference point and their own estimate of their standard is usually wrong in both directions. Marking their timed papers against the published scheme answers the question the family cannot: is this entry realistic in the time left?

whyPoints.title: We will tell you not to enter
whyPoints.description: A cold timed paper sometimes shows that a series is not achievable, and saying so costs us the work. It is still the right answer, because a second disappointing result plus an entry fee is a worse outcome than a changed plan made in good time.

whyPoints.title: We are clear about what we cannot do
whyPoints.description: We cannot enter a candidate, secure a centre place, supervise a practical, authenticate coursework or change a boundary. Those answers come from the board and the centre, and a provider who answers them confidently without a source is guessing with your fee.

whyPoints.title: Dates from the boards, counted backwards
whyPoints.description: Cambridge closed March 2027 entries on 27 November 2026, months before the February papers, and centres set their own deadlines earlier still. No IB date appears here, because the IB's own site could not be confirmed for this project.

whyPoints.title: The honesty line holds for an unsupervised candidate
whyPoints.description: A student with no teacher reviewing drafts is the easiest person in this market to sell finished coursework to. We teach criteria, question designs and give written feedback on the candidate's own draft, and supply nothing submittable.

faqs.question: My Al Muteena school does not offer a subject my child needs. What now?
faqs.answer: Ask the school first, in writing, whether it will arrange supervised independent study or enter a candidate for a subject it does not teach; the answer varies by school and by year. If it declines, many IGCSE subjects are assessed entirely by written paper, which makes a private entry feasible. What then has to be arranged is a centre that accepts private candidates in that subject, the components it runs, the series and the fee, with deadlines that close months before the paper. Ask in Year 9 rather than Year 10.

faqs.question: Can my child sit an IGCSE as a private candidate in Dubai?
faqs.answer: In many subjects yes, and the determining factor is the assessment structure rather than the student. A subject assessed entirely by written paper is straightforward; one with a compulsory school-assessed coursework component or a supervised practical is not, unless the board offers an alternative component and the centre runs it. Start with the board's own guidance and centre information, confirm components in writing with the centre, and expect the centre's registration deadline to fall weeks before the board's.

faqs.question: What does a private candidate have to arrange, and in what order?
faqs.answer: Six things in sequence. Confirm the subject can be sat without school-assessed coursework. Find a centre that accepts private candidates in it. Confirm which components that centre runs. Register and pay by the centre's own deadline, which precedes the board's. Obtain the correct timetable for the centre's Cambridge administrative zone. Then plan the study sequence backwards from the paper. Each step depends on the previous one, and skipping any of them tends to be discovered too late to fix.

faqs.question: Why does the Cambridge administrative zone matter for a private entry?
faqs.answer: Because Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. A candidate inside a school has an exams officer checking that. A private candidate has nobody, so a revision plan built on a timetable found online can be wrong by days. Ask the centre which zone it is in, in writing, on registration.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with a science subject if we have no laboratory?
faqs.answer: Partly, and the honest division is worth knowing. Experimental design, data handling, uncertainty treatment, graph work and written interpretation of results are taught well over video with genuine data sets, and in most papers those are where the practical marks actually sit. Handling the apparatus requires a laboratory and no tutoring substitutes for it. Whether an alternative component exists for candidates without laboratory access is a question for the board and the centre, answered in writing before any fee is paid.

faqs.question: Should my child resit one subject or repeat the whole year?
faqs.answer: Measure the gap first, because the options differ enormously. Two marks below a boundary in one subject is six to ten weeks of targeted work on the question types that failed, entered into the next series. Several grades below across three subjects usually needs the content rebuilt, which a short window will not deliver. A repeat year restores a teacher and a cohort and removes the self-study burden, at the cost of a year, a year of fees and a real social cost. A cold timed paper settles it in two hours.

faqs.question: Is it ever better to change the subject rather than resit it?
faqs.answer: Frequently, and it is the option families skip. A student who has missed a grade twice in a subject the destination course does not require has a subject-choice problem presented as a performance problem, and a third attempt fixes nothing. Checking what the institutions on the list actually state as prerequisites is free, takes an evening, and should be the first step rather than the last. Where the grade already meets the real requirement, accepting it and moving on is also a legitimate answer.

faqs.question: How does a student study a whole syllabus with no teacher?
faqs.answer: With structure imposed from outside, because the two failures are predictable. Self-studying candidates cover the approachable topics and defer the hard cumulative material, and they self-assess by checking answers rather than marks, which tells them nothing about whether credit would be awarded. The fix is a written sequence across the months with the hard foundations first, weekly targets small enough to meet, checkpoint assessments on fixed dates marked by somebody else, and timed full papers from the midpoint.

faqs.question: How do we know whether an entry is realistic in the time left?
faqs.answer: Have the student sit a genuine past paper cold, under timing, and have it marked against the published scheme rather than an answer key. A candidate working alone has no reference point and their own estimate is usually wrong in both directions. That single exercise answers the question the family cannot answer, and it should be repeated at each checkpoint so that an entry decision can still be changed while the deadline is open rather than after the fee is paid.

faqs.question: What do examination entry fees cost for a private candidate in Dubai?
faqs.answer: This page does not quote a figure, deliberately. Entry fees are set by the board and the centre, vary by subject and series, and a private candidate commonly pays a centre administration charge on top of the board fee. Late entry usually carries a surcharge. Ask the centre for a written quote covering both components before committing, and ask what the refund position is if the candidate withdraws. Any page quoting a single figure for this is not working from a source that applies to your subject and series.

faqs.question: Can a tutoring company enter my child for an exam?
faqs.answer: No, and a provider claiming otherwise is misdescribing what it does. Entries are made by a registered examination centre, and whether a centre accepts a private candidate in a given subject is a matter between the family, the centre and the board. A tutor can help you plan around the deadlines and can teach the syllabus, but cannot register the candidate, cannot secure a centre place, cannot supervise a practical and cannot authenticate coursework.

faqs.question: Can the IB Diploma be taken outside a school?
faqs.answer: Not realistically. The Diploma requires a registered IB World School to deliver it, with internal assessment marked by teachers and moderated externally, alongside Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. A student out of step with a Diploma cohort therefore has a school conversation rather than a private entry ahead of them. The realistic options are school-internal, such as adjusting levels early in Diploma Year 1 or, in some cases, pursuing individual course certificates rather than the full Diploma. Ask the coordinator what is possible and by when.

faqs.question: Which schools around Al Muteena do your students come from?
faqs.answer: The nearest cluster spans Al Muteena, Abu Hail and Al Qusais and includes Al Diyafah High School, The Westminster School, Dubai Scholars Private School, Deira Private School and The Elite English School. The wider ring towards Deira, Al Garhoud and Oud Metha includes The Indian High School, Our Own English High School Dubai, Al Mawakeb School Al Garhoud, Deira International School and St Mary's Catholic High School. These are large schools with efficient rather than broad option blocks, which is one reason subjects sometimes have to be sat outside them. Named as context only.

faqs.question: How does equivalency work for a student with qualifications from two routes?
faqs.answer: The arithmetic is the same but needs doing early. The British track requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, plus one Advanced Level subject at no less than E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are excluded from the five, so a student with those plus three other counting subjects has three. One competitor page says six subjects are required; the sourced figure is five. Equivalency itself is completed through the official channel.

faqs.question: Can a tutor visit a student in Al Muteena who is studying at home?
faqs.answer: No. Tutoring for UAE families is delivered online, one to one, over live video, and IB Gram does not make home visits anywhere in the UAE; home tutoring is a service offered only in India. For a candidate studying a syllabus nobody nearby teaches, online delivery is the only practical route to a genuine specialist in the first place. The in-home Dubai market charges roughly AED 180-500 an hour with travel priced in, and a local in-home tutor is unlikely to know a minority syllabus code at all.

dubai/al-muteena.closingHeading: Measure the gap, confirm the route, then start teaching
dubai/al-muteena.closingBody: If your child needs a subject the school will not run, or a grade retaken, or a year rebuilt, the order of operations matters more than the choice of tutor. First a cold timed paper, marked against the real scheme, so the gap is a number rather than a feeling. Then the administrative questions, answered in writing by the board and the centre. Only then a teaching plan sequenced backwards from the paper, with checkpoints that tell you whether the entry is still realistic. Tell us what the school has already ruled out and we will start at step one. Lessons run online, one to one, over live video.

Each tutor is matched to one subject and one level, so siblings on different curricula do not share a compromise.

intro.heading: One household, two school systems
paragraphs: Al Nahda sits against the Sharjah boundary, and that single geographic fact shapes almost everything a parent here has to plan around. Rents on this side of the line draw families who work in Dubai, and the schools within reach sit in both emirates. It is entirely ordinary for an Al Nahda household to have one child at a Dubai school inspected by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority and another at a Sharjah school regulated by the Sharjah Private Education Authority, on different term dates, different boards and different buses.

Nobody writing about tutoring in this market addresses that. The pages competing for this search describe a neighbourhood, list some subjects and ask for a phone number. None of them mention that Sharjah's authority approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, which is a wider remit than inspection alone, or that the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah while Ras Al Khaimah has its own Department of Knowledge. For a family on this boundary those differences are not trivia; they decide which calendar the household runs on.

The practical consequences show up in small things that add up. Two sets of term dates means the week that is quiet for one child is an assessment week for the other. Two boards means a tutor who knows Cambridge 0580 inside out is the wrong match for a sibling entered for Pearson 4MA1. Two school runs in opposite directions, both crossing or approaching the emirate line in the late afternoon, means the evening has a narrower usable window than the clock suggests.

The traffic is the part every resident already knows. Al Ittihad Road and the approaches to Al Nahda carry a heavy inbound and outbound cross-border flow from mid-afternoon, and the queue is unpredictable rather than merely slow. A tutor driving in from anywhere west of Deira is exposed to it, and so is a tutor coming the other way out of Sharjah. The lesson that only requires the student to be in the room is a different proposition here from a lesson that requires two journeys to succeed.

IB Gram delivers tuition for UAE families one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or Sharjah; the in-home service exists only in India. On this boundary that is less of a compromise than it sounds. A family can run two children in two different curricula in the same evening with two different specialists, something no single visiting tutor could do, and neither session depends on the border queue clearing.

What follows is the detail that matters here specifically: which regulator governs which school and what that changes, how the equivalency rules read for an IGCSE or A Level student, what the mandatory UAE subjects require regardless of curriculum, what the market charges, and how to place a slot that works for a household with two school runs.

dubai/al-nahda.programmesIntro: Families on this boundary meet three routes, and the choice is often made for them by which school had a place. The notes below say what each route means for a household running two systems at once.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two years of eight or nine subjects ending in terminal written papers, with practical or alternative-to-practical components in the sciences. Cambridge tiers many subjects into Core and Extended, and Core entry caps the grade at C or 5. Pearson International GCSE runs single-tier papers in most subjects. The board sets the paper structure, so the board matters more than the subject title.
programmes.countryNote: Schools on either side of this boundary do not use the same board, and some enter different subjects with different boards in one year group. Check the statement of entry, not the prospectus. A household with a child in Dubai on Cambridge and a sibling in Sharjah on Pearson needs two differently prepared tutors, and treating them as one request is the commonest planning error here.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, each with an internal assessment designed and drafted outside lesson time, plus the Extended Essay at 4,000 words, Theory of Knowledge and CAS. The total runs to 45 points including up to three bonus points from the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge matrix.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma provision is thinner on this boundary than IGCSE provision, so Al Nahda students doing the DP are usually travelling, often towards Al Garhoud, Mirdif or into Sharjah. The long return makes weekday coursework sessions difficult and weekend mornings valuable, and it is the main reason families here ask about weekend blocks rather than extra weekday hours.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four criteria out of eight and reported as a grade from 1 to 7. The programme rewards investigation, communication and reflection rather than procedural drill, which means fluency gaps can sit underneath respectable grades until a timed paper exposes them.
programmes.countryNote: Where one sibling is in MYP and another in a terminal-examination system, parents often compare the two children's reports and conclude the wrong thing. They are different measurements. MYP criterion grades describe process quality; an IGCSE percentage describes performance against a mark scheme, and the two cannot be read side by side.

programmes.name: International A Level
programmes.description: Three or four subjects in depth, examined in a June or November series, with little coursework in the sciences beyond a practical component. The choice narrows at sixteen rather than eighteen, which suits a student with a settled direction and penalises one still deciding.
programmes.countryNote: For Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, the published requirement is one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than grade E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, alongside five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic Education are not counted among the five.

dubai/al-nahda.subjectsIntro: Requests from this boundary cover both boards and both emirates, and the list below reflects what households here actually ask for rather than a generic subject menu. Where a code is given, it is the code to check on the entry slip.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: The most requested subject on either side of the line. Cambridge Extended reaches grade 9 while Core caps at C or 5, so a tier review can matter more than extra teaching. Pearson's Foundation and Higher papers ask questions differently, which is why board-specific preparation is not a detail.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof, calculus and algebraic rigour carry the grade, and marks are lost on unjustified steps rather than wrong answers. The exploration is marked out of 20 across five criteria, with the heaviest allocation on use of mathematics, so a topic that stays at course level caps the mark.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Electricity and waves dominate lost marks at IGCSE, fields and thermodynamics at Diploma level. The practical or alternative-to-practical paper tests method and variable control, and students who have read experiments rather than run them cannot supply the detail examiners expect.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and qualitative analysis at IGCSE; energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms at HL. Observation answers need colour and state together. Unit and significant-figure discipline costs about a mark a paper and is the quickest habit to repair.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: A large content base rather than a hard one. Command terms set the ceiling: outline wants a list, explain wants a causal mechanism. Retention responds to spaced review, so frequency of sessions matters more here than their length.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language and as an additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory in Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students. Which stream your child is in determines which content and which language of instruction applies, and a report line here is often the weakest on an otherwise strong record.

subjects.name: English First Language and English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Summary questions carry dense marks and are the most frequently wasted, because students paraphrase a passage instead of selecting discrete points. Directed writing rewards register and audience control. Four marked sessions usually move both.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
subjects.description: Case-study marks go to candidates who use the figures inside the argument rather than quoting them alongside it. At Diploma level, Economics requires three commentaries of 800 words built on news articles, and the article choice decides the mark before any writing happens.

subjects.name: Accounting
subjects.description: Offered at several schools serving this boundary and frequently requested. Marks go to layout discipline and consistent treatment rather than to arithmetic, so the fastest improvement comes from drilling the format of each statement until it is automatic.

sections.heading: A search for a tutor in Al Nahda usually crosses an emirate line
paragraphs: Direct answer first: tuition for Al Nahda students runs online, one-to-one over live video, in slots that typically start at 18:30 or 19:00 on weekdays, and each child is matched to a specialist in the board their own school enters. For a household with children in both Dubai and Sharjah schools, that means two tutors rather than one, because the papers are not the same.

The reason this page leads with the boundary rather than with a list of subjects is that the boundary is the thing that makes planning here different. A parent in a villa community with one school five minutes away has a simple scheduling problem. A parent in Al Nahda with a Year 11 student at a Dubai school and a Year 9 student at a Sharjah school has two term calendars, two assessment weeks, potentially two boards and one evening. Tutoring advice that ignores all of that is advice for somebody else's neighbourhood.

It also changes what a family should check before buying anything. The regulator that licenses a school decides the inspection framework its reports are written in, and in Sharjah's case the authority also approves fees, curricula and assessment methods. Reading a Dubai inspection band and a Sharjah school's documentation as though they are the same instrument will mislead you, and parents do it constantly because the two sides of this boundary look identical from the street. The next section sets the regulator map out properly, because no competing page in this market does it at all.

sections.heading: Which authority regulates your child's school, and what it governs
paragraphs: Five bodies regulate private schools across the UAE, and an Al Nahda family may deal with two of them. Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority is described on u.ae as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. Abu Dhabi's Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools there, and is named by none of the competing pages in this market. Sharjah's Private Education Authority regulates private education in that emirate, Ras Al Khaimah has its own Department of Knowledge, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

The remit is not identical across them, which is the part that matters here. Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. That is curriculum and fee approval, not inspection alone. A parent moving a child across this boundary is not just changing buildings; they are moving between two regulatory instruments with different scope.

Underneath all of them sits a federal baseline. Private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That is the rule every emirate's mandatory-subject requirement is built on, and it explains why a British or IB school on either side of this line still teaches Arabic and Islamic Education.

For practical purposes, the table below is what an Al Nahda parent needs: who governs what, where attestation goes, and what each means for a tuition plan. Verify any specific school's licensing on its regulator's own listing rather than on a third-party page, including this one.

sections.heading: The Al Ittihad Road afternoon, and when a session can start
paragraphs: Residents here do not need to be told about the border queue. What is worth saying is how it should change a tuition plan rather than how long it lasts. The cross-boundary flow builds from mid-afternoon and the problem is variance, not duration: a journey that takes twenty minutes one day and fifty-five the next cannot be planned around, and a schedule built on the good day fails on the ordinary one.

The planning rule that works is to build against the worse realistic journey and accept the occasional early start. For a student at school in Al Qusais, 17:30 holds. For a student travelling to or from a Sharjah school in Muweilah or University City, 19:00 is the dependable hour. For a student going out towards Mirdif or Al Garhoud, 18:00 to 18:30. Weekend mornings from 09:00 are open for everybody and are the best hours in the week.

Then there is the question of what a late hour can carry. Concentration is not flat across an evening, and spending a 19:30 session on new abstract content wastes the money. That hour is good for marked-script review, worked examples, command-term drilling and short timed sections, where the paper supplies the structure. New material and anything demanding sustained working memory belongs in a weekend block or an earlier weekday slot where one exists.

The asymmetry that favours online delivery here is simple arithmetic. A lesson with a visiting tutor needs two uncertain journeys to coincide. A lesson over live video needs one person to be home. In a district where the afternoon is this variable, that difference shows up as the number of sessions actually delivered in a term rather than as a philosophical preference.

sections.heading: What changes when the school is in Sharjah rather than Dubai
paragraphs: Parents on this boundary often assume the differences between a Dubai school and a Sharjah one are cosmetic. Some genuinely are, and a child crossing between them will find the same curricula and frequently the same exam boards. Several differences are not cosmetic at all, and the ones that matter for a tuition plan are the calendar, the board and the documentation trail. A household running both needs to know which is which before committing to a weekly schedule rather than after the first clash.

Term dates are the most immediate. Where two schools publish different assessment weeks, the household has two pause windows rather than one, and a tuition plan that treats the family as a single unit will collide with one of them. Mapping both calendars onto one sheet in September takes twenty minutes and prevents a term of friction.

The board is the second. Schools on either side use Cambridge or Pearson and some mix the two across subjects within a year group, so the assumption that siblings can share a tutor is frequently wrong. A tutor prepared on Cambridge 0620 Chemistry meeting a student entered for Pearson 4CH1 is teaching correct chemistry against the wrong paper, and the student will not notice until a mock.

The third is documentation, which matters at the end rather than the beginning. Equivalency and attestation go through the Ministry of Education regardless of which emirate the school sits in, and the requirements are published by curriculum rather than by emirate. sections.heading: The mandatory UAE subjects, and what the rules actually say
paragraphs: This is the largest content gap in the whole competing field. Arabic appears on competitor pages as a subject chip and nowhere as a section, which is strange given that these subjects are compulsory for every student in a Dubai private school regardless of the licensed international curriculum. For a family on this boundary with children in two systems, the rules are worth reading properly.

KHDA's mandatory-subjects guidelines require that schools organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and state that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students, and the school's licensed-curriculum language applies for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in moral, social and cultural studies.

Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit. Schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and the guidance advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should be at least 25 minutes. Schools are required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, which is a concrete and checkable credential point. Using different or additional content for these subjects without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited, which is a real constraint on how any tutoring material for them can be described.

For a parent the practical consequences are three. Which stream your child sits in determines what they are being taught and assessed on, so a weak Arabic report line means something different for an Arab first-language student than for a non-Arab additional-language student. Tutoring in these subjects has to work within approved content rather than importing a parallel syllabus. And for Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, Arabic and Islamic Education are explicitly not included among the five required GCSE or IGCSE subjects, which surprises most families the first time they hear it.

sections.heading: Equivalency and attestation, written out by curriculum
paragraphs: Every family on this boundary eventually meets the equivalency question, usually a year later than they should. Equivalency is the Ministry of Education's recognition of a school certificate for use in the UAE, and it is a ministry process with published requirements. It is not something a tutoring service performs, guarantees or accelerates, and anyone implying otherwise should be treated with scepticism.

On the British track the published requirements are specific. A student must show one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level with the same grade, and must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five required subjects. One page currently ranking in this market states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects, which does not match the published rule.

On the American track the requirements are different in kind. English proficiency is evidenced by a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT. Mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. The source clarifying these requirements does not mention EmSAT and states no IB points threshold.

That last point deserves emphasis because it is where pages in this market invent numbers. No IB equivalency figure appears in the sourced material, so none is published here. If your child is on the Diploma and you need the equivalency position, read it on moe.gov.ae or ask the attestation authority directly rather than trusting a tutoring page, including this one. What a tutor can legitimately do is help a student reach the grades the ministry asks for; the process itself is yours and the ministry's.

sections.heading: What tutoring costs around this boundary, and who publishes the figures
paragraphs: Three of the six strongest pages competing for searches like this one publish no price at all, and the two that do quote US dollars. That is not useful to a family paying rent in dirhams. The table below gives the market bands in AED with the provider who published each figure named, so the number can be checked rather than believed.

These are market rates and not an IB Gram price list. Their value is calibration. A quote of AED 500 an hour for Year 10 mathematics sits in the premium examiner band and should come with a reason. A quote of AED 50 an hour for a Chemistry HL internal assessment sits in the university-student band, which is a legitimate purchase for content revision and the wrong purchase for criterion-based coursework work.

Format moves the figure more than subject does. Published in-home bands run above online bands for a tutor of comparable standing, and the gap is travel. On this boundary, travel means the border queue. Monthly packages in this market run at roughly AED 799 for eight online sessions and about AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits, and Bestimate's 2026 estimates for one weekly hour span AED 240 to 600 at the budget end up to AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support.

For households running two children, the honest arithmetic is that two specialists at the qualified-tutor band usually costs less than one premium tutor and teaches both children properly. Where a budget genuinely only covers one, the better use is the child closer to a terminal examination, with the younger sibling picked up later. A tutor who tells you to buy both regardless is selling.

sections.heading: Where the academic-honesty line sits, and who in this market crosses it
paragraphs: A family on this boundary will be offered coursework help by somebody, and some of what gets offered is dangerous. Operators in this SERP sell completed internal assessments at four-figure dirham prices. Submitting bought work is malpractice under IB rules and the penalty lands on the student: a withdrawn grade, possibly a withdrawn diploma, and a problem that follows a university application. No parent should be anywhere near this, and the sellers rely on parents not knowing the rule.

What a tutor may legitimately do is wide and genuinely valuable. Teach the content the project requires. Discuss whether a research question can be answered with the equipment and time available. Explain what each criterion descriptor rewards and at what mark. Read a draft the student wrote and state in writing which descriptor is not yet met. Build a timeline backwards from the school's own internal deadline and hold the student to weekly checkpoints.

What a tutor may not do is narrow and absolute. No supplied text. No restructuring of a draft for the student to copy back. No generating or analysing the student's data on their behalf. No material from another student's project. Each of those transfers authorship, and authorship is the thing being assessed.

The safeguard a parent should insist on is documentation. Ask how coursework feedback is recorded and ask to see an example. Written feedback against criterion descriptors, kept and shareable with the school, protects the student in the only moment that matters, which is a coordinator asking where the work came from. A verbal-only arrangement leaves nothing to show and nothing to defend.
bullets: Permitted: content teaching, question scoping, criterion explanation, written feedback
Prohibited: supplied text, generated data, editing a draft to a finished state
Ask to see how coursework feedback is documented before the first session
Keep every draft and every piece of feedback until the grade is confirmed

sections.heading: Starting, and the limits we will tell you about
paragraphs: The sequence is short and the useful part is what you send. Subject, level, board and the thing that prompted the call, with a marked script or a report attached if one exists. For a household with two children, send both sets of details at once rather than sequentially, because the slots have to be planned together and a second request a fortnight later usually means the first child's hour has to move.

A trial session then runs at the hour you actually intend to use, with the tutor who would teach the term. That matters more than it sounds. A trial at a convenient midday slot proves nothing about whether a 19:00 session works for a child who crossed the boundary twice that day. After the trial the tutor says what they think the problem is and roughly how many sessions it takes, and a plan without a number attached is not a plan.

The limit worth disclosing is availability. Evening hours between 17:00 and 19:00 Gulf time are the most requested in the network and in mock season they run out. Narrow components take longer to match: Computer Science solution development, Further Mathematics, Arabic as a first language at Diploma level. For those we give a dated alternative rather than a vague reassurance, which is more than any competing page in this market does, because none of them acknowledges a coverage limit at all.

On timing, earlier is cheaper. A Year 10 student starting in the autumn needs fewer sessions than the same student starting in February, and a DP1 student who scopes an internal assessment question in the first term avoids the rescue job that an unworkable question creates in the second. Six weeks before a paper is still worth doing, and the work at that distance is technique, pacing and triage rather than teaching the course again.

process.title: Tell us which emirate each school sits in
process.description: Which school, which side of the boundary and which board on the entry slip. That decides the regulator, the term calendar and the paper your child sits, and for a household with two children it determines whether one tutor or two is the right answer.

process.title: Send the component, not just the subject
process.description: Subject, level and the specific trigger: a mock grade, an internal assessment with no start, a fortnight missed. Syllabus codes help most, because 0580 and 4MA1 need different preparation and a tutor matched to the wrong one wastes the first three sessions.

process.title: Both school calendars on one sheet
process.description: Where two schools are involved we map both sets of assessment weeks before setting slots, so the plan has two pause windows built in rather than discovering them in November. It takes twenty minutes and saves a term of weekly renegotiation.

process.title: Trial in the real slot
process.description: The trial session runs at the hour you intend to keep, after the cross-border return, with the tutor who would teach the term. The first session works from a marked script where one exists, because repeated error patterns are more useful than a fresh diagnostic.

process.title: Review against each school's own marks
process.description: Progress is judged on the school's assessment points rather than on how the sessions felt, and each child is reviewed against their own school. If a plan is not working the tutor changes or the scope narrows, instead of the hour continuing out of habit.

whyPoints.title: Built for a two-regulator household
whyPoints.description: Children at a KHDA-inspected Dubai school and a SPEA-regulated Sharjah school get separate tutors matched to their own boards and calendars. A single visiting tutor cannot do that, and treating two different papers as one request is the most common planning error on this boundary.

whyPoints.title: Regulator and equivalency facts are sourced
whyPoints.description: The regulator map comes from u.ae, the mandatory-subject rules from KHDA's own guidelines, the equivalency requirements from reporting on the ministry's clarification. Where no source exists, as with the IB equivalency figure, this page says so rather than inventing a number.

whyPoints.title: No journey inside the fee
whyPoints.description: Published in-home rates run above online rates for a comparable tutor, and here the difference pays for a car in the border queue. Online delivery removes that cost and the cancellation risk that travels with it, which in this district is the larger of the two savings.

whyPoints.title: Coursework support that keeps the student safe
whyPoints.description: Internal assessment and Extended Essay work is teaching, question scoping and written feedback on the student's own draft, documented so a coordinator can see its scope. Operators in this market sell finished coursework, and the penalty for that lands on the student's diploma.

whyPoints.title: Coverage limits disclosed before payment
whyPoints.description: Where an hour is full or a component thinly covered, we say so and give a dated alternative. No competing page in this market publishes a coverage limit, which is worth noticing: a provider who never runs short is a provider filling slots with whoever is free.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling that assumes the queue
whyPoints.description: Slots are placed against the worse realistic journey rather than the average one, and they move for either school's exam weeks, Eid travel or Ramadan timing instead of being lost. That is the difference between a plan that exists in March and one that quietly ended in October.

faqs.question: Our flat is in Al Nahda but the school is in Sharjah. Which regulator applies to us?
faqs.answer: The school's regulator is set by where the school sits, not where you live. A school in Sharjah is regulated by the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which u.ae states regulates private education in the emirate and which approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. A school on the Dubai side is overseen by KHDA. If you have children on both sides, both apply to your household, with two inspection or approval frameworks and often two term calendars. Equivalency and attestation go through the federal Ministry of Education either way, so that part does not change with the boundary.

faqs.question: Does it matter for university whether the school is licensed by KHDA or SPEA?
faqs.answer: What universities read is the qualification, not the licensing authority: a Cambridge or Pearson IGCSE, an A Level, an IB Diploma. For use inside the UAE the relevant process is Ministry of Education equivalency, which is federal and applies whichever emirate the school sits in. On the British track the published requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one A Level at E or two AS Levels at the same grade. Verify the current rule on moe.gov.ae before relying on it.

faqs.question: How does the border queue affect what time an evening session can start?
faqs.answer: It makes the afternoon unpredictable rather than simply slow, and unpredictability is worse for a schedule. For students attending school in Al Qusais, 17:30 holds. For students travelling to or from Muweilah or University City in Sharjah, 19:00 is the dependable hour. For those heading out towards Al Garhoud or Mirdif, 18:00 to 18:30. Build the slot against the worse realistic journey and accept an occasional early start, because an optimistic hour that collapses twice a month teaches far less across a term than a later one that always happens.

faqs.question: Can one tutor teach two children on different curricula in the same evening?
faqs.answer: One tutor rarely should, and online delivery means they do not have to. If one child is entered for Cambridge 0580 and the other for Pearson 4MA1, the papers differ in structure, tiering and question style, and a tutor prepared for one is working against the wrong assessment for the other. Two specialists can run back to back or simultaneously in different rooms, with no travel gap between the sessions and a separate written note for each child. That is the arrangement a visiting tutor cannot provide, and it is the main reason households here end up online.

faqs.question: Is Arabic compulsory for my non-Arab child at an Al Nahda private school?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and the federal rule behind it is that private schools must teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies whatever curriculum they follow. KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and prohibits combined classes because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. For non-Arab students, Islamic Education and moral, social and cultural studies are taught in the school's licensed-curriculum language.

faqs.question: Do Arabic and Islamic Education count towards the ministry's five-subject requirement for an Al Nahda student?
faqs.answer: No. On the British track the published equivalency requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are explicitly not included among those five. That surprises most families, and it matters for subject selection in Year 9: a student taking nine subjects of which two are Arabic and Islamic Education needs five qualifying passes from the remaining seven. One competing page in this market states six subjects are required, which does not match the published rule. Check the current requirement on moe.gov.ae before planning around it.

faqs.question: Do Sharjah schools really approve their own curricula and fees?
faqs.answer: Not by themselves, but the approval sits with the emirate rather than only with the federal ministry. u.ae states that Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. That is a wider remit than quality inspection alone and is a genuine difference from how a Dubai parent reads a KHDA inspection report. For a family on this boundary the practical effect is that school documentation on the two sides answers different questions, and comparing a Sharjah school with a Dubai one requires reading each in its own framework.

faqs.question: How much does an IB tutor cost for a household in Al Nahda?
faqs.answer: Market bands in Dubai for an online IB specialist run roughly AED 200 to 450 an hour and above, with TutorChase publishing AED 270 and Bestimate's 2026 table putting the specialist band at AED 200 to 450 or more. A qualified subject tutor online sits at AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200. In-home visits are quoted at AED 180 to 500 because travel sits inside the fee. Those are the providers' published figures, not an IB Gram price list. For two children, two tutors at the qualified band typically costs less than one premium tutor and covers both properly.

faqs.question: My son moved from a Sharjah school to a Dubai one mid-year. What usually needs catching up?
faqs.answer: Three things, in this order. First, board alignment: if the new school enters a different board, the paper structure, tiering and question style change even where the content overlaps, and that is the fastest fix. Second, the mandatory UAE subjects, because the stream and content may differ and a weak line here is common after a move. Third, the assessment calendar, since the new school's internal deadlines for coursework may sit earlier than the old one's. A diagnostic from a marked script at the new school is worth more than any general assessment in sorting out what actually transferred.

faqs.question: Are IGCSE grades from a Sharjah school treated differently in Dubai?
faqs.answer: No. The qualification is awarded by Cambridge or Pearson, not by the emirate, so a grade 7 in Pearson 4PH1 means the same thing whichever side of the boundary the school sits on. What differs is the regulatory paperwork around the school and, for use inside the UAE, the equivalency process, which is federal and applies identically. If you are planning a move between emirates, the useful questions are which board the receiving school enters and whether its internal assessment deadlines differ, rather than whether the grades will be recognised.

faqs.question: Can a tutor come to our building in Al Nahda instead?
faqs.answer: Not through IB Gram. Tuition for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or Sharjah; that service exists only in India. Independent in-home tutors do work in this district and published rates for them run higher, roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour, because travel sits inside the fee and the journey here crosses the border queue. If presence in the room is genuinely the requirement, for a younger child who will not work unsupervised, that is a reasonable thing to buy elsewhere, and saying so is more useful than pretending we offer it.

faqs.question: Which exam board do schools around Al Nahda use for IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Both, and sometimes both inside one school. Schools on either side of this boundary enter Cambridge or Pearson depending on the subject and the department, and it is common for a single year group to sit Cambridge mathematics and Pearson sciences. The code on the statement of entry is the only reliable guide: 0580, 0620 and 0625 are Cambridge, while 4MA1, 4CH1 and 4PH1 are Pearson. Ask the school for the entry codes rather than reading the prospectus, because a tutor prepared for the wrong board teaches correct content against the wrong paper.

faqs.question: What slot do you use for families who cross the emirate line daily?
faqs.answer: Usually 19:00 on weekdays, with weekend mornings from around 09:00 for anything that needs a longer block. The reasoning is that a session has to start after the return journey has definitely finished, not at the hour it finishes on a good day. At 19:00 the useful work is marked scripts, worked examples, command terms and short timed sections, where the paper carries the structure. New abstract content belongs in a weekend block. During Ramadan the same households usually move to a post-iftar slot at around 20:30 or later, which works better than any afternoon hour.

faqs.question: What happens if nobody is free for the subject we need this week?
faqs.answer: We tell you and give a date rather than taking the booking and sorting it out later. Evening hours between 17:00 and 19:00 Gulf time are the most requested in the whole network, and in mock season they genuinely run out. Narrow components take longer: Computer Science solution development, Further Mathematics, Arabic as a first language at Diploma level. The alternatives we offer are a different hour with the right specialist, a weekend block, a dated wait, or a deliberately different tutor profile where the work does not need the specialism. No competing page in this market admits a coverage limit at all.

dubai/al-nahda.closingHeading: Send both schools, not just the subject
dubai/al-nahda.closingBody: If your household runs children in two emirates, tell us both schools, both boards and roughly when each child gets home, and we will plan the slots together rather than one at a time. Where a marked script or a school report exists, send it: it tells a specialist more in five minutes than a conversation does in half an hour. We will say honestly whether the right tutor is free at the hour you need, and give you a date rather than a maybe if they are not. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, with a trial session before any commitment.

dubai/al-quoz.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach IB and IGCSE subjects to students across Al Quoz and the central corridor, including a number who specialise in mid-course arrivals. The first job with a transfer student is working out which part of the syllabus they have genuinely never met, rather than assuming the whole course needs repeating.

intro.heading: Al Quoz is a crossing point, and transfer students need different help
paragraphs: Al Quoz is four numbered sectors stretched along Sheikh Zayed Road and Al Khail Road, part industrial, part gallery district, part residential, and it sits between Downtown, Business Bay, Al Jaddaf, Meydan and the Nad Al Sheba and Sobha Hartland developments. Families here are unusually mixed by income, nationality and curriculum history, and the tutoring enquiries reflect that. Roughly half concern a specific weak topic in a settled student. The other half come from households that arrived in the last eighteen months.

Transfer is the thing this page is about, because it is handled badly almost everywhere. A child moving from a CBSE Class 10 into a Cambridge IGCSE Year 11, or from an American high school into the first year of the IB Diploma, is not behind. They are differently placed. They may be ahead on algebraic procedure and behind on extended written explanation, ahead on content coverage and behind on the assessment format, or entirely fine in four subjects and missing two full units in a fifth. Treating that as general catch-up wastes months.

The second thing transfer families have to deal with is paperwork, and nobody writes about it. Dubai's private schools are regulated by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. Move to Abu Dhabi and the regulator is the Department of Education and Knowledge; Sharjah has its own authority; Ras Al Khaimah has a Department of Knowledge; and the federal Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Those five bodies govern different things, and a family that assumes the UAE has one school regulator will be surprised.

Behind that sits equivalency. Students who will apply to a UAE university, or who need a UAE certificate equivalency for any other reason, have to satisfy published Ministry of Education requirements that differ by curriculum. For the British track the published requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from the count of five. One page currently ranking for these searches publishes a six-subject figure, which is wrong.

What follows is written for the family in the middle of that: a transition map by subject, the regulator map for all seven emirates, the equivalency requirements as published, what the KHDA-mandated Arabic and Islamic Education provision adds to a transfer student's week, who may legally tutor in the UAE and how to verify it, and what the first six weeks after a mid-year arrival should look like. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE.
