dubai/al-quoz.programmesIntro: The four routes below are the ones Al Quoz transfer students most often move between. The notes concentrate on the entry point and the gap rather than on a description of each programme, because that is the decision a transferring family is actually making.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: A two-year course, usually eight or nine subjects, with Cambridge subjects tiered as Core or Extended and Pearson structured by paper instead. The codes are not interchangeable: Cambridge 0580, 0620, 0625 and 0610 against Pearson 4MA1, 4CH1, 4PH1 and 4BI1. Assessment of practical skills, formula provision and tiering all differ between the two boards.
programmes.countryNote: This is the most common destination for an Al Quoz transfer, and the most common source of misplacement. A student arriving from an Indian-curriculum Class 9 is frequently placed into Year 10 on age and then found to be strong on procedure and short on extended explanation. The tier decision, Core or Extended, is the one worth getting right in the first month.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, with Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS alongside. Internal Assessments carry a substantial share of most grades and are marked against published criteria by letter. The two years are continuous rather than modular, which makes mid-course entry genuinely difficult after the first term of DP1.
programmes.countryNote: Transfers into the Diploma mid-DP1 are workable; transfers into DP2 are usually not, because coursework deadlines and Internal Assessment work are already under way at the receiving school. Families arriving in Dubai in a DP2 year are usually better served by finishing the original qualification remotely where that is possible.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each judged out of eight against published band descriptors, with grades from one to seven derived from the total. The Personal Project runs in the final year. Assessment rewards process and written reasoning rather than recall, which is the single largest shift for a student arriving from a content-and-test system.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP is the gentlest landing for a mid-year arrival into the central corridor, because the criterion model allows a student to be assessed on what they can show now rather than on a two-year accumulation. It is also the one where the shift in marking style unsettles a transferring student most.

programmes.name: Mandatory UAE subjects alongside any curriculum
programmes.ageRange: All year groups in private schools
programmes.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and prohibits combining the two groups because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ.
programmes.countryNote: For a transfer student this is often the real shock: a subject they have never studied, sometimes examined, timetabled from the first week. KHDA calculates the instructional time in forty-minute lesson units and advises that no mandatory subject lesson falls below twenty-five minutes, and the Ministry prohibits the use of different or additional content without prior permission.

dubai/al-quoz.subjectsIntro: Requests from Al Quoz and the central corridor skew towards the subjects where a curriculum change bites hardest, which are the written ones, plus the mandatory UAE stream that a transferring student has usually never met.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Required of non-Arab students in Dubai private schools, taught in separate classes from Arabic as a first language. Support has to follow the school's own scheme of work, because the Ministry prohibits different or additional content without prior permission. Progress comes from regular short spoken practice rather than vocabulary lists.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: Taught with Standard Arabic as the language of instruction, in classes kept separate from the additional-language stream. Transfer students from outside the region who are heritage speakers often find the written register, rather than the spoken language, is what costs them marks.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.description: Required of Muslim students, with Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Arabs and first-language Arabic students, and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arabs. Schools must ensure teachers of this subject hold the appropriate KHDA approval to teach it.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: Where transfer students are most often ahead on procedure and behind on presentation. An Indian-curriculum arrival can usually do the algebra and loses marks because working is compressed into a single line that a marker cannot follow. The tier decision matters more than the content gap.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language and English First Language
subjects.description: The subject that decides how quickly a transfer student settles everywhere else, because every other subject is assessed through written English. Extended written explanation is the specific skill, and it is different from conversational fluency, which transfer students often already have.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Content maps across systems reasonably well; assessment format does not. A student arriving from a system of short numerical questions meets structured multi-part questions with explanation marks attached, and loses marks on the explanation rather than the physics.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Moles and electrolysis at IGCSE, energetics and organic mechanisms at Diploma. The characteristic transfer problem is a student who can calculate correctly and cannot describe what is happening at an electrode in the words the mark scheme wants.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Management
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0455 and 0450
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy and evaluation decide the marks, and both are usually new to a transfer student. Students from content-heavy systems write knowledgeable answers with no judgement in them, which is the single most expensive habit in these subjects.

subjects.name: History and Geography
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0470 and 0460
subjects.description: Source handling and case-study use are assessed skills, not background reading. A transferring student who has learned the content will still lose marks for narrating it, and the fix is rewriting the same answer against different question stems.

subjects.name: Hindi and French
subjects.description: Often the continuity subject for a transferring family, and worth protecting for that reason. Productive skills decide the grade and are the hardest to maintain alone, which is where a weekly hour spoken entirely in the target language earns its place.

dubai/al-quoz.regionsIntro: The central corridor is a set of very different housing types within a few kilometres of each other, and the schooling patterns differ accordingly. The notes below describe who sends children where and what each pattern means for a tutoring plan.

regions.name: Al Quoz 1 and 2
regions.note: Residential pockets between the industrial and gallery areas, with a long-settled Indian and Arab community. An IGCSE tutor in Al Quoz is most often asked for Mathematics and English here, frequently for a student who transferred within the last two years.

regions.name: Al Quoz 3 and 4
regions.note: More mixed and more transient, with families who move between emirates for work. This is where regulator and equivalency questions come up most, because a household that has already changed emirate once expects to again.

regions.name: Downtown Dubai and Business Bay
regions.note: Apartment living, international postings, shorter tenancies. An IB tutor in Business Bay is often working with a student who has been in three school systems and needs the assessment format explained more than the content.

regions.name: DIFC and Al Jaddaf
regions.note: Professional households with a high share of two-to-four-year postings. Diploma transfers are common and timing is everything: a mid-DP1 arrival is workable, a DP2 arrival usually is not.

regions.name: Meydan and Nad Al Sheba

dubai/al-quoz.modesIntro: Transfer work and settled subject work need different shapes, and the three patterns below reflect that. The first two are specific to arrivals; the third is the ordinary weekly arrangement a settled student uses.

modes.title: Six-week transfer block
modes.description: A fixed block that starts with a diagnostic against the receiving syllabus rather than against the student's previous one, identifies the units genuinely never covered, and closes them in order of exam weighting. It ends on a defined date with a written statement of what is now covered and what still is not, which is a document a school will read.

modes.title: Assessment-format sessions
modes.description: Short, concentrated work on how the new board asks questions, for a student whose content knowledge is sound. It covers command terms, mark allocation, structured multi-part questions, and the specific written conventions the receiving board rewards. Often four sessions are enough, and it is the highest-return work available to a transfer student.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one for a settled student
modes.description: The ordinary arrangement: one or two sessions a week on a named subject at a named level, with work marked between sessions and one finishable task set each time. Nobody travels, so an evening slot on either side of the corridor's traffic is equally workable, and a second sibling can take the following slot.

sections.heading: Why Al Quoz enquiries split into two quite different kinds
paragraphs: The first kind is familiar everywhere: a settled student, a specific weak topic, a parent who wants somebody who knows the subject at the right level. That request is answered by matching on syllabus code and tier and then doing weekly marked work. Nothing about Al Quoz makes it different from the same request in any other part of Dubai, and most of the second half of this page applies to it only loosely.

The second kind is a transfer, and it needs a different first conversation. A student who arrived eight months ago from a CBSE Class 9, an American ninth grade or a British Year 10 in another country is sitting in a Year 10 or Year 11 class whose teacher reasonably assumes a shared starting point. The student may be well ahead in some respects. What they are missing is usually two things: specific units that their previous course either placed later or never included, and the receiving board's assessment conventions.

Confusing those two is the standard error. A parent sees low marks and buys general tutoring, which repeats content the student already knows and does not touch the format problem. Or the school recommends support in Mathematics when the actual issue is that every subject is assessed through extended written English and the student writes compressed, procedural answers. Separating content gaps from format gaps in the first session is the single most useful thing a tutor can do for a transfer student, and it takes one marked script to do it.

sections.heading: A curriculum transition map for students arriving mid-course
paragraphs: The table below maps the transfers we see most often in this corridor. The fourth column is the one worth reading twice, because it names the gap rather than describing the destination. In most cases the gap is narrower than a parent fears and more specific than a school has time to diagnose, and in a few cases, particularly a late Diploma arrival, it is wider than anyone wants to admit.

The weeks column is an estimate of focused one-to-one support, assuming the student is also in the class and doing the ordinary homework. It is not a promise and it varies enormously with the student. What it is useful for is budgeting a decision: a family weighing up whether to transfer in January or wait until August should know that an IGCSE Mathematics transfer is a matter of weeks and a DP2 transfer is a matter of whether it should happen at all.

One structural point applies to every row. Where a student is moving into a two-year linear course partway through, the receiving school's internal assessment timetable governs everything. Coursework deadlines, mock windows and Internal Assessment submission dates are set by the school, not by the board, and they differ between schools in the same emirate. Ask the receiving school for its internal calendar before the transfer rather than after, because that document decides whether the move is viable.

A last word on where the weeks go. In almost every row above, the largest single block of time is spent on how the receiving board asks questions rather than on what it asks about. That is counter-intuitive for a parent who has just moved countries and expects the content to be the problem, and it is the reason a transfer block should start with a timed paper rather than with a textbook. A student who can already do the mathematics and loses method marks to compressed working will recover faster than one who has four units missing, even though the second student usually looks calmer in class.

sections.heading: Who regulates private schools in each emirate, and what each one governs
paragraphs: Families moving within the UAE frequently assume there is one school regulator. There are five, and they do not govern identical things. Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. In Abu Dhabi and Al Ain the Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools. Sharjah's Private Education Authority regulates private education in that emirate, and Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge does the same in its own.

The federal Ministry of Education plays a pivotal part in supervising private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. There is also a federal baseline behind all of it: private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That single rule is why every emirate requires the mandatory subjects whatever international curriculum a school is licensed to teach.

The differences matter practically. Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, so curriculum and fee approval sits with the emirate regulator rather than only inspection. Dubai's regulator confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in the emirate would not increase for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package. A family budgeting a move between emirates should know that fee governance, inspection frameworks and reporting formats all change at the border.

sections.heading: Ministry of Education equivalency: what each curriculum has to show
paragraphs: Equivalency is the process by which a school-leaving certificate earned on an international curriculum is recognised in the UAE. It matters for UAE university applications and for a range of administrative purposes, and it is one of the eighteen things nobody writing about tutoring in this market covers. The requirements were clarified publicly in July 2026 and differ by curriculum track, which is why a transfer decision taken for academic reasons can have a paperwork consequence two years later.

For the British track the published requirement is proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, together with passes in five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. For the American track, English proficiency requires a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL internet-based test, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Mathematics test.

For the International Baccalaureate, no points threshold is published in the source that sets out the other two tracks, and this page will not invent one. If your child is on the Diploma and equivalency matters to you, verify the current requirement on the Ministry's own website or with the emirate attestation authority before you plan around it. IB Gram describes this process; we do not perform it, we are not part of it, and no tutoring arrangement is required for it. Any page implying that tutoring is needed to secure equivalency is making a false-urgency claim about a regulatory process.

sections.heading: Indian-curriculum families moving into IGCSE: what actually changes
paragraphs: This is the most common transfer in Al Quoz, and the most commonly misread. A student arriving from a CBSE or ICSE school is usually not behind on content. In Mathematics they are frequently ahead, having met quadratics, trigonometry and coordinate geometry earlier. In the sciences the content overlap is substantial. What changes is almost entirely how the answer has to be presented, and that is a smaller problem than it looks and a different one from what the first set of marks suggests.

Three specific habits cost marks. The first is compressed working: an answer arrived at correctly in two lines, where the Cambridge or Pearson mark scheme allocates method marks that are unavailable because the steps are not visible. The second is the explanation mark, which rewards a sentence of reasoning that a procedural answer does not contain. The third is the command term, because a student trained to produce the answer tends to answer every question the same way regardless of whether it asked them to state, describe, explain or evaluate.

The tier decision sits on top of that. Cambridge subjects are tiered, Core and Extended, and the grade ceiling differs. A transfer student placed on Core because their first assessments were weak may be capped below where they can actually reach, and moving tier later in Year 11 is awkward. This is worth a conversation with the school in the first term, backed by a diagnostic that distinguishes procedural ability from presentation, rather than left until mock results make the decision for everyone.

sections.heading: The mandatory UAE subjects, and what they add to a transfer student's week
paragraphs: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA's current requirements had to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 the equivalent date for schools whose year begins in April. For a transferring family this is often the surprise: subjects nobody mentioned at the admissions interview, timetabled from the first week, sometimes assessed.

The organisation of these classes is prescribed in detail. For Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for first-language Arabic, Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students, and non-Arabs are taught Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural studies in the school's licensed-curriculum language.

Two further constraints shape what tutoring can look like here. Schools are required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, and for the mandatory subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is strictly prohibited. The practical consequence is that support in this stream must work from the school's own scheme and materials. A tutor who arrives with their own Arabic course is not helping; a tutor who builds short, frequent spoken practice around the school's unit is.

Separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs; combining the groups is prohibited

Instructional time calculated in forty-minute units, with twenty-five minutes advised as a floor

sections.heading: Who may legally tutor in the UAE, and how a parent checks
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years. The service is listed by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation as the issuance of a new work permit for private tutor licensing, with a two-working-day completion time, applied for through the Ministry's smart app, website and e-services system. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged fifteen to eighteen, and university students.

Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published; a figure circulating online could not be verified against any official source, and this page will not repeat it. What a parent should take from that is simply that the permit is free, quick and verifiable, so a tutor who does not hold one has chosen not to.

Two further distinctions are worth knowing. A tutoring operation with premises and staff in Dubai is a different legal entity from an individual tutor and needs a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, with initial approval first and annual renewal requested at least thirty days before expiry. And in Abu Dhabi, professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, a restriction the permit's own code of conduct echoes. Nobody should be marketing your child's own teacher to you privately.

sections.heading: The first six weeks after a mid-year arrival
paragraphs: Week one and two are for information, not teaching. Get the receiving school's internal assessment calendar, the syllabus code and tier for every subject, and a marked piece of work from each of the two or three subjects causing concern. Most families skip this and start tutoring on the basis of the previous school's reports, which describe a different course assessed differently and are close to useless for planning.

Weeks three and four are the audit. For each subject, separate three categories: content the student has met and can use, content met in a different order or notation, and content never taught at all. Only the third category needs teaching from scratch, and it is usually much smaller than it feels. The second category needs translation rather than instruction, which is fast. The first category needs nothing, and tutoring it is the commonest way a transfer family wastes money.

Weeks five and six go to format. One paper per subject sat under time and marked out loud, with the focus on working, command terms and mark allocation rather than on content. By the end of six weeks a family should have a written statement of what is covered, what is not, and which two subjects warrant continued weekly support. That document is also worth sharing with the school, because a tutor's subject-level audit is information the school does not otherwise have.

Two things commonly derail this sequence. The first is a school that cannot supply the internal calendar quickly, in which case ask the subject teachers directly rather than waiting on the office. The second is a parent starting weekly tutoring in week one because the first set of marks was alarming. Those marks were produced by a student who did not yet know the format, and they will improve on their own once the format is learned. Spending the first fortnight gathering information feels passive and saves a term of misdirected effort.

sections.heading: Starting from Al Quoz, including what we will not do
paragraphs: The first conversation is short and factual: which school, which year, which board and code, how long your child has been in the UAE system, which subjects are causing concern, and whether UAE equivalency is likely to matter. If a transfer is involved, the receiving school's internal assessment calendar is the most useful document you can send. If it is a settled student, a marked script is.

We then look for a specialist in that subject at that level who is free in the slot you have, and arrange a trial lesson and a consultation before any block is booked, with terms set out in writing. Where no specialist is free in your slot, we say so rather than offering a near-match quietly; that happens most often for the Arabic and Islamic Education streams, where school schemes are prescribed and KHDA approval requirements apply to the subject's teachers, and for narrow Higher Level combinations close to the May papers.

There are things we do not do, and they are worth stating. We do not send tutors to homes in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; lessons are one-to-one over live video, and home tutoring at the door is a service we run only in India. We hold no accreditation from any UAE regulator or examination board and operate no premises here. We do not handle attestation or equivalency, which belong to the Ministry and the emirate authority. And we do not supply text for an Internal Assessment, Extended Essay or Personal Project, because the candidate carries the malpractice risk and must be the author.

process.title: Establish where the student is actually coming from
process.description: Previous system, previous year group, how long in the UAE, and whether equivalency will matter later. These four facts change the plan more than the subject does, and they are the ones a generic enquiry form never asks for.

process.title: Get the receiving school's internal calendar
process.description: Coursework deadlines, mock windows and Internal Assessment submission dates are set by the school rather than the board, and they differ between schools in the same emirate. That document decides what is achievable this term.

process.title: Audit each subject into three categories
process.description: Content met and usable, content met in a different order or notation, and content never taught. Only the third needs teaching from scratch. Most of what feels like a large gap is in the second category and closes quickly.

process.title: Work on format before working on breadth
process.description: One timed paper per concerning subject, marked out loud, focused on working, command terms and mark allocation. For a transfer student this is usually the highest-return four hours available.

process.title: Write down what is covered and what is not
process.description: At the end of the block you get a plain statement of coverage by unit, which is worth sharing with the school. It also tells you honestly whether weekly support should continue and in which subjects.

whyPoints.title: Transfer treated as a mapping problem
whyPoints.description: A mid-course arrival is not behind; they are differently placed. Separating content never taught from content taught in a different order usually shrinks the job by half and stops a family paying to re-teach what their child already knows.

whyPoints.title: The regulator map stated in full
whyPoints.description: Five bodies govern UAE private schools and they do not govern the same things. Abu Dhabi's regulator is named by none of the competing pages for these searches, and Sharjah's by almost none, which is unhelpful for a family moving between emirates.

whyPoints.title: Equivalency quoted, not guessed
whyPoints.description: The British and American track requirements are set out as published, with the exclusion of Arabic and Islamic education from the five-subject count stated. Where no figure is published, as for the Diploma, we say so instead of inventing one.

whyPoints.title: The mandatory UAE stream taken seriously
whyPoints.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are required in every Dubai private school and prescribed in detail down to class organisation and language of instruction. Support here follows the school's scheme, because the Ministry restricts additional content.

whyPoints.title: The permit position made checkable
whyPoints.description: The private tuition work permit is free, issued for two years, and takes two working days. That makes it a reasonable thing to ask any tutor for, and a reasonable thing to refuse to proceed without.

whyPoints.title: Clear about the limits
whyPoints.description: Lessons are online one-to-one. We hold no regulator accreditation, operate no UAE premises, do not perform attestation, and do not supply text for assessed work. Where nobody suitable is free in your slot, we tell you.

faqs.question: What are the UAE Ministry of Education equivalency requirements for British curriculum students?
faqs.answer: As published in July 2026, a student on the British track must show one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, together with passes in five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five. Verify your own case on the Ministry's own website or with the emirate attestation authority before planning around it. IB Gram describes the process and plays no part in it.

faqs.question: Do the mandatory UAE subjects count towards the five-subject equivalency total?
faqs.answer: No. The published requirement states explicitly that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects for the GCSE and IGCSE count. That is a useful detail because at least one page currently ranking for these searches tells UAE families they need six IGCSE subjects, which does not match the published rule. Your child still has to take the mandatory UAE subjects at school, because KHDA requires them of every Dubai private school regardless of curriculum; they simply do not form part of the five accredited subjects the equivalency count uses.

faqs.question: We are moving to Al Quoz mid-year from a CBSE school. Where does my child start?
faqs.answer: It depends on the year group and the subject audit, not on age alone. A Class 9 arrival generally slots into Year 10 and does well, often ahead on content and behind on presentation. A Class 10 arrival moving into Year 11 needs a unit-level audit first, because some IGCSE units will be missing outright and the practical-skills assessment conventions will be new. Ask the receiving school for the syllabus code and tier for each subject, then get a diagnostic that separates procedural ability from written presentation. The tier decision, Core or Extended, is worth settling in the first term.

faqs.question: Which regulator oversees my child's school if we move from Dubai to Sharjah?
faqs.answer: The Sharjah Private Education Authority, which regulates private education in that emirate and approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. That is broader than inspection alone, so school-level assessment practice can vary more than a family used to Dubai expects. In Dubai the regulator is the Knowledge and Human Development Authority; in Abu Dhabi and Al Ain the Department of Education and Knowledge; in Ras Al Khaimah the Department of Knowledge; and the federal Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Verify any school against its own regulator's listing.

faqs.question: How does IGCSE compare with the UAE Ministry of Education curriculum?
faqs.answer: They are different qualifications with different purposes, and in a private school they coexist. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations, which is why an IGCSE student in Dubai also sits mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies. For UAE university entry the question is equivalency rather than comparison: the British track has published requirements covering five accredited IGCSE subjects plus A Level or AS Level attainment, which you should verify on the Ministry's own site.

faqs.question: Who can legally offer private tutoring in the UAE, and how do I check?
faqs.answer: Anyone holding the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible categories include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. The Ministry lists a two-working-day completion time through its smart app, website and e-services system. Individuals tutoring without a permit face fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so treat any specific amount with scepticism. Ask any tutor to show the permit before the first lesson.

faqs.question: Does my child have to take Arabic in a Dubai private school?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and the current KHDA requirements were to be implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year. The organisation is prescribed: separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes for the two groups prohibited because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Non-Arab students take Arabic as an additional language, which is a different course from the first-language stream.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects does my child need in the UAE?
faqs.answer: For the Ministry of Education equivalency count on the British track, five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from those five, plus one A Level at no less than E or two AS Levels at the same grade. Schools typically enter students for eight or nine subjects, which is a school decision rather than a regulatory minimum. One competing page states six as the requirement; the published rule says five. Confirm your own position on the Ministry's own site before relying on either figure.

faqs.question: What support is there for a student switching from an American curriculum into the IB Diploma?
faqs.answer: The move works best at the standard entry point, into the first Diploma year after grade ten or eleven. The content overlap is usually reasonable and the gaps are structural: Internal Assessments marked against published criteria by letter, Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay, and examined papers that select across the whole course rather than the current unit. Four to eight focused sessions on the core components and on examination format tend to cover it. Entry into the second Diploma year is rarely viable, because coursework is already under way and the receiving school's internal deadlines will already have passed.

faqs.question: Which schools do families in Al Quoz and the central corridor use?
faqs.answer: The pattern spreads across three clusters. On the Sheikh Zayed Road side, GEMS Our Own Indian School, GEMS Wellington International School, Dubai International Academy Al Barsha and Repton Al Barsha. Towards Nad Al Sheba, Meydan and Sobha Hartland, GEMS Modern Academy, North London Collegiate School Dubai, Kent College Dubai and Hartland International School. On the creek side, Swiss International Scientific School Dubai, Dubai English Speaking College, Safa British School and Jumeirah College. These are named as local context only. IB Gram has no affiliation with, endorsement from or contract with any of them.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with Arabic as an additional language for a non-Arab student?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a real constraint. For the mandatory UAE subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is prohibited, so support has to work from your school's own scheme of work and assessment rather than from a separate Arabic course. In practice that means short, frequent spoken practice built around the school's current unit, plus work on the written register, which is usually what costs marks. Schools must also ensure that their own teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education hold the appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects.

faqs.question: How long does it take to close a curriculum gap after a mid-year move?
faqs.answer: For an IGCSE transfer from an Indian-curriculum Class 9, typically six to ten sessions across two subjects, because content is usually ahead and the gap is presentation and command terms. From Class 10 into Year 11 it is longer, often ten to sixteen, weighted towards units never taught. From a British Year 11 or IGCSE into the first Diploma year, four to eight, mostly on the core components. A mid-second-year Diploma transfer is not a tutoring problem at all; it is a placement decision, and finishing the original qualification is usually the better route. These are planning estimates, not promises.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram handle the attestation and equivalency paperwork?
faqs.answer: No, and nobody offering tutoring should suggest otherwise. Equivalency and certificate attestation belong to the Ministry of Education and the relevant emirate authority, and they are administrative processes with published requirements and official channels. We describe them on pages like this one so that families can plan, and we point you to the official route. Tutoring is not required for equivalency, for university admission or for school progression, and any page implying that it is has made a false-urgency claim about a regulatory process rather than an educational argument.

faqs.question: Is online tutoring suitable for a student still working on the language of instruction?
faqs.answer: It can be, and for extended written English it is often better than the alternative, because the student's own writing is on screen in front of both people and can be edited and discussed line by line. Screen sharing also lets a tutor model the structure of an answer in real time rather than describing it. What live video does not replace is volume of spoken practice in a classroom, so for a student in the early stages of English acquisition the useful pattern is frequent shorter sessions focused on one skill rather than a single long weekly hour.

faqs.question: What happens if my child arrives in Year 11 partway through an IGCSE course?
faqs.answer: Treat it as an audit before anything else. Get the syllabus code and tier for every subject from the receiving school, plus its internal mock and coursework calendar, then work out which units were genuinely never taught as against taught in a different order. Entry deadlines also matter: Cambridge final entries for a March series fall months before the papers, so the school's entry decisions may already be made. Expect ten to sixteen focused sessions weighted to the missing units, and expect the practical-skills assessment conventions to need separate attention.

dubai/al-quoz.closingHeading: If you have just arrived, start with an audit rather than a tutor
dubai/al-quoz.closingBody: The most expensive mistake a transferring family in Al Quoz makes is buying general tutoring before anybody has worked out what is actually missing. Send us the receiving school's internal assessment calendar, the syllabus code and tier for each subject, and one marked piece of work, and the first session will tell you which units were never taught, which were simply taught differently, and which subjects warrant continued weekly support. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, the terms are written down before any block starts, and we will tell you plainly if nobody suitable is free in your slot.

intro.heading: The hour you actually have, and how to spend it
paragraphs: Al Quoz 4 is a quiet residential pocket wedged between the warehouse blocks of Al Quoz Industrial and the villa streets that run towards Al Safa and Umm Al Sheif. It has shops, a mosque, a scattering of low-rise villa compounds and a steady flow of traffic heading for Al Khail Road. What it does not have is a school. Every child living here leaves the community each morning and comes back to it in the late afternoon, and that single fact decides more about tutoring than any choice of tutor does.

Ask ten households on these streets where their children study and you will collect four or five different answers: an Indian-curriculum school in Al Quoz 1, a British school in Al Barsha, an IB continuum school in Al Barsha or Nad Al Sheba, a bilingual school towards Al Safa. The school bus leaves early, often before seven, and returns somewhere between half past two and four depending on the route and the day of the week. A Year 11 student with a swimming squad on two evenings and Arabic homework on the others has perhaps two usable slots in the week. Choosing which subject gets them is the real decision.

This is why the format matters more here than the marketing around it. A visiting tutor who has to reach Al Quoz 4 from Deira or Dubai Silicon Oasis at five in the afternoon is pricing in the drive whether the invoice shows it or not, and the first casualty of a late arrival is the end of the lesson rather than the beginning. Lessons delivered online, one-to-one, over live video remove the drive from both sides of the arrangement. The slot that exists on paper is the slot that gets used. IB Gram does not send a tutor to any address in the UAE; visiting tutors are something we arrange only in India.

The second thing that changes with format is the size of the pool. A household in Al Quoz 4 that wants a Chemistry Higher Level specialist, or someone who has taught Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics specification 4MA1 rather than Cambridge 0580, is not well served by whoever happens to live twenty minutes away. On live video, the search is for the person who knows that paper, which is a different search with a much better answer at the end of it.

Dubai's private-school sector gives you plenty of choice and very little guidance on what to do with it. KHDA, the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate, and Dubai's media office reported 387,441 students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, offering 17 different curricula. UK-curriculum schools accounted for 37% of that enrolment, Indian schools 26%, US schools 14% and the International Baccalaureate 7%. Those proportions explain the mix of boards inside a single Al Quoz street and the mix of syllabus codes a tutor has to keep straight.

What follows is written for a household here rather than for Dubai in general: when a lesson can realistically start, what each session length can do, what the market charges per hour and who published those figures, and the Cambridge March series counted backwards from its own published dates. The pricing in this page describes the market, not an IB Gram rate card. Ask us for the trial and the consultation if you want our own figures.

dubai/al-quoz-4.programmesIntro: Al Quoz 4 children sit across the IB continuum and the Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE routes, often with siblings on different ones. Each programme below carries a note on what it means specifically for a household that commutes out of this community every day.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus the three core components: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Each subject carries an internally assessed piece of work marked against published criteria and moderated externally. The written papers sit in a single window, so a weak Paper 1 cannot be repaired by a strong Paper 2 in the way a modular qualification allows. Most of the workload that decides the final grade happens outside taught lessons, in drafting, data analysis and past-paper practice the student manages alone.
programmes.countryNote: For an Al Quoz 4 Diploma student the binding constraint is usually the autumn of DP2, when school deadlines for internally assessed work stack up against university application dates. Working backwards from those deadlines rather than forwards from today is what keeps the term survivable. A fixed 90-minute online slot at the weekend tends to do more for a Diploma student here than two rushed weekday half-hours squeezed either side of the Al Khail Road return.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, labelled A to D, with command terms that mean something precise and task-specific rubrics rather than percentages. Reports arrive as criterion levels out of eight, which parents new to the system often read as marks out of ten. The Personal Project in the final year is a long independent piece with its own criteria, and MYP eAssessment, where a school offers it, produces an externally validated certificate. The step from criterion levels into Diploma marks catches strong students off guard.
programmes.countryNote: Several IB continuum schools serving this part of Dubai sit in Al Barsha and Nad Al Sheba, which means a long bus run from Al Quoz 4 and a child who arrives home tired. MYP work rewards process over speed, so a 45-minute online session on criterion language and task planning is often better value here than an hour of content revision. We also help parents translate a criterion-level report into something actionable before any tutoring is bought.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses in eight to ten subjects, examined externally, with Cambridge syllabuses carrying four-digit codes such as 0580 Mathematics, 0620 Chemistry and 0625 Physics, and Pearson International GCSE codes such as 4MA1, 4CH1 and 4PH1. Cambridge sciences and mathematics are tiered into Core and Extended, which sets the grade ceiling before a single paper is sat. Pearson's modular structure in some subjects allows a unit to be resat in a later series; Cambridge's linear structure usually does not.
programmes.countryNote: The practical question for an Al Quoz 4 family is which board the school actually entered, because the same subject name hides different papers, different formula sheets and different past-paper banks. We ask for the statement of entry before the first session. If the school enters the Cambridge March series, the calendar is tighter than the June one and the entry deadline falls in November, which surprises most parents.

programmes.name: IB Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: An inquiry-led programme organised around transdisciplinary themes rather than separate subjects, finishing with the Year 6 Exhibition. Reports describe approaches to learning and conceptual understanding instead of giving marks, which makes it hard for a parent to tell whether reading fluency, number facts or written structure is the thing to work on. The skills that matter most later — reading stamina, arithmetic automaticity, writing at length without prompting — are mostly built in the primary years and are rarely itemised on a PYP report.
programmes.countryNote: Primary tutoring from Al Quoz 4 works best in short, early slots, before the evening collapses. Thirty to forty-five minutes on live video, three times a week, beats a single long session for a seven-year-old. We ask for the most recent report and a sample of unaided writing, then say plainly whether tutoring is the right purchase at all; for many PYP children twenty minutes of reading a night is the better intervention.

dubai/al-quoz-4.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Al Quoz 4 households ask about most, with what each one actually assesses and where marks tend to leave the page. Levels are listed because the Higher Level and Extended routes are different courses, not the same course with extra homework.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The proof-heavy Diploma mathematics route, with calculus, algebraic manipulation and reasoning weighted far more than modelling. Higher Level adds a third paper drawn from an optional topic and sat without the comfort of familiar question shapes. Marks go missing in method lines that are skipped rather than in final answers, and in the exploration where students choose a topic too wide to control.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and technology-led work, with the graphic display calculator central rather than incidental. Students who move here from Analysis and Approaches often underestimate the writing: interpreting a model in context carries real marks. Higher Level is demanding in its own right and is accepted for many engineering and economics routes, so the switch should be an evidence-based decision rather than a retreat.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE Core and Extended
subjects.description: Electricity and magnetism, waves, mechanics and, at Higher Level, fields and quantum phenomena. The reliable losses are unit errors, misread graph axes and experimental-design questions that ask for a control variable and get a method instead. For Cambridge 0625 and Pearson 4PH1 the formula provision differs, which changes what has to be memorised.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE Core and Extended
subjects.description: Stoichiometry, bonding, energetics and organic mechanisms, with Higher Level extending into reaction pathways and more quantitative equilibrium work. Most lost marks come from careless mole arithmetic and from writing a description where a mechanism was asked for. The internally assessed investigation needs a question narrow enough to generate real data in school conditions.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL · IGCSE Core and Extended
subjects.description: Cell biology, genetics, physiology and ecology, with a heavy command-term load: state, outline, explain and evaluate all attract different mark tariffs. Students who revise by rereading notes plateau quickly; those who practise structured answers against mark schemes do not. Data-analysis questions reward reading the axes before the question.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Microeconomics, macroeconomics and the global economy, assessed through essays, data response and the internal assessment commentaries built on news articles. Diagram accuracy decides more marks than most students expect, and the evaluation sentence at the end of a fifteen-mark answer is where the grade separates. Higher Level adds quantitative work that rewards disciplined practice.

subjects.name: English
subjects.levels: IB Language A HL and SL · IGCSE First Language
subjects.description: Textual analysis, comparative work and, in the Diploma, the individual oral and the higher level essay. The common failure is retelling the text instead of analysing how its language produces an effect. For Cambridge 0500 and Pearson equivalents, directed writing is scored on audience and register as much as on content, which is teachable in a handful of sessions.

subjects.name: Business Management and Business Studies
subjects.description: Organisational structure, marketing, operations and finance, with case-study papers that reward applying a tool to the specific business in front of you rather than describing the tool. Students lose marks by writing textbook definitions where the question asked for a recommendation. Ratio calculations at IGCSE must be shown line by line to earn method marks.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Algorithms, data structures, networks and system fundamentals, with pseudocode conventions that differ between boards and matter in marking. The internally assessed solution needs a client with a real problem and a scope small enough to finish. At IGCSE, trace tables and binary arithmetic are high-yield topics that most students can secure in a few focused hours.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Arabic is mandatory in Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. For most expatriate families this is the subject that quietly costs grades on the school report while the tutoring budget goes entirely to maths and science.

sections.heading: The Al Quoz 4 afternoon, timed from the school gate
paragraphs: The earliest a lesson can start for a child living in Al Quoz 4 is set by the bus route, not by the tutor's diary. Work it out once, write it down, and the rest of the arrangement stops being guesswork. The pattern below is what families on these streets describe: an early departure, a long return, and a gap of forty to ninety minutes between arriving home and being able to think about anything academic.

Three things reliably push the start time later. The first is the number of stops on the route — a bus serving Al Quoz, Al Safa and Umm Al Sheif in one loop drops Al Quoz 4 children towards the end. The second is the school's own finish time, which varies by a full hour between primary and secondary phases in the same building. The third is extracurricular activity: a squad training session or a music lesson at school adds ninety minutes and shifts the arrival into the worst of the evening traffic.

Against that, an online lesson has one structural advantage that a visiting arrangement cannot match. Nothing in the chain depends on a second journey. If the bus is twenty minutes late, the family moves the start by twenty minutes and the full session still happens. If a visiting tutor is twenty minutes late, the session is twenty minutes shorter, because the next household is expecting them. Over a term that difference compounds into several hours of teaching that either happened or did not.

Use the table to find the row closest to your own route, then pick a slot fifteen minutes after the earliest workable start. That buffer is not politeness; it is what stops the first ten minutes of every lesson being spent settling a child who has just walked in.

sections.heading: Why no school sits inside Al Quoz 4, and what that changes
paragraphs: Al Quoz was zoned around light industry, warehousing and workshops, with residential pockets layered in later. Al Quoz 4 is one of those pockets: villa compounds and low-rise housing with commercial land on two sides. Schools went where the master plans put residential density, which is why the nearest campuses sit in Al Quoz 1, Al Safa, Al Barsha and towards Nad Al Sheba rather than inside the sub-community itself.

The consequence is that Al Quoz 4 has no single dominant school and therefore no dominant curriculum. Households on the same street can be running the Cambridge IGCSE route, a Pearson Edexcel route, the IB continuum and an Indian board simultaneously. A neighbour's recommendation is close to worthless in that situation, because the tutor who was excellent for a Cambridge 0580 Extended candidate may never have taught Pearson 4MA1, let alone an MYP criterion-based course.

It also means there is no walkable fallback. In a community built around one school, a parent can book a teacher who lives three streets away and the arrangement survives a late afternoon. Here, every arrangement that depends on travel depends on Dubai traffic, and the traffic on the Al Khail Road and Sheikh Zayed Road approaches between four and seven is the single least predictable variable in the week.

What that argues for is matching on syllabus rather than on geography. Ask for the statement of entry or the school's curriculum page, identify the board and the code, and then look for someone who has taught that exact paper. Delivered on live video, that search covers a far larger pool than a twenty-minute drive radius does, and the pool is where the specialist actually is.

sections.heading: Choosing between a 45, 60 and 90-minute session
paragraphs: Session length is treated as a billing detail and it is really a teaching decision. A 45-minute lesson can rehearse one technique properly. A 60-minute lesson can review set work, teach one new idea and leave the student with something to practise. Only a 90-minute lesson has room for a full past-paper section under timed conditions followed by marking it line by line, which is the single most useful thing a Diploma or Year 11 student can do with a tutor.

For Al Quoz 4 the practical implication is that the 90-minute slot almost always has to live at the weekend, because the weekday evening after the commute cannot hold it without pushing bedtime. That is not a compromise; it is a better design. Weekday sessions carry the short, high-frequency work — command terms, mark-scheme language, a single topic — and the weekend session carries the timed practice.

Parents often ask whether two 30-minute sessions beat one of 60. For a primary child, yes, clearly. For a Year 10 or Year 11 student, no: half an hour is consumed by settling, reviewing and setting, leaving almost nothing for teaching. The crossover sits somewhere around Year 7 and depends more on the child's concentration than on the subject.

One more variable is worth planning for. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a 40-minute lesson unit and advises that no mandatory-subject lesson should be shorter than 25 minutes. Schools therefore think in 40-minute blocks, and a student used to that rhythm often works well with a 45-minute tutoring session that mirrors it.

sections.heading: What fifteen minutes of travel costs over a school term
paragraphs: Do the arithmetic once and the format question answers itself. A weekly hour-long session across a fourteen-week term is fourteen hours of teaching. If a visiting arrangement loses fifteen minutes at the start because of traffic on the approach roads, and the end time is fixed because another family is waiting, the term delivers ten and a half hours instead. Three and a half hours have evaporated, and nobody issued a credit note for them.

The same arithmetic applies to the household's own time. A parent who drives a child to a tuition centre near Al Safa or Al Barsha spends between forty and seventy minutes in the car for a one-hour lesson, twice if they wait. Over a term that is fifteen to twenty hours of adult time, which is why tuition centres in Dubai quietly cluster their secondary classes at the weekend.

There is a second, less visible cost. A child who has just been in a car for thirty-five minutes does not start a lesson in a working state. The first portion of the session gets spent restarting them. Lessons that begin at home, after food, in a familiar room, start closer to full speed, and over a term that is worth more than the travel time itself.

None of this makes a tutor in the room worthless. For a young child who needs an adult physically turning pages, or for a student who will not engage with a screen at all, the room wins. It is simply worth pricing honestly rather than assuming presence is free.

sections.heading: What tutoring costs around Al Quoz, in AED per hour
paragraphs: Three of the six best-ranking tutoring pages for Dubai queries publish no price at all, and two of the others quote in US dollars, which is not the currency a Dubai household transacts in. The figures below are market rates in AED collected from the providers' own published pages and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table. They describe the market. They are not an IB Gram price list, and any provider quoting you a figure should be willing to say what is inside the hour.

The spread is wide for a reason. At the bottom sit university students and generalist online tutors; in the middle sit qualified subject teachers working online; at the top sit specialists in a single Higher Level subject and tutors who market examiner experience. A visiting arrangement adds the travel, which is why in-home hourly figures in Dubai run materially above online ones for comparable experience.

Put the numbers in context before deciding anything. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that private-school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion. A household whose school fees are flat for a year has a clearer view of what tutoring it can sustain, and sustaining one subject for two terms beats three subjects for six weeks.

Ask three questions of any quoted rate: is it per hour or per session, does it include the marking of work set between sessions, and does it change in the exam term. The answers vary more than the headline figures do.

sections.heading: A visiting tutor on Al Khail Road against one-to-one online
paragraphs: This is the comparison most Al Quoz 4 parents are actually running when they search for a home tutor, so it deserves a straight answer rather than a sales pitch. A visiting tutor has genuine advantages: physical presence, the ability to take a pen to a page, and no dependence on a household's bandwidth. For a child under about nine, or for a student with attention needs that a screen aggravates, those advantages can be decisive.

The costs sit on the other side of the ledger. The pool shrinks to who will drive to Al Quoz 4 at five in the afternoon. The rate carries the travel. The arrangement is fragile: one accident on the Al Khail Road and the lesson is half a lesson. And the specialist you want — a Chemistry Higher Level teacher, or someone fluent in Pearson 4PH1 rather than Cambridge 0625 — may be in Mirdif or in Mumbai, and either way is not coming to this street at five.

IB Gram delivers tutoring to Al Quoz 4 as one-to-one online lessons over live video. We do not send tutors to addresses in the UAE; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India. That is stated plainly because the alternative, implying a visit and then explaining later, wastes a parent's time and is the sort of thing this market does too often.

The honest summary is that the room wins on presence and the screen wins on everything measurable: who you can reach, what the hour costs, whether the full hour happens, and whether work can be marked and annotated in a shared document that both sides still have next week.

sections.heading: The Cambridge March series, counted backwards from its own dates
paragraphs: Some Dubai schools enter the Cambridge March series rather than June, and the families affected usually discover the implications in November when the entry deadline has already passed. Cambridge publishes its key dates for the March series, and they are worth reading as a calendar rather than a notice: the exam period runs 3 February to 4 March 2027, final entries are due 27 November 2026, forecast grades are due 27 February 2027, results reach centres on Cambridge International Direct on 13 May and certificates follow in late June.

Read backwards, that means the decision about whether a child sits a subject in March has to be made in October or early November, before the autumn mocks have told anyone much. It means the Christmas and New Year break is the last useful revision block, not a rest period. And it means a student who wants a tutor for the run-in needs to have found one by the start of December, because the slots in January go first.

Cambridge also allocates every exam centre to one of six administrative zones and warns that the correct version of the timetable for the centre's zone must be used, noting that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong zone timetable was used. Parents should take the timetable from their own school rather than from any tutoring website, including this one.

For June and November candidates the shape is the same and only the dates move. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November, with the November 2026 final timetable finishing on 19 November 2026; June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. For the IB Diploma we do not publish session dates on these pages, because they could not be confirmed against ibo.org directly — ask your school's IB coordinator and treat the May session as the one UAE schools sit.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies in the same week
paragraphs: Most tutoring budgets in this community go to mathematics and the sciences, and most school reports that worry a parent at the end of the year carry a weak grade in Arabic. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA's requirements were to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April.

The rules are specific enough to matter for tutoring. KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language; Social Studies is taught in Arabic for Arab students; non-Arab students take Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural studies in the language of the school's licensed curriculum.

There is also a content restriction worth knowing before anyone offers your child extra material. For the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. Tutoring in these subjects therefore means teaching the school's own material properly — vocabulary, reading fluency, written structure, memorisation technique — rather than importing a parallel syllabus.

One more thing surprises British-track families every year. Arabic and Islamic Education are not included among the five accredited subjects required for Ministry of Education equivalency on the GCSE and IGCSE route. They still appear on the school report and still affect progression decisions inside the school, so they are not optional in any practical sense; they simply sit outside the equivalency count.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do with internally assessed work
paragraphs: Every IB Diploma subject carries an internally assessed component, and the IGCSE routes carry coursework in several subjects. These pieces are assessed as the student's own work, and the IB's academic-honesty rules treat a breach as malpractice, with consequences that fall on the student rather than on whoever helped. Any provider willing to hand over a finished piece is selling your child a risk, not a service.

Here is the line in plain terms. A tutor may teach the assessment criteria and what each letter actually rewards. A tutor may discuss a proposed research question and say honestly whether it is narrow enough to generate usable data. A tutor may read a draft the student has produced and give feedback on structure, reasoning, use of evidence and clarity. A tutor may teach the skills the task needs — referencing, graph conventions, uncertainty treatment, evaluation language — using a different example.

A tutor may not author any sentence that appears in the submission, supply text for the student to adapt, build the student's data set, or hand over a model answer to the student's own question. Where a school's own rules are tighter than the board's, the school's rules apply; some Dubai schools limit external feedback to a single draft, and a tutor should ask about that at the start rather than find out at the end.

The market around these pages includes at least one operation selling completed Internal Assessments at a published price. We will not do that, and a parent who is offered it should understand what is being sold: a piece of work the student cannot defend in a viva, submitted under a declaration of authenticity they have to sign.

sections.heading: Starting from Al Quoz 4, and what happens when the slot you want has gone
paragraphs: The first conversation is short and mostly diagnostic. We want the board and syllabus code, the current grade or criterion levels, the most recent marked script if there is one, the two evenings that are genuinely free after the commute, and what you want to be true in twelve weeks. That last answer is the one that shapes everything else; 'improve in maths' and 'secure a 6 in Analysis and Approaches Standard Level for a university offer' lead to different plans.

A trial session follows, taught rather than sold. The tutor sets a short diagnostic, works through it live, and sends a note afterwards saying what they found and what they would do with the first six weeks. If the diagnosis is that tutoring is not the right purchase — and for some students it genuinely is not, because the problem is sleep, workload or subject choice — we would rather say so in week one.

Slots are finite and the good ones go early. The 16:30 to 18:00 window on weekdays is the most requested in Dubai, and in January, before the Cambridge March series, it is effectively full. If the subject and slot you want are not available, we will say so and offer the options honestly: a different weekday, a weekend slot, a different tutor with the same syllabus experience, or a wait. For a small number of niche Higher Level subjects the tutor who knows the paper may be based outside the UAE and teaching into a UAE evening; we tell you where a tutor is based when you ask, because that is a reasonable thing to want to know.
What we will not do is invent availability to hold an enquiry. A term of lessons in the wrong slot with a tutor who does not know the board is worse than four weeks of waiting for the right one.

process.title: Tell us the board and the code
process.description: Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are different exams with the same subject name. The statement of entry, the school's curriculum page or a past assessment paper settles it in a minute, and it prevents the commonest matching error in this market.

process.title: Fix the two evenings that actually exist
process.description: Track the real bus arrival time for a fortnight, add the decompression gap, and name the two slots that survive. A slot chosen from the timetable you wish you had is the slot that gets cancelled in week three.

process.title: Sit a diagnostic in the trial
process.description: A short written task, worked through live, tells a tutor far more than a conversation about weaknesses does. You receive a note afterwards naming the specific gaps found and what the first six weeks would target.

process.title: Agree the session length deliberately
process.description: Forty-five minutes for a weekday technique session, sixty for weekly IGCSE review, ninety at the weekend for timed paper work and marking. Choosing length by what the lesson has to achieve beats choosing it by price.

process.title: Review at six weeks against the diagnosis
process.description: The same diagnostic is repeated and compared with the original. If the gap has not moved, we change something: the tutor, the method, the subject that gets the hour, or the honest advice that the problem is not one tutoring can solve.

whyPoints.title: The whole hour happens
whyPoints.description: Nothing in an online arrangement depends on a second journey through the Al Khail Road evening. A late bus moves the start; it does not shorten the lesson. Across a fourteen-week term that is several hours of teaching that otherwise quietly disappears.

whyPoints.title: Matched by syllabus, not by driving distance
whyPoints.description: Al Quoz 4 has no school of its own and four or five curricula in one street. Matching on the exact board and code — Cambridge 0620 or Pearson 4CH1, Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation — is the difference between a tutor who knows the paper and one who knows the subject.

whyPoints.title: Prices described, not disguised
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure on this page is a market rate with the provider who published it named. We do not present the market's numbers as ours, and we will tell you what is inside our own hour before you book anything, including whether marking between sessions is part of it.

whyPoints.description: Criteria taught, research questions tested for scope, drafts read and given feedback. No sentence in a submission originates with the tutor. Where a school's rules on external feedback are tighter than the board's, the school's rules apply.
