process.title: Send the roster, not this week
process.description: Lay out the full three or four-week cycle rather than the week you happen to be in. We look for the hour that works on the worst week, because a slot that only exists some of the time is what ends most arrangements in this district.

process.title: Send one marked script and the code
process.description: A recent marked paper shows whether marks were lost to content, technique, vocabulary or timing, and the syllabus code tells us which board's papers to use. Cambridge and Pearson practice materials are not interchangeable.

process.title: Hand the student the controls
process.description: The student holds the login, the calendar reminder and a notebook with the week's set tasks. Removing the adult from the critical path is what makes the arrangement survive a month when nobody is home to open a laptop.

process.title: Run a diagnostic first session
process.description: The first session tests the hypothesis from the script and ends with a written note naming the gap, the order to address it and a realistic timescale, including the case where the honest recommendation is no tutoring at all.

process.title: Bracket the travel, review at six weeks
process.description: Trips get a session before departure that sets specific independent work and a session on return that marks it. At six weeks we compare the school's next assessment against the starting point and decide whether to continue, change or stop.

whyPoints.title: Built to run without an adult present
whyPoints.description: The student holds the login and the task list, and a written note follows every session. In a household where somebody is away on a pattern, that single design choice is the difference between an arrangement that holds and one that quietly stops.

whyPoints.title: The slot is chosen for the worst week
whyPoints.description: We test the proposed hour against the whole roster cycle rather than the week you enquired in. A worse hour that exists every week beats a better hour that exists one week in four, because consistency is most of what makes a subject move.

whyPoints.title: The schedule follows the family
whyPoints.description: Households in this district travel more and for longer than the Dubai average. An online slot continues from another country with the same tutor and the same plan, which an in-home arrangement cannot do at any price.

whyPoints.title: A written note any adult can pick up
whyPoints.description: Where two parents work different patterns, the person who knows what was covered is often not the person at home. A short note after each session naming what was taught and set removes the need for a handover conversation.

whyPoints.title: Figures in dirhams, each attributed
whyPoints.description: Every rate here belongs to the provider that published it, in the currency Dubai families use, and we also publish the cost of the sessions a bad schedule loses. Fixing the slot is the cheapest rate reduction available.

whyPoints.title: The honesty line taught to the student
whyPoints.description: Students with less adult oversight meet the worst offers in this market first. We teach the test directly: if the help would work with you absent, it is substitution, and the consequence falls on you rather than the seller.

faqs.question: How do you schedule tutoring around cabin crew or shift rosters in Al Rashidiya?
faqs.answer: By choosing the slot that works on the worst week rather than the week you enquire in. Lay out the full three or four-week cycle and find the hour that is viable in every one of them; it is often earlier, later, or on a weekend morning. Then remove the adult from the critical path: the student holds the login, the reminder and the week's task list, and a short written note after each session lets any parent pick up the thread from another country.

faqs.question: What happens to lessons when our family travels for three or four weeks in term time?
faqs.answer: The sessions continue from wherever you are, with the same tutor and the same slot adjusted for the time zone. Where that is not practical, we bracket the trip: one session before departure that sets specific independent work with worked examples, and one on return that begins by marking what was actually done. Ask the school which assessed tasks fall in those weeks before booking, because a trip crossing two criterion-assessed tasks costs considerably more than one crossing none.

faqs.question: What time can a lesson start for a family near Dubai Airport?
faqs.answer: Later than the distance suggests. Airport Road and the Garhoud interchange carry airport and logistics traffic on top of school traffic, so congestion builds earlier and clears more slowly than in a purely residential district. For schools towards Al Garhoud and Dubai Festival City, 4:00pm to 4:15pm is realistic. For the Mirdif direction, 4:30pm. For Al Mizhar and Al Khawaneej with long bus routes, 4:45pm. Students using the Red Line from the Rashidiya terminus arrive on a more predictable schedule and need a smaller buffer.

faqs.question: Can a fourteen-year-old really manage online tutoring without a parent at home?
faqs.answer: Many can, and the test is three weeks rather than a guess. The responsibilities are specific: hold the login and join two minutes early, keep a notebook with the week's set tasks written down, photograph attempted work if asked, report when something was not done rather than letting it be discovered, and know the date of the next school assessment. Students who cannot sustain that need a weekly format with a parent-facing reminder, which is useful information rather than a failure.

faqs.question: When are the Pearson Edexcel International GCSE exams and results?
faqs.answer: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations are available in May/June and November each year. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, including International GCSE November 2027, so check the live official PDF rather than a restated date before booking travel.

faqs.question: Why do entry deadlines matter so much for a family that travels?
faqs.answer: Because they sit months before the papers and they are not flexible. Cambridge's published key dates for the March 2027 series put the examination period at 3 February to 4 March 2027, with final entries due on 27 November 2026, more than two months earlier. A family abroad in November who assumed the decision could be made in January has missed the door for that series. Put entry deadlines, the examination window and the results date in a shared calendar before the revision plan.

faqs.question: Do you send tutors to homes in Al Rashidiya?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. In this district there are two extra reasons it matters: a tutor driving in during the late afternoon crosses airport traffic, so the arrival becomes an estimate rather than a time; and an in-home visit needs somebody home to admit the tutor, which is precisely what a roster household cannot promise.

faqs.question: How much does a missed session actually cost us?
faqs.answer: More than the hourly rate suggests. A family paying AED 200 an hour who loses one session in four is paying about AED 267 for each session that happens, and losing the continuity that makes a subject move. In-home arrangements are worse again, because a wasted journey is rarely recoverable and monthly packages seldom carry unused sessions over. Fixing the schedule so it survives the whole roster is the cheapest rate reduction available to a household in this district, and it costs nothing.

faqs.question: Which subjects are easiest for a student to keep going alone during a trip?
faqs.answer: Biology at IGCSE, because the losses are mark-scheme vocabulary and that can be drilled from flashcards and a marked script. Economics diagrams, because accuracy can be practised against worked examples. Set texts in English, because reading is reading. The hardest to park are chemistry calculations and Higher Level mathematics, where students usually need somebody present to start a problem and where fluency decays fastest. Set the work before departure and have the return session begin by marking it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help our Diploma student with an Extended Essay while we are abroad?
faqs.answer: Within the boundary, yes, and the Extended Essay is the component most affected by a household being away, because it depends on sustained independent work between school supervisor meetings. A tutor can explain the criteria, say whether the research question is viable, warn where the method will not produce usable material, and read a draft to name the weak criterion. A tutor cannot supply text, rewrite sections or edit a draft into a finished state. The school supervisor owns the formal process.

faqs.question: How do we spot a tutoring offer that would get our child into trouble?
faqs.answer: Apply one test: if the help would still work with your child absent, it is substitution rather than teaching. Offers to produce finished coursework, supply completed Internal Assessments or deliver a draft ready to submit all fail that test. One provider in this market sells completed Internal Assessments outright. Under board malpractice rules the consequence falls on the candidate who declared the work, not on the seller, and no refund exists for a withdrawn diploma.

faqs.question: Are fortnightly sessions a sensible way to cut the cost?
faqs.answer: For some students, yes, and we will say so. A fortnightly review with weekly tasks costs less and demands more: the tutor sets a week of work, the student completes it unprompted, and the session reviews and resets. It suits older, reliable students in households where weekly scheduling genuinely cannot hold. If two consecutive cycles slip because the work was not done, the honest move is back to weekly, because paying for a review of work that does not exist is worse value than a full slot.

faqs.question: Do private tutors in Dubai need a permit, and how long does it last?
faqs.answer: Yes. Individuals providing private lessons need a MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, and it is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Those tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. The official application route is MoHRE's private tutor licensing service.

faqs.question: What should we send you before booking anything?
faqs.answer: Three things, and the third is the one families leave out. One recent marked script or school report so a specialist can see where the marks went. The board and syllabus code, with the tier for Cambridge subjects. And the full roster cycle rather than this week's availability, because the slot has to be tested against the hardest week rather than the easiest. With those three, the first session can be a diagnostic that ends in a written recommendation instead of an hour of fact-finding.

dubai/al-rashidiya.closingHeading: Fix the slot that survives the whole cycle
dubai/al-rashidiya.closingBody: Tutoring in Al Rashidiya fails for scheduling reasons far more often than for teaching reasons. A session booked into the easy week of a roster looks fine for a fortnight and then starts disappearing, and nobody records the moment it stopped. The remedy is unglamorous: map the full cycle, pick the hour that holds on the worst week even if it is a weekend morning, hand the student the login and the task list, and have the tutor write three lines after every session so any adult can pick up the thread from anywhere. Then send a marked script and the syllabus code, and we will build the first session around it. Every lesson is one-to-one over live video.

dubai/al-safa.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover the subjects Al Safa households most often buy hours for, and they are the subjects where the price difference between a generalist and a specialist actually shows: Diploma Mathematics, HL Sciences, IGCSE Extended Maths and the English papers.

intro.heading: Why nobody in this market will tell you the price
paragraphs: Of the competing pages ranking for tutoring searches in Dubai, three publish no price at all. One of them runs a frequently asked question titled how much does tutoring cost and then declines to answer it. Two publish prices in US dollars, which is not the currency an Al Safa family pays in. The one competitor with a published hourly rate contradicts it in its own structured data. That is the state of pricing transparency in this market, and it is why a parent can collect four quotes and still have no idea what a fair number looks like.

The spread is enormous and it is real. Published online rates in Dubai start around AED 33 to 65 an hour at the budget end and run to AED 650 for a premium named tutor. That is a twentyfold range for something all five providers describe as one-to-one tutoring. Without knowing what each band buys, a parent cannot distinguish a reasonable quote from an opportunistic one, and the usual outcome is paying mid-market money for budget-tier teaching.

This page is organised around money rather than around pedagogy. It models what a full academic year costs for a Year 11 IGCSE student and for a Year 12 Diploma student, across six provider models. It names the extras that change the real hourly figure once you account for minimum session lengths, cancellation terms, resource fees and travel. It sets out how many hours a subject genuinely needs, because the hourly rate is the smaller half of the decision.

Al Safa is a useful place to do this honestly. It sits across Sheikh Zayed Road from Al Wasl, holds several of the coast cluster's British-curriculum secondaries inside its own boundaries, and its households span villa plots on the Jumeirah side and apartment stock towards City Walk. The budgets differ enormously, and the same hourly rate means very different things to two families two streets apart.

On format, there is nothing hidden. IB Gram arranges tuition as one-to-one lessons over live video, with a shared whiteboard and the student's own work on screen. Tutors are not dispatched to UAE addresses; in-home visiting exists only in the India service. Part of the reason is cost: published in-home rates in Dubai carry travel time inside the hourly figure, and a family pays for a commute as well as for teaching.

Every figure below names its source and the month it was read. Where a number could not be verified against a primary source, it has been left out rather than estimated, including the fine amounts circulating for unlicensed tutoring, which the ministry has not published. That rule costs this page some confident-sounding sentences and gains it the only thing a parent comparing quotes actually needs, which is a figure they can check themselves against the page that printed it. If a band below looks wrong against a quote you have been given, the source is named and you can go and read it.

dubai/al-safa.programmesIntro: Price varies by programme more than most parents expect, and it varies for structural reasons rather than arbitrary ones. The notes below explain what drives the cost of tutoring at each stage, which is the part a rate card never shows.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: No external examination, inquiry-led units, and reporting against learner attributes rather than marks. Tutoring at this stage is the cheapest tier in the market because it needs a strong generalist rather than a subject specialist, and sessions are usually thirty to forty-five minutes. The spend is low; the risk is buying weekly hours for something a reading routine at home would fix.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Safa the commonest primary purchase is English literacy or number fluency support for a child who has moved curriculum mid-primary, which is frequent in this part of Dubai. Six to eight focused sessions is a normal block. A term-long weekly commitment at this stage is rarely the efficient use of a budget.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight, converted to a 1-7 grade. Prices sit in the qualified-subject-tutor band because the criteria are specific enough that a generalist underperforms. The Personal Project in Year 11 is the single most expensive item families buy at this stage, and it is the one where the boundary on what a tutor may do matters most.
programmes.countryNote: Al Safa families with a child at an IB continuum school often buy MYP support in Years 9 and 10 to protect the Diploma entry, which is a sensible use of money. Buying it in Year 11 as emergency cover for the Personal Project is the expensive version of the same decision.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. This is where the market's specialist band applies: Bestimate puts specialist exam-year support at AED 200 to 450 and above, and Higher Level work in scarce subject combinations sits at the top of that. A two-year Diploma plan is the largest single tutoring commitment a Dubai household makes.
programmes.countryNote: The Diploma's cost curve is not flat. It peaks in the spring of Year 12 when Internal Assessments, the Extended Essay draft and the TOK exhibition cluster, and again in the final term of Year 13. Al Safa families who budget evenly across two years usually under-fund the first peak and over-fund the quiet months.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects examined at the end of Year 11. Unitors publishes IGCSE tutoring from AED 150 an hour against AED 200 for IB, and that gap is typical across the market. The cost driver is subject count: a family supporting three IGCSE subjects at two sessions a week each is buying six hours weekly, which is a larger bill than most Diploma plans.
programmes.countryNote: The practical cost-control move for an Al Safa IGCSE household is to triage by what will be continued post-16 and by which papers are closest to a grade boundary. Supporting every weak subject equally is how a budget disappears without a grade moving.

dubai/al-safa.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Al Safa families most often pay for, with a note on what drives the price and the hours in each. Scarcity, not difficulty, is what moves a rate: the fewer tutors who have taught a specification to examination, the higher the band.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL
subjects.description: The most expensive single combination in the Dubai market, because the pool who have taught it to examination is small. Non-calculator Paper 1 technique and proof work need drilling rather than explaining, which means homework between sessions does most of the work and the session count can be lower than families fear.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Mid-band pricing and frequently under-bought, because parents assume it is the lighter course. The statistics content is where hours go: interpreting regression and significance correctly is a learned habit, and students lose marks describing output rather than naming variables and levels.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Specialist band. Energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms carry the HL difficulty, and the Internal Assessment adds a separate block of hours around the school's internal deadline. Costing a Chemistry year without budgeting for the IA window is the commonest planning error here.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Specialist band, and the hardest slot to fill at a Gulf-evening hour. Extended-response technique is the highest-yield work: students describe where the command term asked them to explain, and lose marks they already knew the physics for.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Mid to specialist band. Content density means hours are spent on retrieval practice rather than explanation, which makes short frequent sessions better value than long ones. Command-term discipline separates a 5 from a 7 more reliably than extra content coverage does.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Mid-band for teaching, specialist band for the three Internal Assessment commentaries. Each commentary is capped at 800 words and built on a news article, and the marks sit in the link between theory, diagram and article rather than in the theory itself.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.description: Often the best value per hour, because the Individual Oral and Paper 1 respond quickly to structured coaching. Rehearsed, timed practice on unseen extracts moves grades faster than reading more texts, and that is a short block rather than a term-long commitment.

subjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics Extended
subjects.description: The highest-volume purchase in Dubai and the most competitively priced. Surds, algebraic fractions, graph transformations and bounds questions appear in every series and are the fastest marks to recover, which makes a targeted six-week block viable.

subjects.name: IGCSE Separate Sciences
subjects.description: Three subjects rather than one, so three times the hours if bought uncritically. The practical-skills paper is where marks are cheapest to recover, because candidates are asked to criticise a method and instead describe it, which is a technique fix rather than a content one.

subjects.name: IGCSE English First Language and ESL
subjects.description: Low to mid band. Register and form control carry more marks than vocabulary range, and the penalty for writing an article in letter form applies regardless of language quality. A handful of marked pieces usually achieves more than a term of weekly conversation.

dubai/al-safa.regionsIntro: Budgets and logistics differ sharply between the communities around Al Safa, and both change what format makes financial sense. These notes are about cost and scheduling rather than scenery.

regions.name: Al Safa 1 and 2
regions.note: Villa plots with study space, so a desk and a wired connection are usually available. In-home tutoring is easy to arrange here, which is also why local in-home quotes tend to sit at the upper end of the published AED 180 to 500 band.

regions.name: Al Wasl
regions.note: Immediately north across the main road, sharing the same school run. Families here frequently compare quotes with Al Safa neighbours, which is the single most useful price check available and costs nothing.

regions.name: Jumeirah 3
regions.note: Longer secondary school runs push a workable first slot later, and a later slot narrows the tutor pool for in-home work, which pushes the rate up. Online removes that constraint entirely at no price premium.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim
regions.note: Weekend morning sessions are common here because weekday evenings compete with activity schedules. Weekend rates are not usually higher, but minimum session lengths often are, so check the terms.

regions.name: City Walk
regions.note: Apartment living with no dedicated study room. The practical cost here is equipment rather than hours: a stylus tablet and decent headphones make an online session materially more productive for Maths and Science.

regions.name: Al Manara
regions.note: Inland towards Al Khail Road. Drive times in from a tutor's side of the city are the hidden component of any in-home quote, and in this direction they are the reason a two-hour minimum is standard.

regions.name: Pearl Jumeira and La Mer
regions.note: Newer stock with fewer schools inside the community, so longer runs and later starts. Families here often split a block across two children, which is the cheapest way to use a specialist's hour.

regions.name: Al Quoz 1
regions.note: Just inland of the Al Safa boundary and home to several schools. Worth noting because tutors quoting in-home rates for Al Safa often live on this side and price the crossing into the hour.

schoolClusters.city: Al Safa and the Jumeirah secondaries

Fee bands across these schools vary widely, which is why a tutoring budget should be set against a household's total education bill rather than against what neighbours spend.

sections.heading: What a full year of tutoring actually costs an Al Safa household
paragraphs: An hourly rate is almost useless on its own. What a family needs is the annual figure, because that is what competes with the school fee, the activity bill and everything else. The table below models a year at three different intensities, using the published Dubai bands rather than invented numbers, and sets them next to the other costs an education budget already carries.

The modelling assumes a thirty-six week academic year with sessions paused through the long summer break and the examination period itself, which is how most Dubai families actually run it. One session a week at the qualified-tutor band is the commonest pattern for a single IGCSE subject. Two sessions a week at the specialist band is typical for a Diploma Higher Level subject in an examination year. The Internal Assessment block is a separate, finite purchase.

The figures that surprise parents are usually the multi-subject ones. Supporting three IGCSE subjects at one session each is three times the hourly cost, and it arrives in the same month. That is the arithmetic behind the advice to triage: pick the subjects where a grade is genuinely close to a boundary and where the subject will be continued, and leave the others to the school.

One piece of context is unusually helpful this year. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package. For a household budgeting education spending, a flat fee bill makes the tutoring line easier to plan than it has been in several years.

sections.heading: Six provider models, and what each one is actually selling
paragraphs: Every competitor page in this market compares itself favourably against an unnamed set of other platforms. That comparison is worthless. What a parent needs is a neutral description of the models available in Dubai, what each charges, and what each does and does not include, so they can work out which one matches their problem.

There are six. A specialist agency charges a premium and takes responsibility for matching and replacement. An international marketplace charges less and leaves the matching to you. A freelance independent tutor is the cheapest per hour and carries the most variability in quality and continuity. A tuition centre group class is cheaper still per student but is not one-to-one. A school-run support session is usually free and is constrained to that school's staff and timetable. And a platform like IB Gram arranges one-to-one online teaching matched to a named syllabus.

The table compares them on the dimensions that matter when something goes wrong, not when everything goes right. Whether the rate is published. Whether in-home is even on offer. Whether the tutor's MoHRE permit has been checked. What happens if the match is poor after two sessions. Whether a trial exists and on what condition. Every rate in it is attributed to whoever published it.

Two columns deserve attention. The permit column matters because individuals offering private tutoring in the UAE need a MoHRE private tuition work permit under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, and a parent is entitled to ask to see it. The replacement column matters because a mismatched tutor is the commonest way money is wasted in this market, and a model with no replacement route turns a bad match into a sunk cost.

sections.heading: The extras that quietly change the real hourly figure
paragraphs: A quoted rate is the start of the arithmetic, not the end of it. Several common terms move the real cost per hour of teaching substantially, and none of them are dishonest if they are stated. The problem is that they usually appear after the first session rather than before it.

Minimum session length is the biggest. A two-hour minimum is standard for in-home work in Dubai, partly because a tutor cannot justify a crossing for sixty minutes. For a fifteen-year-old, two hours in one sitting is frequently less productive than two separate hours in the same week, so the family pays for two hours and receives rather less than two hours of useful teaching.

Then there is cancellation. A twenty-four hour policy is normal and reasonable. A policy that charges in full for a session cancelled because a child is ill, in a market where school absence is common, changes the annual figure by several sessions. Ask what the policy is and whether the session can be moved rather than lost. Resource fees, registration fees and examination-season surcharges are all worth asking about explicitly, as is whether the rate rises in the final term, which it does with several providers.

The last one is VAT. Whether tuition is taxed is not something this page will assert without a Federal Tax Authority citation, and nor should any other page. What a parent can and should establish is simply whether the number they have been quoted is the number that will be charged. Ask for the all-in figure per month, in writing, before the first paid session.

sections.heading: How many hours a subject actually needs
paragraphs: Hours needed is a bigger lever on total cost than the hourly rate, and it is the question providers are least willing to answer, because the honest answer is usually fewer hours than they would like to sell. It depends on three things: whether the gap is content or technique, how far the next assessment is, and how much work the student does between sessions.

A technique gap is cheap. If a student knows the material and loses marks on command terms, working-out discipline or timing, six to ten sessions with marked past papers in between will usually shift the pattern. A content gap is more expensive because the teaching has to happen before the drilling can. A two-term gap in algebraic fluency is not a six-session purchase, and anyone selling it as one is taking the money and hoping.

The multiplier nobody prices in is homework. A student who does the work set between sessions roughly doubles the value of each hour paid for, because the session is then spent on diagnosis and correction rather than on first exposure. A student who does none converts every session into a lecture, and lectures are the most expensive way to learn anything. That is worth saying to the student, not only to the parent paying.

The table sets out indicative blocks for the commonest Al Safa purchases. They are starting points for a conversation with a tutor after a diagnostic session, not quotations. A diagnostic that concludes fewer hours are needed than you expected is the most valuable thing a first session can produce.

sections.heading: Online, in-home or group: what each format buys in Al Safa
paragraphs: This choice is often framed as a quality question and is really a cost and access question. In-home tutoring in Al Safa is genuinely available and widely used; villa households here have the space for it and the published rate band is AED 180 to 500 an hour. What that rate buys is a tutor physically present and a supervision problem solved. What it does not buy is a wide choice of specialist, because the pool is whoever can reach this part of Jumeirah at the hour you need.

Group classes at a tuition centre are cheaper per student and are a different product. Four students sharing an hour means each gets a quarter of the tutor's attention, which works for revising known material and works badly for diagnosing why one particular student keeps losing method marks. For IGCSE revision in a strong subject it can be good value. For a Diploma Higher Level weakness it rarely is.

Online one-to-one sits between them on price and above both on tutor choice. IB Gram delivers lessons in this format: live video, shared whiteboard, the student's own script on screen, one student and one tutor. Tutors are not sent to addresses in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE, and home visiting is confined to the India service. The gain is that a specialist in a scarce combination becomes reachable regardless of where they sit at five in the afternoon.

The table makes the comparison on the dimensions that actually differ. Note the travel column: in Al Safa a tutor crossing from the inland side is pricing the crossing into the hour whether or not it is itemised, and that is a real part of why the in-home band sits where it does.

sections.heading: Why cheap coursework help is the most expensive thing in this market
paragraphs: There is a tier of provider in this space selling finished work. One operator advertises completed Internal Assessments at a fixed price in dirhams. Measured by the hour it looks like a bargain against a specialist's rate. It is the most expensive purchase available in Dubai tutoring, because the price of being caught is the Diploma.

The IB's authenticity requirement sits on the student. A coordinator who reads a draft that does not sound like the person who wrote the rest of the course is required to act, and a malpractice finding can remove the award. The provider who sold the work faces nothing. The asymmetry is the entire point, and it is why this needs saying plainly on a page about cost.

Legitimate coursework support is substantial and worth paying for. A tutor can teach the content the investigation rests on, explain what each criterion asks for in the IB's own wording, read the student's own draft and put the criteria to them as questions, and teach referencing, uncertainty handling and a research question narrow enough to answer in the word limit. That work genuinely moves marks and leaves the authorship where it belongs.

The test to apply to any provider is one question: what will you do with my child's draft, and what will you refuse to do? A tutor who answers that clearly is a teacher. A provider who is vague about it, or who offers to tidy it up, is selling the student a risk nobody has quoted them for.

sections.heading: Checking a tutor is permitted to teach, which costs nothing
paragraphs: Verification is free and almost nobody does it. Private tutoring by individuals in the UAE is regulated through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and, on the government's own account, is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged fifteen to eighteen.

MoHRE lists the service as Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, applied for through its smart app, website or e-services system, with a stated two-working-day completion time. Because the permit is free and quick, a tutor who does not hold one has no cost-based excuse. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are, in the government's wording, subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No schedule of amounts has been published, so any page quoting a specific figure is quoting something unverified.

Two further points are worth knowing before paying anyone. Dubai's schools are overseen by KHDA, which is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate, but KHDA does not license individual tutors; the permit it issues to training institutes with premises is a different instrument, and no provider should imply otherwise about itself. In Abu Dhabi, ADEK's professional-ethics framework has been reported as barring school staff from paid private tutoring of students at their own school.

So the free check is: ask to see the MoHRE permit, and ask whether the tutor teaches at your child's own school. Both questions take a minute and both are things a straightforward provider answers without hesitation.
bullets: The MoHRE private tuition permit is free and valid two years

sections.heading: Spending an Al Safa tutoring budget in the right order
paragraphs: If the budget is finite, and for most households it is, the order of spending matters more than the total. The sequence below is the one that tends to produce the most movement per dirham, and it starts with something free.

First, ask the subject teacher whether the lost marks on the last assessment were on content never covered or on questions the child could have answered. That single question is free and it determines everything that follows. Second, buy a diagnostic session rather than a term. A diagnostic produces a named topic list and an honest statement of how many hours are needed, which is the information the rest of the budget depends on.

Third, spend on technique before content where the diagnostic allows it, because technique is the cheaper fix and it compounds across subjects. A student who learns to read command terms properly carries that into every paper they sit. Fourth, protect the subjects that will be continued post-16 ahead of the ones that will not. A grade in a subject being dropped in August is worth less than a grade in the subject that will carry a university application.

Last, keep a reserve for the coursework window. Diploma families consistently under-budget the spring of Year 12, when Internal Assessments, the Extended Essay draft and the TOK exhibition arrive together. A block held back for that month is better value than the same money spread thinly across the quiet autumn.

process.title: Send the board, the level and the last marked script
process.description: A syllabus code and a recent marked paper tell a tutor more than a paragraph of description. Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are different papers; Standard and Higher Level are different courses. The script shows where marks are going, which is what the plan should be built on.

process.title: A diagnostic session with an hours estimate attached
process.description: The first session watches the student work rather than teaching at them, and ends with a named topic list and a realistic number of sessions. If the honest number is six rather than a term, you hear six. An estimate that always comes back as a term is not an estimate.

process.title: An all-in figure in writing before anything is paid
process.description: Rate, session length, cancellation terms, whether the figure changes in the examination term, and what is included. Al Safa families routinely collect four quotes on different bases and cannot compare them. One written monthly figure solves that in a sentence.

process.title: Weekly work, marked before the session not during it
process.description: Homework is set each session and marked before the next one starts, so the paid hour is spent on correction rather than on reading. That single discipline is the difference between an hour of teaching and an hour of supervision, at the same price.

process.title: A stop review at the next assessment point
process.description: The plan is reviewed when the next graded piece of work comes back, with stopping treated as a legitimate outcome. Sometimes the answer is fewer hours in that subject and a block in another. A provider who never recommends reducing is not reviewing.

whyPoints.title: Published bands with named sources
whyPoints.description: Every dirham figure on this page names who published it and when it was read, from EdFlik's AED 45 to 65 through to BartyED's AED 650. Three of the pages competing for this search publish no price at all, and two publish dollars.

whyPoints.title: Annual cost, not just an hourly rate
whyPoints.description: The hourly figure is the smaller half of the decision. Hours needed, session minimums and cancellation terms move the annual total far more, so those are modelled here rather than left for a parent to discover after the first invoice.

whyPoints.title: Hours estimated honestly after a diagnostic
whyPoints.description: A technique gap is a six to ten session purchase and a two-term content gap is not. A diagnostic that concludes you need less than you expected is the most valuable output a first session can have, and it is the one most providers avoid producing.

whyPoints.title: Online delivery, with the reason stated
whyPoints.description: Lessons run one-to-one over live video, with the student's own work on screen. Tutors are not dispatched to UAE addresses. Part of the rationale is cost: published in-home rates carry travel time inside the hourly figure, and a family pays for the commute.

whyPoints.title: The coursework boundary priced in
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches, explains criteria and reviews the student's own draft. Nobody writes or completes an assessed submission. Completed coursework sold cheaply is the most expensive purchase in this market, because the malpractice consequence lands on the student.

whyPoints.title: Coverage limits disclosed before payment
whyPoints.description: Some level and time-slot combinations have no UAE-based specialist free, Higher Level Physics at a Gulf evening hour among them. Where that applies you are told before booking, not afterwards, and offered the wider network at the same online one-to-one format.

faqs.question: What is a fair hourly rate for IGCSE tutoring in Al Safa?
faqs.answer: Judged against published Dubai rates, a qualified subject tutor working online sits around AED 150 to 300 an hour, based on Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. Below roughly AED 150 you are generally buying a generalist or a university student, which EdFlik and Tutopiya price from AED 33 to 65. In-home work runs AED 180 to 500 because travel sits inside the figure. Ask which band a quote belongs to and what the tutor has actually taught to examination, rather than negotiating the number alone.

faqs.question: Why do so few Dubai tutoring sites publish their prices?
faqs.answer: Because the spread is wide and publishing a number invites comparison. Across the pages competing for these searches, three publish no price at all, one asks the price in its own frequently asked questions and then does not answer, and two quote in US dollars rather than dirhams. One provider's published rate contradicts the figure in its own page data. The practical consequence for a parent is that quotes arrive on different bases and cannot be compared, which is why asking for a single all-in monthly figure in writing is worth more than any amount of negotiation.

faqs.question: How much should I budget for a full Diploma year in Dubai?
faqs.answer: For one Higher Level subject at two sessions a week across a thirty-six week year, the published specialist band of AED 200 to 450 an hour gives roughly AED 14,400 to 32,400. One subject at a single weekly session halves that. Add a finite block of eight to ten sessions for the Internal Assessment window, which lands in the spring of year one. Most families under-budget that spring and over-budget the quiet autumn, so holding a reserve for the coursework crunch is more useful than spreading the same money evenly.

faqs.question: Is a tuition centre group class worth it instead of one-to-one?
faqs.answer: For revising material a student already broadly understands, yes, and the cost per student is clearly lower. For diagnosing why one particular student keeps losing method marks or misreading a command term, no, because four students sharing an hour each receive a quarter of the attention. The useful test is whether the problem is coverage or diagnosis. Coverage problems suit a group; diagnostic problems need one-to-one. A Higher Level weakness is almost always diagnostic, which is why group revision rarely shifts it.

faqs.question: Do tutoring rates go up closer to the exams in Dubai?
faqs.answer: With several providers, yes, and it is rarely mentioned at the point of quotation. Bestimate's Dubai figures place specialist exam-year support at AED 200 to 450 and above, which is the top of the market, and demand for the final term concentrates on a small pool of specialists. The sensible step is to ask directly whether the rate changes in the examination term, and to secure a slot earlier at a stated rate rather than negotiating in March. Getting that commitment in writing costs nothing and removes the commonest unpleasant surprise.

faqs.question: Does the quoted price include VAT, and how do I check?
faqs.answer: Ask for the all-in figure that will actually be charged, in writing, before the first paid session. This page will not state the UAE VAT treatment of tuition as fact, because that requires a Federal Tax Authority citation and none is offered here. What matters practically is simply whether the number quoted is the number invoiced, and whether a tax registration number appears on the invoice. A provider who cannot give you one monthly figure in writing is a provider whose annual cost you cannot forecast.

faqs.question: What hidden extras catch Dubai parents off guard?
faqs.answer: Five recur. Minimum session length, with a two-hour minimum standard for in-home work, which often means paying for more sitting than a teenager uses productively. Cancellation terms that charge in full rather than moving a session. Registration or resource fees added on top of the hourly rate. A rate that rises in the examination term. And travel time priced inside an in-home hour without being itemised. None are improper if disclosed. All are worth asking about before the first session rather than after the first invoice.

faqs.question: How many tutoring sessions should an Al Safa family book to start with?
faqs.answer: Book one diagnostic session, not a term. The diagnostic should watch the student work through a past paper question or a recent marked script and end with a named topic list plus a realistic session count. A technique gap usually needs six to ten sessions with marked practice between them. A content gap spanning two terms needs considerably more and anyone promising otherwise is overselling. Committing to a full term before the diagnosis exists is how budgets are spent without a grade moving.

faqs.question: Is in-home tutoring in Al Safa worth the premium over online?
faqs.answer: It depends on what the premium buys. For a younger child who needs physical supervision to stay on task, often yes. For a Diploma Higher Level subject, usually not, because the in-home pool is limited to tutors who can reach this part of Jumeirah at the hour you need and the published band of AED 180 to 500 includes their travel. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE, delivering one-to-one tuition over live video instead, which removes the drive-time constraint on which specialist you can reach.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE subjects give the best return on tutoring money?
faqs.answer: Extended Mathematics and the practical-skills papers in the separate sciences, because in both the recurring question types are finite and drillable. Surds, algebraic fractions, graph transformations and bounds questions appear in every Mathematics series and are routinely skipped by candidates who have not been shown them. In the sciences, candidates asked to criticise a method frequently describe it instead, which is a technique correction rather than a content one. Both are short-block purchases rather than term-long commitments, which makes them the cheapest marks available.

faqs.question: What should I do first if my child's grades have slipped?
faqs.answer: Something free. Ask the subject teacher whether the lost marks on the most recent assessment were on content never covered or on questions your child could have answered, and ask to see the marked script rather than the summary grade. Content gaps and technique gaps need different interventions at different costs, and an organisation problem needs neither. Buying weekly subject tutoring before that question is answered is the commonest way an Al Safa household spends a term's budget without changing anything.

faqs.question: Are Dubai school fees going up for 2026-27?
faqs.answer: No. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in the emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, as part of Dubai's second economic incentives package. KHDA also reported seven new private schools opening for 2026-27, four British curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 additional places, after six new schools opened during 2025-26. For a household planning a tutoring budget, a flat fee bill makes the rest of the education line considerably easier to forecast this year.

faqs.question: What happens to my money if the tutor is not the right match?
faqs.answer: That depends entirely on the model you bought from, which is why it is worth asking before paying. An agency usually operates a formal rematch. A marketplace leaves you to search again. A freelance arrangement has no mechanism at all, so a poor match becomes a sunk cost and the search restarts from nothing. Ask specifically what happens after two sessions if it is not working, and get the answer in writing. A mismatched tutor is the single commonest way tutoring money is wasted in this market.

faqs.question: Can I reduce the cost by sharing a tutor between two of my children?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking, but check the subjects and levels first. A tutor fluent in Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Extended is not automatically fluent in Diploma Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and the two need different preparation. Where the levels are close, sharing a specialist's hour across two children is genuinely efficient and keeps the vocabulary consistent at home. Where they are not, two tutors at the right level will cost more and waste less. Ask what each tutor has taught to examination, not what they are willing to cover.

faqs.question: Is a free trial lesson genuinely free?
faqs.answer: Ask what the condition is, because there usually is one. Common conditions include a shorter session than a paid one, a requirement to book a block afterwards, a card held on file, or a trial with a different tutor from the one who would teach the course. None of those are improper, but a trial is only informative if it is with the tutor who would actually teach your child, at the level they would teach, using your child's own work. Confirm all three before scheduling it.

dubai/al-safa.closingHeading: Know the bands before you take the first quote
dubai/al-safa.closingBody: The reason tutoring money gets wasted in Al Safa is not that rates are high. It is that the bands are invisible, the hours are never estimated honestly, and the terms arrive after the first session. Those three things are fixable in an afternoon: read the published bands above, ask the subject teacher the free question, and insist on one all-in monthly figure in writing. IB Gram arranges one-to-one lessons over live video, matched to the syllabus code your child's school entered, with an hours estimate after a diagnostic rather than before it.

dubai/al-satwa.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are the ones whose availability matters in Satwa: evening and later-evening slots across Diploma Mathematics, the sciences, Economics and the IGCSE core subjects, with weekend mornings held for families whose weekday window closes entirely.

intro.heading: In Satwa the scheduling problem comes first
paragraphs: Al Satwa sits in a tight triangle between Jumeirah, Al Hudaiba and the Bur Dubai side of the creek, and it is one of the few central Dubai neighbourhoods with almost no private secondary schools inside its own boundary. Satwa children travel. They travel by school bus to Jumeirah, to Al Quoz, to Oud Metha and to Al Garhoud, and the journey home in the afternoon is the single biggest constraint on whether tutoring works.

That makes Satwa a different proposition from a villa community where a child walks in at half past three. A bus route that collects from four schools and threads back through the Satwa roundabout at peak does not arrive at a predictable minute, and a tutoring slot booked for 4pm on the assumption that it will is a slot that gets missed, rescheduled or wasted. Families here lose more money to mistimed sessions than to overpriced ones.

So this page treats time as the subject. It sets out how to build a slot from the bus arrival rather than from a generic after-school hour, what a realistic weekly pattern looks like when prayer times and siblings are in the mix, and how to plan a term around the examination calendar instead of reacting to it. It then counts the Cambridge and Pearson deadlines backwards from each series, using dates published by the awarding bodies themselves.

Delivery is online and that matters more here than in most Dubai neighbourhoods. IB Gram arranges one-to-one lessons over live video, with a shared whiteboard and the student's own paper on screen. No tutor travels to a UAE address; the in-home option exists only in the India service. In Satwa, where parking is tight, the streets are dense and an in-home tutor would be arriving in the same traffic the bus is sitting in, removing the travel from both sides of the arrangement is the difference between a slot that holds and a slot that slips.

Satwa households also tend to be apartment households, which changes the practical setup. There is often no spare study room, a younger sibling is usually in earshot, and the connection is shared. Those are solvable problems but they need solving before the first paid session rather than discovered during it, so there is a section on exactly that below.

On examination dates, one rule is applied throughout. Cambridge and Pearson dates are quoted only where the awarding body has published them, and the source is named. No IB session or results date appears anywhere on this page, because the IB's own site could not be verified for this project; for IB timings, ask your child's Diploma coordinator or check ibo.org directly. Secondary sources circulate IB windows freely and they do not always agree with each other, which is a poor basis for deciding when a block of tuition should start.

dubai/al-satwa.programmesIntro: Each programme has its own rhythm of deadlines, and the rhythm is what a Satwa family needs to plan around. These notes describe when the pressure actually arrives rather than what the programme contains.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four assessment criteria per subject, each out of eight, with no terminal paper in the IGCSE sense. The deadline pattern is continuous rather than seasonal: investigations, reflections and tasks land through the year, which means a student falls behind gradually instead of suddenly. Year 11 adds the Personal Project, with internal deadlines set by the school rather than by the IB.
programmes.countryNote: For a Satwa student the continuous pattern is both the risk and the opportunity. There is no single cliff edge, so a weekly slot that holds through the term is worth more here than a crash block. Equally, a term of missed slots does not announce itself until a report arrives in February.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three Higher and three Standard, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Every subject carries an Internal Assessment with a school-set internal deadline and an IB upload deadline behind it. UAE schools sit the May session. The planning problem is that internal deadlines cluster, and the school sets them, not the IB.
programmes.countryNote: Ask the Diploma coordinator for the school's internal deadline calendar in September and build the year from it. No IB date is published on this page because the IB's own site could not be verified for this project, so confirm every IB deadline with the coordinator or on ibo.org before relying on it.

programmes.name: Cambridge International GCSE and O Level
programmes.description: Cambridge runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states it is essential that the correct version of the timetable for your zone is used, because it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong one.
programmes.countryNote: That zone rule is the single most consequential administrative fact on this page and almost nobody writes about it. Ask your school's examinations officer which Cambridge zone your centre sits in, and check the paper times on that zone's timetable rather than on a general one found online.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Pearson runs International GCSE examinations in May and June and again in November each year. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026; November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series.
programmes.countryNote: Because Pearson publishes provisional timetables that can be revised, the right habit is to work from the live official timetable on the Pearson qualifications site rather than from a date copied into a planner in September. A Satwa family planning a November entry should check it again in October.

dubai/al-satwa.subjectsIntro: Subject by subject, the planning question is how much of the work has to happen between sessions rather than inside them, because that is what determines how badly a missed slot hurts. Each note below says where the time actually goes.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The most homework-dependent subject on the list. Fluency in algebraic manipulation and non-calculator arithmetic is built by daily short practice, not by long sessions, so a Satwa student with an unreliable weekday slot is better served by thirty minutes daily and one weekly review than by two long sessions.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics and modelling, calculator permitted throughout. The session time goes into interpretation rather than computation: naming the variables, the test and the significance level the question asked about. That is teachable in a slot and does not decay as fast as algebraic fluency between missed weeks.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: HL and SL · Cambridge 0625 and Pearson 4PH1 at IGCSE
subjects.description: Mechanics and electricity are the two topics Satwa families ask for most. Extended-response technique is the highest-return session work, because students describe a phenomenon where the command term asked them to explain it with a named quantity.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: HL and SL · Cambridge 0620 at IGCSE
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and equilibrium carry the HL difficulty. The Internal Assessment sits on a school-set deadline, so the sessions around it have to be booked against the school calendar rather than slotted into a weekly pattern.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: HL and SL · Cambridge 0610 at IGCSE
subjects.description: The most content-dense subject here, which makes it the most sensitive to missed weeks. Retrieval practice between sessions does most of the work; a session spent re-covering content a student forgot is the most expensive hour in the plan.

subjects.name: Business Management and Economics
subjects.description: Deadline-shaped rather than content-shaped. Economics requires three Internal Assessment commentaries of up to 800 words, each built on a news article, and each has its own school-set submission date. Planning sessions around those dates is more useful than a weekly slot.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.levels: HL and SL · Cambridge 0500 and 0510 at IGCSE
subjects.description: Rewards timed practice above all. A Satwa student with a fragile weekday window can do the timed writing independently and use the session purely for marking and correction, which makes English the most schedule-tolerant subject on this list.

subjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1
subjects.description: Extended is required for almost any post-16 Maths route. Bounds, surds, algebraic fractions and graph transformations recur in every series and are the fastest marks to recover, which makes a short targeted block a realistic plan even late in Year 11.

subjects.name: IGCSE Combined and Separate Sciences
subjects.description: Separate Sciences means three timetables, three entry codes and three sets of practical-skills technique. Candidates lose marks describing a method where the paper asked them to criticise it, which is the cheapest correction available in the subject.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Required in Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and sat alongside everything else. For a Satwa household it is usually the subject that gets squeezed out of the week, and the one most often requested late.

dubai/al-satwa.regionsIntro: These are the communities a Satwa enquiry sits inside or beside. Each note is about journeys and timing, because in this part of central Dubai that is what decides whether a lesson happens.

regions.name: Al Satwa
regions.note: Dense, low-rise and central, with few private schools inside the boundary. Almost every secondary student here is on a bus route out of the neighbourhood, so arrival home is between a quarter past three and half past four depending on the route.

regions.name: Al Hudaiba
regions.note: Immediately north towards the beach road. Shorter runs to Jumeirah-side schools, but the 2nd December Street corridor is slow at pick-up, which pushes a safe first slot to 4.30pm or later.

regions.name: Al Bada'a
regions.note: Between Satwa and Al Wasl Road. Mixed apartment and villa stock, and a common bus-route overlap with Satwa, which means households here face the same arrival uncertainty and can usefully compare notes on timings.

regions.name: Al Mankhool
regions.note: Across towards Bur Dubai, with several schools within a short run. Students here often arrive home earlier than their Satwa neighbours, so a 4pm start is more often workable.

regions.name: Jumeirah 1
regions.note: The destination for many Satwa bus routes rather than a residential option for most Satwa families. Worth knowing because a route that terminates in Jumeirah 1 on the way back adds fifteen to twenty minutes at peak.

regions.name: Karama
regions.note: Short hop across Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Road. Families often share activity schedules between Satwa and Karama, which is why evening slots after 6pm are in heavier demand on this side of the city than on the coast.

regions.name: Oud Metha
regions.note: A frequent school destination for Satwa students. The run back crosses the creek-side traffic, and in the cooler months it is the least predictable leg of any Satwa bus route.

regions.name: Al Quoz 1
regions.note: Another common school destination, inland along the Al Khail corridor. Buses returning from here are the latest arrivals, and families on these routes are the ones who most often end up with weekend sessions instead.

dubai/al-satwa.modesIntro: Three formats, chosen in Satwa mainly by how reliable the household's weekday window is. All are one-to-one over live video, and the right answer changes as the term progresses.

modes.title: A fixed weekday evening slot
modes.description: Booked at 5pm or later, after the bus has landed and before the evening fragments. This works when the route is predictable and the household has one student in the window. It is the format that lets a tutor track a syllabus continuously, which matters most in content-dense subjects like Biology.
bullets: Set the start twenty minutes after the usual bus arrival, not at it
Keep the same weekday so it becomes a habit rather than a decision
Agree in advance what happens when the bus is late

modes.title: Weekend morning sessions
modes.description: The format most Satwa families end up with for at least one subject, and often the more productive hour. A Saturday morning session is not competing with a full school day, a bus journey and an activity schedule, and it allows a longer block without the fatigue that makes a weekday double unproductive.
bullets: Better for a subject needing sustained concentration
Lets a sibling pair use consecutive slots on one morning
Survives a term more reliably than a fragile weekday slot

modes.title: A deadline-shaped block
modes.description: Hours bought against the school's own internal coursework calendar rather than weekly. Sessions sit before and after each submission date: one to plan, one to review the student's own draft. The tutor reads and questions the draft and does not write, rewrite or complete any part of it.
bullets: Built from the school's internal deadline list, obtained in September
Two sessions per submission rather than a continuous weekly slot
Authorship boundary stated to the student at the start

sections.heading: Why the question in Satwa is when, not who
paragraphs: Searches for tutoring help in central Dubai almost always begin as a search for a person. In Satwa the binding constraint turns out to be the clock. The neighbourhood has very little private secondary provision inside its own streets, so the children who live here are on buses out to Jumeirah, Oud Metha, Al Quoz and Al Garhoud, and they come back into one of the most congested road networks in the emirate at exactly the hour everyone else is moving.

The practical consequence is that a slot booked optimistically fails. A 4pm start assumes a 3.45pm arrival. If the route collects from three schools and threads back through the Satwa roundabout, 4.25pm is just as likely, and a student who walks in at 4.25pm for a 4pm lesson has lost a quarter of the hour and all of their composure. Repeated across a term, that is a meaningful amount of money spent on nothing.

The fix is unglamorous. Establish the actual arrival time across a fortnight rather than the scheduled one, add twenty minutes, and book from there. Agree in advance what happens if the bus is late, so a delayed arrival shortens a session rather than forfeiting it. And if the weekday window genuinely cannot hold, move the subject to a weekend morning rather than fighting the traffic every week.

None of this is about the quality of teaching, which is why no competitor page covers it. It is about whether the teaching happens at all, which for a Satwa household is the question that actually determines the outcome.
bullets: Measure the real bus arrival across two weeks, not the timetable
Add twenty minutes before the lesson starts
Agree the late-arrival rule before the first paid session
Move a fragile weekday subject to the weekend rather than repeating the problem

sections.heading: The Satwa bus run, and what it does to a lesson slot
paragraphs: School finish times across the schools Satwa children attend cluster between about 2pm and 3.30pm, but the arrival home does not cluster at all. It depends on route length, how many schools the bus serves, and which corridor it uses on the way back. A route returning along 2nd December Street at pick-up behaves differently from one coming in off Sheikh Zayed Road.

The table below works through the common patterns. It pairs a typical school location with the finish, the realistic arrival window in Satwa, the earliest workable lesson start and the slot that tends to hold across a full term. The last column is the useful one, because the earliest workable start and the one that actually survives a term are rarely the same time.

Two patterns are worth naming. Students on the Al Quoz and Al Garhoud routes are the latest arrivals and the ones who most often end up with weekend sessions, because a 5.30pm start on a weekday leaves no room for homework afterwards. Students at schools within Al Mankhool or Jumeirah 1 have the widest window and are the households for whom a conventional weekday slot works well.

The second pattern is sibling splitting. Primary-age children on separate routes frequently arrive forty minutes before a secondary sibling, which means a household with two students has two different windows rather than one shared one. Booking consecutive slots in a single weekend morning is the usual solution and it is cheaper in attention as well as in logistics.

sections.heading: Building a weekly pattern that survives a whole term
paragraphs: A timetable that works in September and collapses in November is the normal outcome, and it collapses for predictable reasons. Three things break it: an activity schedule that starts mid-term, a prayer time that moves with the season, and the arrival of a second student's commitments into the same evening.

Prayer times shift through the year, which means a slot that sat comfortably between two obligations in September may not in December. The straightforward response is to place the session so that the whole hour falls between prayer times at the latest point in the season rather than the earliest, and to build the schedule around that worst case once, rather than renegotiating monthly.

Activities are the second issue, and the common mistake is assuming the week is empty until something is booked into it. In practice the opposite is true: the week fills, and the tutoring slot is the item most often moved because it is the one with the most flexible counterpart. Treating it as fixed from the start, and moving other things around it, is what makes it survive.

The third is the homework question. A slot with no space after it is a slot that produces nothing, because the work set in the session has nowhere to go. A 5.30pm session followed by dinner, a sibling's bedtime and nothing else leaves the homework for the following morning, which is better than nothing but worse than the same session at 4.30pm with an hour behind it. When choosing between two workable slots, pick the earlier one for that reason alone.
bullets: Place the hour against the latest seasonal prayer time, not the earliest
Fix the tutoring slot first and move activities around it
Choose the earlier of two workable slots so homework has room
Review the pattern at half term, before it breaks rather than after

sections.heading: The examination calendar counted backwards
paragraphs: Almost no competing page in this market names an examination series at all, let alone a deadline. That is a strange omission, because the deadlines are what determine when tutoring has to start. An entry closes months before a paper is sat, and a family that discovers this in January has lost the option.

Cambridge runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. The March series offers the clearest worked example of how far ahead the administration sits. For the March 2027 series, Cambridge publishes an examination period of 3 February to 4 March 2027, with final entries due 27 November 2026, forecast grades due 27 February 2027, results released on Cambridge International Direct on 13 May and certificates issued in late June.

Read that sequence again in order. The entry deadline falls more than two months before the first paper, and it falls before the winter break. A family deciding in January that their child should sit a subject in the March series has missed the entry by six weeks. That is the single most useful piece of administrative information on this page.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations run in May and June and again in November. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, including for future November sittings, so the live official timetable is the only version worth planning from. For the IB, UAE schools sit the May session, but no IB date appears on this page: confirm every IB deadline with your Diploma coordinator or on ibo.org.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the shortened school day and where revision goes
paragraphs: Ramadan moves roughly eleven days earlier each year against the Gregorian calendar, which means its position relative to the examination season changes from year to year rather than staying fixed. In some years it sits clear of the spring assessment run; in others it lands squarely in the weeks a Year 11 student would normally be doing timed papers. Planning for it in September is far easier than reacting to it in the month itself.

Dubai schools typically run a shortened timetable during Ramadan, with each school publishing its own hours. The effect on tutoring is twofold. The school day finishes earlier, which widens the afternoon window and is genuinely helpful. But energy levels in the late afternoon drop for fasting students, which narrows the useful part of that wider window considerably.

The pattern most families settle on is a move to post-Iftar sessions, which works well for older students and badly for younger ones. The alternative is a late-morning slot on non-school days, which suits the content-heavy subjects where concentration matters most. What does not work is keeping a 5pm weekday slot unchanged and hoping, which is the default and the reason the month shows up as a gap in progress.

The practical move is to agree the Ramadan arrangement with a tutor a month in advance, not in the first week. Slots move for everyone at the same time, and the post-Iftar hours are the most heavily contested in the calendar. A family that asks early gets the hour it wants.
