sections.heading: Making an online lesson work from a Satwa apartment
paragraphs: Satwa is apartment country, and that changes the practical setup in ways worth sorting out before the first paid hour rather than during it. The three issues are space, sound and the device, and all three are cheap to fix compared with the cost of a wasted session.

Space first. Most households here do not have a spare study room, which means the lesson happens at the dining table or in a shared bedroom. Either works, provided the surface is clear and the student is sitting rather than lying down. What does not work is a sofa with a laptop on a cushion, because the camera cannot see written working and a Maths tutor who cannot watch the working appear is teaching blind.

Sound next. A shared apartment with a younger sibling needs headphones with a microphone, not the laptop's own speakers, and the student needs to be audible to the tutor without raising their voice. That single item removes most of the friction in an online session and costs less than one hour of tuition.

The device matters most for Mathematics and the sciences. A tablet with a stylus, or a cheap graphics tablet attached to a laptop, lets the tutor see each step as it is written rather than see a finished answer. That is the difference between feedback on a result and feedback on a method, and method is where the marks are. Test the whole arrangement on a call the day before the first session, not fifteen minutes before it.
bullets: A clear, flat surface with the student sitting upright
Headphones with a microphone, not laptop speakers
A stylus device so the tutor sees working as it happens
A full test call the day before the first paid session

sections.heading: When a session is missed rather than cancelled
paragraphs: In a neighbourhood where arrival times are unpredictable, the policy on missed sessions is not a small print issue. It is the difference between a plan that tolerates reality and one that punishes it. Most providers operate a twenty-four hour cancellation rule, which is reasonable and solves nothing for a bus that is forty minutes late on the day.

The arrangement worth negotiating is a shortened session rather than a forfeited one. If the student arrives at 5.20pm for a 5pm slot, forty minutes of teaching is worth having and the tutor has already blocked the hour. Agreeing that in advance costs nothing and removes the argument from the moment it would otherwise happen, which is while a tired teenager is standing in the doorway.

The second thing to agree is what happens to the work when a session is genuinely lost. A session that disappears without the homework being marked costs more than the fee, because the following week starts with the tutor reading work rather than correcting it. Sending the completed work regardless, even when the session itself cannot happen, keeps the sequence intact.

Finally, be honest about chronic slippage. A slot that is missed or shortened three weeks in four is the wrong slot, and the answer is to move it rather than to keep paying for a quarter of it. That conversation is easier if the pattern has been written down, which is a reason to keep a simple record of what actually happened each week.
bullets: Negotiate a shortened session rather than a forfeited one
Send the homework even when the session cannot happen
Keep a simple weekly record of what actually took place
Move a slot that fails three weeks in four rather than tolerating it

sections.heading: Deadlines, drafts and the honesty line
paragraphs: Timing is also where academic honesty problems begin. A student who has left an Internal Assessment or an Extended Essay draft until the week before a school deadline is the student most likely to accept help they should not accept, and the market around these searches contains providers selling exactly that. One advertises completed Internal Assessments at a fixed price.

The consequence falls on the student. The IB's authenticity requirement means a coordinator who reads a submission that does not sound like its author is obliged to act, and a malpractice finding can cost the award. The provider who sold the work carries nothing. Which is why the honest version of coursework support is scheduled early rather than sold late.

What a tutor can legitimately do is considerable and is best done well before the deadline. Teach the content the investigation rests on. Explain each criterion in the IB's own wording. Read the student's own draft and put the criteria to them as questions. Teach referencing, data presentation and uncertainty handling. Help narrow a research question until it is answerable inside the word limit. None of that touches authorship.

What a tutor must not do is produce any part of the submission, including a rewritten conclusion or an edit heavy enough that the words stop being the student's. Booking review sessions against the school's internal deadlines in September, rather than in the panic week, is the practical way to make sure that boundary never comes under pressure.

sections.heading: What a Satwa family should establish before booking anything
paragraphs: The useful preparation is almost entirely administrative, and all of it is free. Four questions settle the plan, and a tutor can do far better work with the answers than without them.

First, which board and which syllabus code. Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are both called International GCSE Mathematics and are different papers. The entry statement from the school carries the code. Second, which Cambridge zone the centre sits in, if the school enters Cambridge, because Cambridge states plainly that using the wrong zone's timetable is the candidate's own risk and it cannot accept responsibility for a missed paper.

Third, the school's internal coursework deadline calendar. These dates are set by the school, not the awarding body, and they are the dates a tutoring plan actually has to fit. Most Diploma coordinators will provide them on request in September. Fourth, the real bus arrival time across a fortnight, which determines the slot.

With those four things a plan can be built that holds. Without them a family is booking an hour at a guess, against a syllabus that may be the wrong one, ahead of deadlines nobody has written down. That is how a term of tutoring in central Dubai ends up producing less than it should, and it has nothing to do with the quality of the teaching.

It is worth adding a fifth, which is optional but useful: the most recent marked script rather than the most recent report. A report summarises; a script shows. Five minutes with a marked paper will usually tell a tutor whether the problem is content never covered or marks dropped on questions the student could have answered, and those two diagnoses lead to completely different plans at completely different costs. Schools release scripts on request after internal assessments and after mocks, and the request is routine rather than awkward.
bullets: The board and syllabus code from the entry statement
Which of the six Cambridge zones your centre is in
The school's internal coursework deadline calendar
The measured bus arrival window, not the scheduled one

process.title: Send the syllabus code and the real arrival time
process.description: Two pieces of information do most of the work: the code from the entry statement, and when your child actually gets home across a normal fortnight. The first stops a tutor drilling the wrong paper; the second stops a slot being booked at a time that will not hold.

process.title: Pick the slot against the worst case
process.description: The start time is set twenty minutes after the latest usual arrival, not the average, and against the latest seasonal prayer time rather than the current one. A slot chosen against the worst case survives a term; one chosen against a good week is renegotiated by November.

process.title: Diagnostic session from a marked script
process.description: The first session works from a real marked paper rather than a conversation, because the pattern of lost marks is visible in the script and invisible in a grade. It ends with a named topic list and an honest estimate of how many sessions are needed.

process.title: Agree the late and missed session rules
process.description: What happens when the bus is late, and what happens when a session is lost entirely. A shortened session beats a forfeited one, and homework is sent regardless so the next session starts with correction rather than reading. Agreeing this in advance removes the argument.

process.title: Plan the term against the deadline list
process.description: Sessions are placed against the school's internal coursework dates and the awarding body's entry deadlines, not spread evenly. For Cambridge entries that means working back from the published entry date, which for the March 2027 series falls on 27 November 2026.

process.title: Review at half term, not at the end
process.description: The pattern is checked before it breaks. If a slot has slipped three weeks in four it is moved; if the diagnosis has turned out wrong, the plan changes. Reviewing in June tells you what happened; reviewing at half term changes it.

whyPoints.title: Slots built from measured arrivals
whyPoints.description: A start time is set from the bus arrival observed across a fortnight plus twenty minutes, not from a generic after-school hour. In a neighbourhood where almost every secondary student travels out and back through peak traffic, that is the difference between an hour taught and an hour partly attended.

whyPoints.title: Published deadlines, with the source named
whyPoints.description: Cambridge's final entry date for the March 2027 series, its examination window, forecast grade date and results date are all quoted as Cambridge publishes them. Pearson's November 2026 window and its summer results dates likewise. No IB date is published here, because none could be verified.

whyPoints.title: The zone rule stated plainly
whyPoints.description: Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that the correct zone timetable must be used, because it cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who misses a paper otherwise. Almost no page in this market mentions it.

whyPoints.title: No travel on either side of the lesson
whyPoints.description: Teaching runs one-to-one over live video, so neither the tutor nor the student sits in the same traffic the school bus is in. Tutors are not sent to addresses in the UAE, and in Satwa, where parking is tight and streets are dense, that removes a real failure point.

whyPoints.title: Ramadan planned a month ahead
whyPoints.description: Shortened school days widen the afternoon and fasting narrows its useful part, so the arrangement changes rather than persisting unchanged. Post-Iftar and late-morning slots are the usual answers, and they are the most contested hours in the year, so they are agreed early.

whyPoints.title: A missed session policy that fits reality
whyPoints.description: A late arrival shortens a session rather than forfeiting it, and homework is submitted even when a session cannot happen. Both are agreed before the first paid hour, because a policy negotiated in the doorway at 5.20pm is negotiated badly.

faqs.question: Our school bus gets back around 4.45pm. Is a 5pm lesson too soon?
faqs.answer: It is tight and it usually fails. A student needs a few minutes to put a bag down, eat something and sit at a clear surface, so a start twenty minutes after the usual arrival is the realistic minimum, which puts you at 5.05pm or later. If the route is variable, a 5.15pm start that holds every week is worth more than a 5pm start that loses ten minutes in three weeks out of four. For routes returning from Al Quoz or Al Garhoud, a weekend morning often works better than any weekday slot.

faqs.question: When do Cambridge IGCSE entries actually close?
faqs.answer: Much earlier than most families expect. For the Cambridge March 2027 series, final entries are due on 27 November 2026, against an examination period of 3 February to 4 March 2027. That is more than two months ahead of the first paper and before the winter break. Forecast grades are due 27 February 2027, results are released on Cambridge International Direct on 13 May and certificates follow in late June. Cambridge also runs June and November series, so confirm which series your school is entering before planning a tutoring block around it.

faqs.question: What is a Cambridge exam zone and why does it matter to us?
faqs.answer: Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones, and each zone has its own version of the timetable with different paper times. Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version for your zone, and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong one. Ask your school's examinations officer which zone your centre sits in, and check paper times against that zone's timetable rather than against a general version found online. It takes one email and removes a genuine risk.

faqs.question: When are Pearson Edexcel International GCSE exams and results?
faqs.answer: Pearson runs International GCSE examinations in May and June and again in November each year. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. For the summer series, June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and the previous November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series and these can be revised, so plan from the live official timetable on the Pearson qualifications site rather than a date copied in September.

faqs.question: What happens to our weekday tutoring slot during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: It should change rather than persist unchanged, which is what most families do by default and why the month often shows up as a gap in progress. Dubai schools typically shorten the day, widening the afternoon, while a fasting student's concentration in the late afternoon narrows the useful part of that window. The two arrangements that work are a session after Iftar for secondary and Diploma students, or a late-morning slot on non-school days for younger ones and content-heavy subjects. Ask a month ahead, because those hours fill quickly.

faqs.question: Why are there so few schools inside Al Satwa itself?
faqs.answer: Al Satwa is a dense, long-established central district with very little land available for new campuses, so its private school provision sits in the neighbourhoods around it rather than inside it. Satwa children travel out by bus to Jumeirah, Al Mankhool, Oud Metha, Al Garhoud and Al Quoz. For tutoring that is the defining fact, because it means the afternoon window is set by a bus route through peak traffic rather than by a short walk, and a lesson slot has to be built from the arrival rather than the school bell.

faqs.question: Does an unpredictable school run make online tutoring better than in-home?
faqs.answer: In Satwa it usually does, for a practical reason rather than a pedagogical one. An in-home tutor is travelling through the same congestion the bus is in, so a late arrival on one side meets a late arrival on the other and the session shrinks from both ends. Parking in Satwa is also genuinely difficult. IB Gram does not provide home visits in the UAE and delivers one-to-one lessons over live video, which removes travel from both sides and makes a 5pm start mean 5pm.

faqs.question: What happens if my child arrives twenty minutes late for a session?
faqs.answer: That should be agreed before the first paid hour rather than settled in the moment. The sensible arrangement is a shortened session rather than a forfeited one: the tutor has blocked the hour, and forty minutes of teaching is worth having. Agree also that homework is submitted even when a session is lost entirely, so the next session begins with correction rather than with the tutor reading work for the first time. Any provider unwilling to put a late-arrival rule in writing is worth asking twice.

faqs.question: How do I set up an online lesson properly in an apartment?
faqs.answer: Three things, all cheap. A clear flat surface with the student sitting upright, because a laptop on a sofa cushion shows the tutor a face and not the working. Headphones with a microphone rather than laptop speakers, which removes most of the friction when a sibling is in earshot. And a stylus tablet or cheap graphics tablet for Mathematics and the sciences, so the tutor watches each step appear instead of seeing a finished answer. Test the whole arrangement on a call the day before, not fifteen minutes before.

faqs.question: Should we use the winter break for intensive sessions?
faqs.answer: Short intensive blocks work well across a break and weekly slots do not, because the routine that holds a weekly pattern together is gone. Three or four longer sessions in the first week, built around a specific topic list from a marked script, achieve more than six scattered hours. The arrangement needs agreeing before the break starts rather than during it, since availability tightens as soon as term ends. The one thing to avoid is treating the break as recovery time and arriving in January with the same gap.

faqs.question: Which subject suffers most when a weekly slot keeps slipping?
faqs.answer: Biology and any content-dense subject, because the loss compounds. Content learnt and not revisited decays, so a missed week is not a week's delay but a week's regression, and a session spent re-covering forgotten material is the most expensive hour in the plan. Mathematics suffers differently: fluency decays fast, which is why short daily practice protects it better than a long session does. English is the most tolerant, since timed writing can be done independently and the session used purely for marking.

faqs.question: Can my child sit exams as a private candidate if the timing does not work?
faqs.answer: Private candidate entry exists for Cambridge and Pearson qualifications and is arranged through a registered examination centre rather than through a tutor or platform. The centre handles the entry, the fees and the timetable, and entry deadlines are the same ones the awarding body publishes, which for the Cambridge March 2027 series means 27 November 2026. Contact centres early, because capacity for private candidates in specific subjects is limited and practical components in the sciences can restrict which subjects a centre will accept.

faqs.question: How early should we start planning for the May exam season?
faqs.answer: Work backwards from the entry deadline rather than from the papers. For Cambridge series the entry closes months ahead, and the forecast grade deadline shortly before the examinations means the school needs evidence of the student's standard well before that. Practically, content building should be finishing as the mock scripts come back, and the final stretch should be timed papers and technique rather than new material. A family that begins in the term before the series has room; one that begins six weeks out is doing triage.

faqs.question: Is Arabic tutoring available alongside the IB or IGCSE subjects?
faqs.answer: Yes, and in Dubai it is more than an optional extra. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in Dubai private schools regardless of which international curriculum the school is licensed to teach, so an IGCSE or Diploma student is carrying them alongside everything else. In practice it is the subject most often squeezed out of a Satwa family's week and the one most often requested late. Booking it as a modest regular slot rather than an emergency block works considerably better.

faqs.question: What should I have ready before the first conversation with a tutor?
faqs.answer: Four things, all free to obtain. The board and syllabus code from your child's entry statement, since Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are different papers. Which of Cambridge's six administrative zones your centre sits in, if the school enters Cambridge. The school's internal coursework deadline calendar, which the Diploma or key stage coordinator will usually provide on request. And the real bus arrival time measured across a fortnight. With those four, a plan can be built that holds rather than guessed at.

dubai/al-satwa.closingHeading: Fix the hour first, then the teaching
dubai/al-satwa.closingBody: In most Dubai neighbourhoods the limiting factor on tutoring is finding the right specialist. In Al Satwa it is finding an hour that holds every week once the bus, the prayer times and a sibling's schedule have all had their say. Measure the real arrival across a fortnight, add twenty minutes, agree what happens when the bus is late, and get the school's internal deadline list in September. IB Gram arranges one-to-one lessons over live video, so no part of the arrangement depends on anybody driving across central Dubai at five in the afternoon.

dubai/al-sufouh.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach the Diploma, the Middle Years Programme and both IGCSE boards. In a transition year, ask for the specific step your child is making rather than for the subject, because the teaching differs sharply between them.

intro.heading: The step up nobody timetables
paragraphs: Students in Al Sufouh rarely fall behind gradually. They fall behind at a step. A child who was comfortable throughout Key Stage 3 meets IGCSE in Year 10 and discovers that a question now carries a mark allocation they are supposed to read. A Year 11 student with a column of A grades arrives in the Diploma and loses a grade in every science because the questions no longer scaffold the answer. A Middle Years Programme student who writes fluently meets a timed paper and runs out of time at question four. Each of those is a transition failure rather than an ability failure, and each has a different fix.

Al Sufouh makes this unusually visible. The district runs along the coast between Madinat Jumeirah and Media City, with Dubai Knowledge Park and the university campuses in the middle, and the secondary schools in and around it do not all continue in a straight line at sixteen. Some run IGCSE then A Level. Some run the IB continuum from the Primary Years Programme through to the Diploma. A few offer both routes at sixth form, which means a Year 11 cohort here is genuinely choosing rather than defaulting, usually in the January before they commit.

What the school covers in class is the content. What it cannot timetable is the retraining of habits. The IGCSE leaver has two years of practice at answering structured questions and no practice at an unscaffolded 4,000 words. The Middle Years leaver has two years of extended writing and no practice at finishing a paper. The Year 9 student moving into IGCSE has never been marked against an external scheme. Those habits were correct in the previous system and they are the thing that costs marks in the next one.

This page is built around those steps. The four transitions students here actually make, with the gap in each one named. Why the strongest Year 11 students stall in the first Diploma term. Higher Level against Standard Level set out component by component rather than as a sentence about difficulty. The Mathematics Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation choice, and what the degree a student wants will expect of it. Then the decision between A Level and the Diploma, which in this district is a real decision rather than a formality.

IB Gram matches tutors online, one-to-one, over live video. There is no Dubai centre and no tutor is sent to an Al Sufouh address; home visits are offered only in India. For transition work that is an advantage rather than a compromise, because the person you want is someone who has taught both sides of the specific step your child is making, and that person is unlikely to be the one available to drive to Al Sufouh Road at half past four.

dubai/al-sufouh.programmesIntro: The programmes below are described by what each one asks a student to do that the previous one did not. That is the part a transition year exposes, and it is where tuition in this district earns its place.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses examined terminally, syllabus by syllabus, in a June or November series. Cambridge uses four-digit codes such as 0580 for Mathematics, 0625 for Physics and 0620 for Chemistry; Pearson Edexcel uses codes such as 4MA1, 4PH1 and 4CH1. Several Cambridge subjects are tiered into Core and Extended, and the entry is submitted months before the papers.
programmes.countryNote: The step into IGCSE from Year 9 is the first time an Al Sufouh student is marked against an external scheme rather than a teacher's judgement. Mark allocations become instructions, command terms become binding, and a well-written answer to the wrong question scores nothing. Students who read the question for content and ignore the tariff lose marks in every subject simultaneously, which is why the diagnosis is so often the same across a report.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Each subject carries an internally assessed component worth a fifth or more. Three further points come from the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay matrix, so a candidate can gain or lose a university offer on the two components nobody teaches as a subject.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Sufouh the Diploma is entered from two directions. IGCSE leavers arrive with strong technique and no experience of sustained independent research. Middle Years leavers arrive with research habits and no experience of a timed external paper. Neither is better prepared overall; they are differently prepared, and a tutor who does not know which route a student came by will spend the first month teaching the wrong thing.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, marked out of 8 and converted to a 1-7 grade by published boundaries. Assessment is continuous and criterion-referenced, using task-specific clarifications written by the teacher, with no compulsory external examination unless the school enters students for on-screen examinations or eAssessment in Year 11.
programmes.countryNote: The useful signal for an Al Sufouh family deciding at sixteen is not the overall Middle Years grade but the criterion profile underneath it. Criterion C and D in Mathematics and the sciences sit closest to Diploma Higher Level demands. A student at 6 overall on the strength of Criterion A alone is a weaker Higher Level candidate than one at 5 whose marks are evenly spread, and the report shows this if you read the strands.

programmes.name: A Level route after IGCSE
programmes.description: Three or four subjects studied in depth with no compulsory core, examined terminally at the end of two years in most international centres. Depth over breadth: a student drops everything they dislike at sixteen and specialises immediately, which suits some students enormously and leaves others with no route back if they change direction at seventeen.
programmes.countryNote: Several schools near Al Sufouh run A Level while others run the Diploma, and a few offer both, so this is a live choice here rather than a theoretical one. The decision turns on whether the student is already certain of a direction and on how they handle breadth. The Ministry of Education equivalency rule for the British track also expects either one Advanced Level subject at no less than grade E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade, which is worth knowing before subjects are dropped.

dubai/al-sufouh.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects where the transition gap is widest in this district. Each note names what the next level assumes a student can already do, which is usually the thing nobody taught them explicitly.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Assumes algebraic fluency from IGCSE Extended and then asks for justification, which IGCSE never required. At Higher Level, Paper 3 is an extended multi-part investigation worth a fifth of the grade, and it rewards sustained reasoning. Students who can execute every technique and explain none of them plateau here.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Assumes comfort with statistics and with a graphic display calculator as a working tool. The transition failure is treating calculator output as the answer: a correlation coefficient without a sentence interpreting it in context earns the calculation mark and loses the communication marks above it.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Assumes the IGCSE content and then changes the question type entirely, from recall and substitution to explanation and uncertainty. The scientific investigation worth a fifth of the grade is unlike anything in IGCSE practical work, because it is marked on research design and evaluation rather than on measurement accuracy.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Assumes mole calculations are automatic, which for most IGCSE leavers they are not quite. Energetics and organic mechanisms then arrive quickly at Higher Level. The data-based questions expect a structured error analysis that no IGCSE paper asks for, and that single skill accounts for a surprising share of the first-term drop.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Assumes an ability to answer to the command term and the mark allocation. The content volume is larger than IGCSE but the real change is that six-mark questions expect a structured answer with named terminology. Fluent paragraph writing without the terminology scores in the lower bands, which surprises able Middle Years students.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is unseen analysis under time pressure, which is the opposite of the drafted coursework a Middle Years student is used to. Higher Level adds an essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words on a studied text. The Individual Oral needs a global issue narrow enough to argue from two specific extracts.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Usually a new subject at sixteen, so there is no prior grade to reason from. Three internally assessed commentaries, each within 800 words, each on a different unit and a different article. Higher Level adds a quantitative Paper 3 that students arriving from a humanities background routinely underestimate.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A 1,600-word essay on a prescribed title plus an exhibition of three objects, contributing with the Extended Essay to three bonus points. Students treat it as opinion writing. The assessment rewards precise knowledge claims, genuine counterclaims and named real-world examples, which is a technique rather than a talent.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: A 4,000-word independent research piece with a handful of supervisor meetings. For an IGCSE leaver it is the single largest new demand of the Diploma, and most failures are scoping failures from week one: a question too broad to argue in the word limit or too narrow to find sources for.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended / Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The gateway to both sixth-form routes. An Extended or Higher entry keeps Analysis and Approaches open; a Core or Foundation entry closes the top grades and with them several degree pathways. The tier is set at entry, months before the papers, and amendments are only possible inside the board's window.

subjects.name: Sciences (Cambridge 0625 / 0620 / 0610)
subjects.description: Triple award keeps all three Higher Level science doors open; Combined or Co-ordinated Sciences compresses the same ground and leaves gaps that surface in the first Diploma term. Worth confirming which award a student holds before planning any sixth-form science choice.

subjects.name: English Language (Cambridge 0500 / Pearson 4EA1)
subjects.description: Directed writing and composition assessed on structure and register as much as accuracy, plus a reading paper that rewards selective quotation and punishes narration. The plateau at grade B is almost always a register and structure problem rather than a vocabulary one.

modes.title: Transition diagnostic before the step
modes.description: Three or four sessions in the term before a student changes level, run against the syllabus document of the course they are about to join rather than the one they are leaving. The output is a written gap list: what transfers, what has to be rebuilt, and which habit will cost marks in the new system. Booked in the spring of Year 9 or Year 11.

For an IGCSE leaver that usually means justification and extended explanation; for a Middle Years leaver it means timed papers and command terms. sections.heading: The four transitions, and the gap inside each one
paragraphs: Treating transition as a single phenomenon is why schools run generic induction programmes and families still pay for tuition in October. The four steps students in this district make are genuinely different problems, and the useful exercise is to name which one applies before buying anything.

Year 9 into IGCSE is a change in who marks the work. For the first time an external scheme decides, which means mark allocations are instructions and command terms are binding. The student who writes everything they know about a topic in response to a two-mark question is not lazy; nobody has ever penalised them for it before.

Year 11 into the Diploma is a change in scaffolding. IGCSE questions lead a student through a problem in parts. Diploma questions state a situation and expect the student to decide what is relevant. Add an internally assessed component with no fixed brief and a 4,000-word Extended Essay, and the demand is not harder content so much as unfamiliar independence.

The Middle Years Programme into the Diploma is the same change in the opposite direction. These students research, draft and redraft comfortably and have rarely sat a strictly timed external paper. The first mock reveals a student who knows the material and reaches question four of six. That is a pacing problem and it is fixable in weeks, provided it is diagnosed as pacing rather than as a knowledge gap.

The fourth is arrival from another system entirely, which in Al Sufouh 2 happens mid-year with some regularity. These students are placed on the basis of a report from a school nobody at the new school knows, and they are the group most likely to be in the wrong set or entered for the wrong tier. The table sets out all four with the honest length of each fix.

sections.heading: Why the strongest Year 11 students stall in the first Diploma term
paragraphs: The pattern is consistent enough to predict. A student finishes IGCSE with a column of top grades, chooses three Higher Levels on the strength of them, and receives a first set of Diploma marks two grades lower. The family reads this as the school being harder or the child losing motivation. It is usually neither.

IGCSE rewards accurate execution of known procedures. Questions are broken into parts, each part signalling the method expected, and a student who has drilled past papers can score heavily without ever deciding what to do. Diploma questions remove the signalling. A Physics question presents a situation; the candidate must decide which model applies before any algebra starts. The student who was excellent at the second half of that process has never practised the first half.

The second cause is the internally assessed component. A fifth or more of each subject grade comes from work with no fixed question, assessed against lettered criteria with published mark allocations. A strong IGCSE student has never been assessed on choosing a question, designing a method or evaluating a limitation. They write something competent, score in the middle bands, and cannot see why.

The third is simply volume. Six subjects, three at Higher Level, two core components and a service requirement. A student who coped on four hours of homework a week now needs a system, and the ones who stall are rarely the ones who cannot do the work; they are the ones with no method for deciding what to do first.

All three respond quickly to the right intervention. Unscaffolded practice with the method step explicit. Criterion-by-criterion work on a draft the student has already written. A weekly plan that names what gets done and when. Eight to fourteen sessions across the first two terms is the usual requirement, and it is far cheaper than the alternative, which is discovering the problem in the February of the final year.

sections.heading: Higher Level against Standard Level, component by component
paragraphs: Families ask whether Higher Level is harder, which is the wrong question. Higher Level is longer, deeper in defined ways, and carries an extra paper in several subjects. The decision should be made on which of those specific differences a student can absorb, and the differences are published rather than mysterious.

Taught time is the first. A Higher Level subject is allocated around 240 hours over two years against roughly 150 at Standard Level. That ratio is not a measure of difficulty; it is a measure of how much content arrives per week, which is what actually determines whether a student keeps up.

The additional paper is the second and it is where the marginal grade lives. In Mathematics, Paper 3 at Higher Level is worth a fifth of the grade and consists of extended multi-part problems that reward sustained reasoning. In Economics, Paper 3 is quantitative. In the sciences the extended-response and data-handling questions play a comparable role. Students practise the papers that exist in abundance and neglect the one that decides their grade.

The third difference is that the internally assessed component does not get easier at Standard Level. The criteria are the same, the mark allocations are the same, and the time it takes is the same. A student taking a subject at Standard Level purely to reduce workload still owes the full exploration or investigation, which is the part of the course that sits outside lessons entirely.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation
paragraphs: This is the most consequential single choice a Diploma student makes at sixteen, and it is routinely made on the wrong information. The two courses are not an easy version and a hard version of the same subject. They are different mathematics with different purposes, each offered at both levels.

Analysis and Approaches is the algebraic and proof-oriented route: calculus, functions, trigonometry and formal reasoning, with less emphasis on real-world data. Applications and Interpretation is statistical and modelling-oriented, with the graphic display calculator assumed as a working tool throughout. A student strong at manipulation and weak at interpretation is better served by the first; a student who reasons well about context and dislikes abstraction is better served by the second.

The constraint that matters later is admissions. Many engineering, physics, mathematics and computer science programmes expect Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and some will not accept Applications and Interpretation for those degrees at all. Other subjects are relaxed about which course, provided the level is right. The rule is not universal and it is published by each institution, which is exactly why a student should read the requirement for the degrees they are naming rather than relying on a general claim, including this one.

The honest advice to an Al Sufouh Year 11 is therefore sequential. Name three or four plausible degree directions. Read the published mathematics requirement for each. Then choose the course that keeps those open, and only then ask whether Higher or Standard Level is realistic given the student's actual profile in justification and in statistics. Doing it in the other order is how a student ends up with a course they can pass and a degree they cannot apply for.

sections.heading: The Diploma or A Level at sixteen, decided on evidence
paragraphs: In many parts of the world this is not a choice, because the school offers one route. Around Al Sufouh it genuinely is, and families here are often choosing in January with brochures that describe both routes in terms neither parent nor student can test.

The structural difference is breadth against depth. The Diploma keeps six subjects, a second language, a science, a mathematics course and two core components in play, plus a service requirement. A Level narrows to three or four subjects and nothing else. A student certain of their direction and impatient with everything outside it will usually do better and be happier on the narrower route. A student who is good at several things and sure of none keeps more doors open on the broader one.

The decision should be made on three pieces of evidence rather than on temperament alone. First, the mock or criterion profile: is attainment even across subjects, or concentrated in two? Second, how the student handles work with no fixed brief, because the Diploma core is unavoidable and large. Third, the degree direction, since some programmes state preferences and the Ministry of Education equivalency route for British qualifications expects either one Advanced Level at no less than grade E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade.

What should not drive it is the belief that one route is intrinsically harder. Both are demanding in different places. The Diploma's difficulty is volume and the core; A Level's is depth with no fallback if a single subject goes wrong. Matching the difficulty to the student is the whole exercise, and it is worth one or two structured conversations with the student in the room rather than a decision made over a dinner table in the week the form is due.

sections.heading: Command terms, tariffs and the written-answer discipline
paragraphs: Across every transition in this district the same mechanical skill decides a grade, and almost nobody teaches it explicitly. A question carries a command term and a mark allocation, and together they specify the answer's shape. State expects a fact. Outline expects two or three lines. Explain expects a causal chain. Discuss or evaluate expects judgement with both sides addressed.

Students who revise by rereading notes answer every question at roughly the same length. The consequence is systematic: low-tariff questions are over-answered, which costs time, and high-tariff questions are under-answered, which costs marks directly. Across a three-hour paper that single habit can account for a full grade, and it shows up as a mysterious gap between what a student clearly knows and what they score.

The fix is dull and fast. Take fifty past questions in the subject, sort them by command term, answer them in timed batches, and mark them against the published scheme rather than against a sense of whether the answer was good. Three or four sessions of that produces a visible change, because the student starts reading the tariff before the content.

The same discipline applies to internally assessed work, where the lettered criteria do the job the command term does on a paper. A student who writes an exploration without reading the criteria first has written an essay about mathematics. Reading the criteria before starting, and again against the finished draft, is worth more marks per hour invested than any additional content revision at this stage.

sections.heading: What transition support costs in this market
paragraphs: Published Dubai rates span an order of magnitude, so it is worth naming who charges what rather than offering an average. One Dubai content provider advertises online tuition from AED 45 to AED 65 an hour and one platform from roughly AED 33 to AED 52. A Dubai agency publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 an hour and IB tuition from AED 200. A Dubai cost survey puts specialist exam-year tuition at AED 200 to AED 450 and above and in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350; independent home tutors advertise AED 200 to AED 500. One premium provider publishes AED 650. Those figures belong to those providers and are reproduced here as market context, not as IB Gram's prices.

Transition work has a different shape from ongoing tuition, which changes the arithmetic. A diagnostic is three or four sessions. A bridging block is eight to fourteen across one or two terms. A decision conversation is one or two. Nothing here is a two-year commitment, and a family that budgets for a block rather than for an indefinite weekly habit tends to finish it rather than abandoning it in January.

The timing matters more than the rate. A diagnostic in the spring of Year 11 costs the same as one in the November of Year 12 and is worth considerably more, because the choices it informs have not yet been made. Bridging sessions in the first term of a new level are worth more than the same sessions in the second, because habits set early and then have to be unlearned.

IB Gram quotes a rate after a trial session rather than publishing a figure here, because it depends on level, subject scarcity and session length. What this page can do is set out the market so that any quote, from anyone, can be judged against something real.

sections.heading: Academic honesty when the work is new to the student
paragraphs: A transition year is exactly when the pressure to outsource peaks. A student who has never written 4,000 words is facing an Extended Essay; a student who has never designed an experiment is facing an investigation worth a fifth of a grade. Services in this market sell finished Internal Assessments at a fixed price. Buying one is malpractice under IB rules and the penalty falls on the candidate.

The permitted work is wide and genuinely useful. A tutor may teach the content, explain what each lettered criterion asks for and how marks are allocated, interrogate a research question until it is answerable, say that a planned method will not yield usable data before three weeks are lost to it, read the student's own draft and name the criterion not yet met, and teach the referencing convention the school requires.

The prohibited work is equally clear. A tutor does not author any part of the piece, does not supply sentences to be inserted, does not rewrite a paragraph into its final form, does not provide the data, and does not hand over a finished example to be adapted. A supervisor tests authenticity by asking the candidate to explain their own method and reasoning, and a student who cannot do that is exposed regardless of how good the document looks.

This is why support here is sold as a block timed to the school's internal deadlines, with the student drafting between sessions. It is slower. It is also the only version that survives an authenticity check, and in a first Diploma year the habit it builds is worth more than the marks it recovers.

sections.heading: Getting started in a transition year
paragraphs: Bring three things: the most recent report, the latest marked paper with the mark shown, and the subject list with syllabus codes or the Diploma course selections. If the step has not happened yet, bring the course the student is about to join as well, because the diagnostic runs against that rather than against what they are finishing.

Then name the step rather than the subject. Help with Physics is hard to act on. Help with the move from 0625 to Physics at Higher Level, where the student can substitute into any equation and cannot explain a field in words, is a brief a tutor can start on in the first fifteen minutes.

The trial runs on that named gap. What you should receive at the end is a count of sessions and a first target, not a general impression of the child. If a tutor cannot say what they intend to fix first, the match is probably wrong and it is cheaper to discover that in a trial than in November.

Availability is finite and the pattern is predictable. Higher Level Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry and Economics are requested across every Dubai district in the same late-afternoon window, and transition demand concentrates further into the spring of Year 11 and the first term of Year 12. If nothing suitable is free at the hour you want, the honest options are a different weekday, a weekend morning or a short wait. Lessons are online, one-to-one, over live video; there is no Dubai centre to attend and no tutor arriving at an Al Sufouh address, because that is not the service on sale.

process.title: Identify which step is actually happening
process.description: Year 9 into IGCSE, IGCSE into the Diploma, Middle Years into the Diploma, IGCSE into A Level, or an arrival from another system. The four have different gaps and different fixes, and buying generic weekly tuition for a transition problem is the most common wasted spend in this district.

process.title: Send the report, the marked paper and the course list
process.description: Syllabus codes matter because 0580 and 4MA1 are different courses, and Diploma course selections matter because Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation are different subjects. Without both, any match is approximate and the first two sessions go on finding out.

process.title: Take a diagnostic against the incoming syllabus
process.description: Three or four sessions measured against the course the student is joining rather than the one they are leaving. The output is a written gap list separating what transfers, what must be rebuilt and which habit will cost marks, which the school can use as well as the family.

process.title: Book a bridging block, not an open-ended slot
process.description: Eight to fourteen sessions across the first one or two terms of the new level, with one named habit per half-term. A defined block gets finished. An indefinite weekly commitment started in September is the one most often abandoned in January, usually just before it would have worked.

process.title: Review against the first internal assessment
process.description: The school's own first assessment at the new level is the real test of whether the bridging worked. Compare it with the tutor's view. If they disagree, that disagreement is the most useful information available and should change the plan rather than be argued away.

whyPoints.title: Tutors who have taught both sides of the step
whyPoints.description: Bridging an IGCSE leaver into Higher Level Physics needs someone who knows what 0625 did and did not require. That is a narrower qualification than teaching the subject, and it is the one transition work actually depends on.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis before a teaching plan
whyPoints.description: A transition diagnostic runs against the syllabus the student is joining, not the one they are leaving, and produces a written gap list. Plans written without that baseline spend their first month teaching content the student already holds.

whyPoints.title: Blocks with an end date
whyPoints.description: Transition support is sold as a defined block of sessions with a named target rather than as an indefinite weekly habit. Families finish blocks; open-ended arrangements get abandoned in the term when they are starting to work.

whyPoints.title: The route choice made on the student's own marks
whyPoints.description: Diploma or A Level, Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation, Higher or Standard Level: each decided from the criterion or mock profile in front of you and the published entry requirements, rather than from a general claim about which is harder.

whyPoints.title: A national tutor pool, not a drivable one
whyPoints.description: Delivery over live video removes the twenty-minute-drive constraint, so the match is made on who has taught the specific transition rather than on who can reach Al Sufouh Road at half past four on a weekday.

whyPoints.title: No claim that cannot be evidenced
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no accreditation, licence or partnership with KHDA, ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board, and has no Dubai premises. Schools are named as context for routes and boards, never as relationships.

faqs.question: My child had top IGCSE grades but dropped two grades in the first Diploma term. What went wrong?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly nothing about ability. IGCSE questions are broken into parts that signal the method expected, so a well-drilled student scores heavily without deciding what to do. Diploma questions present a situation and leave that decision to the candidate. Add an internally assessed component with no fixed brief and six subjects at once, and the demand is unfamiliar independence rather than harder content. The fix is unscaffolded practice with the method step made explicit, plus criterion work on a draft the student has already written. Eight to fourteen sessions across the first two terms is the usual requirement.

faqs.question: Is Higher Level actually harder, or just longer?
faqs.answer: Longer and deeper in specific, published ways. A Higher Level subject gets around 240 taught hours over two years against roughly 150 at Standard Level, so content arrives faster and a missed fortnight costs more. Several subjects add a third paper, and that paper often carries a fifth of the grade with extended multi-part problems. What does not change is the internally assessed component: same criteria, same weight band, same hours outside lessons. A student taking Standard Level to reduce workload still owes the full exploration or investigation, which surprises most families.

faqs.question: Which Diploma Mathematics course should my child take?
faqs.answer: Decide it backwards from the degree direction, not from which looks easier. Analysis and Approaches is the algebraic and proof-oriented route; Applications and Interpretation is statistical and modelling-oriented with the calculator assumed throughout. Engineering, physics, mathematics and computer science programmes commonly expect Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and some will not accept the other course for those degrees. Business and social science programmes widely accept Applications and Interpretation. Requirements are published per programme and vary, so read the actual entry criteria for three or four plausible degrees before choosing, then check the level is realistic.

faqs.question: How do we choose between the Diploma and A Level in Year 11?
faqs.answer: On three pieces of evidence. Is attainment even across subjects or concentrated in two, because uneven profiles are diluted by six Diploma subjects and exposed by three A Levels. How does the student handle work with no fixed brief, since the Diploma core is large and unavoidable. And what does the degree direction expect. The Ministry of Education equivalency route for British qualifications expects five accredited IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, plus one Advanced Level at E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at E, which is worth knowing before anything is dropped.

faqs.question: What is the gap when a Middle Years Programme student starts the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Usually pacing rather than knowledge. These students research, draft and redraft comfortably and have rarely sat a strictly timed external paper. The first mock then shows someone who knows the material and reaches question four of six. That is a timing problem and it responds quickly: timed batches of past questions, marked against the published scheme, with the clock enforced rather than approximate. Command-term discipline is the other half, because criterion-referenced writing rewards fullness while an exam paper rewards answering to the tariff and moving on.

faqs.question: When should a transition diagnostic be booked?
faqs.answer: The spring of the year before the step, which for most Al Sufouh families means Year 9 term three or Year 11 term two. It costs the same as a diagnostic in the November after the step and is worth considerably more, because the course choices it informs have not yet been made. It runs against the syllabus document of the incoming course rather than the outgoing one, and the output is a written gap list: what transfers intact, what must be rebuilt, and which habit from the old system will now lose marks.

faqs.question: Does Combined Science at IGCSE close off Higher Level sciences?
faqs.answer: Not formally, but it leaves gaps that surface in the first Diploma term. Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences compress all three sciences, so everything is examinable and nothing is revisited. A student then carrying one of those sciences alone at Higher Level meets depth in a subject they covered at speed. The practical answer is to confirm which award your child holds, identify the compressed topics in the subject they intend to continue, and front-load those in the term before the Diploma starts rather than discovering them in October.

faqs.question: Will a tutor come to our home in Al Sufouh?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not make home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE; home visits are offered only in India. Sessions run one-to-one over live video at a fixed slot. For transition work that is an advantage, because the tutor you want is someone who has taught both sides of the specific step your child is making, and that is a narrower pool than people able to drive to Al Sufouh Road at half past four. Choosing online changes the selection criterion from geography to syllabus experience.

faqs.question: How many sessions does bridging into a new level usually take?
faqs.answer: Eight to fourteen across the first one or two terms, depending on the step. A Year 9 into IGCSE move is often six to eight, because the change is mainly about reading tariffs and command terms. An IGCSE into Diploma move at Higher Level is the longest, because two habits change at once: unscaffolded questions and independent coursework. A mid-year arrival from another system needs a three or four session diagnostic first, since planning before that baseline usually means a month spent reteaching material the student already holds.

faqs.question: What does it cost to bridge a student into the Diploma in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Work from the block, not the hour. Market bands published by Dubai providers run from AED 45 to AED 65 an hour at the budget end and from around AED 33 on one platform; a Dubai agency publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200; a Dubai cost survey reports specialist exam-year tuition at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with one premium provider publishing AED 650. A ten-session bridging block therefore ranges widely, and that total is the number worth comparing. Those figures belong to the providers who published them, not to IB Gram.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Extended Essay in the first Diploma year?
faqs.answer: Yes, within limits that matter. A tutor may interrogate the research question until it is answerable in 4,000 words, explain what each assessment criterion asks for, suggest where to look for sources, teach the referencing convention, read the student's own draft and name which criterion is not yet met. A tutor may not author any part of it, supply sentences for insertion, rewrite a paragraph into final form or hand over a model to adapt. Supervisors test authenticity conversationally, so a candidate must be able to explain their own argument and method.

faqs.question: Why does my child lose marks on questions they clearly understand?
faqs.answer: Usually because the answer is the wrong shape for the tariff. A command term and a mark allocation together specify what is expected: state wants a fact, outline wants two or three lines, explain wants a causal chain, evaluate wants judgement on both sides. Students who revise by rereading answer everything at the same length, which over-answers cheap questions and under-answers expensive ones. Across a long paper that single habit can cost a grade. Fifty past questions sorted by command term and marked against the published scheme changes it within a few weeks.

faqs.question: Is it too late to start if my child is already halfway through Year 12?
faqs.answer: No, but the plan changes. Coursework becomes the priority, because the exploration and Extended Essay deadlines sit months before the papers and cannot be recovered afterwards. Content gaps from the first term are addressed second, and timed-paper technique last, since it responds fast and is best done closer to the series. What does not work at this stage is booking four tutors at once across six subjects. One coursework block to clear the largest deadline, then weekly sessions in the two weakest subjects, is the arrangement that actually gets completed.

faqs.question: What should a transition diagnostic produce for us to read?
faqs.answer: A written gap list, not a verdict on the child. It should separate three things: content that transfers intact, content that has to be rebuilt before the new course needs it, and the habits from the previous system that will now cost marks. It should name the specific components at risk, with the syllabus reference, and it should estimate a session count. Something you can take to a head of year or a Diploma coordinator and have a concrete conversation about is the test of whether the diagnostic was worth the money.

faqs.question: Are there enough tutors for Higher Level sciences at the hour we want?
faqs.answer: Not always, and you will be told rather than seated with a generalist. Higher Level Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry and Economics are requested across every Dubai district in the same late-afternoon window, and transition demand concentrates further into the spring of Year 11 and the first term of Year 12. The honest options when the slot is gone are a different weekday, a weekend morning, or a short wait for the right match. A tutor who has not taught the specific step is worse value than waiting a fortnight for one who has.

dubai/al-sufouh.closingHeading: Name the step, then buy the help
dubai/al-sufouh.closingBody: Tuition in Al Sufouh works best when it is bought for a transition with an end date rather than as an indefinite weekly habit. Identify which step your child is making, send the latest report, the most recent marked paper and the incoming course list with its syllabus codes, and ask for a diagnostic against the course they are joining. What you should get back is a written gap list, a session count and a first target. Lessons run one-to-one over live video; no tutor is sent to an Al Sufouh address. Every AED band on this page belongs to the provider or survey that published it.

dubai/al-twar.tutorsIntro: Tutors here cover Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE and the IB Diploma at both levels, plus the mandatory UAE subjects where a family needs them. Each tutor takes one subject and one level, which is what makes it possible to support three children in a household without compromising any of them.

intro.heading: Three kinds of household, three different requests
paragraphs: Al Twar does not have one parent profile, and a page that writes as though it does will be useless to most of the people reading it. The district holds older villa plots with long-settled Emirati and Arab families, apartment blocks along the Damascus Street side with large expatriate households, and a steady flow of families who moved in from Sharjah or Deira for space. Those three groups arrive at a tutoring search from completely different directions.

The villa households often have children in the Arabic first-language and Islamic Education streams running alongside a British or IB curriculum, and the pressure point is usually a report where everything is strong except one mandatory subject, or the reverse. These are the families most likely to be managing two assessment systems inside one child's week, and the ones least well served by the existing pages in this market, which treat Arabic as a subject chip and never mention it again.

The apartment households tend to have more children and a harder budget question. Three school-age children, one income earner, fees already substantial, and a realistic ceiling on what tuition can cost per month. For them the useful information is not a list of subjects but an honest answer to which child should get help first, how many sessions actually change an outcome and what the market charges, so they can tell a fair quote from a chancer.

The families who moved in from elsewhere in the northern emirates carry a different problem again: a child mid-course at a school that uses a different exam board, or one who has moved from a curriculum that counted differently. Their first question is what actually transferred and what has to be rebuilt, which is a diagnostic job rather than a teaching one, and it is quick to do from a marked script.

What all three share is geography. Al Twar sits between Al Qusais, Al Nahda and the airport district, so the afternoon is slow and the school run goes in several directions at once. Tuition for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai; that service exists only in India. For a household with three children in three year groups that is an advantage rather than a concession, because three separate specialists can teach in one evening and no journey sits between them.

The sections below are organised around those household types rather than around a generic subject menu: who asks for what, how the mandatory UAE subjects work, what tuition costs set against the fees you already pay, how to read a KHDA inspection report for your own child's year group, and when sharing a tutor between siblings works.

dubai/al-twar.programmesIntro: Al Twar families meet three main routes, and which one a child is on usually reflects which school had a place rather than a considered choice. The notes below describe what each route demands of a household, not what the programme claims to be.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Eight or nine subjects over two years, examined in terminal written papers with practical or alternative-to-practical components in the sciences. Cambridge tiers several subjects into Core and Extended, with Core entry capping the grade at C or 5. Pearson International GCSE is single tier in most subjects. Volume rather than conceptual difficulty is what defeats most students.
programmes.countryNote: In a household running Arabic first language and Islamic Education alongside nine IGCSE subjects, the week is genuinely full and a third weekly tuition hour will not fit. The decision that matters is which two subjects get the hours. For most Al Twar families that is mathematics plus whichever science the last report flagged, with the rest managed by better use of past papers.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, each with an internal assessment the student designs outside lesson time, plus a 4,000-word Extended Essay, a 1,600-word Theory of Knowledge essay and CAS. Up to three bonus points come from the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge matrix, inside a total of 45.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma provision is not on this doorstep, so Al Twar students doing the DP travel, most often towards Mirdif, Al Garhoud or Festival City. The journey takes the afternoon, and coursework consequently lands at the weekend. Families who plan a Saturday morning block in September rather than discovering the need in February save themselves a rescue job.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, marked out of eight and reported from 1 to 7. The programme rewards investigation, communication and reflection, and deliberately does not drill procedure, so a student can look strong on criterion tasks and weak the moment a paper is timed.
programmes.countryNote: This is the single most common source of confusion in households with children in two systems. An MYP 6 and an IGCSE 73 per cent are not comparable measurements, and parents who read them side by side usually conclude the younger child is doing better. They are measuring different things, and a timed diagnostic settles it in one session.

programmes.name: Mandatory UAE subjects
programmes.ageRange: All year groups in Dubai private schools
programmes.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum. KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ.
programmes.countryNote: For Al Twar's Arab first-language households this is a real assessed load rather than an add-on, and it sits in the same week as nine IGCSE subjects. For the federal equivalency count on the British track, Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required GCSE or IGCSE subjects, which changes how a Year 9 subject choice should be made.

dubai/al-twar.subjectsIntro: The subject list below is ordered by what Al Twar households actually ask for, which differs from the generic Dubai list in one respect: the mandatory UAE subjects appear high up, because in this district they often are the problem.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: A full assessed subject for Arab students in a Dubai private school, taught in Standard Arabic as required by KHDA and in a class separate from the additional-language stream. A weak line here on an otherwise strong report is common and is usually a writing-accuracy problem rather than a comprehension one.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.description: Taught in Standard Arabic for Arab students and in the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arab students. Content is tightly controlled: using different or additional material without prior Ministry of Education permission is prohibited, so support has to work inside the approved syllabus rather than around it.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: The most requested subject in every Dubai district including this one. Extended reaches grade 9, Core caps at C or 5, so a tier review in Year 10 can be worth more than a term of extra teaching. Multi-step problems and algebraic manipulation carry most of the marks.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Calculus, proof and notation discipline decide the grade, and marks go on unjustified steps rather than wrong answers. The exploration is marked out of 20 across five criteria, and the largest allocation is use of mathematics, so a topic pitched at course level caps the achievable mark.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Electricity and waves dominate losses at IGCSE; fields, thermodynamics and the Higher Level extension at Diploma. The practical or alternative-to-practical paper rewards specific method detail, and students who have only read about experiments cannot produce it under time pressure.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and qualitative analysis at IGCSE; energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms at Higher Level. Observation answers need colour and state together to score. Significant figures and units cost roughly a mark a paper, which is the cheapest habit to repair.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The content base is large rather than difficult, so session frequency matters more than session length. Command terms set the ceiling: outline wants a list, explain wants a causal chain, and students who answer the wrong instruction lose marks they clearly knew.

subjects.name: English First Language and English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Summary questions are mark-dense and routinely wasted, because students paraphrase a passage rather than selecting discrete points. Directed writing rewards register and audience. Both respond to four marked sessions, which makes them good value for a household with a tight budget.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
subjects.description: Case-study marks go to candidates who use the figures inside the argument rather than quoting them beside it. At Diploma level Economics needs three commentaries of 800 words on news articles, and the article choice sets the ceiling before any writing starts.

subjects.name: UAE Social Studies and Moral Education
subjects.description: Required alongside the licensed curriculum, with Arabic as the primary language of instruction for Arab students and the school's curriculum language for non-Arabs. Often treated as low stakes by students until it appears on a report, and the fix is usually structured revision rather than teaching.

sections.heading: Who lives in Al Twar, and what each household actually asks for
paragraphs: The direct answer to the search: tutoring for Al Twar students runs online, one-to-one over live video, with a specialist matched per child and per subject, in slots that generally start between 17:30 and 19:00 on weekdays. What varies by household is not the delivery but the request, and getting the request right saves a family both money and a term.

A villa household with four children, two of them in the Arabic first-language stream, is managing a wider assessed load than the brochure version of a British curriculum suggests. Their request is usually diagnostic: which of these four children is actually at risk, and is the weak report line a subject problem or a writing-accuracy problem. The answer is often that one child needs a term of help and the others need nothing, which is not what a sales-led provider will tell them.

An apartment household with three children and a hard monthly ceiling asks a different question, and it is the better question: who gets the hour. The honest ranking is by proximity to a terminal examination and by how much of the grade is still movable. A Year 11 student twelve weeks from a series is a better use of a limited budget than a Year 8 student with four years to recover, even when the Year 8 report looks worse.

A family that arrived mid-course from another emirate or another country asks what transferred. That is a one-session job, not a term. A marked script from the new school, read against the new board's mark scheme, usually shows the gap is narrower than feared and specific rather than general. sections.heading: The Arabic and Islamic Education load nobody else writes about
paragraphs: Across the competing pages in this market, Arabic appears as a subject chip and never as a section. That is a strange omission in a city where these subjects are compulsory for every student in a private school, and it is a particularly unhelpful one for Al Twar, where a large share of households have children in the first-language streams.

The rules are published and specific. Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum. KHDA requires schools to organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction.

Language of instruction is set per stream. Standard Arabic is required as the main language for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language. Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students. For non-Arab students, Islamic Education and moral, social and cultural studies are taught in the school's licensed-curriculum language. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and the guidance advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should run at least 25 minutes. Schools are required to ensure teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects.

Two consequences follow for a parent. First, support in these subjects has to work inside the approved content, because using different or additional material without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. That rules out importing a parallel syllabus and makes the useful work writing accuracy, structure and examination technique. Second, for the federal equivalency count on the British track, Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required GCSE or IGCSE subjects, which should change how a Year 9 option sheet is filled in.

sections.heading: A villa week and an apartment week are not the same week
paragraphs: Housing shapes study more than parents expect, and in a district with both villa plots and apartment blocks the difference is visible in how tuition has to be scheduled. It is a practical point rather than a social one, and ignoring it is how a sensible plan falls apart in the second month.

In a villa with four children there is space but rarely quiet. A session at 18:00 competes with three younger siblings, a kitchen and a living room, and a student who is nominally in their own room is often not. The fix is not a better internet connection; it is agreeing which room is the study room for that hour and treating the slot as an appointment the household respects. Families who do this get a different standard of session from families who do not, with the same tutor.

In an apartment the problem reverses. There is quiet when the household is out and no spare room when it is in. The best available hour is frequently later than the parent would like, after younger children are settled, and the right response is to accept a 19:00 or 19:30 slot and use it for work that suits a tired student: marked scripts, worked examples, command-term drilling, short timed sections. Trying to teach new abstract content at that hour wastes the fee.

Both patterns point the same way on one question. Headphones, a shared document the student types into and a tutor who can see the work rather than just the face are what make a session productive in a busy home. None of that requires an extra room, and all of it is harder to arrange around a visiting tutor who needs a table and a door.
