sections.heading: What tuition costs set against the fees you already pay
paragraphs: No competing page in this market puts tutoring cost into the context of what a Dubai family is already spending, which makes their price pages hard to act on. The anchor is useful and checkable: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there would be no increase in school fees for private schools in the emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. A household budgeting tuition is therefore working against a flat fee rather than a rising one.

The emirate's market gives the other half of the picture. The Dubai Media Office reported 387,441 students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, offering seventeen curricula, with the UK curriculum at 37 per cent of enrolment, Indian at 26, US at 14 and the IB at 7. Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places, after six opened during 2025-26 and enrolment rose 6 per cent.

Against that, the tutoring decision is a monthly one rather than hourly. Monthly packages published in this market sit at roughly AED 799 for eight online sessions and around AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits. Bestimate's 2026 estimates for a single weekly hour run from AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support.

For a household with three children the arithmetic is worth doing explicitly rather than by feel. One specialist hour a week for one child, for one academic year, is a predictable number. Three children at two hours each is a different order of commitment, and the honest advice is almost always to concentrate the spend rather than spread it. A tutor who recommends the opposite without seeing a single marked script is selling, not advising.

sections.heading: What the market charges per hour, and what each band buys
paragraphs: Hourly rates in this market span a factor of ten, and most of the spread is explained by format and seniority rather than by subject or neighbourhood. The table below names who publishes each band so a parent can check rather than trust. These are market figures, not an IB Gram price list.

The practical use of the table is spotting a mismatch between what you are paying and what you need. At the budget band a tutor supervises homework and revises content, which for a Year 8 student with a confidence problem may be exactly right. At the specialist band a tutor diagnoses from a marked script, knows what a particular paper's scheme rewards, and can judge in one session whether an internal assessment question will survive. Buying the first while expecting the second is the commonest way families feel cheated.

Format is the other half. Published in-home bands run above online bands for a tutor of comparable standing, and the difference is travel. In Al Twar that travel crosses the Damascus Street and Al Nahda Road afternoon, which is slow and unpredictable, so the premium pays for a car journey that sometimes fails. Groups cost less per student and set the pace by the group rather than by your child's gaps, which is a fair trade for content revision and a poor one for a specific weakness.

On IB Gram's own figure, the honest answer is that it depends on subject, level and weekly frequency, and that a trial session comes first. Publishing a single number would be tidier and less truthful. What this page can do is give you the bands to measure any quote against, including ours.

sections.heading: Reading a KHDA inspection report for your own child's year group
paragraphs: KHDA is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in Dubai, and it inspects private schools annually against a six-band scale running from Outstanding down to Very Weak. Most parents in Al Twar know their school's headline band. Far fewer have read past it, which is where the useful information lives.

A headline band is an average across phases, subjects and aspects. A school rated Good overall can be Very Good in primary and Acceptable in secondary, or strong in English and weaker in mathematics at the phase your child is actually in. For a parent choosing a tutor, the phase-and-subject judgements are directly actionable in a way the overall band is not: they tell you where the school itself has been told it is weaker, which is often precisely where independent support pays.

The second thing worth reading is the recommendations and whether last year's were addressed. A report that repeats the same recommendation three years running is telling you something about the pace of change. A report showing a subject moving up a band is telling you the department has been reorganised, which may mean a new scheme of work your child's older sibling never saw.

None of this makes a school good or bad for your child in isolation, and no tutoring service should pretend to interpret a regulator's report on your behalf. Read it yourself on KHDA's own site, for the right year, and take the phase that matches your child. sections.heading: When siblings can share a tutor, and when they cannot
paragraphs: Every household with more than one child asks this, and the honest answer has a clear line through it. Sharing works where the assessment is the same and the gap is similar. It fails where either differs, and it fails expensively, because the weaker child disengages and the stronger one is bored while both hours are paid for.

The clearest case for sharing is two children in the same year group, same subject, same board and similar standing, which in practice usually means twins or a year group split across two schools with the same entry. There, a single session genuinely covers both, and the dynamic can help: explaining a step to a sibling is one of the better ways to consolidate it.

The clearest case against is a difference in board or tier. A child entered for Cambridge 0580 Extended and a sibling entered for Pearson 4MA1 Higher are preparing for differently structured papers. A child in Core and a sibling in Extended have different grade ceilings and should be taught different content. A year-group gap of two or more makes shared sessions almost always wasteful.

Sequence is the better arrangement in most Al Twar households, and it is only practical because no travel is involved. Two or three children, each with their own specialist, taught back to back across one evening, with separate plans and separate notes. A visiting tutor cannot do that without either compromising on subject match or taking three evenings, and the fee for the second option would be higher than the sum of the online sessions.

sections.heading: Online delivery, and the questions Al Twar parents actually raise about it
paragraphs: Parents here raise three objections to online tutoring, and all three deserve a straight answer rather than a brochure. The first is attention: will a teenager stay engaged on a screen. The second is the younger children: can a ten-year-old work this way at all. The third is simply preference, a belief that a person in the room teaches better.

On attention, the honest position is that the format is less forgiving of a badly run session and no worse when the session is run properly. A shared document both parties type into, the paper on screen with annotation, a visible timer on timed sections and a written note afterwards produce a session with no hiding place in it. A tutor talking at a muted teenager for an hour produces nothing, and that is a tutoring failure rather than a technology one.

On younger children the answer is more qualified. Primary-age students generally need a parent within earshot for the first few sessions and shorter slots, thirty to forty minutes rather than an hour. Where a child genuinely will not work unless physically supervised, a tuition centre or an in-home tutor is the better purchase, and saying so costs us a sale and saves a family a term. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai, and that is a disclosure rather than a comparison we are neutral about.

On preference, the trade is specific and worth naming once. What is given up is presence in the room. What is gained is a tutor chosen for the exact paper your child sits rather than from the pool prepared to drive into Al Twar between 17:00 and 19:00, plus the ability to run three children through one evening. For most secondary students in this district that trade favours online, and for some younger ones it does not.

sections.heading: Starting, and the limits worth knowing first
paragraphs: Send three things: the subject and level, the exam board from the statement of entry, and a marked script or report if one exists. For a household with several children, send all of them at once. Slots have to be planned together, and a second request three weeks later usually means moving the first child's hour.

A trial session then runs at the hour you intend to keep, with the tutor who would teach the term. After it, the tutor says what they think the problem is and roughly how many sessions it takes. If the honest answer is four sessions on examination technique rather than a year of subject teaching, that is what should be said, and for a household watching a monthly figure it is the difference between a sustainable arrangement and an abandoned one.

The limits are worth stating. Evening hours between 17:00 and 19:00 Gulf time are the most requested in the network and run out during mock season. Arabic as a first language at Diploma level, Islamic Education at examination level, Computer Science solution development and Further Mathematics all take longer to match than mainstream IGCSE subjects. For those we give a dated alternative instead of a reassurance, which is more than any competing page in this market manages, since none of them acknowledges a coverage limit at all.

On the legal question a parent should ask every tutor: private tutoring in the UAE requires a work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, issued through MoHRE and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without it is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. Since it costs nothing, a tutor who has not obtained it has told you something.

process.title: Tell us about the household, not just one child
process.description: How many children, which year groups, which schools and which boards. For a family with three at school the first useful output is a ranking, and that cannot be produced from one name. It usually turns out that one child needs a term of help and the others need a conversation.

process.title: Send the marked evidence
process.description: A marked script, a report or an internal assessment draft tells a specialist more in five minutes than a phone call does in half an hour. It also prevents the commonest waste in this market: paying for general subject teaching when the losses were in technique.

process.title: Name the stream for mandatory subjects
process.description: Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language are different courses in separate classes with different languages of instruction. Islamic Education splits the same way. Getting the stream right before the first session is the difference between useful support and wasted sessions.

process.title: Trial in the real slot, one child at a time
process.description: Each child trials with the tutor who would actually teach them, at the hour the household intends to use. Where siblings are being sequenced, the trials run on the same evening so you can see whether the arrangement holds in practice.

process.title: Half-term review against school marks
process.description: Progress is judged on the school's own assessment points rather than on how sessions felt. If a child is stable we say so and the hour stops or moves to a sibling, instead of continuing out of habit at a cost the household is still paying.

whyPoints.title: A specialist per child, in one evening
whyPoints.description: Three children can be taught back to back by three different subject specialists because nobody is travelling between sessions. A visiting tutor must either compromise on subject match or take three separate evenings, and the second costs more than the sum of the online hours.

whyPoints.title: The mandatory UAE subjects are taken seriously
whyPoints.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies are compulsory in every Dubai private school, and competing pages in this market mention them only as subject chips. We identify the right stream, work inside the approved content and focus on accuracy and technique.

whyPoints.title: We rank the household rather than selling to all of it
whyPoints.description: Where a budget covers one hour, the honest recommendation is the child closest to a terminal examination with the most movable grade, even when another child's report reads worse. A provider who recommends tutoring for everyone before seeing evidence is selling.

whyPoints.title: Costs set against Dubai school fees
whyPoints.description: Tutoring is a monthly decision taken alongside fees, and KHDA confirmed no fee increase for 2026-27. This page puts the market's own published monthly and hourly bands next to that, with sources named, rather than quoting rates in a vacuum.

whyPoints.title: Coverage limits stated before you pay
whyPoints.description: Where an hour is full or a component thin, we give a dated alternative. No competing page in this market discloses a coverage limit, which is worth noticing: a provider who never runs short is a provider filling slots with whoever happens to be free.

whyPoints.title: Coursework help that protects the student
whyPoints.description: Internal assessment and Extended Essay support is content teaching, question scoping and written feedback on the student's own draft, documented so a coordinator can see its scope. Operators in this market sell completed coursework, and the penalty for that falls on the student.

faqs.question: What do Al Twar families usually ask for when they first get in touch?
faqs.answer: Three patterns dominate. Villa households with several children usually want a diagnostic: which child is genuinely at risk, and is the weak report line a subject problem or a writing-accuracy problem. Apartment households with a firm monthly ceiling want to know which child should get the only available hour. Families who moved in from another emirate want to know what transferred between boards. All three are answered faster from a marked script than from a conversation, which is why we ask for one with the first enquiry rather than after the trial session.

faqs.question: My son is in the Arabic first-language stream. Can a tutor support that alongside his IGCSEs?
faqs.answer: Yes, within the rules that govern the subject. Arabic as a first language is a separate course from Arabic as an additional language, taught in a separate class as KHDA requires, with Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction. Content for the mandatory subjects is tightly specified, and using different or additional material without prior Ministry of Education permission is prohibited, so the useful work is writing accuracy, structure and examination technique inside the approved syllabus rather than a parallel course. Tell us which stream he is in before the first session, because the two streams need different tutors.

faqs.question: We have three children at school in Al Twar. How do we decide who gets a tutor?
faqs.answer: Rank by how close the child is to a terminal examination and by how much of the grade is still movable, not by whose report reads worst. A Year 11 student twelve weeks from a series has a grade that can still move several bands with technique work. A Year 8 student with a poor report has four years to recover and usually needs a conversation with the school rather than a paid hour. Concentrating the spend on one child reliably produces more than spreading the same money across three, and any provider who tells you otherwise before seeing a marked script is selling.

faqs.question: What does a KHDA inspection band actually tell me about my daughter's year group?
faqs.answer: Less than parents assume, because the headline band is an average across phases, subjects and aspects. A school rated Good overall can be Very Good in primary and Acceptable in secondary, or strong in English and weaker in mathematics at exactly the phase your daughter is in. Read the phase and subject judgements for her own year group, and read the recommendations and whether last year's were addressed. KHDA inspects annually on a six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak, and the report is published on its own site, which is where you should read it rather than on a third-party page.

faqs.question: Can two of my children share one tutor if they are in different years?
faqs.answer: Generally no, and it is an expensive mistake. Two or more school years apart means different stages, different vocabulary and different pace, so one child disengages while the other is bored and you pay for both. Sharing works only where year, subject, board, tier and standing are all close, which in practice usually means twins. The better arrangement for an Al Twar household is sequence: two or three children taught back to back on the same evening by their own subject specialists, which is only practical because nobody is travelling between the sessions.

faqs.question: How does tutoring cost compare with the school fees we already pay?
faqs.answer: It is a monthly decision alongside a fee that is not rising: KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for 2026-27, under the emirate's second economic incentives package. Against that, Bestimate's 2026 monthly estimates for one weekly hour run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. Published packages in this market include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions. Those are market figures from the sources named, not an IB Gram price list.

faqs.question: Is Islamic Education taught in English or in Arabic at a Dubai private school?
faqs.answer: It depends on the stream. KHDA requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and for Arabic as a first language, and Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students. For non-Arab students, Islamic Education and moral, social and cultural studies are taught in the school's licensed-curriculum language. Schools must organise separate classes for the two groups and combined classes are strictly prohibited, because the curriculum expectations and the language differ. Instructional time is counted on a 40-minute lesson unit, with at least 25 minutes advised for any mandatory-subject lesson.

faqs.question: We live in a villa in Al Twar with no quiet room. Does online tutoring still work?
faqs.answer: It works, with one agreement in place. Decide which room is the study room for that hour and treat the slot as an appointment the household respects, including younger siblings. Headphones and a shared working document the student types into matter more than a dedicated study. Families who make that agreement get a noticeably better session from the same tutor than families who do not. If the real issue is a child who will not work unless physically supervised, a tuition centre or an in-home tutor is the better purchase, and IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai.

faqs.question: Which subjects are hardest to find a specialist for in this part of Dubai?
faqs.answer: Arabic as a first language at Diploma level, Islamic Education at examination level, Computer Science solution development, Further Mathematics and Economics Higher Level commentaries during a shared deadline week. These take days rather than hours to match, and occasionally the right person is not free at the hour you want. The alternatives we offer are a different hour with the right specialist, a weekend block, or a dated wait. What we do not do is put a general science or general maths tutor in front of a specialist component and let you discover the mismatch in week three.

faqs.question: My daughter has strong MYP grades but struggles in tests. What is going on?
faqs.answer: Usually nothing is wrong with either measurement; they measure different things. MYP reports criterion grades out of eight across four criteria per subject, rewarding investigation, communication and reflection, and deliberately not drilling procedure. A timed paper removes the criteria, the redrafting and the time, and tests fluency instead. A student can be genuinely strong on the first and slow on the second. One timed diagnostic settles it, and the fix is usually procedural practice rather than more content teaching.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week should a Year 10 student in Al Twar have?
faqs.answer: One protected weekday hour, with a second only if the first is clearly holding after half a term. A Year 10 week in this district already contains nine subjects, the mandatory UAE subjects for most students, and a slow afternoon return. Three tuition hours do not fit, and families who book them usually end the term doing one, because the third was always the session sacrificed. Where two subjects genuinely need support, put the second in a weekend morning block rather than adding another weekday evening, and keep at least one evening completely free.

faqs.question: Do you cover UAE social studies and moral education?
faqs.answer: We can support them, with the same caveat that applies to Arabic and Islamic Education: the content is specified and may not be supplemented with different or additional material without prior permission from the Ministry of Education. Arabic is the primary language of instruction for Social Studies for Arab students, and the school's licensed-curriculum language applies for non-Arab students in moral, social and cultural studies. In practice the useful work is structured revision and written-answer technique, which is where marks are usually lost, rather than teaching content the school has already delivered.

faqs.question: Does a tutor need KHDA approval to teach Arabic privately?
faqs.answer: Two different things are being asked here. KHDA requires schools to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, which is a requirement on schools and their staff. A private tutor working independently needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years. IB Gram holds no KHDA permit, accreditation or endorsement of any kind and does not claim one. Ask any tutor directly which of these they hold, and treat a vague answer as an answer.

faqs.question: What happens if the subject we need has no specialist free in the week we ask?
faqs.answer: We say so and give you a date. Evening hours between 17:00 and 19:00 Gulf time are the most requested across the whole network and they genuinely run out during mock season. The options are a different hour with the right specialist, which for technique and coursework work is usually better than an earlier hour with a generalist; a weekend block, which is less contested and suits coursework anyway; or a dated wait. No competing page in this market publishes a coverage limit at all, and a provider who never admits one is filling slots with whoever is available.

intro.heading: What a very large year group can and cannot do for one student
paragraphs: Al Warqa is villa and low-rise housing on the eastern side of Dubai, between Mirdif and Al Aweer, with some of the largest school cohorts in the emirate either inside it or a short drive away. Several of the schools serving this area run year groups several times the size of a typical international school's, which is not a criticism: large schools in Dubai frequently achieve strong results, hold good inspection ratings and retain experienced staff for years.

Scale does, though, change what one student receives. A subject teacher in a very large cohort can plan a strong lesson, deliver it to thirty students, set a sensible homework task and mark it. What they cannot do, however good they are, is sit beside one child, watch them answer a five-mark question, stop them at the second mark and make them notice the pattern. There are not enough hours in a week in which several hundred scripts need marking.

That is the specific gap Al Warqa families most often come to us about, and naming it correctly matters. If a child has missed content, the school's own revision support is the right and free answer. If a child understands the content and answers it the same wrong way in every assessment, no amount of further teaching helps, because the problem is a habit that nobody has had the time to observe.

The second feature of this district is the breadth of curriculum within it. Indian-curriculum schools with very large cohorts sit a few minutes from IB continuum schools with much smaller ones, and British and American curriculum schools in between. A family moving a child between those schools is moving between genuinely different experiences of being taught, and the tutoring question changes with the move.

Third, reporting. A large school reports to a lot of parents, which tends to push reporting towards formats that scale: percentages, grade bands, effort grades, comment codes. Those are legitimate and they are also compressed. A percentage tells you where a child sits relative to a cohort; it does not tell you that eleven of their fifteen lost marks came from not stating units. Reading past the format is a skill, and this page sets out how.

So what follows covers the topics a timetable reliably short-changes, what good homework looks like compared with the task most students are set, how to track a grade on evidence rather than impression, what the market charges in dirhams, and what a tutor may and may not do with internally assessed work. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every Al Warqa lesson is one-to-one over live video.

dubai/al-warqa.programmesIntro: Four systems are taught within a short drive of Al Warqa. For each, the relevant detail is how a very large or very small cohort changes what an individual student experiences.

programmes.name: Indian-curriculum stages
programmes.description: Board examinations at Grade 10 and Grade 12, with unit tests through the year and a final paper that examines the full syllabus. Breadth and retrieval are rewarded, which makes consistent revision unusually effective and makes a weak term recoverable in a way terminal tiered systems do not allow.
programmes.countryNote: The very large cohorts in this part of Dubai are mostly on this route, and the practical consequence is that individual feedback is scarce while structured content coverage is excellent. Tutoring here should almost never be re-teaching; it should be marking attention and question technique.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Terminal papers at sixteen on one of two boards. Cambridge examines in June and November series and tiers many subjects into Core and Extended, which caps the grade available; Pearson Edexcel examines in May/June and November on a 9-1 scale. Eight or nine subjects run in parallel.
programmes.countryNote: For Al Warqa students the Core or Extended decision is the one to ask about early, because it is made from Year 10 performance in a large class where an individual's potential is harder to see than their current output. A tier set by last year's marks is difficult to argue with later.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four lettered criteria with task-specific descriptors rather than percentages. Assessment is continuous, so feedback arrives more often and in a different language from the percentage reporting most families in this district are used to.

The second is usually the harder adjustment, and it can be prepared for in a short block.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internally assessed components carry real weight, are marked against published criteria and are moderated, with school deadlines well ahead of any board date.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma cohorts in this part of Dubai are small, which means individual attention is better and subject choice is narrower. A student wanting an unusual Higher Level combination may find the school cannot timetable it, and that constraint, rather than ability, decides more subject choices than parents realise.

dubai/al-warqa.subjectsIntro: Requests from Al Warqa cluster around the subjects where a large class makes individual marking attention scarcest, and where a single repeated error costs the same marks in every assessment.

subjects.name: Mathematics 0580 and 4MA1
subjects.levels: Cambridge IGCSE Extended and Pearson Edexcel
subjects.description: The volume subject in every large cohort. Method marks are awarded for reasoning written on the page, and a student who has been trained towards efficient final answers forfeits them silently in every assessment until somebody watches them work.

subjects.name: Science as a combined or separate award
subjects.description: Large cohorts often run combined science alongside separate sciences, and the entry decision affects the grade ceiling and the content depth. Ask which your child is entered for before buying tutoring aimed at the other one.

subjects.name: Chemistry 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and quantitative questions, where the upper grades are decided. In a big class the recurring issue is that students follow the worked example and cannot begin an unseen calculation, which only shows up one-to-one.

subjects.name: Physics 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Circuits, waves and the practical paper. Practical questions credit a method precise enough to repeat, and precision in writing is the hardest thing to give individual feedback on at scale.

subjects.name: Biology 0610 and 4BI1
subjects.description: Mark-scheme vocabulary carries the marks. A fluent paraphrase scores nothing where a specific term is required, and students in large classes can lose this consistently for two years without anybody naming it.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The proof-heavy Diploma route. Small Diploma cohorts mean better attention and narrower timetabling, so a student may be steered towards a route by the timetable rather than by suitability. Worth checking before the choice is locked.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with heavy calculator use. Marks are lost on interpretation rather than computation, which means a student can be numerically strong and still score in the middle of the range.

subjects.name: Accountancy and Business Studies
subjects.description: Widely taken in this district. Marks depend on format and on applying a tool to a named organisation, both of which are checkable in a one-to-one session and almost impossible to correct individually across a very large class.

subjects.name: English Language and English A
subjects.description: Extended writing is the component where individual feedback matters most and is scarcest at scale. Essay plans against past questions are the efficient drill, because a plan takes fifteen minutes and tests the skill being marked.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first and additional language
subjects.description: Compulsory in every Dubai private school, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students because expectations and the language of instruction differ. Streaming errors are common when a family changes school, and they take a term to surface.

sections.heading: A class of thirty and a five-mark question
paragraphs: Here is the arithmetic that explains most tutoring enquiries from this district. A subject teacher with several classes marks a few hundred scripts after a mock. To give each student genuinely individual written feedback on a long paper would take minutes per question per student, which multiplies into a working week that does not exist. So feedback is given to the class: here are the questions the cohort did worst on, here is what the scheme wanted, here is how to answer it.

That briefing is useful and your child may have been present for several of them. What it cannot do is catch an individual pattern. If your child loses marks by answering around the command verb, and the class briefing is about circuit diagrams, nothing in that briefing addresses the thing costing them a grade. They will nod, agree, and lose the same marks next time.

A one-to-one session inverts the ratio. The tutor is looking at one script, which means they can find the pattern in twenty minutes and then watch the student reproduce it live, which is the part that actually changes behaviour. A student who is stopped mid-answer and asked what the verb is asking for learns something a briefing cannot deliver.

This is why we ask for a marked script rather than a subject name, and why the first session is a diagnostic. In a very large cohort the information a parent has is necessarily cohort-level: a percentage, a grade band, a comment from a list. The individual pattern is in the script, it is usually visible within a page, and almost nobody has had the time to look.

sections.heading: The topics a timetable reliably short-changes
paragraphs: Every syllabus contains topics that get taught properly and topics that get squeezed, and the pattern is consistent enough across schools to be predictable. Topics late in the course order are squeezed because the course runs out of weeks. Topics that need equipment are squeezed when a laboratory is shared between large cohorts. Topics that are hard to teach to a mixed-ability class of thirty get covered rather than embedded.

The useful consequence for a parent is that you can anticipate rather than react. If a topic sits in the last term of a two-year course, assume it will be covered quickly and plan independent work on it. If a topic requires practical work and the cohort is large, assume the written method skills around it will be thinner than the content knowledge.

The table below lists the topics families in this district most often bring to us, with the reason each one gets compressed and a realistic estimate of how long it takes to fix. The estimates assume a student who already understands the surrounding material; where they do not, the figure is longer and we will say so after the first session rather than before it.

One caution. A topic being hard is not the same as a topic being badly taught, and parents sometimes arrive convinced of the second when the first is true. Organic chemistry is difficult. Electricity is difficult. A student struggling with them in a strong school is usually struggling with the subject rather than with the teaching, and the remedy is practice with feedback rather than complaint.

sections.heading: Homework that checks nothing, and what a good task looks like
paragraphs: In a large cohort, homework has to be settable for thirty students and markable at scale, which pushes it towards tasks with clear right answers and quick marking. Those tasks are useful for coverage and weak for diagnosis. A student can complete a worksheet of twenty routine questions, get eighteen right, and learn nothing about whether they can handle an unseen five-mark question under time pressure.

A good independent task has three properties. It is attemptable alone, so the student does not stall and give up. It produces something checkable, so the student finds out whether they were right without waiting a week. And it targets a named weakness rather than general coverage, so the time spent is aimed at the thing actually costing marks.

The most reliable task of that kind is a small set of past-paper questions on one topic, closed book and timed, marked by the student against the scheme. Four questions done that way teaches more than twenty routine ones, and it takes less of the evening. The barrier is that students have to be taught to mark honestly, which takes a few sessions and is the most transferable thing a tutor can give them.

What we will not set is more of what the school already sets. If a child is completing a weekly worksheet adequately and the grade is static, adding a second worksheet changes nothing. The intervention has to change the type of work, not the volume, and in a district where evenings are already full that is also the only version a family can sustain.

sections.heading: Tracking a grade rather than a feeling
paragraphs: Large schools report on a schedule, and between reports a parent is working on impressions. That is how a tutoring arrangement runs for two terms without anybody being able to say whether it worked. The remedy is to decide in advance what evidence you will look at, how often, and who holds it.

The baseline is the easy part and the part most often skipped. Before the first session, write down the last marked grade or percentage, the assessment it came from, and the specific fault the tutor says they expect to find. Those three lines are what makes a six-week review a measurement rather than a conversation.

Between reports, the useful evidence is not a feeling about the sessions; it is artefacts. A marked script with the student's own annotations. A timed paper with a date and a mark. A tutor's note naming one habit targeted and the evidence it is improving. A parent who cannot read the subject can still read those, because either the mark went up or it did not, and either the named habit appears in the next script or it does not.

The table sets out what to collect and how often. It is deliberately short, because a tracking system a family will not maintain is worse than none: it produces guilt rather than information. Four items, collected at sensible intervals, are enough to tell whether an arrangement is working.

One habit makes the whole thing easier. Keep the timed papers in date order in one folder, paper or digital. A sequence of four marks with dates on them answers the question a report cannot, because it shows direction rather than position. Two papers is an anecdote; four is a trend, and a trend is what you want in front of you at the review rather than a memory of how the sessions seemed to be going.

sections.heading: What tutoring costs around Al Warqa, with the figures attributed
paragraphs: Pricing in this market is unusually hard to find. Several of the most visible pages publish no figure, and two of the ones that do quote US dollars rather than dirhams. Everything below is a market rate published by the provider named, presented as the market and not as an IB Gram price list.

Budget online tutoring from university students or generalists is advertised from roughly AED 45 to AED 65 an hour, with one platform quoting from about AED 33. Qualified subject tutors working online sit between about AED 150 and AED 300, with one agency publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one visits run roughly AED 180 to AED 350 on one published index and AED 200 to AED 500 among independent tutors, with travel inside the rate. Specialist IB, IGCSE and A Level tutors are quoted at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, one agency at AED 270, and one premium provider at AED 650.

For a family whose problem is marking attention rather than content, the band that matters is the one with examining and marking experience, which sits in the mid and specialist ranges. The cheapest band supervises practice well and does not reliably read a mark scheme the way an examiner reads it. Paying for the wrong band is a more common error in this district than paying too little overall.

Monthly figures seen in this market include about AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits. One published index estimates weekly one-hour tutoring at roughly AED 240 to AED 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 or more for specialist examination-year support. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that Dubai private school fees would not increase for 2026-27, which is the right context for judging whether a tutoring line is proportionate.

sections.heading: An in-home tutor for an Al Warqa villa against one-to-one online
paragraphs: In-home tutoring is a real option here and the comparison should be made honestly. A villa usually has a room that can be given over for an hour, which removes the main practical objection that applies in apartment districts. An adult at the table sees written working without asking and can annotate a page directly, and for younger children that presence genuinely helps.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. The reason that matters specifically for a large-cohort problem is selection. The thing a student in a very large class is missing is marking attention from somebody who reads a mark scheme the way an examiner does. That is a narrow skill. The local pool willing to drive to Al Warqa at five in the afternoon is selected for proximity and availability, not for that skill.

There is a second point about the shape of the work. A marking-led session works from the student's own script, which can be photographed, shared on screen and annotated digitally just as well as on paper. The format loses very little online, unlike, say, a practical demonstration. The gap online delivery has to work hardest to close, immediate unprompted sight of the page, is smaller in exactly the kind of session this district needs most.

What we lose and will state: the social presence of an adult in the room, which matters more for younger students, and independence from a connection. Both are genuine, and for a nine-year-old we would often say an in-home tutor from another provider is the better choice.

sections.heading: Reading a report: percentages, grades and criterion levels
paragraphs: Within a short drive of Al Warqa a parent can encounter four reporting languages. A percentage from an Indian-curriculum school. A letter grade from a Cambridge school. A number from one to nine from a Pearson school. A criterion level from one to seven from an IB school. Each measures something slightly different, and each hides something different, which is why families moving between schools so often misread a first report.

A percentage measures performance against a particular assessment and is comparable only against the same assessment. It hides the distribution: seventy per cent may be near the top of the cohort or near the middle, and without the cohort context it says less than it appears to. Ask for the position relative to the year group, not because rank matters in itself, but because it tells you whether the number is good.

A letter grade or a 9-1 number from an IGCSE board is referenced to grade boundaries for that series and is therefore more stable across time, but it is coarse: a low grade 6 and a high grade 6 are different situations and look identical. Ask for the raw mark and the boundary if the decision matters, which it does for tier entry and for advanced course entry.

A criterion level measures a specific strand of performance against a descriptor, and it is the most informative format for diagnosis and the least intuitive for parents used to percentages. A 5 in one criterion and a 3 in another is far more useful than an average of both, and averaging them, which many families instinctively do, destroys the only information the format was designed to give.

sections.heading: Where the tutor stops on an Internal Assessment or a Personal Project
paragraphs: This boundary matters in every district and it matters in a specific way here, because large cohorts mean a deadline arrives for several hundred students at once and the market around them responds. One provider found in this search sells completed Internal Assessments outright. Under board malpractice rules the consequence falls on the candidate who declared the work as their own, and no part of that risk transfers to the seller.

The permitted boundary is specific enough to hold anybody to. A tutor may teach the content the assessment rests on, explain each criterion and what its marks reward, say whether a research question or project goal is viable before weeks are spent on it, warn that a method will not generate usable evidence, read a draft and name the criterion that is under-served, and ask the questions that make a student see their own gap. A tutor may not supply text, rewrite sections, generate data, pick the question, or edit a draft into a finished state.

For a student in a very large cohort there is an additional practical point. A teacher supervising many coursework students cannot give each of them extended line-by-line criterion feedback, which is exactly the legitimate space a tutor occupies. That is a real service, it is valuable, and it is also the thing the essay mills imitate badly by offering to do the work instead.

We also do not redistribute board material. Syllabuses, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB. We reference them, name the official source and work from what the school has issued. The simple test for a parent with no subject knowledge: if the offer would still work with your child absent from the room, it is substitution rather than teaching.

sections.heading: The first session as a diagnostic, not a lesson
paragraphs: The first session is where most tutoring arrangements are won or wasted. Used as a lesson, it teaches a topic chosen on insufficient information and tells nobody anything. Used as a diagnostic, it produces a written statement of what is actually wrong, which is worth more than the hour cost even if the family goes no further.

To make that possible we need three things beforehand. A recent marked script or report, so the tutor has evidence rather than description. The board and syllabus code, with the tier for Cambridge subjects, so the right papers are in front of them. And a realistic arrival time on a weekday, because a session booked before a child is actually home loses its first ten minutes every week.

What the session itself looks like: the tutor works through the marked script with your child, has them re-attempt one or two questions live, watches where the answer goes wrong, and tests one hypothesis about the cause. Then they write a short note naming the gap, the order to address it in, and a realistic view of how long that takes.

Occasionally the note says something a tutoring company is not supposed to write: that the child does not need a tutor, and a fortnight of structured independent practice with the school's own materials would do more. In a district where families talk to each other and cohorts are large, being the provider that says that when it is true is worth considerably more than one additional term of fees.

faqs.question: My child is in a class of thirty in a large Al Warqa school. Is that the problem?
faqs.answer: It depends which problem you have. A large cohort usually delivers content well and cannot observe one student closely, because a teacher with several hundred scripts to mark gives feedback to the class rather than to each child. If your child has missed content, the school's own revision support is the right answer and it is free. If they understand the content and answer it the same wrong way in every assessment, that is the gap scale creates, and it needs one script and one pair of eyes.

faqs.question: Which topics do large cohorts most often rush?
faqs.answer: The predictable ones. Topics late in the course order get compressed because the course runs out of weeks: vectors and transformations in mathematics, organic chemistry and electrolysis. Topics needing shared laboratory time get thinner written method skills. Topics that are hard to teach to a mixed-ability class of thirty, electricity and circuit analysis above all, get covered rather than embedded. Extended writing with individual feedback is squeezed everywhere, because marking load scales badly. Plan independent work on these rather than reacting later.

faqs.question: Why does my child get good marks on homework and poor marks in tests?
faqs.answer: Because scaled homework and examinations measure different things. Homework that can be set for thirty students and marked quickly tends towards routine questions with clear answers, which is useful for coverage and tells nobody whether the student can handle an unseen five-mark question under time pressure. The test to apply at home is four past-paper questions on one topic, closed book and timed, marked against the scheme. That predicts examination performance in a way a completed worksheet does not.

faqs.question: What does good independent work look like for a student in a big school?
faqs.answer: Three properties. Attemptable alone, so the student does not stall and abandon it. Checkable, so they find out whether they were right without waiting a week for marking. And targeted at a named weakness rather than at general coverage. In practice that means a small set of past-paper questions on one topic, timed and closed book, marked by the student against the official scheme. Four questions done that way beat twenty routine ones and take less of the evening.

faqs.question: How do we tell whether tutoring is working between school reports?
faqs.answer: Collect artefacts rather than impressions. The tutor's note after each session naming one targeted habit shows whether the work has a focus. A self-marked script every two or three weeks shows whether your child can now see their own losses. A full timed paper with a mark and a date, monthly in an examination year, gives you movement that is comparable over time. Then the school's own next assessment confirms it independently. Four items is enough; a system you will not maintain is worse than none.

faqs.question: My child's report shows a percentage. How do I know whether it is good?
faqs.answer: Ask for the position relative to the year group. A percentage measures performance on one specific assessment and is comparable only against the same assessment, so seventy per cent might be near the top of a cohort or in the middle. Rank is not important in itself, but it tells you whether the number is strong. If a decision depends on it, such as tier entry, also ask for the raw mark and the grade boundary rather than accepting the band.

faqs.question: What is an IB criterion level and should I average them?
faqs.answer: No, and averaging is the commonest mistake families make when moving from percentage reporting. A criterion level measures one named strand of performance against a published descriptor. A 5 in one criterion and a 3 in another tells you exactly where to work; the average of 4 tells you nothing and destroys the only information the format was designed to carry. Ask the school which criterion is weakest and what the descriptor requires at the next level up.

faqs.question: Do you provide home tutoring for villas in Al Warqa?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. For a large-cohort problem the reason is selection: what your child is missing is marking attention from somebody who reads a mark scheme the way an examiner does, and the local pool willing to drive here at five in the afternoon is selected for proximity rather than for that specific skill.

faqs.question: Is the Core or Extended decision made fairly in a very large class?
faqs.answer: It is made from Year 10 performance, which in a large class is easier to measure than potential. That is not unfair, but it means a student having a difficult year can be entered at a tier that caps their grade before anyone has looked closely at why the year was difficult. If you think the tier is wrong, raise it in Year 10 with evidence from a marked script, not in Year 11. A diagnostic block of four to six sessions is often used for exactly this question.

faqs.question: How much should we spend if the issue is marking attention rather than content?
faqs.answer: The mid or specialist band, not the cheapest one. Published figures put qualified subject tutors online at roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour, with one agency publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200, and specialist IB or A Level tutors at AED 200 to AED 450 and above. The budget band, advertised at around AED 45 to AED 65, supervises practice well and does not reliably read a mark scheme as an examiner would. Paying for the wrong band is the commonest error here.

faqs.question: Can a tutor give the coursework feedback a teacher with many supervisees cannot?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is the legitimate space. Extended line-by-line feedback against each criterion takes time proportional to the draft, which a teacher supervising a large coursework cohort cannot give every student. A tutor working with one student can explain each criterion, say whether the research question is viable, warn where the method will not produce usable evidence and name the weak criterion in a draft. A tutor cannot supply text, rewrite sections or finish a draft.

faqs.question: Should we move our child to a school with smaller classes?
faqs.answer: That is a bigger question than tutoring and it has costs on both sides. Smaller cohorts generally mean better individual attention and narrower subject choice, because a school cannot timetable an unusual Higher Level combination for three students. Larger cohorts mean strong content delivery, wider option blocks and scarce individual feedback. Within a short drive of Al Warqa you can find both. Decide on the subject combination your child needs first, then on class size, rather than the reverse.

faqs.question: How long does it take to fix a habit like ignoring the command verb?
faqs.answer: Less time than families expect, because it is behavioural rather than conceptual. A student who already knows the material can usually move a grade in a term once they are consistently answering inside the verb. The mechanism is repetitive: identify the verb, say what the examiner wants, write the answer, check against the scheme, repeat. Twenty questions done that way is worth more than two hours of further explanation, and the gain shows up across every subject rather than one.

faqs.question: What happens in the first session, and what if you think we do not need tutoring?
faqs.answer: The tutor works through the marked script with your child, has them re-attempt a question live, watches where the answer goes wrong and tests one hypothesis about the cause. You then get a short written note naming the gap, the order to address it and a realistic timescale. If that note concludes a fortnight of structured independent practice with the school's own materials would do more than a term of sessions, it says so. In this district, being the provider that says that is worth more than the fees.

dubai/al-warqa.closingBody: Al Warqa sits beside some of the largest school cohorts in Dubai, and large cohorts are good at exactly the thing parents worry about least. Content gets delivered. What cannot be delivered at that scale is somebody sitting beside one child, watching a five-mark answer go wrong at the second mark, and making them notice the pattern. That is the purchase worth making here. Send a recent marked script rather than a description, name the board and the tier, record a three-line baseline, and ask for sessions that start from your child's own work rather than from the topic. Every lesson is one-to-one over live video, and the first one is a diagnostic.

intro.heading: The decision behind the search
paragraphs: Al Wasl sits on the inland side of Jumeirah, between Safa Park and the Al Wasl Road corridor, and it is one of the few Dubai neighbourhoods where a family can reach a British-curriculum school and a full IB continuum school inside the same fifteen minutes. That geography creates a particular kind of problem. A child who has spent Years 7 to 11 taking Cambridge or Edexcel IGCSEs can realistically move into either the IB Diploma or A Levels without changing postcode, and the two routes ask for very different things from the same student.

Parents rarely phrase the search that way. They type something close to tutors in Al Wasl, because the immediate pain is a Maths grade or a Chemistry report comment. Underneath it, though, the question is usually about the next two years rather than the next two weeks. Buying six months of tutoring to rescue a Year 11 grade is a different purchase from committing to a two-year Diploma support plan, and the honest answer depends on which route the child is heading into.

So this page is organised around that fork. It sets out what changes between the Diploma and A Levels in assessment terms, where Maths splits the two routes, and how to read a school report before deciding that tutoring is the fix. It then publishes what the Dubai market charges in AED, attributes those figures to the sources that printed them, and explains the permit position every parent should check before paying anyone.

On delivery there is no ambiguity. IB Gram arranges one-to-one tuition online, over live video, with a shared whiteboard and the student's own past paper on screen. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; in-home visiting is a service offered only in India. For an Al Wasl family that is usually an advantage rather than a compromise. The pool of tutors who can teach Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, or Edexcel International GCSE Physics paper by paper, is far larger than the pool who happen to live within a twenty-minute drive of Safa Park at four in the afternoon.

Dubai's private-school market is the densest in the country. KHDA inspects 227 private schools serving 387,441 enrolled children across 17 different curricula, with British-curriculum provision taking the largest share of enrolment and the International Baccalaureate around seven per cent of it. That mix is exactly why the Year 11 fork exists in Al Wasl, and why a tutor who does not know which board your child sits is of limited use.

Everything factual below is attributed. Where a figure comes from a competitor's published rate card, the competitor is named. Where it comes from a regulator, the regulator is named. Where a date has not been verified against the awarding body itself, it is left out rather than guessed at.

dubai/al-wasl.programmesIntro: Four programmes matter in Al Wasl, and they matter in sequence rather than in parallel. A child moves through them, and the handover points are where grades usually wobble. The notes below are written from the Al Wasl school mix rather than from a generic programme description.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The PYP is inquiry-led and transdisciplinary: children work through units of inquiry rather than discrete subject syllabuses, and there is no external examination at the end. Reporting is against learner-profile attributes and approaches to learning, which is why a PYP report can look reassuring while a specific gap in number fluency or written structure goes unaddressed. Tutoring at this stage is diagnostic rather than remedial.
programmes.countryNote: Al Wasl families often run a PYP child and an IGCSE sibling at once, because the coast cluster holds both continuum and British schools. The practical effect is two different vocabularies for the same skill. A tutor working with the younger child should be told which words the school uses, so the language at home stays consistent.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The MYP assesses against four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight, and converts the total to a 1-7 grade through subject-specific boundaries. There are no papers in the IGCSE sense. Students write investigations, reflections and the Personal Project in Year 11. The criteria are published and specific, and most lost marks come from ignoring a command in the criterion rather than from not knowing the content.
programmes.countryNote: Al Wasl is one of the areas where a Year 11 student can be sitting MYP while a neighbour sits IGCSE, and the two will not have covered the same ground. If your child is in MYP and heading for the Diploma, the handover gap is narrower in Sciences and wider in Mathematics, where IGCSE students arrive with more drilled algebraic fluency.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Each subject carries an Internal Assessment worth roughly twenty to thirty per cent of the grade, marked by the teacher and moderated by the IB. The breadth is the point and also the pressure: a Diploma student cannot drop the subject they dislike, which is the single biggest difference from A Levels.
programmes.countryNote: For an Al Wasl student the Diploma's workload lands hardest in the spring of Year 12, when three Internal Assessments, the Extended Essay first draft and the TOK exhibition tend to cluster. Families who plan tutoring around that window rather than around the final examination season generally find the two years less brutal.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects examined at the end of Year 11, graded 9-1 or A*-G depending on the specification. Cambridge offers Core and Extended tiers in several subjects, with Core capped at grade C or 5. Pearson Edexcel runs a single tier in most subjects and a modular structure in some. Syllabus codes matter: Cambridge Physics is 0625, Pearson International GCSE Physics is 4PH1, and the papers are not interchangeable.
programmes.countryNote: The Al Wasl and wider Jumeirah cluster is dominated by British-curriculum schools, so IGCSE is the default at sixteen for most households here. Confirm the board and the tier on your child's entry statement before buying tutoring. A tutor drilling Cambridge Extended past papers for a Pearson candidate wastes half the hours you pay for.

dubai/al-wasl.subjectsIntro: Subject demand in Al Wasl skews towards the sciences and Mathematics, because those are the subjects that decide whether the Diploma route or the A Level route stays open. Each entry below names what the assessment actually tests and where marks go missing.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebraic and calculus-heavy, with Paper 1 sat without a calculator. HL adds proof by induction, complex numbers and a deeper calculus option. Marks are lost on unjustified steps rather than wrong answers: the method marks are written into the markscheme and a correct answer with no working scores a fraction of the total.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and technology-led, with the graphical display calculator permitted in both papers. The content is not easier, it is different. Most lost marks come from interpreting a regression or a chi-squared result in loose language instead of naming the variables and the significance level the question asked about.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms carry most of the HL difficulty. The Internal Assessment is a single scientific investigation of the student's own design. Students lose marks by writing a method they did not actually follow and by reporting uncertainty as a single figure rather than propagating it through the calculation.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics and fields reward fluent algebra; the HL options add depth rather than new habits. The commonest avoidable loss is in the extended-response questions, where students describe a phenomenon instead of explaining it with the quantity the command term demanded. Graph-gradient questions are routinely answered without units.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content-dense, with the HL extension sitting mostly in plant biology, genetics and physiology. Command terms separate a 4 from a 6 here more than knowledge does: outline, describe, explain and evaluate carry different mark ceilings, and a well-written answer to the wrong command term scores almost nothing.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Three Internal Assessment commentaries at SL and HL, each built on a news article and capped at 800 words. Diagrams must be drawn, labelled and referred to in the prose. Students lose marks by explaining theory correctly and never linking it to the article, which is the criterion that carries the marks.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is unseen guided analysis, Paper 2 a comparative essay, plus the Individual Oral and, at HL, the HL Essay. The Individual Oral is where most grades move, because it requires a global issue argued across one literary and one non-literary text with timed, rehearsed precision.

subjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1
subjects.description: Extended tier is required for almost any post-16 Maths route. The highest-yield gaps are usually surds, algebraic fractions, transformations of graphs and the bounds questions, which appear every series and are skipped by candidates who have not seen them drilled.

subjects.name: IGCSE Combined and Separate Sciences
subjects.description: Separate Sciences keeps three science grades on the certificate and is the stronger platform for HL Sciences in the Diploma. Marks go missing in the practical-skills paper, where candidates are asked to criticise a method and instead describe it.

subjects.name: IGCSE English as a Second Language
subjects.description: The reading-and-writing paper rewards register control more than vocabulary range. Candidates lose marks by writing an email in essay prose, or an article in letter form, which the mark scheme penalises under the form-and-audience criterion regardless of language quality.

sections.heading: What an Al Wasl parent is usually deciding when they search this
paragraphs: The search phrase is about tutors. The decision underneath it, nine times out of ten, is about the next two years of schooling. In Al Wasl specifically, families sit inside a few minutes of both British-curriculum secondaries that run A Levels and IB continuum schools that run the Diploma, so the post-16 route is a genuine choice rather than something the school decides for them.

That changes what tutoring is for. If the child is going into A Levels, the useful work in Year 11 is narrow and deep: secure the three subjects that will be continued, and let the others land where they land. If the child is going into the Diploma, breadth matters, because no subject can be dropped and a weak sixth subject drags the total. The same hours of tutoring, spent differently, produce different outcomes depending on which route is coming.

There is a second, quieter factor. A Diploma student carries the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and six Internal Assessments through two years. An A Level student carries coursework in some subjects and none in others. Families who have only ever seen the British system often underestimate how much of a Diploma grade is written rather than examined, and that surprise usually arrives in the spring of Year 12 when three deadlines collide.

So the first thing worth doing is not booking tutoring. It is establishing which route the child is actually heading into, what the receiving school requires to let them in, and whether the current grades clear that bar. Tutoring then has a target. Without that, a family buys hours and hopes.
bullets: Ask the school for its published post-16 entry requirements in writing
Check whether the Diploma option at your school caps Higher Level choices
Confirm whether your child's IGCSE Maths tier allows the route they want
Find out when the school's internal coursework deadlines fall in Year 12

sections.heading: The Year 11 fork: IGCSE into the Diploma, or IGCSE into A Levels
paragraphs: Both routes are accepted by UAE and international universities. They are not equivalent experiences, and the difference is structural rather than a matter of difficulty. The Diploma asks for six subjects plus three core components across two years, with internal assessment in every subject. A Level asks for three or four subjects, examined mostly at the end, with coursework in some and none in others.

The table below compares them across the dimensions that actually change a family's planning: subject count, whether a weak subject can be dropped, how much of the grade is written rather than examined, and what the workload curve looks like across the two years. The right-hand column states what each difference implies for tutoring hours, which is the part no school prospectus covers.

One row deserves emphasis. On the Diploma, a student cannot abandon a subject they find impossible without losing the Diploma itself, so a Year 11 weakness in a subject that will be continued at Standard Level is a two-year liability. On A Levels, the same weakness can simply be left behind in August. That asymmetry is the strongest argument for doing diagnostic work in Year 11 rather than Year 12.

The other row that matters is the written-component share. Families who have moved from a British system into the Diploma are often startled that a fifth to a third of each subject grade is produced at home, under deadline, and moderated externally. It rewards organisation as much as ability, and it is the part a tutor can support most usefully without ever touching the student's words.

sections.heading: Mathematics is where the fork is really decided
paragraphs: If one subject settles the post-16 route for an Al Wasl student, it is Mathematics. The Diploma makes Maths compulsory and splits it into two courses that share a name and very little else. Analysis and Approaches is algebraic and proof-oriented, with a non-calculator Paper 1. Applications and Interpretation is modelling and statistics-led, with a calculator permitted throughout.

The mistake families make is treating Applications as the easy option. It is not easier, it is differently hard: the content load is comparable, the statistics is unforgiving, and the modelling questions ask students to justify a choice of function rather than execute a known procedure. The real difference is what each route keeps open at university, and that is where the choice should be made.

Engineering, Physics, Computer Science, Mathematics and most Economics degrees at competitive universities expect Analysis and Approaches, frequently at Higher Level. Medicine and the life sciences are more often satisfied by either. Business, Psychology and most social sciences accept Applications comfortably. UAE universities vary, and the only reliable method is to read the specific programme page on the university's own site rather than rely on a general rule.

A diagnostic in Year 11 is cheap and decisive. A student who can factorise fluently, handle surds without a calculator and differentiate from first principles is ready for Analysis. A student who can do none of those under time pressure will spend Year 12 underwater in Analysis HL, and the sensible move is to fix the fluency in Year 11 or choose the other route deliberately rather than by accident.

sections.heading: Reading an Al Wasl school report before you buy tutoring
paragraphs: A Dubai school report tells you less than it appears to. British-curriculum reports in the coast cluster typically carry a current working grade, a predicted or target grade, and an effort descriptor. The gap between working and target is where parents reach for a tutor, but the gap alone does not say what kind of help is needed, or whether help is needed at all.

Three different problems produce the same two-grade gap. The first is a content gap: specific topics were missed, often through absence or a change of school, and they are recoverable with targeted teaching. The second is a technique gap: the child knows the material and loses marks on command terms, working-out discipline or timing. The third is a confidence or organisation problem, where the knowledge is present and the output is not.

They need different interventions. A content gap responds to teaching. A technique gap responds to marked past papers with a tutor who knows the markscheme. An organisation problem responds to structure and, often, to nothing a tutor can sell. Buying weekly subject tutoring for an organisation problem is the commonest way a family spends a term's budget and sees no change.

The practical move is to ask the subject teacher one question: on a recent assessment, were the lost marks on topics not covered, or on questions the child could have answered? Teachers answer that question readily and it points straight at the right intervention. If the answer is the second, ask to see the script, because the pattern of lost marks is usually visible in five minutes.
bullets: Ask whether lost marks were content gaps or technique gaps
Request the marked script rather than the summary grade
Check whether the target grade is aspirational or data-derived
Separate the subjects that will be continued post-16 from those that will not

sections.heading: What tutoring costs in this part of Dubai, in AED
paragraphs: Most pages competing for this search publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars, which is not the currency a Dubai family transacts in. The figures below are market rates in dirhams, taken from providers' own published rate cards and from a Dubai tutoring cost survey, with the source named in each case. They are not IB Gram's price list.

At the lower end, EdFlik publishes online rates from AED 45 to 65 per hour and Tutopiya from roughly AED 33 to 52, both of which generally mean a university student or a non-specialist generalist. Unitors publishes IGCSE tutoring from AED 150 per hour and IB from AED 200. TutorChase quotes around AED 270. Bestimate's 2026 Dubai cost table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 and specialist exam-year support at AED 200 to 450 and above. BartyED publishes AED 650 for premium named tutors.

Monthly packages circulating in this market include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a single weekly hour run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year work.

The reason to publish this is that the spread is the information. A Diploma Higher Level specialist and a general maths tutor are different products at different prices, and a family that does not know the bands cannot tell whether a quote is reasonable. Ask any provider what tier the quoted rate sits in, whether it is per hour or per session, whether VAT is included, and what happens to the rate closer to the examination season.

sections.heading: Online lessons against an in-home tutor on the Al Wasl Road corridor
paragraphs: This is the comparison that matters most for the Jumeirah cluster, because the in-home option is genuinely available here and plenty of families use it. The honest account is that an in-home tutor solves a supervision problem well and a specialism problem badly. A tutor who will drive to Al Wasl at 4pm is drawn from the set of tutors who live within a reasonable radius and have that slot free. That set is small, and it shrinks fast once you specify Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level or Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Physics.

There is a cost consequence too. Published in-home rates in Dubai sit at AED 180 to 500 an hour against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified online subject tutor, and part of that premium is travel time rather than teaching. A two-hour minimum is common for in-home sessions, which is a long single sitting for a fifteen-year-old and often less effective than two separate hours in the same week.

IB Gram delivers one-to-one tuition to Al Wasl online, over live video, with a shared whiteboard and the student's own script or past paper on screen. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in the UAE; in-home visiting is an India-only service. The trade that an Al Wasl family makes is losing a physical presence in the room and gaining access to a subject specialist who is not constrained by Dubai drive times.

Two practical points decide whether that trade works. The first is the workspace: a desk, a wired or strong connection, and a camera angle that lets the tutor see written working, not just a face. The second is the device. A tablet with a stylus is better than a laptop for Maths and Science, because the tutor needs to watch the working appear rather than see a finished answer.
