sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not touch on an IA or Extended Essay
paragraphs: This is a line worth being explicit about, because the market around these searches includes operators who sell completed Internal Assessments. One provider in this space advertises finished IAs at a fixed price. Buying one is academic malpractice under IB rules and the consequence falls on the student, not the seller: a malpractice finding can cost the Diploma.

What a tutor may legitimately do is substantial. They can teach the subject content the investigation rests on. They can explain what each assessment criterion asks for, in the IB's own language. They can read the student's own draft and ask the questions the criteria ask. They can teach referencing, data presentation, uncertainty propagation and the discipline of a research question narrow enough to answer. They can help a student plan a timeline that does not collapse in March.

What a tutor may not do is produce any part of the submission. Not a paragraph, not a rewritten conclusion, not a cleaned-up method, not an edit so heavy the words stop being the student's. The test the IB applies is authenticity, and a coordinator who reads a draft that does not sound like the student will escalate it. A tutor who offers to write it is selling the student a risk they have not been told about.

In practice the boundary is easy to hold and worth stating out loud in the first session, so the student knows where it sits. Ask any prospective tutor directly what they will and will not do with a draft. The answer separates a teacher from a problem.

sections.heading: The regulator, the permit, and how an Al Wasl parent verifies a tutor
paragraphs: Dubai's private schools are overseen by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which u.ae describes as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. KHDA inspects schools annually and publishes a band from Outstanding down to Very Weak. It does not license individual private tutors, and no tutoring provider should describe itself as approved by KHDA unless it holds the specific Educational Services Permit that KHDA issues to training institutes with premises.

Private tutoring by individuals is regulated separately, through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is open to teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. MoHRE's own service listing for it is Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, with a stated two-working-day completion time through the MoHRE app, website or e-services system.

Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are, in the wording on u.ae, subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No schedule of amounts has been published, so any page quoting a specific fine figure is quoting something unverified. Abu Dhabi adds a further rule for its own schools: ADEK's professional-ethics framework has been reported as barring school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct carries a similar restriction.

For a parent the verification step is simple. Ask whether the tutor holds the MoHRE private tuition permit, and ask to see it. A tutor who holds one will show you. A provider who tells you no permit is needed is wrong, and a provider who claims regulator approval it cannot evidence is a different kind of problem.

sections.heading: Starting mid-year, and what happens if no specialist is free
paragraphs: Families in Al Wasl rarely start tutoring in September. They start after the October assessments, after the January mocks, or in the six weeks before a terminal paper, which is the hardest brief of the three. All of those are workable, but they need different plans and it is worth saying what each realistically achieves.

A start after the first assessment round has the most room. There is time to diagnose, teach missing content, and build paper technique in that order. A start after the mocks is narrower: the diagnosis is already done by the mock script, and the work is almost entirely technique and targeted content repair. A start six weeks before a paper is triage. It can move a grade when the problem is technique and the content is broadly present. It cannot rebuild two years of missing foundations, and a provider who says otherwise is selling something.

On availability, the honest position is that some subject and level combinations are genuinely scarce. A Higher Level Physics specialist who can take a 5pm Gulf Standard Time slot is in shorter supply than a Standard Level Maths tutor at the same hour. When a UAE-based tutor is not available for a specific combination, the match is made from the wider network, with the same one-to-one online format and the same syllabus specificity, and the family is told that before booking rather than after.

The first session is diagnostic and is used to confirm the plan or change it. If the tutor concludes after that session that the problem is not the one you described, you should hear it. A tutor who finds an organisation problem and keeps selling subject hours is not doing the job.

process.title: Tell us the board, the tier and the deadline
process.description: The useful detail is specific: Cambridge or Pearson, Core or Extended, Standard or Higher, and the date of the next thing that is graded. A syllabus code from the entry statement is better than a subject name, because it removes the commonest cause of wasted hours.

process.title: A diagnostic session, not a sales call
process.description: The first session puts the student in front of a past paper question or a recent script and watches how they work. That produces a plan with named topics and a sequence, rather than a promise. If the diagnosis contradicts what the report said, you are told.

process.title: Matched to the syllabus, then to the slot
process.description: Subject and level come first, availability second. For Al Wasl that usually means a 4.30pm to 7pm weekday window or a weekend morning. Where a specific Higher Level combination has no UAE-based tutor free, that is disclosed before any booking is made.

process.title: Weekly work with marked homework
process.description: Each session sets work, and the next session starts by marking it against the board's own criteria. Progress is reported in the language of the specification: criterion letters for an IA, paper and question numbers for examinations, so it can be checked against the school's reporting.

process.title: Review at the next assessment point
process.description: The plan is re-examined after the next graded piece of work rather than on a fixed schedule. Sometimes the answer is fewer hours. A tutor who recommends continuing regardless of what the next assessment shows is not reviewing anything.

whyPoints.title: Syllabus specificity before anything else
whyPoints.description: Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are different papers with different question styles, and a tutor who drills the wrong one is wasting your money politely. Matching starts from the syllabus code on the entry statement, not from the subject name.

whyPoints.title: Prices published with their sources
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure on this page names the provider or survey that published it and the month it was read. That is unusual in this market, where most pages publish no price and two publish dollars. You can check each band yourself.

whyPoints.title: A stated coursework boundary
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches, explains criteria and reviews the student's own draft. They do not write, complete or heavily edit any assessed submission. The boundary is stated to the student in the first session, because the malpractice risk sits with them.

whyPoints.title: No regulator claims we cannot evidence
whyPoints.description: KHDA inspects schools and MoHRE issues the private tuition permit. Neither endorses IB Gram, and this page does not imply otherwise. Any provider claiming approval by KHDA should be asked for its permit number.

whyPoints.title: Disclosed coverage limits
whyPoints.description: Some subject, level and time-slot combinations have no UAE-based specialist free. When that is true, you are told before booking and offered the wider network at the same one-to-one online format, rather than being matched to whoever is available.

whyPoints.title: Built around the Al Wasl school run
whyPoints.description: A realistic first slot in this part of Jumeirah is 4.30pm or later on weekdays, earlier only in the summer timetable. Weekend morning sessions are widely used by Diploma students here and are usually the more productive hour.

faqs.question: Should my Al Wasl child take the IB Diploma or A Levels after IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Both are accepted by UAE and international universities, so the choice is about fit rather than prestige. The Diploma suits a student who is broadly strong, organised and comfortable writing to deadlines, because six subjects plus the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge cannot be narrowed. A Levels suit a student with a clear direction and one or two subjects they would rather leave behind, because dropping is possible. The decisive practical question is whether your child can carry a subject they dislike for two years without it dragging the total. If not, A Levels are the kinder structure.

faqs.question: Is IB Maths Applications an easier option than Analysis and Approaches?
faqs.answer: No. It is different rather than lighter. Applications and Interpretation carries a comparable content load, leans heavily on statistics and modelling, and asks students to justify a choice of model rather than execute a known procedure. Analysis and Approaches is algebraic and proof-oriented with a non-calculator Paper 1. The real distinction is what each keeps open: competitive Engineering, Physics, Mathematics and Computer Science programmes usually expect Analysis, often at Higher Level. Check the specific programme page at each university your child is considering, because general rules are unreliable here.

faqs.question: Do tutors travel to homes in Al Wasl?
faqs.answer: Independent tutors in Dubai do, and published in-home rates run from roughly AED 180 to 500 per hour with travel time inside that figure. IB Gram does not work that way. All UAE tuition is delivered one-to-one online, over live video, with a shared whiteboard and the student's own script on screen; in-home visiting is a service offered only in India. The trade for an Al Wasl family is losing a physical presence and gaining a subject specialist who is not limited to whoever can reach Safa Park by four in the afternoon.

faqs.question: How much should I expect to pay for Diploma Higher Level tutoring in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Market rates for specialist IB, IGCSE and A Level tutoring in Dubai sit around AED 200 to 450 per hour and above, based on TutorChase's published AED 270 and Bestimate's 2026 Dubai range of AED 200 to 450 plus. Qualified online subject tutors who are not level specialists run closer to AED 150 to 300, according to Unitors' published rates. Premium named tutors reach AED 650, as BartyED publishes. Ask which band a quote sits in, whether it is hourly or per session, and whether VAT is included.

faqs.question: My child's working grade and target grade are two apart. Does that mean they need a tutor?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, and the gap alone will not tell you. Three different problems produce the same gap: missing content, weak examination technique, and an organisation or confidence issue. Only the first two respond to subject tutoring. Ask the subject teacher one question: on the last assessment, were the lost marks on topics never covered, or on questions your child could have answered? If it is the second, ask to see the marked script. The pattern of lost marks is usually obvious within five minutes and points straight at the right fix.

faqs.question: Which schools do Al Wasl families usually attend?
faqs.answer: The Al Wasl, Al Safa and Jumeirah stretch holds a dense mix of British-curriculum schools and IB continuum schools within a short drive, including Jumeirah English Speaking School, Jumeirah College, Horizon English School, Jumeirah Primary School, Latifa School for Girls, Jumeirah Baccalaureate School and Emirates International School Jumeirah, with Dubai College and Kings' School Dubai a little further along the coast. These are named as ecosystem context only; IB Gram has no affiliation with any of them, and current inspection bands should be checked on the KHDA site.

faqs.question: Where exactly is the line between IA coaching and IA malpractice?
faqs.answer: The line sits at authorship. A tutor may teach the underlying content, explain each assessment criterion in the IB's own wording, read your child's own draft and put the criteria's questions to them, and teach referencing, data handling and timeline discipline. A tutor may not author any part of the submission, including a rewritten conclusion or an edit heavy enough that the words stop being the student's. The authenticity requirement sits on the student, so the consequence of crossing that line falls on them. A provider advertising completed Internal Assessments is selling a malpractice risk.

faqs.question: Does a private tutor in Dubai need a permit, and how do I check?
faqs.answer: Yes. Individuals giving private lessons need the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Applications go through the MoHRE app, website or e-services system under the service Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing. Ask to see the permit. Tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws.

faqs.question: What time can a weekday lesson realistically start for a Jumeirah-side student?
faqs.answer: For most Al Wasl households, 4.30pm is the earliest reliable weekday start, and 5pm is safer if the school sits further along the beach road or inland towards Al Khail. Younger siblings often finish considerably earlier, which in practice splits a household into two different slots rather than one shared one. Diploma students in this cluster frequently prefer a weekend morning session, which is usually the more productive hour because it is not competing with a full school day and an activity schedule.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting tutoring six weeks before an exam?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on what is wrong. Six weeks is enough to change examination technique substantially: command-term discipline, working-out that earns method marks, timing, and the specific question types a student has been avoiding. It is not enough to rebuild two years of missing foundations, and anyone promising that is overselling. The first session should be diagnostic, working from a recent script, and should produce an honest statement of what the remaining time can and cannot achieve. That statement is more useful than an encouraging one.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects does my child need to pass for UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: On the British track, the Ministry of Education requires five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE with a grade no lower than E or grade 3, plus either one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five required subjects. One competing page in this market states six subjects, which is incorrect. Verify the current requirement on the Ministry of Education's own site, since IB Gram does not perform equivalency.

faqs.question: Does my child need to sit Separate Sciences rather than Combined Science?
faqs.answer: For the most competitive Higher Level Science routes in the Diploma, Separate Sciences is the stronger platform: it produces three science grades and covers more content per subject, so the step up to Higher Level Chemistry or Physics is smaller. Combined Science is not a barrier to the Diploma, and plenty of students make the transition successfully, but it usually means more groundwork in the first term of Year 12. If the plan involves Medicine, Engineering or a Physical Sciences degree, discuss the tier with the school before Year 10 options close.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover both of my children if they are on different curricula?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking, but the honest answer is often no. A tutor fluent in Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 Extended is not automatically fluent in the Diploma's Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and the two need different drilling. Where the subjects and levels are close enough, one tutor across two children is efficient and keeps the vocabulary consistent at home. Where they are not, two specialists is the better purchase even though it is more administration. Ask what each tutor has actually taught to examination, not what they can cover.

faqs.question: What should I ask a tutoring provider before paying anything in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Six questions sort most of them. Which exam board and syllabus code will you teach to? Which tier or level have you taught to examination before? Do you hold the MoHRE private tuition permit, and may I see it? Is the rate per hour or per session, and does it include VAT? What will you do, and refuse to do, with an Internal Assessment draft? And what happens if the match does not work after two sessions? Vague answers to any of those are useful information.

faqs.question: Are school fees in Dubai rising again this year?
faqs.answer: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in the emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package. That matters for tutoring budgets, because a frozen fee bill means a household's education spending plan is more predictable than usual this year. KHDA also reported seven new private schools opening for 2026-27, four British curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, adding 16,846 places, which gradually widens the post-16 options available to coast-cluster families.

dubai/al-wasl.closingHeading: Settle the route first, then buy the hours
dubai/al-wasl.closingBody: If your child is in Year 10 or Year 11 in Al Wasl, the most valuable thing you can do this term is not to book a weekly slot. It is to establish which post-16 route they are heading into, read the receiving school's published entry requirements, and get an honest diagnostic on Mathematics, because that is the subject that closes doors quietly. Once the route is settled, tutoring has a target and the hours do work. IB Gram arranges one-to-one lessons online, over live video, matched to the exact syllabus code your child's school has entered, with the coursework boundary stated in the first session.

dubai/arabian-ranches.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover the subjects where the Year 11 to DP1 gap is widest - mathematics, the three sciences and English A - at both the IGCSE end and the Diploma end. A bridging tutor needs fluency in both specifications, which is a narrower requirement than it sounds.

intro.heading: What actually changes between Year 11 and DP1
paragraphs: Arabian Ranches is a villa community of a dozen clusters - Al Reem, Alvorada, Mirador, Palmera, Saheel, Savannah, Terra Nova and the rest - arranged around a golf course and a souk, with Jumeirah English Speaking School Arabian Ranches inside it and Ranches Primary School alongside. The unusual thing about this community, for tutoring purposes, is that JESS runs both IGCSE and the IB Diploma. Families here are not speculating about the transition; they watch the year above them go through it.

What they see is consistent. A student who took eight or nine IGCSEs and collected good grades starts DP1 in September and is struggling by late October. The parents assume the child has stopped working. Usually the child is working harder than ever and getting less for it, because four specific things changed at once and nobody named them.

The first is depth against breadth. IGCSE Mathematics Extended covers a wide syllabus at a modest depth; Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level covers a narrower syllabus to a depth that assumes algebraic fluency as a starting condition rather than as a learning objective. A student who could get through IGCSE algebra by pattern-matching has nothing to pattern-match against in DP1. The same applies in Chemistry, where moles work that was a topic becomes a tool used in every subsequent chapter.

The second is the shift from recall to justification. IGCSE mark schemes reward correct answers with method shown. Diploma mark schemes reward reasoning, and Diploma internal assessments reward reflection on method. A student who has spent two years producing right answers has not practised explaining why a method applies, and that is a separate skill with its own marks attached.

The third is the volume of independent work. Six subjects each carry an internally assessed component. On top sit a 4,000-word extended essay, Theory of Knowledge and Creativity, Activity, Service. None of those three has a weekly subject class. A Year 11 managed by homework deadlines meets a DP1 in which the heaviest items have deadlines months away and no weekly nagging attached. Students who have never managed a long project learn to, expensively, in DP2.

The fourth is the choice itself. Eight or nine IGCSE subjects narrow to six, three of them at Higher Level, and those six are chosen at sixteen on incomplete information. Some combinations close doors to degree courses that the student has not yet thought about. That decision is made in Year 11, it is cheap to get right and expensive to reverse, and it is the single most valuable conversation a family in Arabian Ranches can have before DP1 begins. A school will normally allow a level change in the opening weeks and almost never a subject change after the first term, so the window is narrower than it looks from the outside.
bullets: Depth replaces breadth: algebraic fluency becomes an assumption, not a target
Mark schemes reward justification, not just a correct answer with working
Six internal assessments plus three core components, none weekly-timetabled
Subject and level choices at 16 can close degree routes quietly
The useful window is the spring and summer before DP1, not January of DP1

dubai/arabian-ranches.programmesIntro: Four routes matter in Arabian Ranches, and the interesting part is not what each one is but what each one assumes a student already has on arrival. That assumption is the gap tutoring has to close.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects examined by terminal written papers, with Cambridge tiering several subjects into Core and Extended and Pearson Edexcel generally running a single tier. The syllabus is broad and the depth modest, which is the right design for a two-year course at 14 to 16. Grades are awarded 9 to 1 or A* to G depending on the subject and board, and the papers are the whole of the assessment in most subjects.
programmes.countryNote: The tier matters more in Arabian Ranches than families expect, because a student entered for Cambridge Core has a capped maximum grade and may find a Higher Level Diploma subject built on that foundation unrealistic. Checking the tier in the first term of Year 10, rather than discovering it on a results slip, is the cheapest intervention available in this community.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, lettered A to D with achievement levels from 1 to 8. There is no terminal written examination unless a school enters students for the optional MYP 5 eAssessment. The programme assesses investigation, communication and reflection as explicitly as it assesses content, which means students arrive at the Diploma already fluent in the language of criteria.
programmes.countryNote: An MYP student entering DP1 faces a different gap from an IGCSE student. They are comfortable with criteria and reflection and frequently short on examination technique and raw content coverage, particularly in mathematics. An IGCSE student is the reverse. Both need bridging; they need opposite bridges, and a tutor who treats them the same will waste a term.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Three Higher Level and three Standard Level subjects plus Theory of Knowledge, the extended essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Higher Level subjects add a further written paper and additional syllabus depth. Every subject carries an internally assessed component marked against published criteria by the teacher and moderated by the IB. Dubai schools sit the May session, with the school's own coursework deadlines falling well before it.
programmes.countryNote: JESS Arabian Ranches takes students through to the Diploma, which means a share of this community never changes school at 16 and therefore never gets the natural reset that a school move provides. The continuity is an advantage academically and a hazard in one respect: habits that worked at IGCSE carry straight into DP1 unchallenged.

programmes.name: A Level, the other destination after Year 11
programmes.description: Three or four subjects studied in considerable depth, assessed by written papers with practical endorsement in the sciences and no equivalent of the Diploma core. Content per subject typically exceeds Higher Level in the sciences, while total breadth is far narrower. There is no extended essay, no Theory of Knowledge and no second language requirement, which suits a student with a settled direction.
programmes.countryNote: Several Arabian Ranches families move a child out of the community at 16 for A Level, usually to Nord Anglia International School Dubai, Safa Community School or a school nearer Al Barsha. The choice between depth in three subjects and breadth in six plus core is worth one informed conversation in Year 11, and it is usually made on the strength of a sibling's experience rather than on the student's own direction.

dubai/arabian-ranches.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects where the Year 11 to DP1 gap bites hardest in this community, with the specific thing that changes in each. The gap is rarely the whole subject; it is one or two assumed skills.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebraic manipulation, calculus and proof. The course assumes fluency in surds, indices, factorising and rearranging rather than teaching them. A student who passed IGCSE Extended by recognising question types finds Higher Level unmanageable within a term, and six to eight bridging sessions on algebraic fluency before September is the highest-value intervention available.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and the graphic display calculator. Often chosen as the easier route after IGCSE and frequently underestimated: the statistics content is heavier than anything at IGCSE, and the exploration requires a real dataset and a defensible method. Students arrive expecting less algebra and meet more interpretation.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Moles work shifts from being a topic to being a tool used in energetics, equilibrium, kinetics and acids throughout. A student with shaky stoichiometry at IGCSE does not have a chapter-sized problem; they have a course-sized one. Uncertainty, significant figures and the scientific investigation's evaluation criterion are the other three recurring gaps.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The step is mathematical rather than conceptual. IGCSE Physics asks for formula substitution; Diploma Physics asks for multi-step derivation, algebraic rearrangement with symbols rather than numbers, and graphs interpreted as relationships. Students who were strong at IGCSE recall and weak at algebra are the ones who struggle, and the fix is mathematics rather than physics.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content volume rises sharply and the marking becomes unforgiving about command terms: a question asking students to explain and receiving a description earns part marks at best. The scientific investigation demands a controlled variable set the student can defend. IGCSE habits of broad recall transfer poorly without precision work.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: IGCSE English rewards clear writing on a set task. Diploma English A rewards analysis of how a text produces meaning, including non-literary texts, across two papers, an individual oral and at Higher Level an essay. The individual oral needs a global issue argued through two extracts, which is the single concept most students arrive without.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Frequently a new subject at 16, taken with no IGCSE foundation at all. The diagram carries marks in its own right, which students who come from a written-essay background consistently under-weight. The internally assessed commentaries ask for a named theory applied to a published article rather than a summary of it.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Also commonly new at 16, and the calculation content surprises students who chose it expecting an essay subject. Break-even, ratios and cash-flow forecasting are the reliable marks on the paper. Case-study papers reward treating pre-released material as a dataset to be analysed rather than as reading to be summarised.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: The move from narrative to argument is the whole transition. IGCSE History tolerates a well-organised account; Diploma History requires a thesis defended against counter-evidence, plus source evaluation tied to a specific question and a historical investigation with reflection on method.

subjects.name: English B and the second-language requirement
subjects.description: The Diploma requires a second language, which catches students who dropped languages after Year 9. Starting a language at ab initio in DP1 is viable with regular contact and unviable with occasional cramming. Short, frequent sessions beat long infrequent ones here by a wide margin.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the extended essay
subjects.description: Two components with no IGCSE equivalent whatsoever. A 4,000-word supervised research essay and an argument about how knowledge is justified are both new kinds of work, and both have deadlines set by the school in DP1. Neither is content-heavy; both are entirely unfamiliar, which is why they are underestimated.

sections.heading: The transition map: subject by subject from Year 11 to Diploma entry
paragraphs: One competing page in this search has a single subheading about the IGCSE to IB gap. Nobody has a structured version, which is strange, because the gap is different in every subject and the bridging work is therefore different in every subject too. Treating it as one general problem produces general advice, and general advice produces a term of wasted sessions.

The table below is the map. Read it as a diagnostic rather than as a syllabus: for each subject a student is taking at Diploma level, the question is whether the assumed skill in the third column is already automatic. If it is, no bridging is needed. If it is not, the course will not stop to teach it, and the student will spend DP1 trying to learn two things at once.

The pattern across subjects is consistent enough to state plainly. Mathematics and physics assume algebraic automaticity. Chemistry assumes stoichiometry. The humanities assume argument rather than narrative. The sciences all assume uncertainty handling and precision with command terms. English A assumes that non-literary text analysis is a thing the student has done. None of these is advanced; all of them are prerequisites that IGCSE treats as outcomes.

The weeks-of-support column is an estimate of the gap rather than a quotation. A student who is genuinely fluent needs none. A student who is not is usually two to six weeks of focused work away from being fluent, which is a summer rather than a year. The expensive version of this is discovering the gap in November of DP1 and trying to close it alongside the new content it blocks.

sections.heading: Choosing six subjects at sixteen without closing doors
paragraphs: Eight or nine IGCSE subjects narrow to six, three at Higher Level. That decision is made in Year 11 by a sixteen-year-old with incomplete information about what they want to do at twenty-one, and it is the one academic choice in Dubai schooling that is genuinely hard to reverse. A school will usually allow a level change in the first weeks of DP1 and rarely a subject change after that.

The reliable failure is a combination that looks balanced and does not meet a prerequisite. Medicine commonly expects Chemistry and Biology at Higher Level. Engineering commonly expects Mathematics Analysis and Approaches and Physics at Higher Level. Economics degrees often specify a mathematics requirement that Applications and Interpretation may not satisfy at some institutions. These are not universal rules - they vary by university and change between admissions cycles - which is exactly why the only safe method is to read the published entry requirements for the specific courses a student is considering.

The second failure is workload rather than prerequisite. Three Higher Levels in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry is a defensible combination for a particular student and an unmanageable one for many others, especially alongside an extended essay in a fourth subject. A student's IGCSE profile is reasonable evidence here: consistent high attainment in a subject with modest effort suggests Higher Level is sustainable, and a strong grade achieved through heavy effort suggests it may not be.

The third, smaller failure is the second language. The Diploma requires one, and students who dropped languages after Year 9 discover this late. Starting a language at ab initio in DP1 works with regular weekly contact and fails with occasional cramming, so the decision should be made with the weekly commitment understood rather than as an afterthought in August.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation: choosing the mathematics route
paragraphs: This is the most consequential single choice in the Diploma and the one most often made on hearsay. Both routes are real mathematics courses and neither is a soft option. They are built for different purposes, and the question is not which is harder but which one matches what the student intends to do and how they think.

Analysis and Approaches is algebraic and proof-oriented. It emphasises calculus, algebraic manipulation and formal reasoning, and it is the route most engineering, physics, mathematics and many economics programmes expect. Applications and Interpretation is modelling and statistics led, with the graphic display calculator assumed throughout, and it suits students heading towards the social sciences, business, design, medicine in some systems, and anything where data interpretation matters more than proof.

The practical test, applied to a Year 11 student in April, is two questions. First: in IGCSE mathematics, were the algebra questions the comfortable ones or the ones they avoided? A student who enjoyed rearranging and factorising will find Analysis and Approaches congenial; one who got through algebra by recognising question shapes will not. Second: does any course on their list name a mathematics route explicitly? If one does, the decision is already made and the only remaining question is the level.

A caution about level. Mathematics Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level is a demanding course and is not a lighter alternative to Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level. Students who want less mathematics should take a Standard Level route, not the other subject at Higher Level. Verify any specific university requirement on that institution's own admissions pages, because these requirements vary and are revised between cycles.

sections.heading: What the transition costs, bridged early against rescued late
paragraphs: The financial case for bridging before DP1 rather than reacting during it is straightforward once the session counts are written down. A summer bridge is six to ten sessions on assumed skills. A reactive rescue is twenty to thirty sessions across DP1 and DP2 attempting to close the same gap while new content keeps arriving, because the gap blocks the content and the content hides the gap.

Market rates in Dubai, in dirhams and attributed: EdFlik advertises online tuition from AED 45 to 65 an hour and Tutopiya from around AED 33 to 52, which buys supervision rather than a specialist. Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. TutorChase publishes AED 270. Bestimate's 2026 Dubai survey puts specialist IB, IGCSE and A Level tuition at AED 200 to 450 and above, with monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions of AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-range, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for exam-year specialist support. BartyED publishes a premium rate of AED 650.

Those are other providers' published figures and the market they describe, not IB Gram's price list. What this page can usefully add is the shape of the spend rather than the hourly number, because the hourly number is the part families already know and the session count is the part nobody tells them.

One further point on honesty: ask whether a quoted rate is per hour or per lesson, and whether VAT is included. A 45-minute lesson quoted at an hourly-sounding figure is around a third more expensive per contact hour than it appears, and that gap compounds across a bridging block. IB Gram quotes after a free consultation and a trial session, against the actual subject, level and session length.

sections.heading: Why the Dubailand commute decides the format
paragraphs: IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. In Arabian Ranches that policy happens to align with the practical reality better than it would almost anywhere else in Dubai, and it is worth explaining why rather than simply asserting it.

Arabian Ranches sits off Sheikh Mohammed Bin Zayed Road and Al Qudra Road, and the communities around it - DAMAC Hills, Mudon, Town Square, Remraam - are further out again. A tutor travelling from Jumeirah or Al Barsha at five in the afternoon is committing an hour each way to deliver a sixty-minute lesson, and that cost appears in the rate whether or not it is itemised. Bestimate's survey puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors at AED 200 to 500, with the travel priced in.

The sharper problem is the pool rather than the price. A bridging tutor has to be fluent at both ends of the transition: the IGCSE specification the student has just left and the Diploma specification they are entering. That is a narrower qualification than either alone, and the number of people holding it who also live within half an hour of the Ranches is small. Over live video the radius is irrelevant and the qualification is the only filter.

There is a timing dividend too. Because the school run here is long, the window after school is short and unreliable. An online session at 6.30pm or 7.00pm, after the child has eaten, is more productive than a 4.30pm session delivered to someone who got home at 4.20pm, and it carries no risk of a tutor sitting on Al Qudra Road while the clock runs.

sections.heading: An MYP student entering DP1 needs the opposite bridge
paragraphs: Families in Arabian Ranches with one child on the British route and another in the Middle Years Programme get a useful natural experiment, and the result surprises them. Both children face a gap entering DP1, and the gaps point in opposite directions. Advice that helps one actively misleads the other.

An IGCSE student arrives with examination technique, mark-scheme instincts and broad content coverage, and arrives short on criteria literacy, reflection and independent project management. They have never been assessed on process. Asked to reflect on their method, they write what happened. Their bridging work is about criteria and about justification.

An MYP student arrives fluent in criteria, comfortable with reflection and used to extended investigation, and arrives short on examination technique and on raw content fluency, particularly in mathematics where the programme's lighter procedural drilling shows. They have rarely sat a timed paper that counts. Their bridging work is past papers, timing and procedural automaticity.

The practical consequence for a family is that a single tutor handling both children with a single approach will shortchange one of them. Two matches, two different bridges, and a plan for each that names the specific gap. It is also worth saying that neither starting point is better; they are different preparations for the same destination, and both are closeable in a summer if they are named in April rather than discovered in November. Schools running both programmes in the same building see this every September, and the coordinators can usually tell a parent which of the two gaps their own cohort struggles with most.

sections.heading: What should already be done by December of DP1
paragraphs: DP1 feels unpressured until it is not, because its deadlines are distant and its workload is cumulative. A short checklist for December of DP1 does more for a student in Arabian Ranches than any amount of content tutoring, and almost none of it is content.

By December, the student should know which subject their extended essay will be in and have at least a candidate research question. They should have the school's internal assessment calendar for all six subjects in one place. They should have read, once, the assessment criteria for every internally assessed component they will produce. They should have sat at least one timed paper in each Higher Level subject. And they should have confirmed that their mathematics route and Higher Level combination still match what they intend to study later.

Each item on that list takes under an hour and all of them together take one afternoon. The reason to do them in December rather than in March is that every one of them becomes harder when it is late: extended essay questions chosen in June are chosen from whatever is left, and criteria read the week before a deadline cannot change the work.

If a family does nothing else, the single highest-value item is the internal assessment calendar. Six subject deadlines plus the extended essay checkpoints plus Theory of Knowledge, laid out on one page, converts an unmanageable year into a sequence. Most schools publish it and most families have never seen it in one piece. Ask the Diploma coordinator.

sections.heading: Getting matched, and the honest limits
paragraphs: The process is short. A consultation establishes what the student has just finished, what they are entering, which assumed skills look shaky and what the household's realistic weekly window is given the commute. A trial session follows, usually opening with a diagnostic on the assumed skills rather than on new content, because the diagnostic is the thing that makes the plan specific. Then a written plan, reviewed fortnightly against marked work.

Two disclosures belong here. The first is availability. Bridging tutors fluent at both ends of a transition are a narrower pool than subject tutors, and the demand for them is concentrated into May, June and July. A family asking in late August for a summer bridge is asking at the worst possible moment. Where no suitable tutor is free, we give a date rather than substituting a generalist, because a generalist bridging tutor is a contradiction.

The second is about what tutoring cannot do. It cannot make a Higher Level combination work if the combination is wrong for the student, and it cannot reverse a subject choice after the school's deadline. Nor is it required for anything: not for Ministry of Education equivalency, not for university admission, not for progression from Year 11 into DP1. Anyone implying otherwise has turned a school process into a sales argument.

On the people doing the teaching: private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit issued through MoHRE under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years, with school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18 all eligible. Tutoring without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no published schedule. IB Gram operates no centre, office or branch in the UAE and holds no regulator approval or accreditation of any kind.

process.title: Establish both ends of the transition
process.description: The first call records what the student finished - board, tier, grades by subject - and what they are entering: the six subjects, the three Higher Levels and the mathematics route. Bridging without both halves of that picture is guesswork.

process.title: Diagnose the assumed skills
process.description: A short diagnostic on the prerequisites the Diploma will not teach: algebraic fluency, stoichiometry, non-literary analysis, argument structure. The output is a named gap per subject rather than a general impression of readiness.

process.title: Check the route against published requirements
process.description: Intended degree directions are compared with the published entry requirements of the actual courses on the student's list, including whether a mathematics route is specified. This happens in Year 11 while the choice is still open.

process.title: Run the bridge before September
process.description: Six to ten sessions per affected subject across the summer, aimed only at the assumed skills. No new syllabus content, because the school will deliver that and the student cannot absorb it while a prerequisite is missing.

process.title: Hold a weekly slot through DP1
process.description: One hour per subject through the first Diploma year, splitting time between the week's content and the technique the course assumes: reasoning written out, criteria read when a task is set, scope settled early.

process.title: Review fortnightly on marked work
process.description: Every two weeks the plan is tested against something marked - a timed paper, a returned internal assessment draft, a mock script. Closed gaps come off the plan; new ones go on.

whyPoints.title: Fluent at both ends, not one
whyPoints.description: A bridging tutor has to know the specification the student has left and the one they are entering. That is a narrower qualification than subject expertise alone, and matching for it is only possible when geography is not also a filter.

whyPoints.title: The gap named per subject
whyPoints.description: Mathematics assumes algebraic automaticity; chemistry assumes stoichiometry; History assumes argument. Each gap is specific and separately closeable, which is why a transition map beats general advice about the IB being harder.

whyPoints.title: Choices checked while they are still open
whyPoints.description: Subject and level decisions are tested against the published entry requirements of the courses a student is actually considering, in Year 11, before the school's deadline. After the first weeks of DP1 most of those decisions are fixed.

whyPoints.title: Early bridging costs less than late rescue
whyPoints.description: Six to ten summer sessions on assumed skills against twenty to thirty across DP1 and DP2 closing the same gap while new content keeps arriving. The session counts are published here so a family can do the arithmetic themselves.

whyPoints.title: Opposite bridges for MYP and IGCSE entrants
whyPoints.description: An IGCSE student needs criteria and reflection; an MYP student needs timed technique and procedural fluency. A household with both gets two plans, because one approach would shortchange one of the children.

whyPoints.title: A format that survives Al Qudra Road
whyPoints.description: Sessions run over live video at a time after the commute rather than during it, so a long school run costs nothing and a late slot carries no premium. Nothing in the arrangement depends on a car arriving at a fixed hour.

faqs.question: Why does my child find DP1 so much harder than Year 11 at JESS Arabian Ranches?
faqs.answer: Four things change at once. Depth replaces breadth, so algebraic fluency becomes an assumption rather than a learning objective. Mark schemes start rewarding justification rather than correct answers with working shown. Six internally assessed components plus a 4,000-word extended essay and Theory of Knowledge arrive with deadlines months away and no weekly class. And the subject choice itself was made at sixteen. None of those is an ability problem, which is why a student working harder than ever can still be falling behind by late October.

faqs.question: When is the best time to start bridging work before the Diploma?
faqs.answer: The spring and summer of Year 11, once the examinations are finished. Six to ten sessions per affected subject across May to August, aimed only at the skills the Diploma assumes rather than at new content, is the cheapest effective intervention available. The alternative is a reactive rescue from November of DP1, which typically takes twenty to thirty sessions to close the same gap, because the gap blocks the new content and the new content hides the gap. Ask in April, not in late August.

faqs.question: Leaving Year 11 here, which IB maths route fits a student who disliked algebra?
faqs.answer: Two questions settle it. In IGCSE mathematics, were the algebra questions the comfortable ones or the ones they avoided? A student who enjoyed rearranging and factorising suits Analysis and Approaches; one who passed algebra by recognising question shapes does not. Second, does any course on their university list name a mathematics route explicitly? If so, the decision is made. Applications and Interpretation is not the lighter course - its statistics content is substantial - and Higher Level in either is demanding. Verify requirements on each university's own admissions page.

faqs.question: Can my child change Higher Level subjects after the Diploma starts?
faqs.answer: A level change between Higher and Standard is often possible in the first weeks of DP1, at the school's discretion. A subject change becomes difficult quickly and usually impossible after the first term, because the student would be joining a course already underway with an internal assessment timetable running. This is why the choice conversation belongs in Year 11 rather than in September. Ask your school's Diploma coordinator for the specific deadline that applies, because it varies between schools.

faqs.question: My child did the Middle Years Programme, not IGCSE. Is the gap different?
faqs.answer: It points the opposite way. An MYP entrant arrives fluent in assessment criteria, comfortable with reflection and used to extended investigation, and short on examination technique and procedural fluency - most visibly in mathematics, where lighter drilling shows. An IGCSE entrant arrives with examination instincts and broad content coverage and short on criteria literacy and reflection. Both gaps close in a summer if named in April. A household with one child from each route needs two different plans rather than one tutor applying one approach.

faqs.question: What should a DP1 student have finished by December?
faqs.answer: Five things, all of which take about an afternoon in total. An extended essay subject chosen with at least a candidate research question. All six internal assessment deadlines plus core checkpoints written on one page. The assessment criteria for every internally assessed component read once. At least one timed paper sat in each Higher Level subject. And a re-check that the mathematics route and Higher Level combination still match the intended degree direction. The internal assessment calendar is the highest-value item and most families have never seen it in one piece.

faqs.question: Do tutors come to villas in Arabian Ranches?
faqs.answer: Not through IB Gram. Lessons here are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video; home visits are a service we run only in India. In this community the policy matches the practical position unusually well. A tutor travelling out from Jumeirah or Al Barsha at five commits an hour each way for a sixty-minute lesson, and that appears in the rate - Bestimate's survey puts in-home tuition at AED 180 to 350, with independent home tutors at AED 200 to 500. The sharper issue is that bridging specialists rarely live within half an hour of the Ranches.

faqs.question: What is the earliest practical session time with a school run off Al Qudra Road?
faqs.answer: For most households here, 6.00pm or later on a school night. A child who leaves school at 3.00pm and reaches a villa in the outer Ranches at 4.15pm needs food before algebra, and a session starting at 4.30pm competes with that. Because delivery is online, a 6.30pm or 7.00pm slot carries no travel premium and no risk of a tutor stuck on the road while the hour runs. Families whose children attend school inside the community can start considerably earlier.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE subject gaps cause the most trouble at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: Algebraic fluency and stoichiometry, in that order. Mathematics Analysis and Approaches and Diploma Physics both assume that surds, indices, factorising and rearranging with symbols are automatic rather than effortful, and a student who pattern-matched through IGCSE Extended has nothing to pattern-match against. In Chemistry, moles work shifts from being a topic to being a tool used in energetics, equilibrium, kinetics and acids throughout the course, so shaky stoichiometry is a course-sized problem rather than a chapter-sized one.

faqs.question: Is the Diploma or A Level better for a student leaving Year 11 here?
faqs.answer: It depends on whether a direction is settled. A Level offers three or four subjects in considerable depth, often more content per subject in the sciences, with no core components and no second-language requirement. The Diploma offers six subjects plus the extended essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS, rewarding breadth and independent project management. A student certain about engineering or medicine often benefits from depth; one still deciding usually benefits from breadth. Families here commonly make the choice from a sibling's experience rather than the student's own direction, which is worth one proper conversation.

faqs.question: How many tutoring sessions does a Diploma year actually take?
faqs.answer: It is easier to budget by block than by hour. A summer bridge is six to ten sessions per affected subject. A route and choice consultation is one or two in total. Weekly support through DP1 is around twenty-five to thirty per subject. A reactive rescue started in November of DP1 runs twenty to thirty per subject and achieves less. Exam-year triage in DP2 is sixteen to twenty across the two weakest subjects. Dubai specialist market rates run AED 200 to 450 an hour per Bestimate's 2026 survey.

faqs.question: Does my child need a second language for the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Yes, the Diploma requires one, and this catches students who dropped languages after Year 9. Starting at ab initio level in DP1 is entirely viable with regular weekly contact and fails with occasional cramming, because language acquisition responds to frequency rather than to session length. If a language is going to be started from scratch, two short sessions a week beats one long one, and the commitment should be understood when the subject list is chosen rather than discovered in October.

faqs.question: Can one tutor bridge both mathematics and physics for the same student?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and in this specific case it is efficient rather than a compromise. The physics gap entering the Diploma is mathematical rather than conceptual: multi-step derivation, rearranging with symbols, reading graphs as relationships. A tutor working on algebraic fluency for Mathematics Analysis and Approaches is addressing most of the physics gap at the same time. For other combinations - chemistry and English A, say - separate specialists are the better arrangement because the gaps share nothing.

faqs.question: What can a tutor do with a Diploma internal assessment, and what not?
faqs.answer: A tutor may teach the content, explain what each assessment criterion rewards, discuss whether a research question is answerable within the limit, confirm a method will produce usable data, and give feedback on a draft the student has written themselves. A tutor may not supply wording for submission, restructure the argument into their own prose, or hand over an analysis to adapt. The school's supervisor signs an authenticity declaration. One page competing for these searches sells completed internal assessments, which is a malpractice exposure for the student rather than a service.

faqs.question: What happens if no bridging tutor is available for the summer we need?
faqs.answer: You are told, with a date, rather than given a subject tutor without transition experience. Demand for bridging work concentrates into May, June and July, and tutors fluent at both ends of a transition are a narrower pool than subject tutors generally. Asking in April usually secures a slot; asking in late August usually does not. Where a specialist genuinely is not free, we will say when one becomes available and what the alternative plan through DP1 would look like, so the choice stays with you.

dubai/arabian-ranches.closingHeading: Bridge it in the summer, not in November
dubai/arabian-ranches.closingBody: The useful conversation for an Arabian Ranches family happens in Year 11, not in DP1. Bring the IGCSE or MYP profile, the six subjects the student intends to take and the three Higher Levels, and a short diagnostic will show which assumed skills are already automatic and which are not. Where a gap exists it is usually two to six weeks of focused work, delivered one-to-one over live video at a time that fits the commute rather than fights it. Ask in April and the summer bridge is straightforward to staff; ask in late August and it may not be.

dubai/arabian-ranches-2.tutorsIntro: The tutors listed below work diagnostically: a timed paper, a mark against the published scheme, and then teaching aimed only at the marks that went missing. It is a different habit from working through a textbook, and it is what Arabian Ranches 2 families ask for most.

intro.heading: When the effort is real and the mark will not move
paragraphs: Arabian Ranches 2 is the second phase of the Ranches: villa clusters called Azalea, Camelia, Casa, Lila, Palma, Rasha, Reem, Rosa, Samara and Yasmin, sharing the souk and much of the school run with the original community. Households here are a few years younger on average, which means the dominant tutoring question is not the Diploma transition but something more immediate: why hard work is not converting into marks.

The sentence arrives in almost identical form from every cluster. The child revises. The teacher says they are engaged. The report says effort is good. The mark sits where it sat last term. Parents then reach for more of the same - more revision, more notes, another textbook - and the mark stays still, because the problem was never the quantity of revision.

In most cases the problem is one of four things, and all four are visible on a marked script. The student answered a different question from the one asked, because a command term was misread. They lost mechanical marks: units, working not shown, premature rounding, an unlabelled axis. They knew the content and could not sequence a multi-step answer under time pressure. Or they ran out of time because the first two questions took a third of the paper.

None of those is a knowledge gap, and that is why revision does not fix them. A student can know every fact in a syllabus and still lose fifteen marks on a paper to execution. Fifteen marks is frequently two grade boundaries. The useful intervention is not more content; it is somebody reading the script with the mark scheme open and naming the pattern.

The reason families rarely do this themselves is practical rather than a failure of will. Marking your own child's paper against a published scheme is slow, it invites argument about whether an answer should have scored, and the pattern only becomes visible across several papers rather than one. Most households try it once and abandon it. An external reader has no stake in whether the answer deserved the mark, which turns a fight into an observation.

The other thing worth saying about this community is that the schools are not the problem. Jumeirah English Speaking School Arabian Ranches, Ranches Primary School, Fairgreen International School, GEMS Metropole and Nord Anglia International School Dubai are all competent schools teaching full syllabuses to classes of twenty-odd. Marking one student's script line by line and tracking their personal error pattern across a term is simply not a thing a class teacher has the hours to do, and it is the single highest-yield hour available. A teacher with five classes and thirty books in each writes a grade and a short comment, and the comment almost never says that the student answered the wrong kind of question. That omission is structural, not negligent, and it is the gap this page is about.

dubai/arabian-ranches-2.programmesIntro: Three programmes run through this community, and what matters here is how each one reports a mark - because the report is what a family acts on, and two of the three report in a form most parents misread.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Assessment is almost entirely terminal written papers, reported as a grade with no breakdown a parent can see. The useful information lives in the school's own mock scripts and in class assessments, because those come back marked and annotated. Cambridge tiers several subjects into Core and Extended, which caps the available grade at Core; Pearson Edexcel generally runs one tier with Foundation and Higher in mathematics.
programmes.countryNote: A grade tells a family nothing about why. A marked mock script tells them whether the marks went on content, on command terms, on mechanics or on timing, and those four require completely different responses. Asking the school for the annotated script rather than only the grade is the first move, and most schools will hand it over without hesitation if asked.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects reported as grades 1 to 7, plus points from the extended essay and Theory of Knowledge. Each subject carries an internally assessed component marked against published criteria. Papers are returned marked within the school, so a DP1 student has genuine diagnostic material from the first term - the difficulty is that nobody treats a returned Paper 1 as data.
programmes.countryNote: The Diploma's internally assessed components come back with criterion-level feedback, which is the most actionable information in the whole programme and the least used. A criterion marked in the middle band with a two-line comment is a specific, closeable gap. Most students read the overall mark, feel the feeling, and file the paper.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject group, lettered A to D, each scored 1 to 8 on achievement levels rather than percentages. No terminal examination unless the school enters students for the optional MYP 5 eAssessment. Reports therefore show a profile of criterion scores, which is far more diagnostic than a single percentage if a parent knows how to read it.
programmes.countryNote: This is the most misread report in Dubai schooling. A criterion B score of 5 out of 8 is not 62% and does not convert to a percentage; it is a descriptor band with published wording. Reading the descriptor for level 7 or 8 in that criterion tells a parent exactly what the child is not yet doing. Families here routinely compare criterion scores between siblings as though they were grades, which they are not.

dubai/arabian-ranches-2.subjectsIntro: Below are the subjects Arabian Ranches 2 asks for, described by where their marks actually leak rather than by what the syllabus contains. The leak is usually narrower and more mechanical than families expect.

subjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics (0580 / 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Marks leak in four places: working not shown on multi-step questions so one slip costs everything, premature rounding carried through a calculation, bearings and transformations treated as optional, and time lost to the first long question. Each is drillable in a fortnight and none requires new content.

subjects.name: IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences (0654)
subjects.description: Three sciences in two papers, so breadth is wide and depth shallow - which rewards precision over insight. The standard losses are unit omissions, state symbols in equations, and describing an observation where an explanation was required. The alternative-to-practical paper is the most predictable component on the course and the least practised.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Stoichiometry errors propagate: a wrong mole ratio costs every mark downstream. Significant figures and uncertainty handling are mechanical marks that disappear through habit. At Diploma level the scientific investigation's evaluation criterion is where a whole criterion goes missing, because students report what happened instead of what limited the method.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The commonest loss is skipping the diagram a question implies, followed by unit handling and by rearranging an equation numerically instead of symbolically. Multi-step derivations under time pressure are a sequencing problem, not a knowledge one, and respond to being written out slowly a dozen times.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Almost all avoidable loss here is command terms. Explain answered as describe, compare answered as two separate descriptions, suggest answered as a guess without reasoning. Data questions on unfamiliar experiments reward practice on past papers rather than another pass through the notes.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Reasoning that is correct but unjustified is the single biggest leak, because Diploma schemes award method and justification separately. Students who write the answer and omit the line that explains why the method applies lose marks they had already earned mentally. Paper 3 at Higher Level punishes unpractised extended problems.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Calculator-dependent working loses marks when the calculator output is reported without the model that produced it. Statistical questions lose marks on interpretation rather than computation: a correlation calculated and not explained earns part marks. The exploration needs a real dataset and a defensible method.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Case-study detail is the mark-earner and the first thing to be forgotten: named places, figures and dates. Students who write generic answers about coastal erosion where a named example was required lose a consistent band of marks on every paper. The fieldwork report fails on method design rather than on writing.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams carry marks independently of the prose, and an undrawn or unlabelled diagram loses them silently. Evaluation questions lose marks when a judgement is asserted without the trade-off being named. The internal assessment commentaries lose marks when the article is summarised rather than a named theory applied to it.

subjects.name: English A and IGCSE English Language
subjects.description: Paraphrase instead of analysis is the standard loss: saying what a text does rather than how its choices produce an effect. Directed-writing tasks lose marks on audience and register rather than on content. At Diploma level the individual oral loses marks when a theme is presented where a global issue was required.

sections.heading: The six mechanical errors that quietly cost a grade
paragraphs: Mechanical errors are the ones that have nothing to do with understanding. A student who knows the physics perfectly still loses the mark if the unit is missing. These errors are boring, they are entirely fixable, and together they routinely account for a grade boundary across a paper. No competing page in this search mentions a single one of them, which is odd given that they are the cheapest marks in the system to recover.

The reason they persist is that nobody counts them. A returned paper shows a total, and a total does not distinguish between ten marks lost to not understanding electromagnetic induction and ten marks lost to dropped units and unlabelled axes. The first requires six weeks of teaching. The second requires a fortnight of nagging and a checklist. Treating them the same wastes the six weeks.

The fix is mechanical in the same way the error is. For each error class, the student writes out the correct habit ten times on real past-paper questions, with somebody checking. Units appended every time. Working written for every multi-step calculation, even the easy ones. Full values carried through a calculation and rounded only at the end. Axes labelled with quantity and unit before a single point is plotted. It is not interesting work and it moves marks faster than anything else available.

There is one caution. Drilling mechanics on a student whose actual problem is content produces a tidy script with the wrong answers in it. That is why the diagnostic comes first: count the lost marks by cause, then decide where the time goes. A student losing twenty marks to content and four to mechanics should not be spending a month on units.

sections.heading: Command terms decoded, with what students write instead
paragraphs: A command term is the instruction word that tells the student what shape the answer must take. Misreading one does not lose a mark; it loses the question. A student who writes a full, accurate description where an explanation was demanded can score one mark out of four while believing they answered well, and the pattern repeats on every paper until somebody names it.

The reason this is so persistent is that ordinary homework does not flag it. A teacher marking thirty books writes a grade and a comment; the comment rarely says that the student answered the wrong kind of question. Across a term the student receives the feedback that their answers are too short, responds by writing more description, and the marks stay where they were.

Naming the pattern takes one session with a marked script. Count the questions where the command term asked for causation and the answer gave observation. In a typical science mock that count is between three and eight questions, worth anywhere from six to twenty marks. Once a student has seen their own script annotated that way, the correction tends to hold, because the error is no longer abstract.

The drill afterwards is short and specific: take ten past-paper questions, write only the first sentence of each answer, and check that the first sentence does what the command term asked. Explanations start with because or by. Comparisons address both items against the same criterion. Evaluations state a judgement. Suggestions give a reason. Ten first sentences takes fifteen minutes and teaches more than an hour of full answers.

sections.heading: How to read a marked script with your child in thirty minutes
paragraphs: This is a method a parent in Arabian Ranches 2 can run without a tutor, and it is worth publishing because it costs nothing and most families have never been shown it. It needs the marked script, the published mark scheme for that paper, a pen in a different colour and half an hour of nobody being defensive.

Go question by question. For each lost mark, write a single letter in the margin: C for content the student did not know, T for a command term misread, M for a mechanical loss, S for a sequencing failure on a multi-step answer, and X for a question not attempted because time ran out. Do not discuss whether the mark was fair. Just classify. The classification is the entire output.

At the end, count the letters. The distribution tells you what to do next, and it is almost always lopsided in a way the total mark concealed. Twelve Ms and three Cs means a fortnight of drills, not a term of teaching. Nine Ts means one session on command terms and then a different student. Four Xs clustered at the end means a timing strategy: which questions to attempt first and when to abandon one and move on.

The rule that makes it survivable is no arguing about fairness. The moment the conversation becomes about whether an answer deserved the mark, the exercise stops being diagnostic and becomes a dispute, and that is why most households give up after one attempt. The mark scheme is the authority, the letters are the data, and the child's job is only to classify honestly. Doing this after each mock across two years is worth more than any amount of generic revision advice.

sections.heading: Timing: the loss that looks like weakness and is not
paragraphs: A student who leaves the last two questions blank has not demonstrated what they know. Yet the mark records it as ignorance, and the family responds by teaching the topics those questions covered, which does nothing at all because the student could already answer them. Timing is the most commonly misdiagnosed loss in examinations and the easiest to correct once identified.

The usual cause is over-investment early. A student meets a four-mark question that interests them, writes a nine-mark answer, and never recovers the eleven minutes. Compounded three times in a paper, that is the last page. The second cause is refusing to abandon a question that is not working, which is a psychological habit rather than an academic one and responds to being practised deliberately.

The drill has three parts. First, a marks-per-minute budget: total marks divided by total minutes, written at the top of the paper, with a checkpoint at the halfway page. Second, permission to abandon: if ninety seconds pass without progress, mark the question, move on, return at the end. Third, a deliberate order - attempt the questions that pay fastest first rather than working strictly front to back, where the specification allows it.

Practising this requires timed conditions, which is the part families skip. An untimed past paper measures knowledge and teaches nothing about timing; it can even entrench the problem by rewarding the student's instinct to write exhaustively. One properly timed paper a week, with the clock enforced, is worth three untimed ones for a student whose diagnosis shows Xs at the end of the script.

sections.heading: What diagnostic-led tutoring costs in this market
paragraphs: Diagnostic work has an unusual cost profile, and it is worth laying out because it is cheaper than families assume. A single diagnostic session on existing scripts is one hour. A command-term correction is typically one to two sessions. A mechanical-error drill is a fortnight of short tasks with two sessions of checking. Those three together often account for most of the available improvement, and they total under five hours.

The Dubai market, in dirhams and attributed to whoever published the figure: EdFlik advertises online tuition from AED 45 to 65 an hour; Tutopiya from around AED 33 to 52; Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200; TutorChase publishes AED 270; Bestimate's 2026 Dubai survey puts specialist IB, IGCSE and A Level tuition at AED 200 to 450 and above; BartyED publishes AED 650 as a premium rate. In-home one-to-one sits at AED 180 to 350 in Bestimate's survey and AED 200 to 500 among independent home tutors, with travel priced in.

Those figures are the market rather than IB Gram's list. What this page adds is the number of hours each job takes, because an hourly rate without a session count tells a family nothing about what the year costs. A diagnostic plus a command-term correction plus a mechanical drill is four to five hours. A twelve-week timed-paper cycle is twelve. A genuine content gap in one subject is fifteen to twenty-five.

Ask two questions of anyone quoting. Is the rate per hour or per lesson - a 45-minute lesson at an hourly-sounding figure is around a third more per contact hour. And is VAT included? IB Gram publishes no price list here; a rate follows a free consultation and a trial session, quoted against the actual subject, level and session length.

sections.heading: Why a marked script works better on a shared screen
paragraphs: IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. For diagnostic work that happens to be an advantage rather than a constraint, and the reason is specific to what this kind of session actually involves.

A diagnostic session is three documents in use at once: the student's script, the published mark scheme and a running tally of error classes. On a shared screen all three sit side by side, the tutor's cursor points at the exact line that lost the mark, and the annotated version is saved and sent afterwards. Across a table it is three paper documents, one pen and nothing retained. The student revising in March has no record of what the February diagnosis said.

Recording matters more here than in content teaching. The whole value of a diagnostic is the pattern, and a pattern is only visible across several sittings. Three recorded diagnostics across a year, with the error counts written down each time, show whether the mechanical losses are actually falling. A verbal conversation in a living room produces a feeling of progress and no evidence of it.

The pool argument applies as usual. A tutor who marks diagnostically against published schemes, by cause rather than by topic, is a particular habit rather than a general qualification, and the number of people with it inside half an hour of Arabian Ranches 2 is small. Over video the half hour is irrelevant. The honest exception remains a young child who needs an adult physically beside them, which is a different job from reading a script.
