faqs.question: My child speaks Arabic fluently at home. Why is their 0508 mark only a C?
faqs.answer: Because 0508 does not assess fluency. It assesses close reading of a passage the student has not seen before and the production of formal written Modern Standard Arabic shaped to a task. A fluent speaker understands the passage completely and then answers from general understanding rather than from the text, which loses marks on inference, summary and language commentary. In writing, the same student drifts from formal Arabic into spoken constructions partway through a composition, and control of register is explicitly what is being marked. Both problems are technique rather than language, and both respond to marked practice within a term.

faqs.question: Which Cambridge Arabic syllabus should my child be entered for, 0508 or 0544?
faqs.answer: 0508 is Arabic as a First Language and assumes the student reads and writes Arabic as a first language; 0544 is Arabic as a Foreign Language and assumes they are learning it. They are different assessments, not two difficulty levels. Dubai schools place students by heritage and their own assessment, following KHDA's requirement that Arab and non-Arab groups be taught separately. The hard cases are Arab children schooled entirely in English who speak dialect at home. Settle it with a marked piece of writing and an unseen passage, not a conversation, and raise any change with the school before the entry deadline.

faqs.question: What does the 0508 summary question actually reward?
faqs.answer: Selection, not expression. The question sets a focus; marks come from identifying the material in the passage relevant to that focus, reorganising it, and writing it in the student's own words within the length allowed. Fluent speakers lose marks here more than anyone, because they rewrite the passage elegantly instead of selecting from it, which scores on style rather than on content points. The procedure is teachable: mark only on-focus material, group what is marked, then write continuously without commentary or examples of your own. It is the single most recoverable block of marks on the reading paper.

faqs.question: Is 0508 marked in Modern Standard Arabic, or is dialect accepted?
faqs.answer: The written components expect Modern Standard Arabic, with register controlled to the task set. Dialect constructions in a formal letter or article read as a register error, and control of register is part of what the writing criteria assess. This is the most common source of lost marks in Dubai scripts, because students here code-switch between English, dialect and a messaging register all day and almost nothing in their week requires sustained formal Arabic. The practical fix is a running register sheet of the spoken construction, the Standard Arabic equivalent, and where each belongs, built over a term.

faqs.question: Does a 0508 grade count towards the five subjects the Ministry of Education requires?
faqs.answer: No. For equivalency on the British track, students must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one Advanced Level subject at E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five. Count your five excluding them. The grade still matters for the certificate, for continuation to A Level Arabic or IB Arabic A, and in the region generally. Equivalency is run by the Ministry, not by any tutoring service, so verify the current rule on its own channel.

faqs.question: Can a non-Arab student in Dubai sit 0508 rather than 0544?
faqs.answer: It happens, and it depends on reading ability rather than on heritage. A non-Arab student raised in Dubai who reads Modern Standard Arabic confidently may be better served by 0508 than by a learner syllabus that under-stretches them. The constraint is the school: KHDA requires separate Arabic classes for Arabs and non-Arabs because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ, and the stream a student sits in usually drives the Cambridge entry. Ask the school for an assessed piece of unseen reading and a written task, then discuss the entry in writing well before the deadline.

faqs.question: Who is permitted to teach Arabic in a Dubai private school?
faqs.answer: KHDA requires schools to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. That is a requirement on schools and their staff, and it is not a credential a private tutor holds, so no tutoring service should present itself as carrying it. What it gives a parent is a reasonable question to ask any Arabic tutor: what is your qualification, which syllabus have you taught to examination, and have you marked against the Cambridge criteria. Separately, private tutors in the UAE need the MoHRE private tuition work permit, which is free and valid for two years.

faqs.question: Our school teaches Arab and non-Arab students in the same Arabic class. Is that permitted?
faqs.answer: KHDA's mandatory-subjects guidance states that for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. If that is not what your child's timetable looks like, the place to raise it is with the school's leadership, in writing, referring to the published guidance. It is a school compliance question rather than something a tutor can resolve, though the practical consequence, a class pitched at the wrong level, is something tutoring can mitigate.

faqs.question: How many hours of 0508 tutoring does a Year 11 student usually need?
faqs.answer: It depends on which repair is needed, which is why the first session is a diagnosis. Patterns we see: summary technique and language commentary are concentrated repairs of four to six sessions; register control in writing takes a term of corrected pieces; reading speed in Modern Standard Arabic improves over months and cannot be compressed. A student arriving twelve weeks before the papers should spend them on summary, commentary and timing. A student starting in Year 10 with weekly sessions gets the reading stamina built, which is the cheapest route to the grade and the least popular one to buy.

faqs.question: Does 0508 prepare a student for IB Arabic A or A Level Arabic?
faqs.answer: It is the right foundation and not a complete one. Both continuations assume secure formal Arabic and analytical writing, which 0508 builds. The shape of the assessment is what changes. IB Arabic A examines oral components and extended written work in ways 0508 does not touch at all, and AS and A Level Arabic pushes further into literary analysis. Students moving from a British-curriculum school into an IB Diploma sixth form in Dubai should expect the oral assessment to be the new demand. Check availability early: fewer Dubai centres offer A Level Arabic than offer 0508.

faqs.question: How do we practise 0508 handwriting and accuracy in an online lesson?
faqs.answer: Answers are written by hand on paper, photographed and submitted for marking, which is how the examination itself works. A student who practises only on a phone or laptop keyboard writes slower and less accurately on the day than their knowledge deserves, and in Arabic script letter forms and diacritical precision matter. Accuracy work is then driven by the student's own marked script rather than by a textbook list: a marked piece typically shows four recurring errors, and those four are the lesson. The unseen passage itself is shared on screen and annotated live by both tutor and student.

faqs.question: What does a Cambridge 0508 tutor cost per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Market rates collected in October 2026 put qualified online subject tutors at roughly AED 150-300 an hour and examination-year specialists at AED 200-450 or more, with in-home one-to-one at AED 180-350 per Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table. Arabic first-language specialists who mark against the Cambridge criteria sit in the upper half, because the overlap between fluent Arabic teachers and tutors who know the 0508 bands is smaller than parents expect. Those are market figures rather than IB Gram's price list; ours is a free trial lesson followed by a written plan with the total stated.

faqs.question: Can a tutor correct my child's 0508 composition drafts?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear boundary. A tutor may mark a composition against the published criteria, explain which band it sits in, point to a sentence where register slipped, model an alternative construction and set a rewrite the student does themselves. A tutor may not supply sentences to transcribe or rewrite a piece into something the student could not have produced. The safe and more effective pattern is correction by category: name the error type, say how many more are in the piece, and let the student find them. That is also the only version that improves the next unseen task.

faqs.question: How does Ramadan affect a 0508 revision plan in Dubai?
faqs.answer: School days shorten and household rhythms change, and Ramadan often falls in the stretch when timed writing practice should be intensifying. The workable adjustment is shorter sessions moved earlier in the afternoon or to after Iftar, planned in advance rather than improvised. Forty-five focused minutes is worth more than ninety minutes nobody is present for. For a language subject the particular risk is that reading practice lapses for a month, so we keep one short unseen passage a week going even when the writing load is reduced. The plan says which weeks are light before the month begins.

faqs.question: What if no Cambridge 0508 specialist is free in our evening slot?
faqs.answer: We say so rather than substituting quietly. The honest options are a different time slot, a weekend morning, or a wait of a week or two for the right tutor. Where a family cannot move the slot, we will say what the alternative is and what it is weaker at, so the choice is theirs with the trade-off visible. What we will not do is place a general Arabic teacher on a 0508 plan and describe them as a specialist. Evening slots between 7pm and 9pm are the most contested in Dubai, so booking a fixed slot early in the term is worth more than negotiating the rate.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-arabic-first-langu.closingHeading: Send one piece of written Arabic
dubai/cambridge-igcse-arabic-first-langu.closingBody: The fastest way to know what your child needs for Cambridge IGCSE Arabic as a First Language is not a conversation about how well they speak. It is one piece of their written Arabic and one unseen passage worked through with a tutor who marks against the 0508 criteria. Book the free trial lesson, send the written piece in advance, and you will get back a specific answer: whether the loss is in selection, in commentary, in register or in timing, and roughly how many sessions that repair takes. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, built around your child's centre and the series they are entered for.

intro.heading: What Arabic 0544 support in Dubai really costs, before anyone quotes you
paragraphs: Ask five providers in Dubai what an Arabic tutor costs and you will get five numbers with no shared unit behind them. One quotes a bare sixty minutes of conversation. One includes a marked writing task and a pronunciation log. One prices a car journey into the hour without saying so. The spread in the market runs from roughly AED 45 at the budget online end to AED 650 for a premium named tutor, and the only way to compare quotes honestly is to force every provider to state what the hour contains. That is the job this page does for Cambridge IGCSE Arabic (Foreign Language) 0544 specifically, because Arabic prices differently from every other language on a Dubai timetable.

The reason is supply. French and Spanish teaching in Dubai draws on a large pool of European-trained graduates who arrived for other reasons. Arabic teaching draws on a much narrower pool, and the strongest candidates are already employed by schools. KHDA requires schools to ensure that every teacher of Arabic and Islamic Education holds appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects, which concentrates the qualified people inside school payrolls rather than on the open tutoring market. The result is a seller's market for genuine 0544 expertise and a crowded market for conversational Arabic that will not move a Cambridge grade.

There is a second cost nobody prints. The Arabic teaching pool in Dubai is clustered towards Deira, Al Nahda, Bur Dubai and Al Mamzar. The families searching hardest for 0544 support live in Dubai Hills Estate, Arabian Ranches, Mudon, Dubai Marina and Jumeirah. A 17:00 start in Arabian Ranches means a tutor leaving Deira at 16:00 and arriving home around 19:30 for one taught hour. Somebody pays for those ninety minutes of driving, and it is not the tutor. In-home rates in the Bestimate 2026 Dubai survey run AED 180 to 350, with independent home tutors quoting 200 to 500, and travel is the single largest reason those numbers sit above the online bands.

IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai, and home tutoring at a UAE address is not a service we sell anywhere in the Emirates. Lessons run one to one over live video, screen shared, with the student's own script on the shared document. For Arabic that is not a compromise. Right-to-left typing, vowel marks, hamza placement and the shape-changing of letters in initial, medial and final position are all easier to demonstrate on a screen a tutor can annotate than on a notebook across a kitchen table. The practical gain is the pool: a Mudon family gets a 0544 specialist rather than whoever is willing to drive to Mudon.

The last piece of the budget is the part most families discover too late. Arabic and Islamic Education are excluded from the five accredited subjects the UAE Ministry of Education counts for British-track equivalency. A 0544 grade is still a Cambridge grade, still mandatory school content under KHDA rules, and still useful on a university application, but it does not fill one of the five slots. Knowing that changes how much a family should sensibly spend on 0544 relative to Mathematics 0580 or English First Language 0500, and no competitor page in this market says it.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-arabic-foreign-lan.programmesIntro: Arabic support in a Dubai school runs from Foundation Stage to Year 13 under KHDA's mandatory-subject rules, and the Cambridge route through it has several entry points. These are the four stages families book most often, with the money question attached to each.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE Arabic (Foreign Language)
programmes.description: The syllabus built for learners studying Arabic as a foreign language rather than as a mother tongue. Listening, reading, speaking and writing are assessed as separate components; confirm the weighting split and timings for your child's exam year on cambridgeinternational.org, because Cambridge revises these by cohort. Most briefs we see run eighteen to thirty taught hours across two years.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai this is the course most non-Arab students on a British curriculum are entered for, after years of in-school Arabic as an additional language. The common pattern is a child with reasonable spoken confidence and almost no unvowelled reading fluency, which is an expensive gap to close in Year 11 and a cheap one to close in Year 9.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE Arabic (First Language)
programmes.description: The mother-tongue syllabus, aimed at students educated partly in Arabic. Text difficulty, writing length and the register expected in composition all sit well above 0544. Briefs here are usually shorter in hours but higher in rate, because the teacher has to be a trained first-language Arabic specialist rather than a strong additional-language teacher.
programmes.countryNote: KHDA requires schools to organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited. A Dubai family that has quietly been placed in the wrong stream usually finds out in a Year 10 mock, and the correction costs a term.

programmes.name: Cambridge Lower Secondary and Key Stage 3 Arabic
programmes.description: The years when reading unvowelled text either becomes automatic or never does. Support at this stage is cheaper per hour and far cheaper per mark eventually gained, because the work is script fluency and core verb patterns rather than exam triage. Fortnightly sessions are usually enough.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools deliver mandatory Arabic on a timetable KHDA calculates in forty-minute lesson units, and advise that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least twenty-five minutes. In a crowded Year 8 timetable that is not much contact time for a language with a new alphabet, which is why Year 7 to 9 support is the best value in the whole Arabic budget.

programmes.name: KHDA mandatory Arabic strand
programmes.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum. This is the strand a family cannot opt out of, and the one that produces the report-card grade parents react to long before any Cambridge entry is made.
programmes.countryNote: KHDA states that for mandatory UAE subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited. A tutor therefore works on the school's own material and on Cambridge 0544 skills, and does not substitute an alternative curriculum of their own.

sections.heading: What a Cambridge IGCSE Arabic 0544 tutor costs in Dubai, by provider model
paragraphs: Arabic tuition in Dubai costs between roughly AED 45 and AED 650 per sixty minutes depending entirely on which kind of provider you approach. The low end is a university student teaching conversationally online. The high end is a named individual with a long teaching record and a waiting list. Neither number is wrong, and neither tells you anything useful on its own, because the two are not selling the same product.

Every figure in the table below was published by the provider named beside it and read in October 2026. None of them is an IB Gram price. We do not publish a rate card on these pages because the honest answer depends on the subject, the level and how many sessions a brief actually needs, and a family deserves that conversation rather than a number designed to win a click. What we will do is show the market we operate inside, with its sources, so a quote can be judged against something.

Read the table across rather than down. A rate of AED 150 that includes a marked writing task, a written session note and a pronunciation log is cheaper in real terms than AED 120 for sixty minutes of unrecorded conversation, because the second one leaves no evidence behind and no way to tell whether it worked. The questions that collapse the price range quickly are these: what gets marked, who marks it, what arrives in writing afterwards, and is travel inside or outside the number.

sections.heading: The seven things that move an Arabic quote up or down in this emirate
paragraphs: The spread in the table is not randomness. Seven specific variables account for almost all of it in Dubai, and six of them are inside a family's control. Knowing which lever you are pulling stops a negotiation turning into a guess.

The first and largest is whether the tutor is a trained Arabic teacher or a fluent speaker. Fluency is not teaching. A speaker can correct a sentence; a teacher can tell you that your child is losing marks because non-human plurals take feminine singular agreement and nobody ever taught them the rule. The second is syllabus specificity: a teacher who has marked 0544 writing tasks against Cambridge criteria prices above one who has not, and is worth it. The third is whether the hour includes marking. Marking is unpaid work for a tutor unless it is in the rate, and the tutors who do it properly build it in.

The fourth is travel, which is the whole reason the in-home band sits above the online band. The fifth is timing: evening slots between 16:30 and 19:30 on school nights are the scarcest commodity in Dubai tutoring, and Arabic specialists fill them first. The sixth is session length, because many providers quote a price for a session rather than for an hour, and a ninety-minute session at AED 250 is a different trade from a sixty-minute one. The seventh is commitment, where a booked block of ten sessions usually buys a better slot rather than a better price, which is the more valuable concession in this market.

sections.heading: Travel, priced as the line item it actually is
paragraphs: In-home Arabic tuition in Dubai is a transport product as much as a teaching one. The qualified Arabic teaching pool is concentrated in the older northern districts, and demand is concentrated in the newer southern and inland communities. Every booking that crosses that gap converts roughly sixty to ninety minutes of a tutor's evening into driving, and that time is paid for whether or not it appears on the invoice.

IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai; lessons are delivered one to one over live video, and in-home tutoring at a UAE address is not something we sell in any emirate. We publish the drive times anyway, because a family comparing our model against a local in-home quote should be comparing real numbers rather than a slogan. If an in-home tutor near your community is genuinely a 0544 specialist and the travel is short, that is a reasonable choice and you should make it with the figures in front of you.

What changes with live video is not the quality of the hour but the size of the pool you are choosing from. A family in Mudon selecting an in-home tutor is choosing from the people willing to drive to Mudon on a Tuesday at 17:00. The same family online is choosing from every 0544 specialist available in that slot. For a subject with thin qualified supply, that difference is worth more than any discount, and it is the one advantage no amount of local driving can buy back.

sections.heading: Arabic 0544 or Arabic 0508: the most expensive mistake in Dubai
paragraphs: The costliest error in Arabic tuition in this city is not overpaying for an hour. It is paying for the wrong syllabus for a year. Cambridge runs Arabic as a foreign language under code 0544 and Arabic as a first language under 0508, and they are different qualifications aimed at different students, with different text difficulty and different writing expectations.

Dubai makes this harder than it needs to be, because many households are partly Arabic-speaking. A child who speaks Levantine or Egyptian Arabic at home and has never written Modern Standard Arabic to a literary register is not automatically a first-language candidate. A child educated in Arabic until Year 6 and in English since is not automatically a foreign-language candidate either. KHDA requires schools to run separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and prohibits combining the two groups, which means the school has already made a streaming decision about your child whether or not anyone discussed it with you.

Two paid diagnostic sessions resolve this cheaply: one unvowelled reading task at each level, one short composition at each level, marked against the relevant criteria. Families who do that in Year 9 spend a small amount to settle a two-year question. Families who discover it in a Year 11 mock spend a great deal more, and sometimes cannot fix it at all before the entry deadline. sections.heading: KHDA's mandatory Arabic rules, and what they do to the price of a tutor
paragraphs: Arabic is not optional in a Dubai private school. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of which international curriculum the school is licensed to teach, and KHDA set a deadline of the start of the 2025-26 academic year for its requirements to be implemented, with April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. Every family on a British curriculum in this city is therefore buying Arabic teaching whether they planned to or not.

The rules go further than attendance. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic must be the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language; Social Studies is delivered in Arabic for Arab students; non-Arab students receive Islamic Education and moral, social and cultural studies in the language of the school's licensed curriculum. Instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and KHDA advises that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least twenty-five minutes.

Two consequences follow for a tutoring budget. First, the qualified people are inside schools, because schools must ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. That is why genuine Arabic expertise prices above French in the same city. Second, for the mandatory subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited, so a tutor works on the school's own material and on Cambridge 0544 skills rather than importing a parallel syllabus. Any provider offering you their own Arabic curriculum for the mandatory strand has not read the guidance.

sections.heading: Why a 0544 grade does not fill one of the Ministry's five subjects
paragraphs: For UAE Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects.

That single line reorders a tutoring budget. If a family has limited money and a child sitting eight IGCSEs, the subjects that carry equivalency weight have a stronger claim on it than Arabic does. One competitor page currently ranking in this market states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects; the sourced rule is five, excluding Arabic and Islamic Education, and getting that right is worth more to a family than any discount.

None of which makes 0544 unimportant. It is a Cambridge grade on the certificate, it is the subject the school reports on every term, it is a genuine advantage for a child who will live and work in this region, and for students continuing to AS or A Level Arabic it is the foundation. The point is sequencing. Spend on the subjects that gate the equivalency file first, spend on Arabic early rather than late because script fluency is cheap to build at thirteen and expensive at sixteen, and verify your own equivalency position on moe.gov.ae rather than on any tutoring company's page, including this one. Equivalency is a Ministry process. IB Gram describes it and does not perform it.

sections.heading: Budgeting Years 10 and 11 against the Cambridge series
paragraphs: Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level exams in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. The deadlines that matter to a family's spending plan sit months before the papers. Cambridge's published key dates for the March 2027 series put the exam period from 3 February to 4 March 2027, with final entries due 27 November 2026, forecast grades due 27 February 2027, results on Direct on 13 May and certificates in late June. The pattern holds across series: the entry decision is made a full quarter before the exam.

Every Cambridge centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong zone timetable. Ask your school's exams officer which zone your centre sits in and work from that timetable, not from a date on a blog.

The budgeting consequence is simple and almost nobody acts on it. Arabic specialist capacity in Dubai is thin, and the weeks before a series are exactly when every family wants it. A block booked in the term before a series costs the same per hour as a block booked at the last minute, but the last-minute block frequently does not exist. Counting backwards from the entry deadline rather than forwards from today is the cheapest planning decision in this whole page, and it costs nothing.

sections.heading: Is the tutor you are paying legally permitted to teach in Dubai?
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is permitted work, not unregulated work. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 on private tuition work permits. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. The official route is MoHRE's own service, Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system, listing no fees and a two-working-day completion time.

Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so no amount is quoted here; a figure circulating online could not be verified against any ministry source. A separate regime applies to anyone running a tutoring operation with premises and staff in Dubai, which requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, with initial approval first and renewal requested ahead of expiry. IB Gram holds no such permit and makes no claim to one, because it operates no premises in the UAE.

A reported ethics point matters for Dubai families too. Press reporting on Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules describes school staff being barred from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and notes that the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Verify the current policy wording with the relevant authority before relying on it, and treat any offer of your child's own class teacher privately as a question to ask the school rather than a bargain to accept.

sections.heading: Four ways Dubai families overspend on Arabic support
paragraphs: The first is paying for conversation when the problem is script. A child who chats comfortably and freezes on an unvowelled reading passage does not need more talking; they need timed decoding practice, three short sessions a week rather than one long one, and a written record of every word that cost them time. Families often buy twenty hours of pleasant conversation before anyone diagnoses this, and the money is simply gone.

The second is starting in Year 11. Arabic rewards early, cheap, frequent contact more than almost any other IGCSE subject, because the limiting skill is automaticity rather than content knowledge. Thirty minutes twice a week in Year 8 costs a fraction of the crisis block in the term before a series, and works far better. The third is buying an unexamined bundle. A monthly package of eight online sessions at AED 799 is a real market offer and may be excellent value, but only if the sessions are one to one, with marking, at a slot that exists. Count the hours, check the format, and ask what happens to unused sessions.

The fourth is spending on Arabic before spending on the subjects that gate the Ministry's equivalency file. This is not an argument against Arabic tuition; it is an argument for sequencing. If a family can afford one subject this term and the child is a grade 4 in Mathematics 0580 and a grade 6 in Arabic 0544, the money goes to maths, and the Arabic plan becomes a cheap fortnightly reading clinic that keeps the skill moving. Deciding that deliberately rather than by default is how a Dubai tutoring budget stops leaking.

whyPoints.title: No regulator is presented as an endorser
whyPoints.description: KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoHRE and the Ministry of Education are described here because their rules affect your decisions. None of them approves, licenses or endorses IB Gram, and any tutoring company implying otherwise is making a claim worth checking.

faqs.question: How much does a Cambridge IGCSE Arabic 0544 tutor cost per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: The Dubai market for language tutoring runs from about AED 45 to AED 650 per sixty minutes. Budget online tutors published rates from AED 45 to 65; qualified subject teachers online sit around AED 150 to 300; in-home visits run AED 180 to 500 once travel is priced in; IGCSE and IB specialists AED 200 to 450 and above; a premium named tutor has been published at AED 650. Arabic generally sits in the upper half of whichever band you are comparing, because qualified supply is thinner than for French or Spanish. Those are market figures read in October 2026, not an IB Gram price list.

faqs.question: Why is Arabic 0544 tuition in Dubai priced above French or Spanish?
faqs.answer: Supply. French and Spanish teaching in Dubai draws on a deep pool of European-trained graduates who came to the city for other reasons. Arabic draws on a narrower pool, and KHDA requires schools to ensure every teacher of Arabic and Islamic Education holds appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects, which keeps the strongest candidates on school payrolls rather than in the open market. The effect is a shortage of genuine 0544 teaching expertise alongside an abundance of conversational Arabic. If an Arabic quote is not meaningfully above a French one from the same provider, ask precisely what the Arabic teaching qualification is.

faqs.question: Does my child need Arabic 0544 or Arabic First Language 0508?
faqs.answer: It depends on reading and writing, not on what is spoken at home. 0544 is built for learners studying Arabic as an additional language; 0508 assumes an education partly delivered through Arabic, with longer authentic texts and extended composition judged on register. A child who speaks a dialect fluently but has never written Modern Standard Arabic to a literary standard is usually a 0544 candidate. KHDA requires Dubai schools to stream Arab and non-Arab groups into separate classes for first-language Arabic, so your school has already decided. Two diagnostic sessions, one reading task and one composition at each level, settle it cheaply.

faqs.question: Does a Cambridge 0544 grade count towards UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: No. For the British track the Ministry requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, plus one Advanced Level subject at no less than E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five. Your 0544 grade still appears on the Cambridge certificate and still counts for school reporting and university applications. It simply does not fill one of the five slots. Verify your own position on moe.gov.ae, because equivalency is a Ministry process that no tutoring company performs.

faqs.question: Do you send an Arabic tutor to our villa in Dubai for 0544 lessons?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not arrange home visits anywhere in the UAE, and in-home tutoring at a Dubai address is not a service we sell. Every 0544 session runs one to one over live video, screen shared, on Gulf Standard Time. For Arabic that works in your favour: vowel marks, hamza placement and the way letters change shape in initial, medial and final position are easier to demonstrate on an annotated screen than in a notebook. The bigger gain is choice. Online, a family in Mudon picks from every available specialist rather than from the people willing to drive to Mudon.

faqs.question: How many 0544 sessions will my child actually need before the exam?
faqs.answer: A typical two-year brief we see runs eighteen to thirty taught hours, front-loaded onto reading fluency rather than spread evenly. A child whose only real gap is unvowelled reading speed may need twelve short sessions and nothing else. A child entered for the wrong syllabus needs a streaming decision before anyone counts hours at all. Ask any provider for a total-hours estimate as well as an hourly rate, because the total is what decides affordability. A brief at AED 220 for fifteen hours costs less than one at AED 150 for thirty, and the first one finishes sooner.

faqs.question: Does the quoted 0544 rate include marking, resources and VAT?
faqs.answer: Ask, every time, because the answer varies enormously across this market. Marking written Arabic against Cambridge criteria takes a tutor real time, and tutors who do it properly build it into the rate while others treat it as unpaid extra. Resources are a separate question: Cambridge, IB and Pearson syllabus documents, past papers and mark schemes should be referenced and linked from the official sites, never reproduced or supplied as downloads. On tax, insist only that a provider states clearly whether its own quoted AED figure includes VAT, and do not accept a general claim about how UAE VAT treats tuition without a Federal Tax Authority citation.

faqs.question: Is a 0544 Arabic tutor required to hold the MoHRE private tuition permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tuition in the UAE runs on a work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Applications go through MoHRE's own service, Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, via the smart app, website or e-services system. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule has been published, so no amount should be quoted to you.

faqs.question: Do Arabic 0544 rates in Dubai rise closer to the June Cambridge series?
faqs.answer: Published hourly rates mostly hold steady. What disappears is capacity. Arabic specialists in this city fill the 16:30 to 19:30 school-night slots first, and by the final weeks before a series the question stops being price and becomes availability. A block of sessions booked in the term before a series costs the same per hour as one booked a fortnight out, but the fortnight-out block frequently cannot be filled at any rate. Count backwards from the entry deadline rather than forwards from today. Cambridge final entries for the March 2027 series were due on 27 November 2026.

faqs.question: Can a school Arabic teacher tutor my child privately for 0544?
faqs.answer: Possibly, but not if your child attends their school. Press reporting on Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules describes school staff being barred from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and notes that the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Verify the current wording with the relevant authority before relying on it. Practically, treat any offer of your child's own class teacher privately as a question to raise with the school rather than a shortcut to accept, and ask any registered teacher to show their private tuition permit first.

faqs.question: What does KHDA's mandatory Arabic requirement mean for a non-Arab child taking 0544?
faqs.answer: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools whatever international curriculum the school is licensed to teach. For non-Arab students, Islamic Education and moral, social and cultural studies are delivered in the language of the school's licensed curriculum, and Arabic as a first language runs in separate classes from which non-Arab students are excluded. KHDA calculates instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit and advises a minimum of twenty-five minutes for any mandatory-subject lesson. For the mandatory subjects, using different or additional content without prior Ministry permission is prohibited, so a tutor works on the school's material.

faqs.question: Is a native Arabic speaker worth a higher rate for 0544 than a trained teacher?
faqs.answer: Not on its own. Fluency lets somebody correct a sentence; training lets them explain that your child keeps losing marks because non-human plurals take feminine singular agreement, or because the first noun in an idafa construction never carries the definite article. For 0544 the decisive credentials are teaching qualification, experience marking Cambridge written tasks against the criteria, and familiarity with the specific syllabus your centre is entering. A native speaker who has all three is worth the premium. A native speaker who has none of them is selling conversation practice, which is a real product at a much lower price.

faqs.question: What happens to the 0544 fee if we pause lessons during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Ask before you book, because policies differ across this market. Dubai school timetables compress during Ramadan and many families move sessions to post-Iftar slots rather than stopping, which keeps the reading practice ticking without fighting a shortened school day. Our own arrangement is straightforward: sessions move or pause without a travel penalty, because there is no car journey to compensate anyone for. If you pause, expect to lose the slot rather than the money, and if the slot matters, agree in advance how it will be held through the month.

faqs.question: Can we start 0544 support in Year 11 and still see the grade move?
faqs.answer: Often yes, but the arithmetic is tighter and the honest answer depends on the gap. If the problem is exam technique, task structure or vocabulary coverage, a focused block in Year 11 can genuinely change the outcome. If the problem is that your child cannot yet read unvowelled text at speed, that is a skill built by repetition over months, and a late block buys partial progress rather than a transformation. No tutor can promise a specific grade. What we will do is say at the diagnostic which of those two situations you are in, before you commit to anything.

faqs.question: Can we reduce the 0544 bill by booking two siblings into one session?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it depends on how close the two are in level. Two children within a year of each other, both on the foreign-language syllabus, both stuck on reading fluency, can share a timed decoding clinic productively and split the cost. Two children in different streams, or one on 0544 and one on 0508, cannot share an hour usefully; you would be paying for half a lesson each. Small-group rates in the Dubai market sit below one-to-one per student but above nothing, and the saving is only real if the teaching still targets both children's actual losses.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-arabic-foreign-lan.closingHeading: Start with the diagnostic, not the quote
dubai/cambridge-igcse-arabic-foreign-lan.closingBody: The useful first step for Arabic 0544 in Dubai is not a price comparison. It is thirty free minutes that tell you whether you are looking at a reading problem, a writing problem or a streaming problem, because those three cost very different amounts to fix and only one of them is urgent in Year 11. Bring the last school report, the current Arabic set or stream, and the Cambridge series your child is entered for. You will get a written note naming the specific losses and an estimate of total taught hours, with no card details and no obligation. If the honest answer is that a fortnightly reading clinic is enough, that is what we will tell you.

intro.heading: How you will know whether Arabic 0544 tuition is working
paragraphs: Most families judge a tutor on atmosphere. The child seemed engaged, the hour passed pleasantly, the tutor is warm. That tells you whether the arrangement is tolerable, not whether it is working, and in Arabic the gap between those two is unusually wide. A learner can enjoy forty hours of Arabic conversation and arrive at a Cambridge reading paper no faster at decoding text without vowel marks than they were in September. The grade moves on measurable skills, so the sensible thing to demand from the first session is measurement.

There are four numbers worth taking at the start and tracking all year. The first is unvowelled reading speed: how many words a minute your child reads aloud from an unseen passage with vowel marks removed, and how many of those words are decoded correctly. The second is written accuracy on a controlled task, counted as errors per hundred words and broken down by error type rather than totalled. The third is listening retrieval, measured on short audio items under exam conditions. The fourth is speaking fluency, which means time to first response and length of unprompted turn, both of which are audible on a recording and invisible in a parent's memory of the lesson.

Online delivery is what makes those four measurable without extra admin. A session over live video can be recorded with consent, the shared document keeps every correction with its version history, the reading timer runs on screen where both tutor and student can see it, and the speaking file sits in a folder your child can replay on the bus. None of that happens by accident in a room with a notebook. The point of video for Arabic is not convenience; it is that the evidence survives the session.

IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai, and in-home tutoring at a UAE address is not something we sell in any emirate. Lessons are one to one over live video, screen shared, timed to Gulf Standard Time and the Dubai school week. The practical benefit for a thin-supply subject like Arabic is that the tutor is chosen on marking record rather than on postcode. A family in Dubai Creek Harbour is not restricted to the Arabic teachers willing to drive to Dubai Creek Harbour on a Wednesday evening.

What follows is the whole evidence system, written out: what gets measured, when it arrives, how to read a marked Arabic script, what a term of work realistically changes, and the point at which the honest recommendation is to pause or change tutor rather than continue. There is no promised grade anywhere on this page, because no tutor can promise one. There is a promise about documentation, which is a thing we can actually control.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-arabic-foreign-lan.programmesIntro: Arabic appears on a Dubai timetable from Foundation Stage to Year 13, and the evidence worth collecting changes at each stage. These are the four points where families most often ask for help, with the measurable thing each stage is really about.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE Arabic (Foreign Language)
programmes.description: The foreign-language Arabic syllabus, assessing listening, reading, speaking and writing as separate components. Confirm the current weighting and timing for your child's exam year on cambridgeinternational.org, since Cambridge revises components by cohort. The measurable priority at this stage is decoding speed on unseen unvowelled text, because that is what caps the reading and writing marks.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the typical 0544 candidate is a non-Arab student on a British curriculum who has had school Arabic since Foundation Stage and has rarely read independently. The characteristic profile is strong oral confidence with a reading speed well below what the paper assumes, which is exactly the gap a fortnightly marked task exposes within a month.

programmes.name: Cambridge Lower Secondary and Checkpoint Arabic
programmes.description: Cambridge runs Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October, which gives a Dubai family an external reading on their child's Arabic two full years before any IGCSE entry. Treat the Checkpoint report as a baseline document and keep it; it is the only independent measurement most students get before Year 10.
programmes.countryNote: This is the cheapest place in the whole plan to build reading automaticity, and the stage where measurement is most often skipped. A monthly timed reading figure through Years 7 to 9 is worth more to a Dubai family than any amount of Year 11 crisis tutoring, because the curve it produces tells you early whether the foreign-language route is the right one.

programmes.name: Cambridge International AS and A Level Arabic
programmes.description: The continuation route for students who finish 0544 well and want to keep the language. Confirm the exact component codes with your school's exams officer, because Cambridge offers more than one Arabic qualification at this level and centres differ in what they enter. Evidence at this stage shifts from decoding speed to argument structure in extended writing.
programmes.countryNote: Few Dubai students carry Arabic to this level, which makes the ones who do unusually visible on a university application in this region. The practical reason for keeping a measured record from IGCSE onwards is that it lets a family decide in Year 11, on data, whether continuing is realistic.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Arabic B
programmes.description: The parallel route for the many Dubai students who move from a British Year 11 into the IB Diploma. Arabic B at Standard or Higher Level assumes prior study, and students arriving from 0544 usually find the receptive demand steps up sharply while the productive demand feels familiar at first.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai is one of the few cities where a student can realistically choose between Cambridge A Level Arabic and IB Arabic B in the same neighbourhood. A measured reading and writing profile from Year 11 is the single most useful document in that decision, and almost nobody has one.

sections.heading: The four measurements taken in the first Arabic 0544 session
paragraphs: A first session that produces no numbers has wasted an hour. The diagnostic is not a conversation about goals; it is four short tasks that give a starting position against which everything later is judged. All four take about ten minutes each and all four are repeatable, which is the whole point.

Reading comes first and matters most. An unseen passage at roughly syllabus level, vowel marks removed, read aloud against a visible timer. We record words per minute and the proportion decoded correctly, and we write down every word that cost more than a beat. The common finding in Dubai is a student who converses easily and reads at a speed that cannot get through a Cambridge reading paper in the time available. That diagnosis is invisible in a pleasant conversational lesson and obvious within eight minutes of a timed read.

Writing is second: one controlled task on a familiar theme, marked by error type rather than totalled. Agreement with non-human plurals, hamza placement, ta marbuta against final ha, the definite article inside an idafa construction, and tense consistency each get their own count. Listening is third, using short audio items under exam conditions so the figure means something. Speaking is fourth and is recorded with consent, with time to first response and length of unprompted turn both noted. The four numbers go into a written baseline note the same day, and the family keeps it. Nothing in that note is a prediction; it is a starting position, which is a far more useful thing to own.

sections.heading: How to read a marked Arabic script without reading Arabic
paragraphs: Most parents paying for Arabic in Dubai cannot read the language, which puts them in the uncomfortable position of buying something they cannot inspect. The answer is not to learn Arabic. It is to insist that marking is structured so the pattern is legible to somebody who cannot read the words.

A marked task should come back with errors grouped into named categories and a count beside each, in English, above the script. If a returned task shows eleven errors and nine of them sit in one category, you have learned something real: your child does not have a general Arabic problem, they have one specific untaught rule. Agreement with non-human plurals taking feminine singular forms is the single most common of these in our Dubai marking, and it is fixable in two sessions once named. A script covered in undifferentiated red ink, by contrast, tells a parent nothing and usually means the tutor marked quickly.

Three further things belong on a returned task. A one-line statement of the single priority for the next fortnight, so the family can see a plan rather than a verdict. A note of which errors were already corrected from the previous task, which is where progress actually becomes visible. And a mark that is explicitly described as a teacher's estimate rather than a Cambridge grade, because grade boundaries are set by Cambridge after marking and no tutor can convert a practice task into a certificate grade. Any provider presenting a predicted grade as fact is overclaiming.
bullets: Errors grouped into named categories with a count, written in English

sections.heading: What a term of Arabic tuition realistically changes, and what it does not
paragraphs: Families deserve an honest range rather than an inspiring one. Across the Arabic briefs we see, the measurements that respond fastest are the mechanical ones, and the ones that respond slowest are the ones built from years of exposure. That ordering is stable and it should drive expectations.

Written error clusters move quickly. A named rule, practised across three or four marked tasks, usually stops producing errors inside six weeks. Decoding speed moves steadily but not dramatically: frequent short drills shift it over a term, and the curve is gradual rather than stepped. Listening retrieval improves mainly through familiarity with answer formats. Spoken fluency on unrehearsed prompts is the slowest of the four and the one most often oversold, because it depends on retrieval under pressure rather than on knowledge.

What does not change in a term is a fundamental mismatch of syllabus or stream. If a student is entered for a level their current reading cannot support, no amount of weekly tuition closes that in twelve weeks, and the responsible thing is to say so at the diagnostic rather than at the mock. We also decline to attach a grade to a plan. Cambridge sets boundaries after marking, cohorts differ, and a company that tells you a number is selling confidence rather than teaching. The table below is what our own fortnightly evidence tends to show, framed as a direction of travel rather than a promise, and it is drawn from marking records rather than from a survey.

sections.heading: Why live video produces better evidence than a notebook on a table
paragraphs: The case for online Arabic tuition in Dubai is usually made on convenience, which undersells it. The real argument is that a video session leaves artefacts behind and a room does not. Everything written in a shared document is saved with its version history, so the tutor can show a family the same sentence rewritten three times across a month. A notebook shows the final version and nothing else.

Arabic benefits from screen annotation more than most subjects. Vowel marks sit above and below the consonant line and are easy to misplace by hand; on a shared screen a tutor can zoom, colour and label them. Letters change shape in initial, medial and final position, and a tutor can display the same root in all four forms side by side instantly. Right-to-left typing with a visible keyboard overlay teaches a skill the student will need for any digital Arabic task later. None of this is a substitute for handwriting practice, which still belongs in the week, but it makes the teaching inspectable.

Speaking is the clearest case. A recording, taken with the family's consent, turns an unverifiable impression into something a student can replay. Children consistently hear hesitations in their own recording that they did not notice while speaking, and that single moment of recognition does more for fluency than being told. Files are kept only with consent and deleted on request. For context on data: lead forms and session records involving minors should state what is collected, why, and how to have it removed, and the UAE's personal data protection framework under Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 is the reason to take that seriously rather than a marketing line.

sections.heading: IB Gram does not do home visits in Dubai, and why that helps the evidence
paragraphs: This needs saying plainly rather than being buried. IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; in-home tutoring at a UAE address is a service we do not sell, and home visiting is offered only in India. Every Arabic 0544 session for a Dubai family runs one to one over live video. Any page that implies otherwise about us is wrong.

The gain is selection. Qualified Arabic teaching capacity in this city is genuinely scarce, concentrated inside schools, and clustered geographically in the older northern districts. A family choosing an in-home tutor is choosing from the subset of that pool willing to drive to their community in the specific evening slot their child is free. For Mathematics that constraint is tolerable because the pool is large. For 0544 it can mean choosing between two people, neither of whom has marked a Cambridge Arabic script.

There is an evidence argument as well as a supply one. A tutor who travels prices travel into the hour and has a strong incentive to keep sessions long and marking light, because marking is the unpaid part. A tutor with no commute has no such pressure, which is why a fortnightly marked task is a realistic commitment online and an awkward one in-home. We publish in-home market rates elsewhere on this site so families can compare honestly, and if a genuinely qualified 0544 specialist lives ten minutes away, that is a reasonable choice to make with the numbers in front of you.

sections.heading: When the honest recommendation is to pause, switch or stop
paragraphs: An evidence system is only worth building if it is allowed to produce an unwelcome answer. Every sixth session we write a short recommendation with one of four verdicts, and it goes to the family whether or not they asked for it.

Continue is the common one: the measurements are moving in the expected pattern for the stage, and the plan stands. Change the focus is next: the numbers show the original diagnosis was partly wrong, usually because a presumed reading problem turns out to be a vocabulary problem, and the session shape should change. Change the tutor comes third. Personal fit matters in language teaching more than in most subjects, and a flat chart across six sessions with a student who has stopped volunteering in the session is a fit problem, not a motivation problem. We move the student and we do not charge for the handover.

Stop is the fourth verdict and the one almost nobody offers. Sometimes the right advice is that the school is already doing the necessary work, that the measurements have plateaued where the student needs vocabulary breadth rather than teaching, and that the money would do more on a different subject. Arabic and Islamic Education sit outside the five accredited subjects the Ministry counts for British-track equivalency, so for a family with limited funds and a weak grade elsewhere, redirecting the Arabic hours is frequently the better decision. Saying that costs us a booking and keeps the evidence system credible.

sections.heading: Academic honesty: whose Arabic is on the page?
paragraphs: Language subjects attract a particular kind of cheating, and it is worth being explicit about where the line sits. A tutor may teach, model, question, give feedback and mark. A tutor may not supply text for a student to hand in, and a tutor may not improve a piece of assessed work to the point where the sentences are no longer the student's own. That holds for school-assessed tasks, for anything feeding a Cambridge entry, and for the project and essay components of other qualifications.

The practical test we use is simple. After feedback, the student rewrites. The tutor does not type into the submission. If a correction cannot be explained in a way the student can then apply unaided, the correction was pitched at the wrong level and the teaching is at fault. Feedback that produces a better student is legitimate; feedback that only produces a better script is not.

Machine translation deserves its own paragraph in an Arabic page. Free translation tools now produce Arabic prose far better than a Year 10 foreign-language learner can write, and they produce it in a register that is instantly recognisable to anybody who marks these scripts. A student submitting translated text is risking a malpractice finding and learning nothing. We treat the tools as diagnostic rather than forbidden: comparing a student's own sentence with a machine version, and naming exactly why the machine chose a different construction, is a genuinely useful teaching move. Using the output as the submission is not, and we say so to the student directly.

sections.heading: Keeping the evidence trail through the Dubai school year
paragraphs: An evidence trail breaks when sessions stop happening, and in Dubai the predictable interruptions are known a year in advance. The school year runs from late summer to the start of July for most British-curriculum schools, with a long winter break, a spring break, and Ramadan, which compresses the school day and moves family routines later into the evening.

Ramadan is the one most often handled badly. Schools shorten their timetables, children are tired in the afternoon and alert after Iftar, and a 16:30 Arabic slot that worked all year stops working. The straightforward fix is to move sessions to a post-Iftar slot for the month and keep the fortnightly marked task running on the same cycle, rather than pausing and losing six weeks of trend data. Reading drills in particular suit a shorter, later slot well.

The summer holiday is the other break worth planning. A student who stops Arabic entirely for nine weeks loses decoding speed measurably, and the first September measurement usually shows it. Two short drills a week through July and August hold the figure where it was, which is much cheaper than rebuilding it in Year 11. Against the Cambridge calendar, the fixed point to work backwards from is the entry deadline rather than the paper: for the March 2027 series, Cambridge published final entries as due on 27 November 2026, with the exam period running 3 February to 4 March 2027 and results on Direct on 13 May. Ask your school which of the six administrative zones your centre sits in, because Cambridge states it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who use the wrong zone timetable.

faqs.question: How will I know whether Arabic 0544 tuition is actually working?
faqs.answer: By four numbers rather than by impressions. Unvowelled reading speed in words per minute with a decoding accuracy figure, written errors grouped by named category, listening retrieval accuracy under timed conditions, and recorded speaking fluency measured as time to first response and length of unprompted turn. All four are taken in the first session, written into a baseline note the same day, and repeated monthly. A marked written task arrives every second week. If those figures are flat across six sessions, the arrangement is not working and we will say so in writing.

faqs.question: What does a marked 0544 writing task look like when it comes back?
faqs.answer: Errors grouped into named categories in English with a count beside each, above the script, so a parent who does not read Arabic can still see the pattern. One stated priority for the next fortnight. A note of which errors from the previous task have stopped appearing. And any mark clearly labelled a teacher estimate rather than a Cambridge grade. If eleven errors cluster into one category, your child does not have a general Arabic problem; they have one untaught rule, which is usually fixable in two sessions once named.

faqs.question: How fast does unvowelled reading speed improve with weekly drills?
faqs.answer: Gradually and steadily rather than in jumps. Over six weeks of two short drills a week the gains are small and uneven. Over a full term the curve becomes clearly visible on a chart. Over two terms the limiting factor usually shifts from decoding to vocabulary breadth, which is a different teaching problem. Decoding responds to frequency rather than session length, which is why two thirty-minute drills a week beat one sixty-minute lesson for this specific skill, and cost less per week in the Dubai market.

faqs.question: Can my child record the Arabic speaking practice and keep the files?
faqs.answer: Yes, with your explicit consent, and the files are yours. Recording is the most useful single thing we do for spoken Arabic, because children hear hesitations in their own playback that they did not notice while talking. The log that accompanies the recording names specific sounds and constructions rather than offering general comments about fluency. We state what is stored and why, and we delete on request. Session records involving minors deserve that care under the UAE personal data framework, not as a disclaimer but as ordinary practice.

faqs.question: Will you give me a predicted grade for my child's 0544 entry?
faqs.answer: No, and you should be wary of anyone who does. Cambridge sets grade boundaries after marking, and they move between series and between cohorts. What we provide is a teacher estimate on individual practice tasks, explicitly labelled as such, plus a trend across six or more marked scripts that becomes arguable over a term and defensible over two. That is a more useful document than a confident number, and it is the one your school's own forecast-grade process will actually recognise. No honest tutor promises a particular number, and a plan built on one is a sales document rather than a teaching plan.

faqs.question: Does online Arabic teaching really work for the script and the vowel marks?
faqs.answer: It works better than a notebook for exactly those things. Vowel marks sit above and below the consonant line and are easy to misplace by hand; on a shared screen a tutor can zoom, colour and label them. The same root can be displayed in initial, medial, final and isolated forms side by side instantly. Right-to-left typing with a keyboard overlay teaches a skill the student needs for digital Arabic tasks anyway. Handwriting practice still belongs in the week, done on paper, and we set it as homework rather than spending session time on it.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a tutor to our Dubai address for Arabic lessons?
faqs.answer: No. We do not arrange home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE, and in-home tutoring at a UAE address is not a service we sell; home visiting is offered only in India. Every 0544 session runs one to one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For a subject with genuinely scarce qualified supply, that widens the choice from the Arabic teachers willing to drive to your community in your child's free evening slot to every available specialist, selected on marking record rather than postcode.

faqs.question: What happens if the measurements stay flat for a month or two?
faqs.answer: We write to you with one of four verdicts. Continue, if the pattern is normal for the stage. Change the focus, if the figures show the original diagnosis was partly wrong, which most often means a presumed reading problem is really a vocabulary problem. Change the tutor, if the chart is flat and your child has stopped volunteering in sessions, which is a fit issue and ours to fix; handovers are not charged for. Or stop, if the honest reading is that the money would do more elsewhere. That review arrives every six sessions whether you ask for it or not.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Arabic work my child submits to school?
faqs.answer: A tutor can teach, model, question, give feedback and mark. A tutor cannot supply text for submission or polish a piece of assessed work until the sentences stop being the student's own. The working test is that after feedback the student rewrites, and the tutor never types into the submission. If a correction cannot be explained so the student can apply it unaided, the correction was pitched wrongly and the teaching is at fault. Feedback that produces a better student is legitimate; feedback that only produces a better script is not.

faqs.question: How should we handle machine translation in Arabic homework?
faqs.answer: Treat the tools as diagnostic rather than forbidden, and be honest with your child about the risk. Free translators now produce Arabic prose far better than a Year 10 foreign-language learner writes, and in a register that anyone who marks these scripts recognises immediately. Submitting translated text risks a malpractice finding and teaches nothing. A genuinely useful session move is to compare the student's own sentence with the machine version and name exactly why the machine chose a different construction. Using the output as the submission is a different thing, and we say so to the student directly.

faqs.question: How do we keep Arabic sessions running through Ramadan in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Move the slot rather than pausing the cycle. School timetables compress during Ramadan, children are tired in the afternoon and considerably sharper after Iftar, so a 16:30 session that worked all year stops working. Shifting to a post-Iftar slot for the month keeps the fortnightly marked task on its cycle and preserves the trend data, which is the thing a pause actually destroys. Short reading drills suit a later, shorter slot particularly well. There is no travel penalty attached to moving a session, because there is no car journey to compensate anyone for.

faqs.question: Is it worth continuing Arabic drills through the Dubai summer holiday?
faqs.answer: For decoding speed, yes, and the September measurement shows why. Students who stop Arabic entirely for nine weeks typically return with a measurably slower unvowelled reading figure, and rebuilding it costs more than holding it would have. Two short drills a week through July and August are usually enough to keep the number where it was. Writing and listening tolerate a break better. If budget is tight, protect the reading drills and let the rest wait until term starts, because reading is the skill that caps everything else on this syllabus.

faqs.question: Should we use the Cambridge Checkpoint result as a baseline?
faqs.answer: Yes, and keep it. Cambridge runs Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October, which gives a Dubai family an external reading on their child's Arabic two years before any IGCSE entry. It is often the only independent measurement a student gets before Year 10, and it makes our own baseline far quicker to interpret because we can see whether the current figures represent a decline, a plateau or steady progress. Bring it to the diagnostic along with the latest school report and the current set or stream.

faqs.question: Why would we spend on Arabic at all if it does not count for equivalency?
faqs.answer: Because it is still a Cambridge grade on the certificate, a mandatory school subject in every Dubai private school, a real advantage for a child who will study or work in this region, and the foundation for AS, A Level or IB Arabic B. What the equivalency rule changes is sequencing, not value. Arabic and Islamic Education sit outside the five accredited subjects the Ministry counts for British-track equivalency, so a family with one subject's worth of budget and a weak maths grade should spend it on maths and run a cheap fortnightly reading clinic for Arabic.

faqs.question: How many marked scripts do we need before a trend means anything?
faqs.answer: Three is noise, six is arguable, ten is defensible. A single task mark tells you almost nothing because task difficulty, tiredness and topic familiarity all move it. That is the reason for the fortnightly cycle rather than a monthly one: over a term it produces roughly six marked scripts, which is enough to distinguish a trend from a mood. It is also why we report error categories rather than only marks, since a category disappearing from three consecutive scripts is firmer evidence of learning than any single number going up.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-arabic-foreign-lan.closingHeading: Ask for the baseline note before you ask for the rate
dubai/cambridge-igcse-arabic-foreign-lan.closingBody: The first thing to request from any Arabic tutor in Dubai is not a price but a written baseline: four measurements taken in one session, dated, with a named priority attached. A provider who cannot produce that document is selling hours rather than teaching, and you will have no way to tell in February whether the autumn was worth it. Bring the latest school report, the Arabic stream your child sits in, and any Checkpoint result. Thirty minutes, no card details, one trial per family, and a written note the same day with all four figures in it. If the numbers say the school is already doing the work, we will tell you that too.

intro.heading: Why script literacy decides a 0544 grade
paragraphs: The students sitting Cambridge IGCSE Arabic as a Foreign Language in Dubai are in an unusual position for language learners. They live in an Arabic-speaking country. They hear the language in taxis, shops and the school corridor. A good number can greet, thank, bargain and understand a conversation about food. And when a Cambridge reading passage is put in front of them, they cannot decode it at speed, because recognising a spoken word and reading the same word in an unvowelled script are different skills that nothing in their week has connected.

That gap is the single most useful thing to understand about 0544. The alphabet has twenty-eight letters, each with different forms depending on position, several distinguished only by the number and placement of dots, and short vowels that are usually absent from ordinary text. A learner who reads letter by letter can decode a sentence given time, and will run out of time on an examination paper. A learner who reads in chunks has a completely different experience of the same paper. Moving a student from the first state to the second is the project, and it takes months of regular short practice rather than a term of vocabulary lists.

The second thing to understand is that 0544 and 0508 are not two difficulty levels of one subject. Cambridge offers Arabic as a First Language under 0508 and Arabic as a Foreign Language under 0544, and they assess different things for different students. 0508 asks for close reading of unseen text and formal composition from someone schooled in Arabic. 0544 asks a learner to understand, read, write and in most syllabus versions speak at a level appropriate to someone acquiring the language. A student in the wrong one looks weak for reasons unconnected to their ability.

Confirm the current component structure for 0544 on the syllabus page at cambridgeinternational.org for your child's examination year, and ask the school which components it enters. Cambridge revises specifications, syllabus versions differ in how speaking is handled, and a tutor working from an out-of-date printout is a genuine risk on a subject with a small teaching community in this city. What this page does is describe what each skill demands of a learner in Dubai, where marks leak, and what a session can realistically fix.

The third thing is context: Arabic is mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, prohibiting combined classes because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Your child's school Arabic lessons and their 0544 entry are related but not identical: the school stream is a regulatory requirement, and the Cambridge entry is a qualification decision. The two are worth separating in your own mind before any conversation about tutoring.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-arabic-foreign-lan.programmesIntro: Arabic as an additional language runs through a Dubai student's whole schooling, and 0544 is one point on that line. These are the stages families ask about.

programmes.name: School Arabic, additional-language stream
programmes.description: The mandatory Arabic every non-Arab student in a Dubai private school receives, taught separately from the Arab group by requirement. Quality and intensity vary widely between schools, and so does how much reading of real text a student has done by Year 9.
programmes.countryNote: The diagnostic question for a Dubai family is not how many years of Arabic a child has had, but whether they can read an unvowelled sentence at speed. Ten years of additional-language Arabic can end in a student who speaks politely and reads letter by letter, and that is the state 0544 punishes.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE Arabic as a Foreign Language (0544)
programmes.description: The examined learner course: understanding spoken Arabic, reading passages at learner level, writing to a prompt, and in most syllabus versions a speaking element. Topic areas are finite, which is the single biggest advantage a 0544 student has over a first-language candidate.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai students reaching 0544 are usually non-Arab residents whose school entered the additional-language stream for the qualification. The finite topic list means a disciplined eighteen-month plan genuinely works, which is rarely true of a language subject.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE Arabic as a First Language (0508)
programmes.description: The parallel route for students schooled in Arabic, assessed by close reading of unseen text and formal composition. Named here because placement between the two codes is the most consequential decision a Dubai family makes about this subject.
programmes.countryNote: A handful of students each year sit the wrong code: an Arab child schooled entirely in English placed in 0508, or a strong non-Arab reader left in 0544 and under-stretched. A marked piece of writing and one timed reading passage settle it; a conversation about fluency does not.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Arabic B and ab initio
